When war is declared on you, your allies get defensive calls, except in your own independence war or a war you provoked by a refused demand. An ally who refuses a defensive call breaks the alliance, takes an Oath broken, and gets Abandoned us in your ledger. Refusing an offensive call breaks nothing; the ally just stays out. A call's count adds Our ally's war aim is our concern +30 (the target is their Rival or Hostile, or the aim frees their people or faith), We are at war already −30, and The enemy is far stronger −10 per full multiple up to −40. Calls go out instantly and are answered a month later. An ally keeps its own armies and its own peace voices and is named in the peace so it gets the truce too. When over half its own peace voices say peace it may make a separate peace ; that is no Oath broken, but you lose the tie Answered our call . Joining when asked gives Answered our call +20; fighting on the same side gives Fought side by side +15. Marriages and pretenders. A marriage needs an unmarried heir, son or daughter on each side, and for houses of hostile faiths the religion rule on tolerance. Its count adds Their house is greater +10 (your realm has more people) and A marriage already binds us −10 per existing marriage. While a marriage lives, when either ruler dies without a direct heir the other house gets a 1 in 10 chance per marriage of a claim: a dynastic claim fact and a pretender at that court. Pretenders also come from exiles of a lost succession war or revolt, and from events; a pretender gives the war aim Seat a pretender , and his claim passes to his heir or lapses. When a ruler dies with no heir at all and your house holds the strongest claim (most marriages, then the closest), the realm passes to your ruler as a personal union for Subjects, and each Wavering or Disloyal lord of the inherited realm rolls to rise for a local claimant. Demands are the step before war. Each names exactly one demand with its need met: Demand Needs War aim on refusal Hand over a province a border with it, or a claim Take land (that province) Pay tribute a border Tribute Recognise our pretender a pretender at your court Seat a pretender Release a subject they have a subject Break a subject Tolerate our faith in a named province the persecution flag on a province bordering you Defend the faith Apologise and pay they broke an oath to you or insulted you Punish Expel an envoy / cut an alliance they host your enemy's resident, or are allied with your Rival Punish A demand's count adds We cannot beat you , We have strong friends , and It's our heartland −30 for a province with their capital or of their own culture. If they give in you get exactly what was asked with no war and no truce, and they record Threatened us . If they refuse you gain the matching war aim for 5 years, and the war that follows counts as provoked by them: your non-Warlike lords don't waver, your allies' offensive calls get They refused a fair demand +20, and their allies get no defensive call at all. Passage. Your armies may enter a foreign country only if you are at war, it is your subject or ally, or it granted passage. From G8 you can ask for passage by envoy (base −10, You are marching on our friend −40, You are marching on our enemy +20); before G8 a country at peace is closed to your armies unless it is an ally or subject. Passage lasts 2 years and the granting side can revoke it any time without an Oath broken. A country that refused or revoked your passage blocks your envoys over its land for 2 years. An army that enters without passage commits an act of war: the owner may declare with the aim Punish that turn, and its allies' defensive calls count as answered to a war started by the intruder. Trade pacts and embargoes. A trade pact waives tolls and extra fees for both sides' traders, records the trade agreement fact and adds Trade pact +10 both ways, ending with war or when either side cancels. An embargo (instant) bars both sides' traders from each other's land and ports, closes paths through the embargoing country, and adds Embargo against us −15. Pledges and sworn peace. A pledge is a one-way promise to defend a country; it gives them Pledged to protect us +15. If they are attacked you get a defensive call as if allied, and refusing is an Oath broken. Swear peace (base −20, We fear you +10 per multiple, We want your land −30 if they claim your land) creates a 10-year Truce without a war; breaking it is an Oath broken and Broke a truce with us . Subjects by agreement. Offer overlordship (base −80) adds We need a protector +20 per neighbour Hostile toward them or claiming them, You already protect us +20 with a pledge, and We are proud −10 per castle of theirs beyond two; on yes, Subjects makes them a Tributary. Ask for protection (base −10) asks a stronger country to take you as a subject; on yes you become a Tributary, or a Vassal if you asked for that. Courting a foreign lord. An envoy can work on a foreign Wavering or Disloyal lord: each season he stays, the lord's loyalty to his own ruler drops a step, unless his ruler pays him more or wins a battle he fought in. A Disloyal lord who borders you and has been courted for a year defects with his lands, and his old ruler gains Take land for them. Each season there is a 1 in 4 chance of discovery, which adds Courted our lord and sends the envoy home. Gifts, insults and rivals. A gift of any amount adds Gift (+1 per 5 gold, up to +30, fading over 10 years). An insult makes the insulted side Hostile toward you (ending any friendship between you), adds Insulted us , raises a loyalty step for each of your Warlike lords whose Want is a war with them, and gives them Punish . Declaring a rival needs a named contested object. Funding rebels pays for a revolution that is already brewing in another country (its revolution card shows at least one sign). It needs a free envoy seat and a target that is not your ally or subject, and costs 1 % of the target's yearly income every month. Nobody is told, not even when you stop. While you pay, that country's revolution breaks out sooner. You can also fund an émigré pretender court the same way. Each month there is a 3 in 100 chance of being caught: the envoy is held and funding stops, the target records Stirred revolt in our land −50 (fading over 20 years) and gains Punish against you for 5 years, and you learn it a month later. If the revolution wins, the new regime records Backed our revolution +25 toward you, unless it hates your form of rule. War aims A war aim is held from things in the world: War aim Held when Lasts Take land (named provinces) you held them in the last 50 years; a pretender of yours claims them; they are a homeland of your culture; a lord's Want names them; they refused your demand for them; a lord defected from you with them while the reason holds; a refused demand gives 5 years Seat a pretender a pretender to their throne is at your court, including an émigré court while the pretender lives Tribute you border them and they refused a tribute demand; or you border them and have 3 times their soldiers 5 years / while true Free a people their land holds a homeland of a culture with no country, yours or accepted by you while true Break a subject (the war is on the overlord) they have a subject Hostile toward them or that asked you for help while true Defend the faith the persecution flag on a province bordering you; or they refused your tolerance demand while true Punish they broke an oath to you, insulted you, held your envoy, entered without passage, refused Apologise and pay , or were caught funding rebels in your land 5 years Raid nothing always No aim nothing always Events and national strengths can grant other aims for a stated time. What each aim wins at the peace is set by Warfare. Declaring war You declare war, and offer or ask for peace, from the Diplomacy tab of the other country's card. A declaration needs a target and exactly one aim you hold. Any Alliance, Truce or Pledge with the target must be broken first, each an Oath broken. The same turn, offensive calls go to your allies, defensive calls to the target's allies and pledgers, both sides' subjects come in by their kind (a Union joins at once, a Vassal or Protectorate is called and answers by its loyalty, a March joins when the enemy borders it, a Tributary or Colony stays out), and members of a league against you are brought in; answers arrive a month later. The aim is shown to every country, and for a war with no aim every neighbour of yours records Threatened us . A Union, Colony or Protectorate can't declare war, and a Vassal can't declare war on its overlord's allies; they join their overlord's wars or start an independence war. A realm under a regency may fight only defensive wars and Raids. Hungary prepares to declare war on the Ottomans. Hungary holds the aim Take land for Nikopol from the Want of its lord John Hunyadi. The declaration sheet shows the aim "Take land: Nikopol" and its source, Wallachia and the Papal States as called on Hungary's side, Serbia as an Ottoman tributary that does not join, and how many of Hungary's voices lean to peace. It does not show how the called countries will answer. It offers Send a demand first and Declare . Peace and truces Computer players offer you peace by the same rules they use among themselves: when over half their peace voices want it, or when they are worn out. Their offer arrives in your turn report, waits under Waiting for you and marks their Diplomacy tab until you answer it or put it off. A signed peace starts a truce of 5 years, plus 5 more if it moved provinces or made a subject; a white peace gives 5 years. Both sides may agree to extend a truce. From era III, when three or more countries are on each side, one envoy can carry a single many-sided peace that every warring country signs at once, each by its own peace voices; before that each pair makes its own peace. Leagues against a conqueror Once a year, for each country X whose Lands taken (last 20 years) reaches the era's league threshold (8 in eras I to III, 6 in IV and V, 4 in VI and VII), every country that borders X or a province X took in the last 20 years, and is not X's ally, subject or overlord and not at war with X, makes the count Join a league against X : Reason Number Base −30 Their standing toward X − standing ÷ 4 X took our land +10 per province X's Lands taken +3 per province X could crush us alone balancers +10 per multiple; bandwagoners −10 per multiple Others already in the league +5 per member Same faith as X −10 When at least two say yes, the league forms, named after X ("League against Venice"). If X declares war on any member, every member gets a defensive call; a member who refuses leaves with no Oath broken. Members owe nothing else and are protected against nobody but X. X sees the league, its members and their soldiers on its country card. The league dissolves when X's Lands taken falls below half the threshold, or X makes a peace that gives provinces back to members. Events can also start a league regardless of the threshold; such a league ends only by event or by a peace that gives provinces back. Eras Era Change I the start (1378) to 1500 envoys only travel; residents only with G8 (the Italian states start with it); marriages the strongest tie II 1500 to 1600 G8 spreads; residents give sight of other courts III 1600 to 1700 many-sided peace, or earlier if the event peace of westphalia fires IV 1700 to 1800 league threshold 8 to 6; Married houses +10 V 1800 to 1870 T14 telegraphy makes missions instant between telegraph countries (marriages and residents still travel) VI 1870 to 1914 mobilisation pacts : either ally can mark or unmark an alliance as a pact: a defensive call is then answered automatically, shown to the player as an event, and offensive calls between the partners get +10; league threshold 4 VII 1914 to 1939 gifts count half; the campaign ends 31 August 1939 A revolution can add its own reason row, for example Different form of rule −20 with monarchies in every count for a set time. Events An event's opinion effect adds an event tie or wrong named after the event, fading over 10 years unless it says otherwise. trust is read as 100 − 10 × Oaths broken (never below 0), and an effect lowering it adds an Oath broken. notoriety is 5 × Lands taken plus the notoriety events added that has not yet faded (each point fades over 30 years), capped at 100; adding notoriety n adds Notorious deed −10 × n with every country that shares a border, a sea zone or a trade pact with the actor. A league started by an event needs no minimum number of members and ends only by event or by a peace that gives provinces back. An event setting a relation (alliance, truce, rivalry, war, trade pact, embargo, guarantee, non-aggression) runs the matching action with its conditions. Three new effects are asked for: war aim , league and pretender . The computer players The AI decides with exactly the same counts, adding rows for its posture and negotiation level : Posture Seeks Reason rows Mixed nothing in particular none Bandwagoner alliance with the strongest neighbour +20 alliances with a stronger country; +20 Ask for protection ; −10 per multiple to leagues against the strong Opportunist gains when others are weak +20 joining the side with more soldiers; −20 defensive calls against a stronger enemy; courts lords; Oaths broken count −5 in its own reckoning Isolationist to be left alone −30 alliances and calls; +20 sworn peace and trade pacts; −20 passage Balancer stop any one power growing +10 per multiple to leagues against the strong; +20 alliances against the strongest neighbour Client seeker a protector +30 Offer overlordship and pledges from a stronger, Warm country Hegemon seeker domination makes demands; −20 alliances with a stronger country; offers pledges and overlordship to small neighbours Negotiation level adds very high +15 (and gifts count 25 % more), high +10, moderate 0, low −10, very low −20. Each month an AI with a free seat scores up to 5 candidate actions per free seat toward countries in its horizon (neighbours, neighbours' neighbours, anyone it has a relation or fact with, its rivals' enemies), estimates the other side's count with only what a player could see, sends the best one over zero, and sends a gift first when the best is a close no (−20 or better). It tries a demand before war unless it is an Opportunist and the target's armies are away. Opportunists and hegemon seekers fund rebels in a rival's provinces that already have two or more grievances. Each month Answer letters from last month are delivered; envoys arriving this month have their asks counted; rebel funding is charged and the caught chance rolled; at each season's end resident ties grow and courting rolls happen; truces, passages and timed war aims expire and envoys return; the AI acts. Once a year ledgers fade, leagues are checked and relations decay. What you see - The diplomacy map mode : every country coloured by its relation to you: your colour for you and your subjects; blue for allies and light blue for pledges; green and pale green for Close and Warm; grey for Cool or nothing recorded; orange for Cold or Rival; red for Hostile, Bitter or at war (hatched at war); a red border for a league against you. Envoys on the road appear as small riders with a dotted line, and a crossed-sword icon marks countries you hold a war aim against (regional zoom only). - The country diplomacy card : their standing toward you and your stance, ties and wrongs, relations, your war aims on them, the last answer with a Why? button for the full reasons, and action buttons that show no prediction. In landscape it sits to the right of the map. - The envoy picker : which official goes, the days on the road, and which province loses its official meanwhile. - The envoys strip : each seat as free, on the road (destination and days) or resident (court). - The declare sheet : the Price of war (who is called against you and how, the neighbours alarmed, the lords who will waver, a truce broken, your pay at war, the most one peace can take) above Confirm ; see Warfare. - Your name abroad : your own Diplomacy tab opens with it. Any league against you comes first, with each member and its soldiers; then your notoriety as a word ( Trusted under 25, Watched from 25, Feared from 50, Hated from 75), and your Lands taken in the last 20 years as a bar against the era's league threshold ("6 of 8 before a league"). Notoriety is 5 for each land taken plus notorious deeds, fading over 30 years; courts trust you less for it (less willing to ally, marry or pledge) and are readier to join a league against you. Land taken also leaves the wrong Grabbed land near us with the realms that border it. Every row opens its reason on a tap. - The war card for each war you fight, with both sides' peace voices; see Warfare. - Answer letters , and the country card line "Envoys n of m abroad" and "Leagues against you". Envoys in the game today The first part of statecraft is in the playable build: envoys, alliances, marriages, courtesy visits and gifts. Demands, subjects and passage come next. - Where : open another realm's card and its Diplomacy tab. At the top is what they think of you: the word (Warm, Cool and so on), the number, and every line of their ledger with its weight. Below that is your envoy on the way there, if any, and their last answer; tap Why? to see every reason they counted and the total. - Sending an envoy : under Send an envoy you see how many of your envoys are free, then four missions. Each is a button with one line on what it does, or a greyed button that says why not: you are at war, an envoy is already on the way, every seat is taken, you are already allies, a subject tie, they are hostile, your houses are married already, or you lack the gold. - Propose an alliance : they say yes only if their reasons add up above nothing. - Arrange a marriage : married houses think better of each other (+15), and a marriage can bring a claim on their throne or their whole crown (see Subjects, personal unions). - Courtesy visit : always welcome, +15 fading over 5 years. - Send a gift : 30 gold, +30 fading over 10 years. - How long it takes : the envoy rides to their capital (two days per unit of distance), stays at court a month, and the answer reaches you the month after. While he is away his seat is taken. Most realms have one seat, and one more with over 10 provinces. - Your own overview : your realm card's Diplomacy tab lists your envoys abroad (where, why, and when they arrive or come home) and the last eight answers, each with its Why? . Answers also arrive in the News with a scroll. - Ending an alliance : End the alliance on an ally's tab. It is an Oath broken: they remember it (−40, fading over 20 years), and other courts trust you less. - Courting a lord : tap a province of another realm, open its lord from Governed by ( Lord ), and if he is Wavering or Disloyal, Court him . One of your envoys stays at his court: each season he loses a step unless his ruler wins him back, and once Disloyal for a year with land next to yours he comes over with it (his old ruler remembers Took our land ). Each season there is 1 in 4 they find out: Courted our lord (−25, fading over 10 years) and your envoy comes home. Your courting envoys are listed with your envoys abroad, and Recall your envoy frees the seat. Realms court the lords and subjects of neighbours they hold as rivals or hostile. - The other realms send envoys too: once a year each court picks the neighbour that thinks best of it and weighs an alliance and a marriage there, and sends the best ask its count says yes to, or a gift first when it is close. You see the alliances and marriages they make in the News. - For now an envoy is not a named official, so no province loses its official while he is away; every realm counts two unmarried children; and the royal marriages already made on the start day count from the start. Envoys, letters and alliances are kept in your save. Demands in the game today - Where : under the envoys on another realm's Diplomacy tab, Make a demand (not while you are at war with them). - What you can demand : Demand tribute , or Demand a province of theirs on your border (one button each, their capital marked). A demand needs a reason: a war aim on them (for example, sharing a border with three times their soldiers gives you Tribute ) or a Rival or Hostile stance toward them. If you can't, the tab says why. - How they answer : your envoy carries it like any mission, and their answer comes back with a Why? . They start at −60 and give in only when they cannot beat you (+15 for each time over their soldiers, up to +60), minus half that if their allies would defend them, and −30 if you ask for their capital. What they think of you counts too, so a gift first can tip it. - If they give in : the province is yours at once, with no war and no truce; or they become your tributary and send you 15 in 100 of their tax and trade every month, shown as Tribute in your Treasury tab and on their card. A tributary stays out of your wars; see Subjects for its loyalty and the tribute level. - If they refuse : you hold a war aim on them for 5 years, and a war you start over it brings their allies no call to arms. Either way they remember the threat (−15, fading over 10 years). - The other realms demand too: before a realm goes to war on a neighbour it first demands tribute or a border province, and fights only if refused. For now they make demands only of each other, not of you. Exploration-and-Colonies: Exploration is how your realm sails into the unknown and plants colonies there. Each country sees only the part of the world it has charted, with a parchment fog over the rest; exploration ships push into that fog, and once you can hire colonial governors you can carry one to an unowned coast, keep the colony fed from your ships, and watch it grow until the province becomes yours. How it works Unlocking exploration A country gets the exploration unlock when it knows S4 Carrack and caravel (or S3 Outrigger voyaging ) and the Age of Exploration has begun in its region. Once the age has begun there, the gate stays open for that country even after the age ends. The gating age is one config line, exploration.unlock age , set to the event tree's age of exploration . Regions outside that age's list wait for the first later age that covers them: North America opens with the Age of Atlantic Empires (1520), the Middle East and central Asia with the Age of Reformations (1530). So the Mamluks can know S4 early and still not explore until then. At the 1378 start nobody can explore. Genoa and Venice know S4, but the Age of Exploration has not begun; it starts when Portugal or Castile has the ocean ships or holds the Atlantic islands (earliest 1415, and by 1445 at the latest), see Historical Events. Portugal and Castile don't know S4 yet and must research it first. Ming knows S1 and S2 but not S4. Without the unlock you can't buy exploration ships: no caravel without S4, no voyaging canoe without S3, and the age gate applies to voyaging canoes too. Where an exploration ship may sail is Naval's research rule: with S4 and S1 within 3 zones of a coast, with S5 the open ocean. Early voyages creep along the coasts. The Pacific and Malay way. A country that knows S3 builds the voyaging canoe (outrigger or double-hulled) as its exploration ship: 60 supply, 100 rations of colony stores, crew 20, 5 gold, 1 timber and 1 month, built on any shore with seafolk. It can cross open ocean from the start. S3 also opens colonies with 1 colonial governor slot and a colonial range of at least 10 zones, whatever the government form; T8 and T9 add a slot each on top. The charted map Every country has its own charted map of the land provinces and sea zones it knows, and what it hasn't charted lies under the parchment . - At the start a country has charted every province within 6 steps of its lands, plus every sea zone touching them. - When an exploration ship enters a zone, that zone and every zone and coastal province next to it are charted. - Any army or fleet charts what is next to where it stands. - Charts are never lost: if Portugal charted the coast of Arguin and later loses every ship and province near it, the coast stays charted. - Charts are never shared or handed over: not with allies, subjects or overlords, and not when land is conquered or inherited. Each country charts its own world. - Only exploration ships enter uncharted zones. Trade and military fleets plan routes only through charted zones. Voyages You give a voyage to an exploration ship or a fleet of them by tapping zones one by one, uncharted ones allowed. The preview shows the zones and how many are uncharted, the supply needed out and back and any shortfall, the ports on the way (uncharted or undockable ones marked), and the low-supply choice : - Turn back (the default): when the supply left is just enough to reach the nearest port where it may dock, the ship turns and sails there. - Carry on : the ship sails the path to its end and runs out of supply if it must, losing 1 in 10 of its crew each zone. A voyage is given only to ships in port, so it always leaves with full supply; ships at sea must put into a port first. Supply is naval's: 1 per zone, 60 for exploration ships, refilled by docking (food in friendly ports, gold in neutral ones, nothing in an enemy's or a rival's). Newly charted land shows its terrain, its owner if any and its ports, and nothing else. The São Gabriel. The caravel São Gabriel waits in Lagos with 60 supply. The player draws a voyage of 34 zones, 21 uncharted. The preview shows supply 60 of 60, 34 out and 34 back, 8 short; it lists Arguin as a canoe landing with no dock and Elmina as uncharted, and offers Turn back and Carry on. Castile 1493, the first voyage. Castile has the unlock and knows S5. Three caravels sail from Seville to the Canaries and dock for food from the province, then sail 17 uncharted zones west with 60 supply each. The preview shows enough to get there and back; they chart the Bahamas and the coast of Hispaniola, and come home. Colonial governors and range Knowing S5 Ocean navigation lets a country hire colonial governors . A governor is hired like any official, in any of your ports, for 20 gold and a wage of 5 gold a year . He is a person: 30 when hired, a year older each January, and he can die. He needs a slot : Source Slots S5 Ocean navigation 2 S3 Outrigger voyaging (without S5) 1 T8 Licensed trading companies +1 on top T9 Joint-stock finance +1 on top Slots are never lost. With no free slot you can't hire. A governor holding a slot doesn't count against the government's officials cap. He leaves his slot when his colony is founded (he becomes its ordinary official and the slot frees), when it fails (he dies), by old age or by dismissal. He waits in a port of yours until a ship picks him up, and any ship can carry him. Colonial range is how many sea zones from your nearest port or colony a colony may be founded. It counts from your own ports (your lords' ports and canoe landings included), your subjects' ports and the colonies you have founded, but not from a colony still being founded. The range comes from your government form: Range Government forms 40 company rule 30 merchant republic, constitutional monarchy, constitutional republic 20 feudal realm, diet monarchy, absolute monarchy, party state 15 military order, military junta, colonial government 10 household realm, bureaucratic empire, elective monarchy, city commune, soldier emirs, shogunate 5 prince-bishopric, holy rule, paramount chiefdom, tribute empire, warlord domain 0 peasant commune, clan council, chiefdom, horde, confederation Once a colony is founded, range is measured from it too, so colonies chain across an ocean. Range is checked only when the governor goes ashore: if your government changes and your range shrinks, colonies already being founded carry on. Portugal, a feudal realm with range 20, can found a colony on an unowned coast of Brazil about 10 zones from a Portuguese port in the Cape Verde islands. Founding a colony A province can be colonised only when it is charted, coastal, owned by no country, has at least one free tile, lies inside your colonial range, and nobody else is already founding a colony there. - Land owned by a country, tribal countries (a chiefdom or clan council in the start list) included, can't be colonised; it can only be taken by war or treaty. Hispaniola, held by a Taíno chiefdom, is one such case. - Land that no realm on the map owns belongs to a people with no country, even where old records name a people or tribe there. A colony there takes only the free tiles, and the people's tiles stay theirs. Going ashore. When a ship carrying a governor is in the province's coastal zone and you give Found colony , the governor goes ashore and the colony starts at 10 progress . Its local aggression is rolled at once from the peoples in the province and its neighbours (a coast across one sea zone counts) and shown: Aggression Chance Average progress lost a month Months to 100 on average Food needed on average Peaceful 30 % 0 18 360 rations Wary 30 % 1 23 460 Hostile 25 % 2 30 600 Fierce 15 % 3 45 900 If nobody lives in the province or any neighbour, the colony is Peaceful. Each month a colony being founded gains 5 progress from its settling party, loses the locals' pressure (a whole number from 0 to twice the aggression's average, each equally likely: 0–2 for Wary, 0–4 for Hostile, 0–6 for Fierce), and eats 20 rations of colony food. If it has no food left it loses a further 10 progress that month. Colony food comes only from ships. Exploration ships carry colony stores apart from their supply (a caravel 300 rations, a voyaging canoe 100), loaded in any port where the ship could resupply at the same cost as resupply. Unload stores moves them into colony food in one day from the colony's coastal zone, with no port needed. - Founded : at 100 progress the province becomes one of your own royal provinces with its settlement at settlement . The governor stays as its official (now counting against the officials cap), his slot frees, and left-over colony food goes into the province's store. From there the Provinces rules (settlers, local tiles) take over; it becomes a Colony subject only if you later charter it under the Subjects rules. The event tree's colonial presence counts it, together with the trading posts you hold, but not colonies still being founded. - Lost : at 0 progress the governor dies, the colony food is lost, the slot frees and the province stays unowned. The colony is lost the same way if its governor dies of old age, or if another realm gains the province while you are founding it. A governor at sea dies if his ship sinks. - Abandon : while one of your ships is in the colony's zone you can take the governor back aboard. The colony food left ashore is lost. He can go ashore on another coast at once with Found colony ; otherwise his slot stays used until he is home in a port. Castile 1493, the second trip. Castile has a colonial governor in slot 1 of 2 and a feudal range of 20. Two caravels load 600 rations of colony stores and the governor and sail to an unowned coast on a small island 17 zones from the Canaries. Castile gives Found colony ; the Taíno across the strait make the roll Hostile, and the caravels unload all 600 rations. The colony gains about 3 progress a month. After a bad run of rolls a third caravel brings 300 more rations in year two, and the colony reaches 100 in month 31 and becomes a Castilian province. The governor stays as its official and his slot frees for the next colony. The computer players A country whose catalogue personality favours expansion by sea sends exploration ships along the edge of its charted map, then founds colonies on the nearest unowned coasts, always loading the stores its rolled aggression needs on average plus a quarter: 450 rations for Peaceful, 575 for Wary, 750 for Hostile and 1,125 for Fierce. Land powers never explore. The AI uses the same commands as the player. Charted maps are stored as one bit per province and zone per country, and colonies update once a month with the province. How you play it Most of exploration happens on the fleet card and the map; the Colonies tab is its overview. - Order a caravel on the Port tab of a coastal province, like any ship. It sails in its own fleet of explorers and needs no admiral. - Explore on the fleet card (in port) folds the card away and brings up the voyage bar along the bottom of the map. Tap sea zones, under the parchment or not: each tap adds a leg, the course is drawn in gold, and the bar shows the zones, how many are uncharted, the supply out and back and any shortfall. Pick Turn back or Carry on , then Set sail ; Undo takes back the last leg and Cancel drops the course. A zone too far out for your ships' reach says why when tapped. - As the fleet sails the parchment lifts from every zone and coast next to it, and a news line reports how many places the voyage charted when it ends. - The Colony section of the same card (once you know Ocean navigation): Hire a colonial governor in a port of yours, Load colony stores, then at sea beside an empty coast one Found a colony in … button per coast, each with the reason underneath when it can't be used. Beside your colony, Unload puts the stores ashore. - A colony being founded shows its card on the province: progress and the month's change, the locals, food and whether it will last, and Abandon when a ship of yours lies beside it. On the map it is a small flag over a ring that fills as it grows. - The Exploration map mode (Map mode menu) shows what you have charted, empty coasts inside your colonial range in bright green, empty land beyond it in pale green and colonies being founded in gold. - The Colonies tab of your country card: governors used of slots and the range, where each governor is (tap to go there), colonies being founded with their progress and food, those founded, and how many empty coasts lie in range, with a button to the Exploration map mode. On a phone in landscape the voyage bar sits between the overview button and End turn, wraps its buttons rather than shrinking them, and every reason is written under its button since there is no hover. In the game today. Until the map records regions per province and who works each tile, a realm's region for the age gate comes from the event tree's region list or the scenario catalogue's region, every unowned land province has one free tile, and a founded colony keeps the people living there, who become yours. The computer players that explore are the sea-minded realms of the catalogue (Castile, Portugal, Novgorod): each keeps one caravel exploring the edge of its charts and, once it can hire governors, settles the nearest empty coast in range with the stores it needs. How it connects - Naval: ship families, the caravel and voyaging canoe, 60 supply, colony stores, docking and sailing reach; exploration gives back the unlock and the charted map. - Research: S3, S4, S5, T8, T9 and S1. - Historical-Events: the Age of Exploration and its regions open the gate; founded colonies count toward colonial presence . - Government: colonial range per form, the officials cap and the governor exemption. - Provinces: the founded colony as province state, free tiles and the colonial governor official type. - Subjects: a founded colony is a royal province until it is chartered as a Colony subject; subjects' ports count for colonial range. - World-Map: sea zones, coastal provinces and adjacency. - The 1378 Start: which land is owned at the start and which is unowned with peoples on it. - Your-Realm: the country card line and the governor's gold and wage. - Troop-Movement: the shared planner and day loop voyages use. - Diplomacy: war and rivalry close ports to a voyage. - Map and Map Modes: the parchment, paths, flags, range line and colony card. - Time-and-Turns: the monthly colony update and the day loop. Government: Government decides how your country is ruled and how many people can run it. Your government form (one of 27, from a feudal realm to a party state) sets how many officials and lords you can support, how far your colonies can reach, how many subjects you can watch over and how the next ruler is chosen. You change form by reform, or it is changed for you by a revolution, a coup, a lost capital or an event. How it works The two caps Every country has two caps: - Officials cap = the form's officials + the officials your buildings give (+ any national strength). - Lords cap = the form's lords + the lords your buildings give (+ any national strength). Both show as "x of y". Every lord counts exactly 1 toward the lords cap, however many provinces he holds. While you are within both caps nothing happens. Over the officials cap , the province of each official over the cap gets the grievance Grasping officials , newest hires first. An official's hire date is the day he took up his post, whether he was hired, came from the schools or inherited the post from a lord's line. The grievance goes away when you are back within the cap. Over the lords cap , at each New Year one lord loses a loyalty step for each lord over the cap, lowest loyalty first, then the lord with the most provinces. Great lords. A lord's size affects only his loyalty: a lord with 4 to 7 provinces has one permanent down reason Great lord , and one with 8 or more has two. Buildings that raise the caps Building Officials Lords Needs Palace, step 1 / 2 / 3 6 / 10 / 16 2 / 4 / 6 Landmark palace (step 4): Forbidden City / Topkapı Palace 24 / 20 6 the landmark (provisional) Seat, step 1 / 2 (one per province) 2 / 4 each step 2 needs G11 Chancery 4 G3 Tax registers Court of law 2 G1 Written law codes Diet hall 3 feudal realm, diet monarchy, elective monarchy or confederation only Hostage residence 3 household realm, tribute empire, horde, warlord domain or shogunate only Examination hall 4 G4 Examination system Parliament house 6 G14 Written constitution The buildings themselves (cost, slot, jobs) belong to Buildings. France in 1444 , measured on the 1444 checkpoint world, is a feudal realm with a palace at step 2, 3 seats at step 1 and a court of law. Its officials cap is 22 (form 6, palace 10, three seats 6) and its lords cap 14 (form 8, palace 4, court of law 2). With 18 officials and 11 lords, the government card reads "Officials 18 of 22" and "Lords 11 of 14", within both caps. The Ottomans , a household realm with a palace at step 2, a chancery, 4 seats at step 1 and a hostage residence, have an officials cap of 32 and a lords cap of 11. At the 1378 start that is the Hordes of the steppe (Mamai's Horde, the White Horde of Tokhtamysh and Arab Shah's Horde), Moghulistan, the Northern Yuan and the Qara Qoyunlu. Crimea, Kazan, the Nogais, the Uzbeks and the Oirats are not born yet and form later as hordes (see The 1378 start). How far behind. A steppe horde starts level with anyone in the horse (riding, composite-bow horse archery, horse breeding) and one era level behind its settled neighbours (Muscovy, the Ottomans, the Timurids, Ming) in everything else: no stone castles, no steel or gunpowder, no knights or wagon forts, no feudal grants or royal chancery. It keeps writing, written law and temple schools, and the Islamic hordes keep madrasas. Why it is strong. Horse archers, the Feigned flight style, herds that give horses and horse-only raids make a horde win most field battles in Era I and about half in Era II. Why it fades. Without castles or siege guns it takes castles slowly, so it lives from raids and tribute more than conquest, and a neighbour can often buy peace for less than the raids cost. Few towns, few schools and 2 officials keep its research slow. Once its enemies field field guns (W8) and flintlocks (W11), from Era III, horse archers keep only scouting and raiding. How it catches up. Any realm pays less for an invention from an earlier era than today: 25 % less per era behind, at most 50 %, before the discount from neighbours and trade partners, and never below a fifth of the cost. So what the world already knows is cheap to learn. A horde can also settle : reform to a Household realm (a palace in a town, 150 gold); it keeps everything it knows, horse archers included, and gains officials (2 → 10) but has fewer lords (10 → 4). Where you see it. The Learning tab's overview says how many inventions your neighbours know that you don't, and each invention's sheet shows its "Behind the times" discount. A horde's Government tab says how long its riders stay strong and what settling changes. Another realm's card says how many inventions it is ahead of or behind you. All numbers here are provisional, set against balance targets: a horde's Technology score about half of Muscovy's at the start; a horde that studies closes the gap by about 1550; field wins against an equal settled army 6 in 10 in Era I, 5 in 10 in Era II and at most 1 in 4 from Era III; and at least a third of a horde's gold from raids and tribute in Era I. The start Each catalogue record gets its start form by the first rule that applies: a hand-set override (75 of them), then text rules on the catalogue's government form text in order (some only for certain entity types, some skipping them), then for kingdoms a rule by region (in Southeast Asia tier A and B kingdoms become tribute empires and tier C paramount chiefdoms; a kingdom in a region with no rule becomes a feudal realm), then the entity type table, then the default chiefdom. Nobody starts as an absolute monarchy, constitutional monarchy, constitutional republic, military junta, party state or company rule. Each country starts with the catalogue's historical houses as lords (none if it has only one province), and its caps come from its start form and its start buildings. The computer players The AI uses the same Reform command as the player. Each January it orders the reform to the first of its next forms, in the order the table lists them, whose needs it meets and whose gold it holds twice over. Each month Each month any change that happens by itself is applied, the caps are recomputed after buildings and hiring, and Grasping officials is applied or lifted. At New Year, lords over the cap slip. Reforms resolve when ordered. What you see - The government card : the form and the ruler; each cap as "x of y" with its parts (the form and each building); subjects as "x of y"; the next forms with each need shown met or not; and a Reform action. In the game now Open your realm (tap its name in the top bar) and choose the Government tab, next to General: - Your form and its family. - Officials x of y and Lords x of y , each with a bar and its parts. Until cap buildings can be built, each cap has a part Custom since 1378 : what your realm held above its form at the start, so nobody starts over a cap. Conquests, new officials and a reform to a smaller form can push you over; the cap turns red and says what follows. Tap a cap to open the Officials or Lords tab, where you can move or commission officials and grant or take back fiefs. - Laws of the realm : succession, how far your colonies may reach, and how many subjects you can hold against your reach. - Reform : a card for each form you can become, with the change in officials and lords, each need ✓ or ✗, the gold (the design's gold × 0.2, so 100 is 20) and the lords who will slip. Tap Reform, then confirm. Forms that come only by revolution, event or a condition say so. Needs for buildings, traders, families and alliances can't be met yet; inventions and province, lord and subject counts can. The Government page sits in your Realm book's Realm section, beside the Overview. Other realms' cards show their form. AI realms reform each January when they meet the needs with twice the gold. How it connects - Buildings: which cap buildings stand and at what step. - Provinces: officials hired, Grasping officials , self-run provinces and Ungoverned . - Your-Realm: lords, their provinces and loyalty, the treasury, and succession by form. - Subjects: the subject limit and its change by form. - Exploration-and-Colonies: colonial range and colonial governors. - Revolutions: regimes set forms, era ignored. - Rebellions: a won New ideas rising sets a form. - Historical-Events: the 16 event-tree values and admin capacity . - Research: G1, G2, G3, G4, G6, G9, G11, G14 and W12 as needs. - National-Strengths: additions to caps (for example +2 officials for Venice). - Religion: a change of state faith opens the faith forms' reform; the Inquisition is open to monarchies. - Culture: a province's largest language, which decides "own people" for self-run forms. - Warfare: army coups and the shogun's capital. - Trade: traders abroad and trade debt as reform needs. - Diplomacy: alliances with neighbours as a need. - The 1378 Start: start forms and lords. - Map and Map Modes: the government card. Historical-Events: Historical events are the game's history layer: the turning points of five centuries, from the fall of Constantinople to the Great Depression, arriving as cards with choices. They follow the state of the world rather than a fixed calendar, so history can come early, late, differently or not at all, and every event lets you decide how your realm answers it. How it works The campaign span Events run from the campaign's start to the campaign's end date, which is 31 August 1939 by default (it is one setting). When a campaign loads, every event that history places after that date is dropped and never fires. That covers the Second World War events, the Holocaust, the 1943 Bengal famine, the atomic bombings and everything in the Cold War and decolonization chains: 59 events in the current data. The ages Age of Decolonization, Cold War and Age of Globalization never start, and any age still running on the last day is cut there. An age that would end on a dropped event (the World Wars age ends on the Second World War) simply runs until its other end condition or the end date. The interwar years stay in: the Wilsonian moment, the 1918 armistice, the 1918 influenza, Versailles, the May Fourth movement, the founding of the Soviet Union, Lausanne, the Great Depression, the Italian invasion of Ethiopia and the Second Sino-Japanese War. Principles A few rules shape every event in the tree. - History is a reference, not a script. Each event carries a history block (dates, a summary, why it matters, sources, how confident the record is, and any disputes). That block never drives play. Only the event's availability, trigger and selection decide when it happens. - Roles, not hard-coded countries. An event names slots such as $realm , $sponsor or $resister . When the event becomes eligible, each slot is bound to whichever country, entity or province meets its selector. A selector can be fixed (the historical holders) or a condition, optionally limited to a place. So "a monarchy in deep debt with liberal ideas spreading" can be France, or someone else. - Agency for everyone. Colonised, enslaved and Indigenous actors can hold the initiator and resister roles and choose their own options. - Harm is shown, never rewarded. An event marked narrative only depicts an atrocity. It never offers the perpetrator an option with a positive stat or prestige payoff, and it acts on the people it names (population and forced movement of a population group), not just on a modifier. Enslaved people are never a trade good or a production bonus on the victims' land; enslavement is forced movement of people, with costs on the societies they were taken from. - No invented facts. Contested dates and numbers sit in disputes with lowered confidence, and gameplay magnitudes are labelled as design values. Every source is marked verified or not, and a historian spot-checks citations before release. - Our own model. The tree uses its own words: prosperity, innovations, trade hubs, mean years, notoriety, integration strain. Ages An age is a broad frame over the world with a window, start and end conditions and forced dates. Once the game is inside an age's window it checks the start and end conditions every year. If they never come true, the forced dates start and end the age anyway, so a stalled game still moves on. Several ages run at the same time. Age Window Forced start Forced end Schism and Conquerors 1378 to 1460 1378 1460 Gunpowder Empires 1420 to 1760 1453 1760 Exploration 1415 to 1680 1445 1680 Reformations 1480 to 1700 1530 1700 Atlantic Empires 1480 to 1880 1520 1880 Crisis and Absolutism 1590 to 1790 1640 1790 Revolutions 1750 to 1880 1800 1880 Industrialization 1700 to 1950 1830 1950 Imperialism 1800 to 1945 1860 1945 World Wars 1890 to 1960 1925 1960 Each age also lists its regions, so systems that care whether "the age has begun in your region" (exploration, national strengths, music) can read it. There are 13 ages in the data and these 10 are inside the campaign. The campaign starts on 20 September 1378, the day the Western Schism begins. The Age of Schism and Conquerors covers the years from then to the fall of Constantinople: two popes, Timur's campaigns, the early Ming fleets. It is under way from the first day in every region and ends once the Schism and the Council of Basel are over and Constantinople has fallen. Gunpowder Empires starts when three of the eight great powers (the realms with the most provinces) know Bombards, or when Constantinople falls. Exploration starts when Portugal or Castile has the ocean ships (Carrack and caravel) or holds the Atlantic islands. A fast world starts them early and a slow one waits for 1453 and 1445. The 1444 checkpoint world, opened with ?start=1444 , has all three under way from the start. Periods A period is a regional or thematic situation inside one or more ages, such as a dynastic crisis or a regional war. There are 101. A period becomes active when its start condition holds inside its window (a period marked initial is already running at the start, if the start lies inside its window) and ends when its end condition holds, so it can start early, late or never. Events can also start and end periods directly, and conditions can ask whether a period or an age is active. Which events belong to a period or an age is declared once, on the event itself. From the 1378 start the Western Schism, Timur's conquests, the Caroline phase of the Hundred Years' War, Ottoman expansion, Muscovite consolidation and the Southeast Asian states are under way. Others follow from what happens: the Timurid fragmentation once Timur's conquests are over, the Lancastrian phase when England and France go to war again, the Ottoman Interregnum only if Timur breaks the Ottomans, the Hussite wars with the Defenestration of Prague or when religious rebels rise in Bohemia, the Ming treasure voyages while the Ming are steady, Majapahit's decline, and Late Ming once the voyages are over. Portuguese oceanic expansion waits for the Age of Exploration, and Aztec and Inca expansion for the Triple Alliance and the Inca. From 1378 to 1444: the bridge events of the West Between the 1378 start and 1444, the West meets its history as 54 events. Like every event they wait for their conditions and are only likeliest near their history year, so each can come early, late or not at all. - The Church. France declares for the Avignon pope first. Then every Catholic realm of Europe gets one card: obey Rome, obey Avignon, or stay neutral. France's friends lean to Avignon, England's to Rome. Urban deposes Joanna of Naples, Wyclif's Lollards are condemned or tolerated, and the councils of Pisa, Constance and Basel follow. Constance ends the Schism; Hus's burning and the Defenestration of Prague start the Hussite wars. - The Empire. Wenceslaus follows Charles IV, Austria is split at Neuberg, and the Swiss win at Sempach and Näfels. Wenceslaus can be deposed if his realm is weak and he has ruled ten years or more. Then come Sigismund, Brandenburg to the Hohenzollerns (a union under Brandenburg), Saxony to the Wettins (Saxony takes Saxe-Wittenberg), the Hussite crusades, and Albert of Austria's three crowns (Hungary and Bohemia become unions under Austria). - France and England. The uncles' regency when a child is king of France, the Peasants' Revolt while England pays for the war, Richard II's deposition when his throne is weak, the madness of Charles VI and the princes' feud that follows. If the princes fight, Agincourt can come, and then Normandy passes to England two years later if the war is still on. At Troyes, France may give Paris to England. Joan of Arc and the Congress of Arras can turn it back. - Iberia. Portugal's crisis when its king dies, Aljubarrota, Lancaster's claim to Castile and the Compromise of Caspe. Ceuta, Madeira and the Azores, and Cape Bojador turn Portugal to the sea. Settling the islands can start the Age of Exploration. Alfonso V can take Naples as a union under Aragon. - Italy. The War of Chioggia and the Peace of Turin. Durazzo takes Naples, which gives the French a claim on it. Gian Galeazzo's coup unites Pavia and Milan, Milan is made a duchy and breaks up when he dies, and Florence takes Pisa. Ladislaus marches on Rome, the Lombard wars can give Brescia to Venice, and Sforza's marriage gives the French a claim on Milan. Both claims are what the later Italian Wars need. Deaths, child kings and the Emperor come from the game itself: an event that needs "the king has died" waits until the realm's ruler really changes. A campaign that starts in 1444 counts these events as history already, with their historical choice, so it plays as before. Some 1444 events now need them: the end of the Hundred Years' War needs Agincourt or Troyes first, the Wars of the Roses need Richard II's fall, and the union of Castile and Aragon needs Caspe. Everyday events Between the great events, your own realm asks for small choices. About every three to six months (two or three times a year) something happens to your officials, lords, family or stores, and an event card asks what you will do. No new one comes while another card waits for your answer, so they never pile up. What happens Your choices An official dies in a royal province Raise his deputy (free, starts at half the post's effect), send for a seasoned man (25 gold, keeps the full effect), or give the post to a lord's kinsman (starts at half, that lord grows more loyal) A lord dies Confirm his son (as loyal as his father), ask a fee for the lands (gold, the son less loyal), or take the lands for the crown (they become royal land, your other lords grow less loyal) A lord feels slighted at court Send him a gift (gold), give him an office (another lord grows jealous), or let him sulk (he grows less loyal) A lord speaks well of you Reward him (gold, he grows more loyal) or thank him Two lords quarrel over a mill Judge for one (he grows more loyal, the other less), or fine them both (gold, both less loyal) A lord is hurt hunting Send your physician (gold, he grows more loyal) or your prayers A child is born to your ruler Hold a feast (gold, your two least loyal lords grow more loyal), promise the child to a lord's house (that lord grows more loyal), or give thanks quietly. With no heir, the child becomes your heir Your young heir falls ill Pay the best physicians (gold) or trust in prayer (3 in 10 that the heir dies) Grain rots, burns or is eaten by rats in a store The grain is lost whatever you choose; buy grain (gold) or take it from a lord's barns (he grows less loyal) to make half of it good, or bear the loss Plague reaches one of your provinces Close the province (its trade stops and its tax halves while closed), send physicians (gold: half as many die and it is over sooner), or keep the roads open. Only one plague card waits at a time; the News tells of the rest An option you can't pay for isn't offered, and at least one choice always costs nothing. Other realms get the same events and answer them at once, so their lords die, quarrel and change their minds too. Look at the map on a card about a province opens that province. When an event can happen An event has to pass several gates before it can fire. - Years. It never fires outside its earliest and latest year. - How strongly the date binds. mandatory fires inside the window whenever the trigger holds: in the window's last year it is certain. approximate is weighted toward the historical date: its monthly chance is doubled in the history year and the extra fades away over 10 years either side, so the death of Suleiman is twice as likely in 1566 and half again as likely in 1561 or 1571. reference uses the date only as a guide. - Repeating. one time fires once. recurring can fire again after a cooldown: the Bengal famine of 1770 has a 30-year cooldown, so if Bengal's food security falls below 0.4 again in 1790 it cannot fire yet, but in 1801 it can. process diffuses and can fire for several countries. - Prerequisites. Event chains use all (mandatory), any (alternative paths), not (exclusive) and at least (n of m). A prerequisite can name an outcome: the French revolutionary wars need the French Revolution to have ended as a radical republic, so a constitutional monarchy outcome closes that branch. - Optional events only raise the weight. If the American Revolution has happened, the French Revolution's weight is multiplied by 1.5, but it was never needed for eligibility. - Exclusive events. When one of a pair fires, the other never does. - Invalidation. When an event's invalidation condition holds, it is removed for good. If France becomes a republic by some other path, the French Revolution event is gone. A branch closed because its entity vanished can re-open if a later event creates that entity again. - Trigger. A condition tree over the state of the world. For example, the French Revolution needs $realm to be a monarchy with debt of 2000 or more and liberalism of 0.25 or more, plus any of stability -1 or lower, legitimacy under 40, or the Laki eruption having happened. A France with debt 2100, liberalism 0.3, stability 0 and legitimacy 35 qualifies. Triggers may only use condition types declared in the vocabulary: date, exists, controls, owns, borders, at war, war ongoing, relation, opinion, stat, rank, government, religion, religion share, culture group, innovation, ideology, tech, colonial presence, trade presence, rebels active, subject count, event, event active, period active, age active, flag, any country, all countries and count countries. Logic is all, any, not and at least. The event condition means "this event has happened", optionally with a given outcome, within n years, with a role bound to someone. No condition can ask whether a country is played by a person: you and the computer face the same history. Targets can be a role, an entity id, a province, an area, a region, the whole world, or "this" inside the any, all and count country tests. How an eligible event is chosen Selection What happens Immediate Fires as soon as it becomes eligible. Pool Rolled every month against its mean years (the expected wait once eligible), multiplied by its selection modifiers and any follow-up boost. An event with a mean wait of 4 years, modifiers of ×2 and a boost of ×1.5 rolls with all three applied. Decision Offered to its chooser. Napoleon's invasion of Iberia, with the invader role bound to France, is offered to whoever controls France. To keep the pace sane, no country gets more than 2 pool events a year. A decision a computer country leaves unanswered for 10 years lapses and goes back into the pool if it is still eligible. A decision offered to you never lapses: it waits for you like every other event. Follow-ups. When an event fires, each of its follow-ups gets a weight boost during its delay window. Boosts are capped at ×5, fade out linearly over 10 years after the window closes, and never make an ineligible event fire. Alternate history. When you start a new game, the "Events" choice picks how closely history is followed. Plausible is the default. Events choice Follow-up boost Historical option weight Mean years Historical ×1.5 ×2.0 ×0.8 Plausible ×1.0 ×1.0 ×1.0 Free ×0.6 ×0.5 ×1.3 Options and choices Every event offers two to four options, and exactly one is marked historical, the one that matches the record. An option's chooser is a role: its controller, player or computer, picks. If an option has no chooser, the game rolls between options by weight. An option whose allowed condition is false is hidden. An option's effects add to the event's own effects. When an event is offered to you, the game waits for your answer. Nothing ever answers an event for you: while one is waiting, End turn opens the oldest unanswered event instead. The computer weighs each option by a base weight times named factors: Factor True when at war The country is at war low treasury Treasury is below one year of expenses high unrest More than half its provinces have 4 or more grievances same religion The other party shares the state religion rival The other party is a rival great power The country is in the top 8 by great power score threatened A hostile neighbour has more than 1.5 times its army strength Effects Effects land in tiers: immediate ; delayed after a number of years (or a range); ongoing each month while the event runs; and long term as a permanent change to the world. In the Anglo-Zulu war, the "invade" option starts the war at once and annexes the Zulu kingdom a year later if its war weariness is 10 or more. Some events run for a while. They last their duration, apply ongoing effects, end early if their maintain condition stops holding, and abort if their cancel condition comes true. Samori Toure's resistance runs for 16 years while the Wassoulou empire exists; if the empire falls in year five, the event ends and its ongoing effects stop. Conditions can ask whether such an event is still running. The effect types are: modifier, stat, transfer, create country, annex, vassalize, release, war, peace, reason for war, relation, rebels, spread, population, move population, set flag, start period, end period, unlock, government, religion, trade route and colony. A stat change is a one-off delta, either a flat amount or a percentage. A war started by an event gets a stable id that later events can test. Adding a new condition or effect type takes one engine evaluator and nothing else; everything else is data. A rebels effect is a spark: a rising starts at once in the province, and its men come out of the province's recruit pool. Rebellions then runs it like any other rising. Size Share of the recruit pool From a pool of 1000 Small one eighth 125 Medium a quarter 250 Large half 500 Huge all of it 1000 When a revolution's rising ends, the option you chose applies its "if the rising won" or "if the rising was crushed" effects. Modifiers A modifier is a named, timed bundle of stat changes. There are 159. Each has a scope (province, country, region or global), its changes, a length in years (0 means permanent), a decay (none, linear or exponential) and a stacking rule (none, refresh or stack). A modifier that names no stacking rule refreshes. No modifier stacks more than 3 times. Exponential decay halves the magnitude at half the duration. How a change applies depends on the stat: a plain number holds on a level stat while the modifier is active, and applies once a year on an accumulating stat. A percentage scales a derived stat, or removes that share of population each year. A key ending in growth changes the yearly growth rate. A region-scoped modifier aimed at a country hits all its provinces. The event tree's statistics The tree has its own abstract statistics (prosperity 1 to 60, unrest 0 to 100, stability -3 to +3, opinion -200 to 200, trust 0 to 100 and so on), split into stored values that are kept as state and derived values recomputed every tick. An event never writes a derived value directly, only its inputs or a modifier the formula reads; when a province's devastation rises, its local supply and output are worked out again the next tick. The tree's abstract words never reach your cards. Each change lands as something concrete in the system that owns it: An event changes… …and you see prosperity +2 two new buildings that fit the province devastation +30 30 % of the province's tiles burned unrest up one named grievance from the event fort level +1 the castle one step up infrastructure +1 the road one step up industry +1 one factory disease burden up a plague outbreak trade access the trade ratio gain, for the event's duration notoriety up a notorious deed in every country that knows you trust down an oath broken Integration strain is only read by events, as the share of your provinces with a grievance. Flags, lists and entities Triggers may only read flags that some effect sets or that are declared system flags set by the engine or the scenario (ruler died, succession crisis, succession dispute, regency, female succession, ruler led campaign, Atlantic island bases, potato blight, commercial crisis and the world-state flags). Religion sets its own three: persecution, missionary persecution and an inquisition. Religions, governments, innovations, ideologies, culture groups, rebel types, relation types, period kinds and entity kinds come from closed lists; adding a value needs no engine change. The lists hold nothing first seen after 1939, and there are 43 culture groups. The 625 entities (polities, companies, movements, population groups, organizations) have real existence spans. A population group is never owned and an organization holds no provinces. The data build The event data is checked offline before it ships. The build splits it into runtime layers (history reference, ages, periods, event definitions, triggers, selection, execution, choices, AI, effects, modifiers, statistics, balance and English localization). All player-facing text comes from the localization layer, keyed by id and ready for translation. The build checks that every id exists, every condition and effect type is declared, every event has its roles, two to four options with one historical, that narrative-only events pay no perpetrator, that there are no mandatory prerequisite cycles, impossible triggers or jointly required exclusive pairs, that entities exist at the event's date, that flags read are set or declared, and that ages and periods have start and end conditions. It also reports coverage: any region with fewer than 2 events in an age that lists it, and an agency share (initiator, beneficiary and resister slots over all slots in a region) below 0.35. An error fails the build; warnings do not. The current result is 0 errors and 21 warnings; the anachronism warnings are corrected when a historian checks the sources before release. Realms' historical goals History is a guide, not a script. Realms follow its normal course because each one pursues the goals it really had, for the reasons it had them: the Ottomans want the Balkans for their frontier lords, Florence wants Pisa because it needs a port. Each goal has a window of years, a weight (weak, normal or strong) and an aim the game can read: take some places, hold some places, make a realm a subject , ally with a realm, fight a realm, or free itself from an overlord. Goals about faith, trade or a succession are shown but not weighed. - A goal ends with its reason. A take goal ends once its realm holds every place it names, a hold goal once one of them is lost, an ally goal once the two are allied, and any goal once its target or its realm is gone. A goal pulls from five years before its window and fades over ten years after it. - The AI weighs goals like any other wish. A goal makes its realm look for a war more often, pick the realm holding its places as the target, and ask for those places first; an ally or subject goal sends envoys toward its target. A goal never lets a war past its price: a weak realm does not march however much it wants to. - Every campaign differs. At the start the seed shakes every goal: its weight varies by half either way, and a share of goals goes another way (10 % on Historical, 25 % on Plausible, 50 % on Free), taking the plausible alternative where there is one and dropping out where there is none. Historical also weighs goals ×1.5 and Free ×0.5. - You are never steered. Your realm's goals weigh nothing you do. The 1378 scenario holds about 760 goals, written region by region from the start-date research. The 1444 start has none. Hooks for other systems An event can carry a music tag (good event, bad event, major event, crisis, revolution) that moves the soundtrack. Events marked tutorial only never fire in a real campaign. What you see - The event card. A fired event opens as a modal card with its options. Events open one at a time, queued in date order. - End turn waits for you. Unanswered events block End turn until you choose. - The "Events" choice (Historical, Plausible or Free) is offered among the new game options. - The Chronicle. The News has a History tab. Its first line counts the turning points ahead: on course, bent or gone. Under it, Ahead lists the turning points of history due within 25 years, soonest first, each with its history year. Tap one to see who is heading there: each realm with its goal and why it wants it. Happened lists those that happened, with the year and whether it was as in history (within ten years), early or late. A turning point is bent when it is more than ten years overdue, or when every realm heading there went another way; it is gone when it can no longer happen. At the foot, the closed fold History's plan for your realm holds your own realm's goals as hints, if you want them. - Aims on a realm's card. Another realm's General tab has an Aims fold with its live goals, each with its reason and its years. - The end of the campaign shows the final scores; there is no separate wrap-up event. How it connects - Provinces: event statistics such as prosperity, devastation and unrest land on province numbers. - Your realm: legitimacy, stability, war weariness, prestige, treasury and the engine flags such as ruler died. - Research: the 17 innovations are research-tree inventions with the same ids. - Trade: trade access lands on the trade ratio gain; trade presence and trade route effects. - Government: 16 government values map to forms of rule. - Rebellions: the rebels effect starts a rising; "rebels active" reads it. - Revolutions: built on events, adding a revolution block and the "rising won" and "rising crushed" effects. - Religion, Culture, Subjects, Diplomacy, National strengths, Buildings: each adds its own conditions and effects to the events. - Exploration and colonies: the Age of Exploration gates exploration per region. - Warfare: war, peace and reasons for war; prestige from victories. - Screens and navigation: the event card, the queue and blocking End turn. - Music and sound: music tags on events. - Achievements: your roles and historical or non-historical choices. - Tutorial and help: tutorial-only scripted events. - How a turn works: events run after every other system's monthly, seasonal and yearly steps, just before achievements and the autosave. Each month Turns are a week long, so this runs in the turn in which a new month begins. Each year, in the turn in which 1 January falls, the game checks age and period conditions and applies forced dates. Each month it lets computer decisions older than 10 years lapse, then checks eligibility and binds roles, fires immediate events, rolls pool events under the pacing cap, offers decisions, queues fired events for you in date order (computer choosers answer at once), applies effects, schedules delayed ones, ticks running events and modifiers, fades follow-up boosts and works out derived values again. Home: Pocket Hegemony is an 8-bit grand strategy game for phones, desktop and the web. You lead one of hundreds of realms from 20 September 1378 to the end of August 1939, one week per turn, on a pixel-art map of the whole world that you can zoom from the globe down to a single town. This wiki explains every system in the game and how it works. Each page is written from the game's domain specs, the precise rules the code is checked against, so the wiki and the game say the same thing. Numbers marked provisional are still being balanced, and every page ends with what is not decided yet. Start here - How a turn works: one week per turn, the days inside it, and when the campaign ends. - The 1378 start: which realms exist and which you can play. - Your realm and Provinces: the two cards everything else feeds. - Map and Map Modes: what the map shows at each zoom.
