The context map shows how they depend on each other. In short: the clock, the map and the 1378 start sit underneath everything; provinces and the realm make the gold, food and people; armies, fleets and traders spend and move them; diplomacy, government, culture and religion shape who rules and who obeys; events, revolutions and heritage give history its shape; and the screens, saves, sound and achievements sit on top without ever changing the simulation. For developers - Design principles: how every feature is designed around the player, grouped logically, given an overview and checked on a phone. - Domain specs and feature files: domain/ in the game repository. Each system has spec.md (requirements with ids such as TRADE-004 ) and features/ .feature (Gherkin). - pnpm specs prints how many scenarios each system has, how many are automated and how many pass. - Rules code lives in packages/engine/src/domain/<system / , balance numbers in packages/rules/data/domain/<system .json . - Everything not yet decided is in open-questions.md.
Institutions: Some realms belong to something bigger than themselves. At the 1378 start that is the Empire , whose Emperor is elected by seven seats and is only as strong as his hold over its members. The Shogunate in Japan works the same way: the shogun is only as strong as his hold over the great houses. Every number here is provisional and lives in institutions.json . Hold An institution's office is worth its hold , 0 to 100, named by a word: Hollow (0 to 19), Weak (20 to 49), Firm (50 to 79) and Strong (80 to 100). Some things move it at once (answering a call to defend a member); the rest is added up each January, and the Hold fold shows each gain and loss with its cause. What the Empire's hold counts each year: Hold : No war between members and no imperial land held by outsiders +2 Each war between two members −3 Each imperial province an outsider holds −2 (at most −10) Each member that left −5 Each member whose faith is not the Emperor's (halved after the Peace of Augsburg, none after Westphalia) −1 Defending a member when called +10 Refusing, or not answering, a call to defend a member −15 The Empire Members and imperial land On 20 September 1378 the crown is held by Charles IV of the house of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia, aged 62. In history he dies on 29 November, in the tenth week, and his son Wenceslaus , aged 17 and already elected King of the Romans, follows him without an election. Wenceslaus's deposition (1400) and the reigns of Rupert, Jobst and Sigismund are events. The members are the realms whose capital lies in imperial land, from the Low Countries' fiefs, Lorraine and Savoy to Bohemia, Austria and the north German princes and cities. The hold starts at 35 (Weak); Wenceslaus's Empire is weak, and this first value may be set lower. In the game today the member list in institutions.json is still the one of the 1444 checkpoint (18 members, with Austria and Frederick III holding the crown); the 1378 list replaces it. Imperial land is every province the members held on the start day. It never changes: a province an outsider takes stays imperial land, held by an outsider, and the Emperor holds the war aim Restore imperial land on whoever holds it. A member leaves when its capital is no longer in imperial land, when it becomes the subject of a realm outside the Empire, or when it is gone. The Emperor can ask a realm whose capital lies in imperial land to join; it answers by the reasons count. Seats and the election Seven seats elect the Emperor: Cologne, Bohemia, the Palatinate, Saxe-Wittenberg and Brandenburg, held by those realms, and the church seats of Mainz and Trier, which vote for the candidate the Pope thinks best of. A realm holds at most one seat, but a house can hold two: in 1378 the Luxembourgs hold both Bohemia and Brandenburg. Meissen and Thuringia, the Wettins' land, have no seat yet; the Saxon seat passes to the Wettins (1423) and Brandenburg to the Hohenzollerns (1415) by event. When a seat's realm leaves or is gone, the seat stands vacant until the Emperor grants it to a member without one. The seats elect a new Emperor when the Emperor dies or his realm leaves the Empire. The election sits for a month. The candidates are the sitting house, the three members with the most soldiers and every member whose ruler stands for the crown, all of the Catholic faith until the Peace of Westphalia. Each seat votes for the candidate it rates highest: Reason : Standing toward the candidate ÷ 4 Same faith +10 The sitting house +15 A strong crown: the candidate has more soldiers +5 for each multiple, at most +20 Sought our vote +15, fading over 10 years At war with the candidate −50 Most votes win; a tie goes to the sitting house, then to the candidate with more soldiers. If you hold a seat, you cast its vote yourself while the election sits; if you say nothing, your seat votes by its reasons. Seek their vote sends an envoy with a 30-gold gift to an elector's court. When he arrives, the elector holds the tie Sought our vote toward you. The Emperor - Defend the Empire. When a realm outside the Empire declares war on a member, or holds a member's imperial land in a war, the Emperor is called to defend it. Answering gives +10 hold. Refusing, or saying nothing for a month, costs 15 hold, and the attacked member and every elector hold the wrong Left us to our fate toward him. - Dues. Each month the Emperor receives 1 gold per member times hold ÷ 100, on the Tribute line of the treasury. - He grants vacant seats and asks realms to join. - He is bound by every reform like any member. The Diet and the reforms While hold is 50 or more, the Emperor may call the Diet , at most once every five years, on the next reform of the ladder. The reforms pass in order: Reform What it does Public Peace A member that declares war on another member is a Breaker of the Peace : for ten years the Emperor and every member hold a war aim on it, and the Emperor is called to defend its victim. Imperial Court A member with a war aim on another member's province may take it to court instead of to war. The court rules by the aim, both sides' standing toward the Emperor and the hold. A ruling for the plaintiff moves the province with no war; refusing it makes the refuser a Breaker of the Peace. Saying nothing for a month hands it over. Circles When an outsider attacks a member, every member of its circle joins the defence. The circles: Austrian, Bavarian, Swabian, Upper Rhenish, Electoral Rhenish, Lower Saxon and Upper Saxon. Common Tax Every member pays 5 in 100 of its tax to the Emperor each month, in place of the dues. Imperial Army When the Emperor answers a call to defend the Empire, he raises a contingent of a tenth of every member's soldiers at his capital for the war; it goes home with the peace. Hereditary Crown The Emperor's heir takes the crown; no more elections. One Realm Needs hold 80. Every other member's ruler becomes a great lord of the Emperor with his land, Wavering, and the Empire becomes one realm. The Diet sits for a month. Every member votes yes or no by its reasons; an elector's vote counts twice, and over half the votes pass it. Passing spends 30 hold and failing 10. If you are a member you vote on an answer card; saying nothing counts as no. A member's reason to vote yes : The reform itself Public Peace +10, Imperial Court and Circles +5, Common Tax and Imperial Army −10, Hereditary Crown −25, One Realm −40 The Empire's hold ÷ 10 Standing toward the Emperor ÷ 4 Same faith as the Emperor +10 An outsider holds imperial land next to us +15 Small beside the Emperor (or strong beside him) +5 (or −5) for each multiple, at most 20 Faith and the end - After the Peace of Westphalia an eighth seat goes to the largest member without one, and a member's faith no longer costs hold. - The Empire is dissolved when its hold has stood at 0 for five years in a row, or when a realm outside it that beat the Emperor in a war takes the peace term Dissolve the Empire (from era IV). Every member is then a free realm and every imperial war aim ends. The Shogunate The houses Japan starts as the shogun's realm, with hold 30 (Weak). In 1378 the Southern Court still holds out against the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimitsu as a realm of its own, at war with him. Its fourteen great houses are its lords, each on its own land: Hosokawa, Hatakeyama, Shiba, Yamana, Ōuchi, Uesugi, Imagawa, Toki, Kyōgoku, Ōtomo, Shimazu, Takeda, Date and Nanbu. The rest is the shogun's own: Mie, where the Court sits in Kyoto, the three Nagasaki provinces and Ehime. What the Shogunate's hold counts each year: Hold : No house in revolt +3 Each house in revolt −5 No adult heir −10 At war while over half the houses are Wavering or worse −3 Each house summoned to the capital +1 The closed country +2 Confirming a house's land −5 Each season the houses read the hold: at Firm or Strong each grows a step more loyal, at Weak nothing happens, and at Hollow each grows a step less loyal. The shogun's actions - Summon a house (while hold is Firm or better): its lord lives at the capital, his wealth falls by a tenth each year and he cannot join a rising. The summons ends when you release him or when hold falls below Firm. - Confirm a house's land , once per house for each ruler: the house grows a step more loyal, for 5 hold. - Close the country (from era III, while hold is Firm or better): foreign traders may trade only at the one port you name and foreign faiths send no preachers in. It ends when you open the ports or when the Perry Expedition forces them open. The break At a season's end with hold 0, or as soon as the shogun loses Mie, the Shogunate breaks : each great house becomes its own warlord domain on its land, the shogun keeps only his own provinces, and the Ōnin War begins if it has not. The office of Shogun then stands vacant, and every warlord domain with its capital in Japan is a member. A member that holds Mie and owns, or holds as subjects, over half of Japan's 32 provinces can Ask the Court : it becomes the Shogunate at no cost, with hold 40, and every other member is asked to swear to the shogun . One that swears becomes his great house with its land, Wavering; one that refuses stays a realm, and the shogun holds the war aim Bring to heel on it. If you are asked, an answer card waits a month; silence is a refusal. What a member weighs before it swears: Reasons : Base (keeping its own realm) −10 Standing toward the shogun a quarter of it The shogun has more soldiers +10 for each multiple, at most +30 The shogun's hold (hold − 50) ÷ 5 The end The Shogunate ends when the shogun's realm leaves the shogunate form, by reform to a constitutional monarchy or by a revolution. Where you find it - Your Diplomacy tab has an Institutions row while you belong to one: "The Empire · Emperor: Bohemia · Hold 35 Weak · You: Elector". Tap it for the Empire card. - A member's country card shows a badge, Emperor, Elector or Empire, that opens the Empire card. - The Empire card has a header (the Emperor, the hold bar, your role) and four folds: Election (each seat and whom it would vote for today, the tally, Stand for the crown, a seat's reasons and Seek their vote), Reforms (the ladder with the passed reforms ticked, the next one's effect, its cost and today's forecast, Call the Diet for the Emperor, Vote yes and Vote no while the Diet sits, and Take to court once the Imperial Court has passed), Members (each member with its land, faith, seat and badges) and Hold (the year's gains and losses). - The Shogunate card has a header (the shogun, the hold bar, your role) and three folds: Houses (each great house with its lord, land, loyalty and Summon or Confirm , or each member realm while the office is vacant), The Court (who holds Mie, Ask the Court when you qualify, Close the country or Open the ports ) and Hold . While hold is Weak or lower it warns: "At hold 0 the houses break away". - News carries the call to defend a member, the election's vote, a sitting Diet, a court ruling against you and a request to swear to the shogun as answer cards. - The peace sheet offers Dissolve the Empire when you are at war with the Emperor, not a member, and it is era IV or later. - The Institutions map mode colours the Emperor and the shogun gold and the members light gold, marks the seats, hatches imperial land held by outsiders, and draws Japan by house while it is whole. - On a phone the card is a side sheet in the Wide layout and a bottom sheet in the Tall layout; every row and button is a full 44-point tap.
Map-and-Lenses: The map is home in Pocket Hegemony: you play on it, and cards and screens open over it. This page covers how the map is drawn, what you see at each of the three zoom levels, the map modes that recolour the world by one stat, the parchment over lands you have not charted, how the month plays back after End turn, how screens arrange themselves on phones, tablets, PCs and TVs, and the speed budgets that keep it all smooth on a phone. All of it is presentation only: what a map mode or an icon means is the rule of the system that owns that stat, and nothing the map does ever changes the simulation. How it works Drawing the map The map is drawn with WebGL2. The province id image (which place each pixel belongs to) is uploaded once, and each province's colour comes from a small lookup texture, so recolouring the whole world after a turn costs almost nothing. How a map pixel looks depends on how far you are zoomed in: Zoom How each map pixel is drawn Zoomed out The terrain's colour with hill shading, and the owner's colour washed over it. The sea is shaded by depth, with dithered edges between depth bands. Middle zoom 4 × 4 art pixels (half-size tiles) from the terrain tile atlas Close in 8 × 8 art pixels, with rounded coasts, sand and surf Nation borders are an ink line with a band of the owner's colour inside. Each tile type's average colour is its colour on the far map, so an artist who repaints a tile changes the far map too. Rivers are drawn as one clean line along their traced path. Labels, towns, armies and routes are painted on a separate overlay at the device's pixel ratio, from cached bitmaps, so text stays crisp. The map never unloads during a campaign, and exactly one map mode is active at a time. The three zoom levels There are three zoom levels: World , Region and Local ("Province" zoom in the Naval and Exploration and Colonies pages means Local). The map is at World zoom when zoomed out furthest, switches to Region at camera zoom 2 and to Local at 4. Local zoom is still the map, not a screen: the province's tile row is part of it. World zoom shows the big picture: - Each province's owner colour, with a small icon if it is hungry, rioting or in revolt, and front lines. - Armies as a banner with a men count, each standing on its own tile with its commander's banner and moving tile by tile as the week plays; battles as crossed swords with each side's men and a bar of men and morale left; besieged castles with a ring. Armies on the move are arrows, thick by men and coloured by owner, with no day counts. - Ports as anchor dots in the owner's colour, larger for great ports; fleets as a single ship sprite with a count. - The parchment, voyage paths as dotted lines, and colonies being founded as a small flag with a progress ring. - For diplomacy, only the map mode colours. Region zoom shows a province's life: - Sieges with their progress: how long the castle has held, its breaches, and the garrison and food left. - Town size, the castle and its reach rings, roads, rivers and the busiest trade paths (thicker means more traders), armies and sieges, burned provinces hatched, and plague. - Armies as sprites by troop type (foot, horse, guns) with a food bar on the banner showing days of reserve left; rumours as faded banners; the forage limit while you drag an army; and the full route of a selected army with day counts, month marks, food colour and step icons. - The harbour tile with an anchor icon showing berths used and free (for example 7/20 ), a slipway icon with hulls being built, and fleets with their admiral's banner and course line in days. - Each house of worship as a sprite in the town, preachers as walking figures, and active faith waves as a soft tint spreading from their source. - Envoys on the road as small riders with a dotted route, and the war-aim icon on countries you hold a war aim against. - Traders as icons (caravan, barge, ship) with a purse bar, and a coin on cities with a market. - Colonial range as a faint line on the sea, and colonisable provinces with a pale flag. Local zoom shows the province's tile row as pixel art: - Each tile's building as a sprite, burned tiles in ash, workers moving on busy tiles, ships in the harbour, caravans on the road and barges on the river. - Marching armies as columns of foot, horse, guns and wagons in proportion. - A battle is shown on the province's own tile row, and a siege as the castle tile with breaches drawn in the walls. Commanders, flags and portraits. Each army's commander stands on the map on foot, dressed in their country's flag colours, so a French commander wears blue and white and an English one red and white. Their kit follows the era: plate and sword at the start, halberd and morion from 1500, pistol and buff coat from 1600, then tricorne, sabre, revolver, rifle and field glasses. Their hair greys as they age. The figure stays the same size however far you zoom in. Their country's flag sits in front of their men count, on the same row, and their name shows below. Every country flies its own flag, without a pole: the one you know it by today where it still exists, otherwise its banner of the age. Portraits of commanders, officials and lords stand before their country's flag and show what they do: armour or uniform for a commander, the dress and tool of an official's post (a judge's red robe and gavel, a steward's keys, a tax collector's purse), and a fur mantle and coronet for a lord. Land provinces have no names on the map at any zoom, except each country's capital, so you can see whose capital it is. Every province's name shows on its name tab and card when you select it. Realm names and sea names stay. Realm names never cover each other: your own realm is named first, then the largest; a smaller realm's name moves to another of its provinces or shrinks to fit, and if there is still no room it shows when you zoom in. Route lines are a light dash over a dark outline, so they read on every colour. Every system added after the province and warfare designs has to state what it shows at each zoom, including its map mode. Close in: the living map Pinch in past the Local icons and the map stops showing icons and shows the world itself. There are three bands inside Local zoom: Camera zoom What you see 4 to under 16 The Local icons: settlement sprites, commander tokens, number plates 16 to under 40 The living map : towns, hamlets and roads on the land, armies as small figures, fleets as hulls, traders on their paths 40 to 96 Street level : the same at double detail, with single houses, people and soldiers Between zoom 14 and 16 the icons fade out as the living pieces fade in, so nothing pops. Map scale, not true scale. One map pixel is about 7 km, so at true scale a city would be smaller than a pixel. Close in, sizes show importance instead: a town covers more pixels the more town people it has (craftsmen, market folk, clergy, clerks and scholars), from 1 pixel for a village to 30 for the greatest cities. It grows from the province's land nearest its centre and only ever adds or loses pixels at its edge, once a month at most. The first 60 % of a town is its packed core, the rest its outskirts among fields. What stands in a town. A capital has a keep with its realm's flag; a fort rings the core with a palisade and a castle with stone walls and towers; a market shows its square; every town has its house of worship; a drill yard shows its yard; a coastal town or a harbour has docks with piers and ships at berth. Mines, quarries and lumber camps mark their own pixel, and the countryside has up to 6 hamlets (one per 40,000 country people). Roads join each town to its nearest neighbours' towns, the way the roads of the time ran: a few ways out of each town, with a town between two others carrying the road between them, keeping close to the straight line and winding only round hills, marsh and water. Most are worn footpaths; a cart road with ruts or a paved road appears where both provinces have built their road that far, and hamlets have tracks to the nearest town. Land no realm holds has no towns or roads until someone settles it. Towns take their culture's building style, and some great cities have their own landmark. Town buildings are drawn at twice the ground's art detail (16 × 16 art pixels per map pixel), so houses show their roofs, windows, doors and chimneys and a keep its towers, gate and flag. Armies, fleets and traders. An army is one figure per 1,000 men (one per 250 at street level), up to 12 (40), split between foot, horse, guns and wagons. It stands in ranks, marches in a column behind its banner along the roads, clashes front rank to front rank in battle and loses figures as it loses men, and rings a town it besieges. Rebels carry no banner. A fleet is one hull per 5 ships (one per ship at street level), sailing in a loose formation with a wake behind each hull. In port its hulls lie at berths along the town's waterfront, and any that find no free berth wait just offshore. In a sea battle the hulls turn to face the enemy, with powder smoke drifting off them. Each busy trade path you can see (one through your lands or on your own traders' loops) carries up to three caravans, barges or trading ships in the colours of the realm that sends them. They walk the path there and back with the game clock, keeping to their side of the way, and stand still while the game waits for you. Tap one of yours to open its card in the Trade tab; another realm's caravan gives way to the province beneath it. Reading the numbers. The living map is for seeing; the cards are for knowing. Every number stays in its card. Tap a town to open its province card, and a formation, fleet or caravan to open its own card; a tap goes to the piece first, then the province, and every piece has a tap box of at least 44 points. The Markers switch in the map mode menu brings back the number plates and names over every piece, and the siege marks and battle bars; the selected piece always shows its plate, name and route. The army list, the battle bar and the province's Garrison tab keep every number either way. Map detail. Low keeps the icons at every zoom (closest zoom 40). Medium, the phone default, has the living map but no street level. High has both. With Animations Off every figure stands still, and Reduced moves only marching and fighting armies. Map modes A map mode recolours the map by one stat. You pick it from the map mode picker, a small pop-over in the tool column. The map mode list brings together every system's map mode: Map mode What it colours Owner Food Food in each province Provinces Tax reaching you Tax that reaches your treasury Provinces Days to capital How far each province is from the capital Provinces Grievances Grievances in each province Provinces Faith Majority faith, hatched where another faith is 30 % or more; holy places carry a small icon Religion Language Language family at far zoom, language at region zoom; a toggle to same language, related or foreign colours for your realm; homelands of peoples without a country outlined Culture Ground Each province's ground Provinces Recruits Recruits Provinces Trade ratio Provinces by trade ratio, with the busiest roads and sea lanes as lines Trade Trade value Trade value Trade Traders Only your traders and their routes Trade Diplomacy Every country by your relation to it (see below) Diplomacy Sea Ports shaded by sailors who can still be called; fleets at sea; the month's winds as arrows; zones your ships can enter at current research Naval Works Building sites (green), neglected or damaged buildings (amber), ruined ones (red) Buildings Jobs Empty job slots against homeless people Buildings Subjects Your subjects by loyalty, with a line to each courted subject from the courting country's capital Subjects Revolution Provinces by how many of the revolution's province-level signs they meet; risen provinces hatched in the revolution's colour Revolutions Trade ratio and Trade value replace the older Traders passing and Trade balance map modes. The picker holds 22 map modes: Realms, Terrain, People, Wealth, Walls and Food, plus Tax reaching you, Days to capital, Grievances, Faith, Language, Ground, Recruits, Trade ratio, Trade value, Traders, Diplomacy, Sea, Works, Jobs, Subjects and Revolution. On a phone the picker scrolls. A system with no zoom plan of its own shows its map mode at every zoom and its card only at Local. Diplomacy map mode colours: Colour Means Your own colour You and your subjects Blue (light blue if pledged) Allies Green, pale green Close, Warm Grey Cool, or nothing recorded Orange Cold or Rival Red (hatched at war) Hostile, Bitter or at war Red border A league against you Ambition shimmer. While one of your national ambitions that names places is hot, the map shimmers faintly over the region it concerns, without outlining or naming the target. See National Strengths. Parchment over uncharted lands Land and sea your country has not charted lie under a drawn parchment . The parchment shows your charted map, which only ever grows; it replaces the old rule of showing everything within 6 steps of your lands and armies. Which places you have charted is decided by Exploration and Colonies. The Exploration map mode shows the same charted map with the parchment always on, empty coasts you could settle in green and colonies being founded in gold (see Exploration and Colonies). You can turn off "Hide unexplored lands" in the map mode menu to see the whole world. That switch is display only. It only changes what you see: it never lets you enter uncharted waters, and it is not the fog of war campaign rule. Watching the week The date in the top bar ticks one day at a time while the week plays, and shows the hour of each 4-hour step during one of your battles. While a turn is being worked out, the map stays visible: you can pan and zoom, armies march along their routes, and borders change as results arrive. If the turn takes longer than 1.5 seconds, a small parchment strip says what is being worked out, such as "The courts of Europe deliberate…". A turn is one week. When you end it, the week plays back on the map: armies walk their routes, and castles that stop an army ring red. While one of your battles is being fought, the playback slows to six 4-hour steps a day, about half a second each, and a battle bar shows every battle running. From the bar you can switch between battles, change your standing orders or retreat. The game never stops for a battle, and you cannot skip the playback while one of your battles is running; battles between other realms never slow it. See Time and Turns. Seasons The map shows the season. Lands north of latitude 50 and mountains turn white with snow in winter, wet climates turn green in the rainy months, and northern seas show ice while they are frozen. Sea ice is grey-blue with faint cracks, darker than the white snow on land, so you can tell frozen sea from snowy coast. It grows out from the coasts and the pole as the water cools and melts back in spring, in natural shapes with a soft, textured edge, not as whole sea zones turning white at once. A sea zone closes to fleets once most of it is frozen. The season colours stay readable in every colour vision mode, and there is no switch to turn them off. Layout by window shape Screens are laid out by the shape of the window , not by the device: Window shape Typical device Layout Short wide Phones in landscape (height under 500 CSS px) Map first; cards are side sheets on the left (45 % of the screen); the Realm book's six sections are one row of icons with names; the top bar is one thin row Tall Tablets in portrait, desktop windows taller than wide Cards are bottom sheets (55 % height, draggable); the Realm book's sections the same one row; the tool column on the right edge above End turn Large Tablets in landscape, desktop, Steam Deck (1280 × 800) Side sheets have a fixed width (380 px at UI scale 1); menus centred with a maximum width; nothing stretches edge to edge Far TV and Steam Machine The Large layout with the UI scaled up so body text is about 1/30 of the screen height, thicker focus frames, and nothing in the outer 5 % of the screen Phones play in landscape only , on every screen; a phone held upright shows "Turn your phone sideways". When a card is open on a phone in landscape, the map stays live on the right and is recentred so the selected thing isn't hidden. Every tap target is at least 44 × 44 points with 8 points between neighbours (56 with Large touch targets). End turn and the game menu button sit at opposite corners, and system safe areas stay clear of buttons. Map accessibility - Colour vision modes swap nation colours to a second assignment from the same 32-colour palette, chosen so neighbours stay distinguishable, and switch each map mode to a safe ramp (blue to orange instead of red to green). "No colour" uses greys with patterns. - Patterns on map modes add hatching, dots and stripes by band so every map mode reads without colour. - High contrast borders draw nation borders in black and white ink two art pixels wide. - Route food colours also carry a pattern (solid, dashed, dotted). Day counts stay at least 10 points tall at region zoom and hide rather than shrink when you zoom too far out. - Every map mode the tutorial teaches reads without telling colours apart; for example, hungry provinces also carry the hunger icon on the Food map mode. Staying smooth: performance budgets Budget Limit Panning and zooming 60 fps (16.7 ms a frame) Drawing the overlay at most 2.5 ms a frame on average, 5 ms at the 95th percentile Longest main-thread task while playing 50 ms Frames redrawn while something animates at least 90 % Engine turn, 5,000 provinces and 500 nations 25 ms Engine turn, 20,000 provinces and 2,000 nations 100 ms Worker's answer after End turn on the real map 250 ms Applying that answer on the main thread 16 ms (one frame) Slowest route plan, 5,000 / 20,000 provinces 8 ms / 32 ms To hold these: - The map canvas shades 1 pixel per CSS pixel, never device pixels; the overlay uses the device pixel ratio; close-up tile detail switches in by CSS zoom. - The draw loop never reads layout, takes text and sprites from cached bitmaps, and never plans routes or walks the province graph per frame. - The turn is simulated in the background (a Web Worker, or a Node worker on desktop); only without worker support does it run on the main thread. - The worker sends typed arrays and transfers them, never JSON of the world. Applying a turn updates textures and redraws once; panels re-render only what is open. - Budgets scale with the world, not the player: AI nations run in the same worker turn. - A change that breaks a budget fails the build ( pnpm bench , pnpm --filter @ph/client perf ). Targets are measured at the phone defaults and checked once with Battery saver on. - While nothing moves, the map does not redraw, whatever the frame cap. Performance knobs (in Settings): Knob Steps Sharpness Native (up to 3×), Balanced (up to 2×), Battery (1×) Frame rate cap 30, 60, 120 or the display's rate Map detail Low (no 8 × 8 close-in tiles, no surf, no forest blending), Medium (8 × 8 tiles, still water), High (everything) Animations Full, Reduced, Off (battle results as still frames); Reduced motion sets Reduced or lower Battery saver Caps the frame rate at 30, sets Sharpness to Battery, reduces animations, redraws only on change, and runs the AI turn with a smaller worker budget What you see - The map itself at World, Region and Local zoom, as described above. - The tool column with the map mode picker pop-over, and the map mode menu with the parchment switch and the Language toggle. - Weekly playback , slowed to 4-hour steps during your battles, and the parchment strip during long turns. - Cards as side sheets or bottom sheets depending on the window shape; "Turn your phone sideways" on an upright phone. Commands you give here never reach the engine: picking a map mode, zooming and panning, toggling the parchment, and skipping playback. Picking a map mode and crossing a zoom boundary are passed to Music and Sound (the map mode sound and the music's zoom mix), and the end of playback tells Screens and Navigation to show the turn report. Music-and-Sound: Every sound in Pocket Hegemony, music and effects alike, is synthesized live on PH-5, a small virtual 8-bit sound chip, from note data; the game ships no audio files. The music follows history: it changes with the era, sounds like your own corner of the world, swells when war comes and quiets in peace, and every track carries the same five-note Hegemony motif. Effects tell you what just happened without ever stepping on the music, and everything you hear also has something you can see, so the game is fully playable muted. How it works Original by design All music is original: no melody, track name or soundtrack structure from any other commercial game, no national anthems and no modern copyrighted songs. Public-domain folk tunes may inspire an idiom, but every melody is newly written. Every effect is synthesized too: no samples, no sound from another game, no recorded real-world audio, and no voices anywhere. The PH-5 chip Music voices (at most five at once): Voice What it is P1, P2 Pulse waves, duty 12.5, 25, 50 or 75 %, 16-step volume envelope, vibrato, pitch slide T A 4-bit stepped triangle, on or off only W A 32-sample 4-bit wavetable, swappable per pattern N Noise, long and short, with an envelope W2 A second wavetable for brass and string sections, allowed only in music era V Chords are faked with arpeggios, never played on one voice. Each track stores a tuning table (cents per scale degree), so neutral intervals, slendro, pelog, seven-equal and other tunings are possible. Allowed: pitch slides, vibrato, duty sweeps, volume envelopes, one short echo (a single tap of 60 to 250 ms, used sparingly) and pan up to 30 % off centre per voice. Not allowed: samples, reverb tails, more voices. Bass lines sit an octave higher than on a console, with the triangle's stepped shape kept, so they are heard on phone speakers that reproduce little below about 200 Hz. A gentle low-pass around 9 kHz smooths the master mix. In the game now: the music's soft voices. The first playtests found the strict chip harsh, "noise mostly" (Leroy, 17 Oct). So the music keeps the voices' roles, its tunes and the motif but plays them soft: the pulses and bass are rounded (their buzzing upper harmonics rolled off), volumes glide instead of stepping, a pad holds each bar's chord under the tune, the drums are tuned skins and a woodblock with only a breath of noise for the snare and cymbal, and a small hall gives the music some room. The effects below keep the chip's sound, which playtesters liked as it is. The tunes, rewritten. The tunes are written chord first: each bar has a chord, the tune lands on one of its notes on the beat, the bass walks the chord's root and fifth, and the regional instrument breaks the chord gently under it. Peace tunes use only chords that sound right in every region's tuning, so a nation's music changes colour, not into clashes. The early peace tune is a pastoral air followed by a dance, the late one a march, and every track still carries the Hegemony motif. Effect voices are a separate bank of three, so an effect never takes a music voice: Voice What it is S1 Pulse, the four duties, 16-step envelope, pitch sweep, arpeggio up to 4 steps S2 Noise, long and short, envelope, noise-pitch sweep S3 Stepped triangle, or any music wavetable, chosen per sound Each effect is a short program ticked 60 times a second, each tick setting pitch, volume, duty or noise mode per voice. Effects have their own bus and volume, the same 9 kHz low-pass and 30 % pan limit. Every effect is under 2 seconds (most under 300 ms), except ambience, with no reverb tails and the one-tap echo only for large sounds. Nothing important sits below 200 Hz: a cannon's thump comes from a noise burst and a fast pitch drop that starts high. The Hegemony motif Five notes: scale degrees 1, 5, 4, 5 and the octave above 1, long-short-short-long-long. Every track quotes it at least once. The title track states it plainly, and every age stinger ends on it. When you press End turn, the turn end chime plays notes 1 and 5; when the new turn is ready, turn ready answers with 4, 5 and the high 1. Music eras The era is taken from the game year (the calendar). A technology basis (the average of your three tech tracks) is kept in config but turned off. It reads the screen, the Realm book tab, the camera's region and zoom, and whether the app is in the foreground; your nation's culture group, war state and trend, armies near enemies, sieges, battles this turn, an occupied capital, your lords' loyalty, the share of provinces plotting or risen, and the treasury trend; and the world's year, active ages, periods and event chains with music tags, and how many great powers are at war. It holds one state at a time, chosen by the highest rule that holds: 1. Screen rules: title and main menu play title ; new campaign nation select ; loading load resume ; game over, campaign end and credits their own tracks; the battle screen war tracks; the siege screen war siege . Screens marked "unchanged" keep the current state. 2. Losing a war: war losing . 3. At war: world war , then war naval , war siege , war campaign , war mobilize . 4. Crisis: revolution , then crisis , then unrest . 5. Screen moods: diplomacy on the Realm book's Diplomacy section. 6. Good times: prosperity , exploration . 7. Peace rotation. Changing state. The director only decides at turn end or on a screen change. It waits for the next bar line (war, crisis) or phrase end (peace, at most 8 bars) and crossfades over one bar; layers also fade over one bar. A state is held at least 45 seconds, though even a one-turn war gets its stinger. Going down in priority (a war ends) plays the matching stinger, then 3 to 6 seconds of silence, then the new state from its intro. Going up (a war starts) cuts in at the next bar. Stingers play over the music, ducking it by 6 dB, or in the gap between tracks. A stinger is never a state. An event card plays its stinger and ducks the music without changing state. Peace rotation. Picks are weighted: your own palette 60 %, the era theme 20 %, the palette of the region the camera has looked at for 20 seconds at regional zoom 15 % ("you hear where you look", only at track changes), and a neighbour's palette 5 %. None of the last 3 tracks repeats. Each peace track plays 1 or 2 loops, then 10 to 40 seconds of silence. The era arrangement is chosen when a track starts. When the era changes, the next peace track is that era's theme in full, after the age stinger that caused the change. With variety set to "own palette only", only your palette is picked. Zoom mix. At world view the full arrangement plays; at local zoom percussion drops 3 dB and the lead comes forward 1 dB. Over a battle province in wartime at local zoom, war campaign 's third layer comes in even between battles. On the battle screen at normal speed, sounds follow the order of a bell (orders, shooting, charges, melee, breaking), one per step from the sector nearest the screen centre, other sectors only if a voice is free. Skipping ahead plays only battle start , battle rout and the music stinger. Ambience Ambience is off by default. There is no weather, but in winter months the plain and forest beds are windier. Ambience may fill the silences between peace tracks. Many things at once - Turn results. When a new turn is shown, at most 5 effects play, 150 ms apart: first what happened to your armies, castles or ruler (highest priority first), then what is in view. Everything else is shown silently. With five or more notifications in a turn, notify batch plays instead. - Voice stealing. A new sound with no free voice takes the voice of the lowest-priority sound playing, if that is lower than its own; otherwise it is dropped. - Cooldowns. The same sound does not restart within its cooldown: 50 ms by default, 40 ms for scroll ticks, 20 ms for sliders, 2 s for alerts, 5 s for unrest. - Variation. Repeating sounds vary by up to a semitone and a new noise seed, except sounds whose pitch carries meaning. - Position. A map sound is panned by its screen position up to 30 %, gets quieter toward the edge (0.4 at the edge) and is muted off screen. Notifications always play centred and are never muted. - Zoom. At world zoom only notifications play from the map; at regional zoom also army orders, battle starts, siege breaches, sea battle starts and map sounds; at local zoom everything. Mixing with the music - While a stinger plays, effects of priority 3 to 5 are dropped and priority 1 and 2 are ducked 4 dB. - Effects duck the music only for six sounds ( battle start , siege breach , siege storm , realm rising , realm ruler dies , sea battle start ), by 4 dB for their length. No other sound ducks it, however long. - Ambience ducks 6 dB under any priority 1 or 2 effect and fades out over 2 s when a music track starts. - The game menu leaves the music as it is. - While several of your battles run at once, you hear the battle sounds of the one on screen; switching battles switches the sounds. - A ui tap sits about 6 dB below the music's average, a priority 1 sound peaks about 3 dB above it, and the whole mix aims at −16 LUFS. - Several achievements in one turn play ui achievement once. Platform behaviour - PH-5 runs in an AudioWorklet at the device's sample rate, fed by a main-thread scheduler about 100 ms ahead. If the worklet cannot start, the same voices are built from standard oscillators and a looping noise buffer. - Music and effects together stay under 2 % of one core on a mid-range phone. - Audio starts on the first tap; the title's "Tap to start" is that tap. A mobile cold start has a silent splash and the first sound is frame start ; desktop and Steam play frame logo . - In the background, or with the tab hidden, sound is suspended, and it resumes with load resume . Notifications that arrived while you were away play no sound. - On iPhone the game uses the "ambient" audio session: it mixes with your other audio apps and respects the silent switch; effects follow the same session as music. On desktop, "Play in background" (off by default) keeps the sound going when the window is hidden; on the web it always pauses. - Interface sounds start within one audio block of the tap (about 3 ms) by a direct message to the worklet; map and battle sounds go through the scheduler so they line up with animation. - Haptics on phones (on by default, never on desktop, working with sound off): all light: ui error , turn ready , battle start , siege breach , and realm ruler dies once. The Sound card The speaker button in the side tools, under the map mode and your commanders, opens the Sound card: what is playing now and why (for example "Mobilizing: war has been declared, the armies gather"), the volume, music on or off with its volume, the effects volume, and button sounds on or off. The speaker shows struck through while music is off, so you can tell without opening it. Sound starts with your first tap, as browsers and phones require, and your choices stay on the device. In this first cut the game plays the title theme, two peace tunes for each half of the eras in your palette's own tuning and timbre, prosperity, diplomacy, mobilizing, campaign (whose layers join as your armies close on the enemy and fight), siege, a losing war, unrest and crisis, with stingers for war declared, battles won and lost, and wars won and lost. Turns chime at their end and start (the full motif at a new year), taps click, and marches, levies, battles, sieges, famine and unrest each have a sound. Accessibility - Every sound has a visual partner (a toast, an icon flash or an animation), so the game is fully playable muted. - Sound captions show off-screen sounds as a small caption at the screen edge toward where they came from ("Battle at Troyes" with crossed swords). Off by default, they turn on by themselves when you turn sound off. - Mono turns pan off. - Rising and falling pairs (gain and loss) differ by rhythm or timbre as well as pitch. - Reduced intensity removes the echo, softens priority 1 sounds by 4 dB, and turns off the machine-gun stutter and sharp attacks. Care - Palettes describe musical features, not ethnic stereotypes, and never use a "generic exotic" scale shared across unrelated traditions. Each palette's tracks are reviewed by a musician or scholar of that tradition before release and credited. - Colonized peoples are never written as an "enemy" or "primitive" side, and Indigenous and African palettes get the same development across all five eras as European ones. - A narrative-only event gets no stinger at all. - A peace with neither gain nor loss plays no stinger. - Tutorial steps play ui hint when they appear and ui confirm when done, and a new warning plays notify alert ; none of them lowers the music. - Plunder, razing, massacres, enslavement and narrative-only events never get coins, chimes, fanfares or any rising, rewarding sound (at most realm fire or a single low bell), and plunder adds gold silently. - Colonial conquest has no distinct "victory" sound, and Indigenous and African arms sound by era and type with the same quality as anyone's. - Era VII machine guns, shells and gas sound at a distance without exaggeration: no screams, no wounded, no speech or crowds anywhere. "Shout" sounds are pulse sweeps. How it is made Tracks are written as MML text, one file per track, in packages/rules/data/music/tracks/ , compiled to JSON (patterns, order list, loop point, layers, era variants). Sounds are text blocks in packages/rules/data/audio/sfx/<group .sfx , compiled by the same step. The build checks the voice budget, range per voice, loop length, that the motif appears and that every id the director names exists; for sounds it fails on more than three voices, 2 seconds or longer (ambience exempt), a missing named sound, a missing era variant a troop type needs, a ui sound of 10 ms or less, or a sound with no visual partner named. Every number the director and mixer use lives in music.yaml and sfx.yaml , so balancing needs no code. Events can carry music: and sfx: tags, and a bindings table maps game events to sound ids. Tools: /music.html lists every track with any palette, era variant and layer toggled and live voice use, plus an Effects tab with every sound and a "busy turn" button that fires 40 battle results at once; a render script bounces any track or sound to WAV; and the diagnostics line shows the current music state, track, layer and why it was chosen, and the last five effects with which were dropped and why. The music is written in-house by Claude in MML. Each track ships with a rendered MP3 that Leroy approves by ear before it goes into the game; a failing track is reworked, not shipped. If the first milestone's tracks fail that gate, an outside chiptune composer is commissioned for the title theme and the motif only. National-Strengths: Every playable country has a heritage: what it is good at because of where and what it is, what it becomes good at when its moment in history comes, what it secretly wants, what it has achieved, and what holds it back. Heritage is small on purpose. It fits on one card of at most five rows, and every line changes something you can count somewhere else in the game: gold, officials, lords, recruits, horses, ships, scholars, traders, buildings or grievances. How it works The five parts Part What it is Birthright The one always-on strength that comes from who the country is Golden age A strength tied to one historical age, active while that age is running and its condition holds Ambitions Hidden goals drawn from the country's own pool Legacies Permanent strengths you earned Weakness Something from history that holds you back until you overcome it Venice is a good example. Its birthright "Lagoon and Arsenal" makes galleys build 30 % faster, the capital's garrison 40 % stronger and ports raise 15 % more sailors. In the Age of Gunpowder Empires its golden age "The mude to Alexandria" can be active. It has the weakness "The feared lion", has three active ambitions, and starts with no legacies. Heritage is the game's own system; it uses no mechanic, name or value from another game. Birthright Every country with heritage has exactly one birthright of its own. A birthright can name a needs condition. While that condition fails, the birthright goes dormant: it is shown greyed out and does nothing, and it wakes again as soon as the condition holds. A birthright is never deleted because you lost a war. Golden ages A golden age belongs to one age of the historical events system, and a country has up to 3. Each golden age moves through four states: State When Waiting Its age has not begun Active Its age is running and its start condition holds Inactive Its age is running but the condition fails; years already served are kept Ended Its age ended or its ends condition held; this is for good Portugal's golden age "Carreira da Índia" belongs to the Age of Exploration and begins when Portugal has an Atlantic harbour and knows invention S4. If Portugal loses its Atlantic harbours it becomes inactive, keeping its years. Because golden ages follow the ages as they actually happen in your campaign, an early Atlantic crossing that starts the Age of Atlantic Empires early lets Atlantic golden ages begin early too. Marks. A golden age that was active for 25 years in total leaves a mark when it ends: a permanent legacy worth a third of the golden age, which counts toward the 5 legacies. Carreira da Índia active for 24 years leaves nothing; at 25 years it leaves the mark "Cape charts". A golden age with no mark written for it leaves its first lever at a third of its value, so a golden age with +15 tax reach leaves a legacy of +5. At most 2 golden ages can be active at once. If a third would begin, you are asked which one becomes inactive. Ambitions Each country has a pool of 4 to 7 ambitions (at least 5 for hand-written countries, at least 4 for generated ones). When the campaign starts, 3 are drawn as your active ambitions, and at least one of them is tagged historical. Castile, with a pool of 6 of which 2 are historical, gets 3 drawn with at least one historical among them. If a drawn ambition's goal already holds on the first day, it is put back and another is drawn: no free wins. Ambitions stay hidden. While an ambition is open, its plain goal is never shown. State What you see Hidden Only its theme icon (land, sea, trade, faith, crown, learning, survival or wealth) and a one-line riddle hint, such as Venice's "The Visconti line is ending; the river is a border only by habit." Hinted Its hint condition held, so it is revealed. The hint is still the only words shown, but now you also see its warmth, the name of the legacy it promises and its deadline, if it has one Done The goal holds. You get the legacy, the plain goal is shown for the first time, and a new ambition is drawn Lost The deadline passed or the fail condition held. No penalty: the plain goal is shown as what might have been, and a new ambition is drawn When Portugal holds Calicut, its ambition "Beyond the Cape of Storms" is done and grants the legacy "Estado da Índia". If its window ends in 1560, the ambition is lost when 1561 begins. Warmth is the share of the goal's conditions that currently hold, shown in three bands: cold (under a third), warm (from a third to under two thirds) and hot (two thirds or more). A count condition counts as partly met by how far it has come: a goal of 12 markets with 8 built is two thirds met. A goal that is a single yes-or-no condition goes from cold straight to done. Goal conditions Holding Warmth 3 0 cold 3 1 warm 3 2 warm 3 3 done 4 3 hot Counsel. Once every 10 years you can pay gold to reveal one ambition at once and see its warmth. Its words stay a hint. The price rises by era: Era I II III IV V VI VII Gold 30 50 80 120 180 260 380 Envoys. A country that keeps a resident envoy at a foreign court for 2 years learns the hint and warmth of one of that country's active ambitions, never its plain goal. Milan with an envoy at Venice's court learns one of Venice's. The computer can do the same to you. Age ambitions. Some pool entries name an age; they join the pool when that age begins. History mode. A campaign setting chooses "Drawn" (the default) or "Historical only", which draws only historical ambitions. No setting reveals ambitions. The tutorial teaches ambitions with one ambition whose hint is plain. Legacies Legacies are permanent, and come three ways: an ambition's reward, a golden age's mark, or a turned weakness. Great legacies, the rewards for the hardest goals, get a bigger budget. A country keeps at most 5 legacies; if you would earn a sixth, you are asked which one to let go. Weakness A country has no weakness or one. A weakness has negative points and a condition to overcome it. When that condition holds, the weakness goes and its turned legacy is granted in its place. A weakness can never be bought off: only its condition or a reform event overcomes it. Levers Every heritage effect is a lever: one named effect that changes one rule in the system that owns it by a value. A strength usually pulls one to three levers. Each lever has a unit, a cost in points per unit, its parameters, the design that owns its rule, and whether higher or lower is better. Unit Meaning pct A percent change relative to the base rule steps Whole steps on a ladder the owning design defines count Whole things flag A rule switched on, or access granted There are 64 levers in 13 groups: Group Levers Example cost Treasury (6) tax reach, trade balance, toll gold, loan interest, tribute, loot tax reach 0.1 per % Economy (1) ware output (all wares cost triple) 0.06 Food (5) harvest steps, herd growth, fish, store rot, castle reach rings harvest 1.2 per step People (3) growth, migrants, class slots growth 0.1 Rule (12) official wage, official type, official years to full, official capacity, lord capacity, lord loyalty start, lord loyalty shield, retinue, grievance shield, days to capital, integration years, homeland resistance grievance shield 1.5 (flag) Army (13) recruit refill, troop cap share, levy free months, break point, hits, horses, march days, forage, siege, garrison, hired company cost, commander style, commander skill troop cap share 2.0 per point Navy (5) ship build, crew, ship hits, sea days, storm loss storm loss 0.03 Trade (3) trader count, trader gain, traders passing trader count 1.0 Learning (5) invention cost, scholar output, school seats, spread discount cap, invention known invention known 1.5 (flag) Belief (2) faith shift, language shift 0.05 Abroad (4) envoy count, opinion steps, oath fade, lands taken envoy count 1.2 Building (2) building cost, building unlock building unlock 1.5 (flag) Events (3) event weight, event option, stat stat: by the stat's points Ten levers are provisional because the design that owns their rule is still being written: tribute, official capacity, lord capacity, ship build, crew, sea days, faith shift, language shift, envoy count and opinion steps. The trade levers follow the trade design: trade balance and traders passing raise the trade ratio gain, trader gain raises each deposit, and trader count gives extra traders at the start. Building levers use the buildings design's buildings, and a unique building variant is unlocked the same way. Their owner may rename them or point them at a rule; only the key changes in heritage data. A lever can be limited to a scope with where : realm, capital, coast, core, royal, lords, frontier, a terrain, a culture group, a faith, an area or a region. A limited lever costs less. Conditions Heritage uses the event tree's condition language unchanged, with this meaning the heritage's own country, and adds a few of its own: Condition Meaning knows An invention is known holds place Owns the province holding a named place coastal Owns a province with a harbour on the named sea, or any sea count A counted country-card stat, which can be building:<id and can be relative to the start ("start 2", "start+3") heritage An item is awake , done , lost , shed or held (the data's state names) independent Has no overlord relation {who: A, other: B, type: T} reads as "A is the T of B". Each place name used by holds place is bound once to a map province. Budgets Each part has a budget in points (a point is about a tenth more of something central, for the whole realm). Part Budget Birthright 3.0 Golden age 3.0 Legacy 2.0 Great legacy 3.0 Weakness −2.0 Smaller countries get a size bonus on their birthright and golden ages. Size class is the mean of six catalogue assessments (economic strength, manpower potential, military capability, naval capability, diplomatic influence, trade access), each from very low (1) to very high (5). Size class Bonus 4.5 or more none 3.5 or more +0.5 2.5 or more +1.0 1.5 or more +1.5 below 1.5 +2.0 A scoped lever's cost is multiplied by its scope factor: a single where limit (capital, coast, core, royal, lords, frontier, terrain, culture, faith or region) 0.5, one named area or place 0.25, a terrain or sea parameter 0.5. Factors multiply but never go below 0.25. Ware output without a named ware costs triple, and the stat lever costs by stat: legitimacy 0.1, stability 1.0, prestige 1.0, notoriety 0.5, admin capacity 0.1, literacy 0.2, cohesion 0.1. The build totals every part of every country and reports any part outside its budget by more than 0.6. Who gets what Group Count Heritage Tier A playable countries and subjects 58 Hand-written: birthright, 2 or 3 golden ages, 5 to 7 ambitions, weakness Tier B and C playable countries and subjects 434 Generated from archetypes Decentralised polities 214 Generated from archetypes for societies without a crown Background actors, non-state actors, internal estates, collective institutions 257 None (not played) Generated heritage comes from 27 archetypes. Each has detection rules on catalogue fields and templates for the birthright, golden age and weakness, written in the country's own words. The game scores every generated country against all archetypes: the best gives the birthright and weakness, the second best may add a golden age. A generated golden age gets the first allowed age whose regions cover the country, with percentages scaled to the budget. Ambitions are filled from the catalogue record: likely rivals become "outlast" goals, preferred partners "bind or ally", disputed territories and key locations "hold a place", possible future paths a historical path, and trade routes "win a trade hub". Decentralised polities only take the crownless archetypes (forest, hill, herding, steppe, desert, island, mountain, ocean, chiefdom, commune, raiders, segmentary). A hand-written file overrides whatever generated parts it defines. The current build has 706 countries with heritage (58 hand-written, 648 generated), 3,551 ambitions, 945 golden ages and 706 weaknesses, with 0 errors, 0 warnings, 273 place names to bind (most bind to the map's nearest land province by their name; the rest are bound by hand), and all 64 levers in use. When countries change hands - Annexation. The annexed country's birthright becomes a dormant claim of the annexer. Once the annexer has owned its old capital and held most of its homeland for 30 years, the claim wakes as a second birthright. A country holds at most 2 birthrights. - Subjects keep their whole heritage, and an overlord's legacies never apply to its subjects. - Released countries get their catalogue heritage, or their archetype's generated heritage if they are not in the catalogue. - Formed countries (a union, or a new state made by an event) keep the forming country's birthright and legacies, add the formed country's own heritage if any, and draw ambitions from both pools. Events Heritage proposes four effects and one condition to the event tree. grant legacy grants a legacy; wake heyday makes a golden age active for a number of years even if its condition fails; stir ambition reveals an ambition, keeping its words a hint; shed burden overcomes the weakness. The heritage condition lets events ask about heritage, and the event weight and event option levers raise an event's weight or open an option for the country. The computer The computer always knows its own ambitions and treats them as goals with weight 1.5 next to its personality priorities. When it completes one, it gets the legacy just as you would. Golden ages give it a reason to change course across the centuries. It can read your ambitions through a resident envoy kept 2 years at your court. When a third golden age would begin or a sixth legacy arrives, it lets the weakest one go (the one worth the fewest points). What you see - In the game today. Every realm's card has a Heritage line on its General tab, naming its birthright and its weakness. Tap it, or the Heritage tab, to see the birthright, each golden age with the age it belongs to, and the weakness; tap any of them for its full text and history note. Under them, In 1378 shows how the chronicles judge the realm at the start: Strength (economy, manpower, army, navy, trade, standing abroad), Government (reach of rule, finances, stability, institutions, cohesion, prospects) and Dangers (unrest, threat from outside), each as five steps with a word, with a question mark where the chronicles are unsure. The tab is there for every realm, also before you pick one. 110 of the 137 realms on the map have heritage; the rest say none is recorded yet. Ambitions, legacies and golden ages beginning follow when heritage is checked each turn. - The country card gets one Heritage row: the birthright icon, the active golden age icon, three hidden ambition icons and the weakness icon. Tapping it opens the Heritage sheet. - The heritage card shows five rows, never more: Birthright, Golden age, Ambitions, Weakness and Legacies ("none yet" when empty). Tapping a row shows its full text, its history note and what it changes. A dormant birthright is greyed. - Reveal moments. When a hidden ambition is revealed or warmth rises from warm to hot, a small quiet animation plays and one line goes into the monthly digest. - Map shimmer. While an ambition that names places or areas is hot, the map shimmers faintly over its region, without outlining or naming the target. - The nation picker shows each country's birthright and weakness, a count of hidden ambitions, and its golden ages as the ages they belong to. - Every country has the same system in every tier; the free tier only limits which countries you can pick. How it connects - Historical events: ages drive golden ages; heritage uses the condition language and proposes four effects and a condition. - The 1378 start: catalogue fields, tiers, size assessments, personality and places feed generation. - Your realm: levers on treasury, officials, lords, loyalty, recruits, horses and envoys. - Provinces: levers on tax reach, harvests, growth, class slots, official types and grievances. - Warfare: levers on troop cap, break point, marching, sieges, garrisons and commanders. - Recruiting: recruit refill and retinues. - Research: invention levers, and invention ids for knows . - Trade: trader levers, trade presence and hubs. - Naval: ship build, crew and sea days (provisional). - Buildings: building cost and unlock levers; unique variants and landmarks offered as hooks. - Government: official and lord capacity; reforms that overcome weaknesses. - Religion and Culture: faith and language shift. - Diplomacy: envoys, annexation and release; envoy and opinion levers. - Subjects: tribute; subjects keep their heritage. - Revolutions: reforms and revolutions can overcome weaknesses or grant legacies. - Achievements: suggested achievements for every ambition of a country and for 5 legacies. - Screens and navigation: heritage row and sheet, nation picker, digest lines. - Map and Map Modes: the shimmer over hot ambitions; place names bound to provinces. - Settings: the history mode setting. - Tutorial and help: the tutorial ambition with a plain hint. - How a turn works: dates, eras for counsel gold, and years counted. Each turn Heritage is checked once a turn (a week), right after historical events, and counts time in months by the date: a month is counted in the turn in which a new month begins, 12 months make a year, so a golden age needs 300 active months (25 years) to leave its mark. In order, heritage checks dormant claims and birthright needs; golden ages, counting a month active, granting marks and resolving a third beginning; ambitions, warmth, deadlines and draws, with digest lines; whether the weakness is overcome and a sixth legacy; then publishes its active levers to the systems that own them for the next month. Naval: Naval is how your realm gets ships to sea and keeps them there. Ships need ports, and ports need sailors: you muster sailors from a port's people at a shipyard, order ships there and they are laid down once their crew is in port, put an official in command as admiral, and then keep the fleet paid, supplied and repaired while it sails with the winds. The size of your fleet is always tied to the seafaring people you can put aboard. How it works Ports A port is a province with a harbour on a shore tile. Only a port can give berths, and only a port with a shipyard can muster sailors and build ships (other than small craft). The shipyard is built from the province's Build tab once it has a harbour; it stands with the harbour and takes no slot of its own. A coastal province without a harbour is a plain shore : seafolk fish from the beach, small craft can be launched and armies can land, but no ship can be bought, berthed or crewed there. Any realm can make a new port by building a harbour on a shore tile it holds. Harbour step Berths What it allows 1 Harbour 10 recruiting sailors, buying, resupply 2 Port 25 also refit and hiring foreign crews 3 Great port 50 also coaling for steamships and later ships Shipyard step Slipways Builds 1 Slipway yard 1 galleys, and faster, every hull that needs no slipway 2 Shipyard 2 also carracks, armed carracks, galleons, turtle ships and fluyts 3 Naval dockyard 2 also ships of the line, then ironclads and later hulls 4 Venetian Arsenal 3 builds as a naval dockyard from the start Each ship takes one berth ; a ship of the line or larger takes two. Galleys, cogs and small craft can be drawn up on the beach in a port, taking no berth but rotting at the anchorage rate. Ships beyond a port's berths ride at the anchorage , where they can resupply but not refit, and rot and face storms as if at sea. A lighthouse halves storm losses in its sea zone. Ships crewed in port at a naval base cost upkeep and food but no wages. A harbour burned in a raid or sacked with the town falls a step, and one whose slots are under half filled goes fallow with half its berths. A shipyard that is burned, has no timber in reach or has its slots under half filled stops its slipways. Ports at the start. The port list holds 317 historical port towns (32 great ports, 110 ports, 162 small harbours and 13 canoe landings, 53 with a shipyard). Each is placed into the province under it, or the nearest coastal province within about 80 km. In the 1378 start each town takes its holder of 20 September 1378, and a town whose holder doesn't own that coast on the start day is left out. Each province takes the highest tier among its towns and a shipyard if any town had one. At the start a great port gets harbour 2; a port gets harbour 2, or harbour 1 where the town is smaller than the market town harbour 2 needs; a small harbour gets harbour 1; and a canoe landing (the trading towns of the Americas, Atlantic Africa and Mozambique) gets no harbour, extra seafolk and small craft only. A shipyard starts at step 1, or step 2 where its holder knows S4 Carrack and caravel, and Venice has the Arsenal. Melos and Malé fall on no land of the current map and wait until the map gains small islands. Sailors Sailors are people, counted one by one. Recruiting turns people of a port province into sailors; each leaves their class and their home slot stays empty until released. Every sailor counts the same toward a crew. Recruiting sailors. Recruit sailors is offered on a port, or on the country card for several ports at once, with one slider, only for provinces with a harbour. Of a province's fighting-age men (a quarter of its people), a muster can call 2 in 3 of the seafolk, 1 in 3 of the homeless and 1 in 20 of every other class, each class by its share. Sailors come from the same people as the levy, so a man at sea can't be levied and the levy pool shows the sailors already gone. A muster pays a bounty of 0.05 gold a sailor, lowers the province's fish for the seafolk away, and has the sailors ready in that port after 14 days. The muster queue. Sailors come in batches of 50, each batch two weeks after the one before, like the recruit queue on the Garrison tab: a crew of 200 takes eight weeks. A port holds at most 10 batches on their way, and the last one can be taken off the queue with its bounty and men back. Waiting in port. Each sailor in port eats 1 ration a month from the province store and is paid 0.1 gold. After 6 months with no ship being built for them, 1 in 10 drift back to their slots each month. Recruiting at Lagos. Lagos has 4,600 seafolk and 1,150 fighting-age men, of whom about 770 can go to sea. Portugal recruits 75 sailors: it pays 4 gold of bounty, Lagos loses 5 % of its fish while they serve, and the 75 are sailors in port at Lagos when they are ready. Each month they eat 75 rations from the Lagos store and cost 7.5 gold in wages. Other sources: - Foreign crews : at harbour 2 or better you can hire sailors from a seafaring people whose ships call there. They arrive as sailors in that port, cost twice the wage and leave when unpaid. - Lords : a loyal lord with a port recruits his own sailors by the same rules and brings his ships when called; his ships and crews stay his. - Prisoners : a captured ship's sailors can be taken into service; 1 in 4 desert at the first port friendly to them. - Pressing : with S9 Line-of-battle tactics you can take seafolk men in a port without the bounty, giving the province the Pressed grievance for a year. Sailors move by road to another of your ports at levy marching pace, eating on the way, or aboard any ship with room as passengers. When a crew is paid off (a ship laid up or a fleet disbanded) its sailors walk home and refill the emptiest slots of their own province, and come back homeless where others have filled those slots. What going to sea gives and takes: - A province whose men have served 2 years or more at sea gets +10 % fish and +10 % traders by sea for 10 years. - A fifth of the wages of sailors in port is spent in that port as trade for its market folk. - While sailors are away their fishery, harbour or shipyard slots stay empty; a fishery under half filled is fallow with no fish. Recruiting the seafolk a shipyard needs stops its slipways. - A province that loses more than a tenth of its seafolk at sea within 5 years has fewer births for 10 years and the Lost at sea grievance for 2 years. Buying ships To order a ship you need a port with a shipyard of the step the hull needs, and its gold, paid when you order. The ship joins the port's ship queue (at most 5 waiting). The first ship waiting is laid down on a free slipway as soon as its whole crew waits in port; the crew is assigned to the hull and helps build it alongside the shipyard's own seafolk, and the ships behind it wait their turn. So you can order first and muster after: the Port tab's Muster N for the waiting ships calls exactly the crews still missing. The last ship waiting can be taken off the queue for its gold back. The upgrade path. A port offers only the types your realm has unlocked in the S branch (and the exploration unlock for exploration ships) that its shipyard can build, and only the newest on each path: trade goes cog (junk or dhow by sea), carrack, fluyt, steamer; war goes galley (or war canoe fleet), armed carrack, galleon, ship of the line, and the turtle ship gives way to the ship of the line. An older type disappears once a newer one can be built in that port; a smaller yard that can't build the newer one keeps offering the older. A line under the list names the next types and what they need. At Lagos, with 60 sailors in port, a free slipway at shipyard step 2 and S4 known, Portugal orders a carrack: it pays 60 gold and 12 timber at once, the 60 sailors are assigned to the hull, and Lagos has 0 sailors in port. With only 20 sailors the carrack waits in the queue until 40 more come in. Every type belongs to one family , which sets its supply: trade and military ships carry 15 zones, galleys 6, and exploration ships 60 plus a hold of colony stores. Fleets and ships Ships at sea or ready to sail are grouped into fleets of one admiral and any number of ships. A fleet sails at the pace of its slowest ship and enters only zones every ship may enter. Each ship keeps its crew, hull, supply and age. The hull goes sound, worn, leaking, wrecked. It drops a step for battle hits, every 6 months at sea, in storms, and from rot while laid up or in port. A worn ship sails as normal; a leaking ship sails at half speed and loses a step in each storm; a wrecked ship can only limp to the nearest port and sinks at the next storm. In a berth that allows refit, a worn hull is made sound in a month and a leaking one in 3 months, twice as fast with a shipyard. A ship short of crew fights in proportion to its crew share and needs more days per zone (100 of 200 is half strength and twice the days). Below a quarter of its crew it can't leave port. Admirals A fleet of warships or troop carriers can't leave port without a leader (an admiral, a commodore or a viceroy, see Fleets at sea), though such ships can still defend the port in its own zone. Trade ships sail with no admiral on the routes trade gives them. An official is commissioned as admiral by the same act as an army commander in Recruiting: he leaves the province he ran (left, another official moved in, a deputy named or the lord next door asked) and returns to a province of your choice when released. Years served in a port province count double. A large fleet can have up to two vice-admirals , officials or lords, each leading part of the line. An admiral takes the realm's current sea style.
