Rui Vaz is a customs officer who ran the port province of Lagos for 9 years. Commissioned as admiral, his 9 years in a port count as 18, so he starts with Might 0, Cunning 5 and Logistics 1, and is offered the trait Careful. Others can lead a fleet too: the ruler or an heir (if lost at sea or captured, a succession crisis), a lord (his own ships, or the realm's if loyal; a proud lord won't sail under an official admiral), a hired privateer or corsair for a season (leaves when unpaid, may raid neutral shipping and drag you into a war), or in realms with no officials a chief or elder. Keeping ships State Crew Costs Hull loses a step At sea full, paid 0.2 gold a month each upkeep, supply used every 6 months In port, crewed full, paid 0.1 gold and 1 ration a month each from the port's province upkeep every 3 years Laid up none a tenth of upkeep every 2 years Laying a ship up releases its crew. Fitting it out again needs its crew as sailors in that port and takes a month. A ship left laid up for 10 years is wrecked. Docking. A fleet can dock in ports of your realm, your lords, your subjects and your allies (resupply paid in food), of countries you are not at war with and not rivals (resupply paid in gold), and not in ports of an enemy or a rival. Each zone of supply refilled costs per ship crew ÷ 10 rations of the province's food in a friendly port, or crew ÷ 100 gold to the port's owner in a neutral one. Resupply fills every ship in one day, only as far as the province's food goes. Hulls are refitted only in a berth at harbour 2 or better or at any shipyard, at the upkeep cost in friendly ports and 1.5 times that elsewhere. Supply at sea. A ship uses 1 supply for every zone it sails, and while holding one zone (blockading, hunting, waiting) 1 supply every step-days. Only exploration ships enter uncharted zones, and their colony stores (caravel 300 rations, voyaging canoe 100) are kept apart from supply and loaded when docking. A ship out of supply loses 1 in 10 of its crew for each zone it sails and fights at no more than half strength until it docks. Sailing Fleets are movers on the same map and clock as armies (see Troop-Movement); they may enter sea zones and port provinces through their harbour. Coastal zones are about 150 km across, ocean zones about 300 km. Ship Days per coastal zone Days per ocean zone Galley 1 not allowed Small craft and war canoes 1 2 (S3 only) Cog, junk, dhow 2 3 Caravel 1.5 2 Carrack, armed carrack, galleon, turtle ship 2 2 Ship of the line 2 2 Steamships and later 1 1 - Reach : without S1 Magnetic compass and sea charts, ships keep to coastal zones; with S1 they can go up to 3 ocean zones from a coast; with S5 Ocean navigation, any ocean zone. Galleys never enter ocean zones. Junks and dhows count as ocean-going in their own monsoon seas from the start (T5 Monsoon sailing calendars). - Winds : each sea has a wind calendar by month. Sailing with the wind halves days per zone; against it doubles them. Steamships ignore wind. - Storms come in each zone's storm season, as warfare sets. - Ice : Baltic and White Sea zones freeze in winter; no fleet may enter, and a fleet caught there is iced into the nearest port. - Carrying an army : its food reserve counts as loads, each horse as the room of 4 men and each gun as 20. An army carried by small craft keeps to coastal zones and never passes an enemy war fleet. Against an enemy at sea Sea battles are fought over time, in rounds of 4 hours. While one of your fleets is in a battle, time slows to six 4-hour steps a day, so other fleets can sail in and join. You can't skip a battle, but you can watch it, change its orders or retreat at any step, and switch between battles running at once. Battles between computer players never slow the game. Each round follows warfare's bell rules on at most 3 sectors. On top of them: - Each ship fights with the share of its crew aboard. - When an admiral gives a Close order or a galley rams, its soldiers aboard fight the enemy ship's crew and soldiers by the land bell rules on a single sector, and the ship whose defenders break is taken. - A ship taken, or one that strikes to a stronger fleet in a hunt, becomes the winner's if a prize crew of at least a quarter of its crew is put aboard from the fleet; otherwise it is burned. Its own crew become prisoners or prize crew. - When a ship sinks, a third of its crew swim ashore or are picked up by the winner as prisoners, and the rest drown. - An enemy fleet at war lying still in a port's zone blockades the port (see Fleets at sea). An army that takes a port province's castle takes every ship there that has not sailed and the hulls on its slipways. Pirates. Each pirate coast in config (the wokou in the East China Sea, Barbary and Aegean corsairs, the Orang Laut in the Malacca strait, the Caribbean later) has a pirate fleet with no country, hunting trade ships in its home zones and one zone beyond. Each season in which trade ships passed and no warship hunted there, it gains a ship; ships taken or sunk are removed. Burning its base ends the fleet until trade brings it back. Where a pirate people is also a catalogue record (wokou, Orang Laut), the same fleet can belong to a lord or be hired. The computer players Sea powers (Venice, Genoa, Portugal, the Hanse towns, Hormuz, Malacca, Ryukyu) keep a quarter of their seafolk at sea, buy trade ships first and warships when a rival's fleet grows. Land powers lay up their few ships in peace and fit them out when a war starts across water. Every AI keeps a customs officer in each great port it holds, so it has admirals to commission. AI fleets plan with the same zone graph and wind calendar. A peaceful AI fleet more than 10 zones from the player's realm and ports runs no fleet AI; its voyage is resolved as a day count. Fleets move once a day using a cached shortest path per ship class, research step and month, recomputed only when research or a port changes. Each day and each month Each day of the day loop (7 days a turn) fleets take their step and use supply, and storms, ice, docking and resupply happen on their day; a battle starts on its day and runs in 4-hour steps until one side is beaten or retreats. Each month, in the turn in which the month begins: pay wages and upkeep and feed sailors (unpaid crews desert and foreign crews leave); sailors waiting over 6 months drift home; hulls advance and finished ships launch; rot, the 10-year wreck and refits apply; a fifth of in-port wages is spent in the port; province effects update. Each season pirate fleets grow or stay. Each year ships age and admirals may gain Logistics. What you see - World zoom : ports as anchor dots in the owner's colour (larger for great ports); fleets as one ship sprite with a count. - Region zoom : berths used and free, slipways with hulls building, fleets with the admiral's banner and course line in days. - The port card (province zoom): sailors in port, berths, slipways, ships by state, and the Recruit sailors and Buy ship commands. - The Sea map mode : ports shaded by sailors who can still be called, fleets at sea, the month's winds, and the zones a fleet can enter. - The recruiting preview : who is taken by class, the bounty, fish lost and when they are ready. In the game now The first slice of ships is playable: - Port tab. Tap a coastal province of yours and open its Port tab: its harbour and shipyard, berths and slipways, sailors ready, on their way and still callable. Recruit 30, 100 or 300 calls sailors from the levy pool, ready in two weeks. Order a ship lists every ship the yard can build with its gold, crew, months, fights and carries, or why it can't yet (crew not in port, no slipway, an invention). A hull on the slipway is launched into the port's fleet when its months are up. - Fleets on the map. Every fleet shows as a ship in its realm's colours with its ship count, in its sea zone or just off its port. Tap one of yours to choose it, then tap a sea zone, a port or a shore: it sets sail at once along a dotted course. Tap it again to open its card. - Fleet card. Where it is, Sail, its admiral (a fleet needs one to sail: appoint a commander waiting at court), the army aboard, every ship with its crew, hull and supply, Part off , Join another fleet here and Lay up . - Carrying armies. An army standing in a port shows Board ships ; aboard, it stands off the map and moves with its ships. Sail to a shore you may march into and it lands there; sail into a friend's port and it goes ashore. - Sea battles. Enemy fleets in one zone fight round by round, every four hours, until one side has lost half its strength; the loser's ships take a hull step and it runs for port. The battle is said over the map with Go there. - Navy tab. Your realm card's Navy tab is the overview: ships, sailors, the month's cost, battles, every fleet and every port. The cost is also the Ships and sailors line of the Treasury. - The AI keeps one ship for every two ports (at most four), puts a commander at their head, and at war hunts enemy fleets it outnumbers near by. - Starting fleets. The realms that had ships at the start start with them: one fleet in their best port, by how strong a sea power they were (very low none, low a transport, moderate a warship and a transport, high 3 warships and 2 transports, very high 6 and 3). Warships are galleys where the port has a shipyard, transports its sea's cog, junk or dhow. Venice, Genoa, Aragon, Portugal and Naples start with real fleets; the Americas, with canoes and rafts, start with none. A starting fleet has no admiral: appoint one before it sails. - Hired fleets. The Navy tab's Hired fleets line opens the Hire a fleet screen. Free fleets gather in the seas their people sailed (Genoese galley masters, Basque shipmasters, Hanseatic peace ships, Barbary and Aegean corsairs, Dalmatian ship-owners, Japanese sea clans, Fujian traders, the Orang Laut, Gujarati and Malabar ship-owners); four are for hire at once and some move on each month. Sea powers at peace with everyone also lend an idle fleet of their own; the gold goes to them, and they call it home if they go to war. Each card shows the ships, what they fight and carry, the captain, the port it would reach and the days, and its pay. A hired fleet sails at once for your nearest port under its own captain, costs three times its ships' upkeep and wages a month (a lent fleet twice), keeps its ships together, and leaves when you dismiss it or can't pay. At war and outgunned at sea, the AI hires one too. Prices are the design's scaled to the game's treasury (ships ×0.1, wages ×0.01), and timber is bought in, so any shipyard can build. Winds, storms and piracy come in later slices. Fleets at sea These rules come from Leroy's afternoon playtest of 18 October. Sailing tile by tile. A fleet stands on one water tile of its sea zone. In port it lies at the port's anchorage, the water tile beside the port. A voyage is still planned zone by zone, with the same winds, reach, charts and ice. When you give the order, the fleet plans its whole course over the water tiles at once, as an army plans its march: the shortest way through the zones of its voyage to the spot you tapped, the port it puts into or the shore where its army lands. It never cuts across land from one zone's centre to the next; where a strait is too narrow for the map's tiles, like the Bosporus, it passes through it. Each zone still takes as many days as it always did, spread over the course's tiles in that zone, and the ship sails a little every few hours. So it glides along the coast as the days pass instead of jumping. You can tap any spot of the sea and the fleet sails to that spot, with its whole course drawn through the water and the days to sail at its end. Choosing a fleet. A fleet takes taps as an army does. Its tap box is at least 44 points, fitted to its ship or hulls. Where it overlaps an army, such as a fleet in port beside the town's army, the one nearer your finger is chosen. With a fleet chosen, tapping one of your armies chooses that army instead of sailing. Sighting range. Enemy fleets meet only when they are in the same sea zone, just as armies only meet in the same province. Even then they must come within sight of each other. A fleet sees 20 tiles, plus 1 tile for each point of its leader's Cunning, up to 30 tiles. Armies see only 10 to 15. Choose a fleet and its sighting ring shows on the map. A fleet that comes within range of a sea battle in its zone joins its side. The battle is fought where the defender stands. Fleets in port, fleets running for port after a defeat and fleets of realms not at war never meet. Three posts. Every fleet leader holds one of three posts. You pick it on the fleet card with three buttons in one row, and you can change it at any time for free. When you appoint a leader, the game picks the post that fits the fleet: commodore for trade ships only, viceroy for exploration ships only, otherwise admiral. Any of the three lets warships and troop ships leave port. Post For What he does Admiral war His Might and Cunning count in full in sea battles. Commodore trade Your trade ships pass enemy blockades in the zone where his fleet lies. Your ports beside that zone gain trade ratio 25 % faster. A blockade he holds takes 1.5 times the prize money. His Might counts half in battle. Viceroy exploration and colonies His fleet charts two rings of sea zones around it instead of one. A colony founded from his fleet starts 10 points ahead. His Might counts half in battle. Blockades. A blockade needs no order. A fleet blockades when its realm is at war, it has at least one warship and a leader, and it lies still in a sea zone: not sailing, not landing an army, not fighting and not running for port. It closes every coastal province beside its zone held by a realm at war with it. A closed port gains no trade ratio, and its Port tab says who blockades it. The enemy's trade ships may not sail through the zone. They go round it or wait, and one caught there loses its purse to you as a prize. A commodore of their own lying in the zone takes them through. Prize money. Each month you take half of each closed port's sea trade for the month: its value to ships times its trade ratio. A port worth 20 gold a month to ships at a trade ratio of 40 pays you 4 gold, or 6 gold under a commodore. The fleet card says it plainly: "Blockading 3 ports of Castile: about 4 gold a month in prizes". Blockades also wear the enemy down. Each closed port counts half as much as an occupied province when they weigh making peace. Where to see it. You hear when your fleet starts a blockade and when an enemy closes your ports. Your Navy tab lists the blockades you hold and the ones you suffer, with their ports and prize money, and the month's prize money. On the map a closed port wears a chain mark in the blockader's colour. How the open points were settled - Recruiting sailors takes every class by its share, not seafolk first: from 770 seafolk, 45 homeless and 15 others, 300 sailors are 278 seafolk, 16 homeless and 6 others. The bounty is 0.05 gold a sailor (75 sailors cost 4 gold), the sailors are ready after 14 days, and the province loses fish in proportion to the seafolk away out of the third of its seafolk who fish. - Admirals : commissioning costs 10 gold and the admiral is paid three times his wage at sea. Years an official served in a port province count double, with the usual +1 at 5 and 10 years. A colonial governor cannot be made an admiral. Women can be admirals where the country's history allows women commanders. - Battle damage : a ship that takes hits and stays afloat loses one hull step; hits equal to its strength sink it. Repairs happen at harbour step 2 or a shipyard. - Storms : in storm season each ship at sea has a 1 in 20 chance a month to be struck, less with a good admiral's Logistics and halved next to a lighthouse. A struck ship loses a hull step, and a wrecked one sinks. - Trade ships : the caravel cannot trade; trading ships pay their normal upkeep. - Ships of the line need S9 and a step 3 shipyard (which needs S10), or the Arsenal. - Harbour step 3 only adds coaling and berths; ocean ships don't need it. A naval base saves wages only while ships are in port. A half-crewed ship takes twice the days. - Small craft count as trade ships with 15 days of supply and can be built on any shore with seafolk. Canoe landings start with 100 extra seafolk and 5 small craft. - Junks and dhows may cross their own monsoon seas (the Indian Ocean seas, the South China Sea and the Java Sea) once their realm knows T5, which its home regions know from the start. - Foreign crews : a port can hire up to 100 sailors a year from realms whose trade ships call there. - Pirates : each pirate fleet starts with 2 ships, a season lasts 3 months, and each pirate coast has one base province (Algiers for the Barbary corsairs). Burning it ends the fleet until trade brings it back. - Sea-power AIs keep a quarter of the seafolk they can call at sea. - Frozen seas : from December to March the Gulf of Bothnia, the White Sea and the far northern seas freeze. No fleet can enter them, and their ports can neither launch nor take in ships until spring. - Docking works in ports of realms at peace and not rivals. In a subject's or lord's port, food comes from that province's store and nothing is owed. - Later ships (ironclads, dreadnoughts, submarines and aircraft carriers) have first-guess numbers. Many naval numbers are first guesses and will be tuned. Still open Nothing in the rules. Balancing is a tuning pass on the numbers. Provinces: The province is where your realm actually lives. Gold is taxed here, food grows here, recruits are raised here, lords and officials govern here, and armies burn it. Each province is a row of 4 to 16 tiles with real people working real buildings, and every number on its card is something you can count or point at, with a list of how you gain it and how you lose it. Your country card is mostly the sum of your provinces. How it works The principles - Everything is countable. Tiles, buildings, workers, men, days. There are no abstract levels or meters. - Every stat explains itself. Tap any line on the province card and you get its gain and lose list, so you can always see why a number moved. - One config file. All rates and limits (jobs per building, food per worker, ground tables, slots per town size, toll effects, grievance thresholds) live in one province config file. Every number on this page is a placeholder until balanced. Our running example: Troyes in 1444 (on the 1444 checkpoint world) Troyes is a royal province of France, 3 days from Paris, on farmland with 12 tiles: four farms, one burned field, two ranches, a lumber camp, a second woods tile with no building, a fishery, the castle and the town. It has 72,000 people, a tax collector of 6 years, and Duke Philip of Burgundy as a pretender. We will come back to it throughout this page. Tiles A province is a row of tiles : 4 for the smallest province on the map, 16 for the largest. Each tile has one use , and most uses can hold one building: Use How it changes Fields Turned to pasture in one season. Left unworked 10 years, they grow back into woods. Salted or overgrazed, they become waste. Pasture Ploughed back into fields. Lost to drought and overgrazing (becomes waste). Grassland, savanna and steppe provinces start with many. Woods Cleared into fields in 3 years for gold, giving one load of timber. Gained by fields growing back and, later, replanting; lost by clearing, cutting timber faster than it regrows, and fire. Marsh Drained into fields with Polder drainage . Floods and dykes broken in war turn tiles into marsh. Waste Irrigated into fields with Qanat and canal irrigation . Shore 1 to 3 tiles, only for provinces on a coast, lake or navigable river. Never lost, but a blockade or a silted harbour stops their buildings working. Town Every settled province has one. At 40,000 townsfolk the town takes a second tile, built over fields, and a great city a third. If the town shrinks below a tile's limit, that tile goes back to fields. Castle Placed on any land tile except the Town; that tile stops producing. A destroyed castle leaves waste for 5 years, then fields. Tile states. A tile can have at most one state at a time: State Cause Effect Ends Burned An army forages or loots, you burn your own fields (scorched earth), raiders raid, or rebels act Its building is wrecked, it gives nothing, its workers become refugees or die With people and peace, one burned tile is rebuilt a year, faster with gold Fallow A building has fewer than half its workers Works not at all Enough workers return Worn Fields farmed for decades with more people than needed and no rotation inventions; overgrazed pasture; later, mines and factories Half output Five years without use. Three-field rotation , Fodder crops and Four-field rotation make wearing rarer War damage is shown as burned tiles, never as a meter. Ground Each province has one ground , taken from the World Map's terrain. It sets the starting tile mix and how troops fight, how buildings work and how people work without buildings. Ground and the economy (build cost, building output, output of people working without a building): Ground Build cost Building output People output Farmland 100 % +25 % 100 % Grassland 100 % 100 % +50 % herding Savanna 100 % 100 % +25 % herding Drylands 125 % −25 % until irrigated 100 % Desert 150 % −50 % except mines and irrigation works 100 % herding and caravans Hills 125 % 100 % (mines +25 %) 100 % Mountains 200 % farms −50 %, mines +50 % −25 % Forest 150 % 100 % (lumber +50 %) +25 % hunting and gathering Jungle 200 % −25 % +25 % gathering Marsh 200 % −50 % until drained +25 % fishing Tundra 150 % −50 % 100 % herding Buildings in the province Buildings owns the full building rules; here is how they sit in a province. - Every building stands on a tile, and the castle is a building too. Each land tile holds at most one building. - Each building has job slots for one class. With all slots filled it works fully, with fewer people in proportion, and below half it is fallow. - Buildings are gained by building them (cost times the ground's build cost), by conquest, by events, and some appear by themselves. They are lost when their tile burns, when the town is sacked, when upkeep goes unpaid, when demolished by you or a peace treaty, or when their tile changes use. - A tile with no building still has slots for up to 3,000 people of the matching class, working at the ground's people output. - Mines show the years of digging left in their ore deposit. Ore deposits are gained by prospecting events and mining inventions and lost every year the mine is dug. A mine that runs out closes; its miners overflow into other slots or become homeless, and the town shrinks. - Shipyards and mines need timber from a lumber camp in the same province or within reach (one ring, more with roads and rivers). Without timber no ships are built. - The Town tile has building slots by town size: Town size Hamlet Village Market town Town City Great city Building slots 1 2 4 6 9 12 - An almshouse shelters 3,000 homeless, who then stop counting toward theft, the Homeless grievance and shanty camps, at a cost in gold upkeep and clergy. - While a town has a market, homeless people and the raw ware nearby, craft buildings now and then appear by themselves. Craftsmen fleeing persecution abroad may found one too. Job slots per building (people, with their families): farm 12,000; rice paddy 18,000; terrace, raised fields and plantation 12,000; ranch and horse stud 3,000; lumber camp 1,500; mine 6,000; irrigation works 1,500; fishery 3,000; saltworks 1,500; harbour 1,500; shipyard 3,000; loom house, forge, kiln and tannery 1,500; press 900; brewery or winery 900; market 1,500; caravanserai or warehouse 900; house of worship 600; seat 300 plus the official; almshouse 600; powder mill 900; hospital, wells and drains 600; factory 6,000; rail station 600. Food The province's harvest is the sum of its food tiles. Each gives: people in its slots × food per person × the ground's output × the harvest roll × inventions. Food tile People fed per worker Rolls a harvest? Farm, terrace, raised fields 1.5 Yes Rice paddy 1.5, two harvests (rolled twice) Yes Ranch 1.33 No: drought and hard winter events instead Fishery 1.33 No: storms and blockades instead Empty fields, woods, pasture 0.67 × the ground's people output Fields yes; woods and pasture no Harvest roll Bumper Good Normal Poor Failed Food × 1.3 1.15 1 0.7 0.3 Three-field rotation , Fodder crops , Seed drill and Four-field rotation each make the harvest one step better. With Maize, potato and cassava , a failed harvest becomes poor. Troyes, a normal year: - 4 farms × 12,000 farmers × 1.5 × 1.25 (farmland) = 90,000 fed - 2 ranches × 3,000 herders × 1.33 = 8,000 fed - 1 fishery × 3,000 seafolk × 1.33 = 4,000 fed - The second woods tile has no building: 3,000 woodsmen hunt and gather, 3,000 × 0.67 = 2,000 fed. The burned field gives nothing. - Total: about 104,000 fed , for 72,000 eaters. A good year in Troyes feeds the castle; a failed one, with a field burned, leaves Troyes hungry. Burn two more fields and it can't feed itself. Wares Every non-food ware is made by the people in a building's slots × the ground's building output × inventions. Craft buildings that turn raw wares into finished ones add value: wool into cloth is worth three times as much. Wares made fall with burned and fallow tiles, plague killing workers, missing inputs (a forge without iron stops) and a mine running out. The ware list lives in config: grain, rice, wine, olive oil, wool, cloth, flax, linen, silk, cotton, salt, fish, timber, furs, hides, leather, horses, iron, tools, arms, copper, tin, silver, gold, gems, spices, pepper, sugar, tea, coffee, cocoa, tobacco, incense, ivory, pottery, porcelain, dyes, paper, books, saltpetre and powder; later eras add coal, rubber and oil. Enslaved people are never a ware. People: births, deaths and famine Each month every class gains births and loses deaths from yearly base rates: Class Births a year Deaths a year Land classes 4.0 % 3.0 % Miners 3.5 % 4.0 % Craftsmen, market folk, clerks 3.0 % 3.5 % Clergy 0.5 % where clergy don't marry, otherwise as townsfolk 3.0 % Scholars 1.0 % 3.0 % Homeless 4.0 % 5.0 % Birth rate goes up with a food store above 6 months (+0.5) and 10 years of peace in the province (+0.5), and down with a store under 3 months (−1), the Hungry grievance (−2), war in the province (−1), plague (−1) and, in later eras, in towns by era. Death rate goes up with plague (+5 % at rumour, +15 % at outbreak, +30 % at its worst), war in the province (+1 %), each burned tile (+0.5 %), fever land for people born elsewhere, and smoke (+1 % for town classes). It goes down with hospitals, wells and drains (−0.5 % in town) and with sanitation and vaccination (each −0.5 %). Troyes, with 72,000 people, well fed and at peace, has about 2,800 births and 2,200 deaths a year, so it grows by about 600 a year until the food runs short. Famine. Each season the province compares the food it has (its share of the harvest, its local store and castle deliveries) with the people who must eat. If there is enough, everyone eats and the rest goes to the store. If not, the people the food can't feed die that season, spread over the classes by size, except that a quarter of them flee as refugees if a neighbouring province has food. If Troyes has food for 64,000 one season, 8,000 can't be fed: 2,000 flee to Sens, which has food to spare, and 6,000 die. With no fed neighbour, all 8,000 die. A year's famine never kills more than a fifth of a province, so even two failed harvests in a row kill at most about a third of its people; past that the unfed go hungry instead. Classes and job slots Every person belongs to one class, and each class works in certain slots: Class Their slots are in Farmers Farms, rice paddies, terraces, raised fields, plantations, irrigation works, empty fields Herders Ranches, horse studs, empty pasture Woodsmen Lumber camps, empty woods Miners Mines, saltworks Seafolk Fisheries, harbours, shipyards, empty shore; fleet crews are raised from them Craftsmen Loom houses, forges, kilns, tanneries, presses, breweries, factories, rail stations Market folk Markets, caravanserais, warehouses Clergy Houses of worship, almshouses, hospitals Clerks Seats Scholars Schools Homeless No slots How people move: - Newborns join their parents' class the month they are born. - When a class has more people than slots, the extra move to the class whose slots are least filled (lowest share filled), ties going to food classes first. This is overflow . - Overflow never goes into scholars or soldiers. Scholars only come from graduating students, and soldiers only from raised recruits. - When every slot in the province is full, overflow becomes homeless . - When a slot opens (a new building, deaths, plague, a levy), homeless people move into it first. - Each month a share of the homeless moves to the neighbouring province with the least-filled slots, in your own realm first. - A class with fewer people than slots leaves them empty until overflow arrives. In Troyes the farms are full. A new loom house opens 1,500 craftsman slots, now the least filled. The 3,600 homeless move in first: 1,500 become weavers and 2,100 stay homeless. From then on the farmers' extra people overflow into whichever slots are emptiest, or join the homeless. Countryfolk and townsfolk are shown, not stored. Town size comes from townsfolk, and townsfolk grow no food. Homeless Homeless people eat from the local store, make nothing, pay no tax, and die at 5 % a year. They come from overflow with every slot full, burned tiles, buildings closing, and soldiers and refugees returning with no slot free. They leave through new slots, rebuilt tiles, almshouses, levies, settlers sent to a colony or a frontier with free tiles, and drift to neighbours or abroad. Homeless share Effect Over 5 % Theft: for every 5 % homeless, 5 % less tax reaches you and 5 % fewer traders pass Over 10 % The Homeless grievance Over 20 % (shanty camps) Homeless counts as two; plague starts here first and spreads twice as fast; town classes die 1 % faster; each year a town building may burn Rebels muster from the province's recruits, like any levy. Other people - People is everyone in the province, summed over classes. - Refugees shelter outside the classes, eat without working at first, go home when it is safe, and after 2 years settle and overflow into slots (or become homeless). Fleeing craftsmen and scholars keep their class if a slot is free. If 2,000 refugees from Troyes shelter in Sens, they go home once Troyes is safe. - Faith and language mix store the top three of each; the country's Faith and Language percentages are their people-weighted sums. Persecution makes people flee and take their faith and crafts elsewhere. See Religion and Culture. Recruits, students and scholars - Each year the province adds to recruits here a share of every class except clergy and scholars, more from homeless men. Recruits of royal provinces go to the ruler; a lord's go to his retinue. Raised recruits leave their class slots; soldiers who come home rejoin as homeless and overflow. - While recruits are below a quarter of the pool, the province has the Conscription grievance, ending when refilled to half. - Local recruits fill local school seats first, then the realm's. Students are lost by graduating, being called to arms, plague and the school being sacked. - Scholars are gained by graduation and by foreign scholars settling in towns with schools and peace, and lost by old age, war here, persecution and a richer neighbour hiring them. See Research and Recruiting. Tolls The owner sets a toll rate of none, low or high on each toll point : a bridge, ford, pass, river mouth or strait. A free-trade charter sets it to none. Tolls count as trade income; see Trade. Tax Each province has its own tax rate : none, light, normal, heavy or crushing. It defaults to the realm default set on the Tax screen and can be overridden per province. Presets such as Even , Spare the frontier , Squeeze the towns and War chest fill in every rate at once. - Tax owed is the gold the province owes each year at its rate, from the value of what its buildings make and its townsfolk. It falls with burned and fallow tiles, homeless people, and riots (half). - Reaches you is the part that arrives: half without an official, half kept by a lord, a share lost for every day of travel beyond 5, less with enemy armies on the road, and nothing while occupied. - In a lord's province, the rate is what you demand from the lord. He keeps half of what is collected either way, and a heavy or crushing demand makes him waver. - Riots or rebels may force the rate down, and a tax cap charter keeps it at light or below. - A heavy rate gives the Heavy taxes grievance; crushing counts as two. Troyes, at normal tax, owes 11 gold a year and all 11 reach you: it is 3 days from Paris and its official is a full-strength tax collector. Tax is paid a twelfth each month. Each day of travel beyond 5 loses 5 % of it, a tax collector makes up to 20 % back, and you never get more than the province owes. Roads, rivers and days to capital - Each province has one road step : track, road, paved road, turnpike, railway. Each step is unlocked by an invention and built for gold × the ground's build cost. Roads are lost by neglect without upkeep, fighting and floods. - A navigable river is fixed and shown as shore tiles; canals add one ( Grand canals , Canal locks ), and a wrecked canal or silting removes it. River provinces count one ring closer for castle food spread. - Days to capital is the travel time to the capital or nearest seat by the fastest road, river or sea route, longer in winter, with enemy armies, broken roads or a sea route closed in war. Above a limit (for example 30 days), the province has Far from the throne . Who owns and governs it - Owner : gained by conquest, inheritance, purchase, a lord joining with his land or a colony; lost by losing a war, a lord defecting, rebels breaking away or ceding it. - Governed by one of: Governed by Effect An official Full tax and recruits, plus the effect of his type A lord Half tax; recruits go to his retinue; run by his own officials No one Half of everything, and the Ungoverned grievance A subject ruler See Subjects Occupied Tax, recruits, food and trade go to the occupier - When a lord's line dies out, his province returns to royal and needs an official. - Officials at work. Who governs a province is the first thing on its card. Each official's type helps the province he runs: a tax collector brings in more tax, a steward more food from the harvest, a muster master refills recruits faster, a customs officer adds trade, a warden makes the garrison harder to storm, a judge keeps riots down. He gives half his effect in his first year and all of it after 5 years there, shown as five pips. The country card's Officials tab lists every official with his post, province, effect and years; open one and Move to another province lists your royal provinces, the best fit for his type first, to swap him with the official there or move him into an empty post. Whoever moves starts again at half. A lord's officials serve the lord: you can't move or commission them. - Occupied : while an enemy holds the castle, or holds a province with no castle for a season. Months of occupation are counted. - Years held counts years since this owner gained it. The longer it is held, the faster language and faith shift and the faster Foreign rule fades. - Homeland of : set at start from the catalogue; a people gains it by making up most of the province for 100 years and loses it after being gone 100 years. A homeland held by a ruler of another language has Foreign rule , and separatist events start there. - Pretenders are gained by inheritance and marriage, by losing the province in war (the old ruler keeps a right for 50 years) and by buying a title; lost by death without heirs, renouncing in a peace, marrying into your house, and time. Officials Every official has a type and runs one province ; a seat needs one of its own. He gives half his effect in his first year in a province, rising to full after 5 years there. Moving him starts him again at half: a tax collector of 6 years moved from Troyes to Rouen is back to half. Type Effect in his province Tax collector +20 % of tax owed reaches you Steward +10 % food from the tiles; local store rots half as fast Judge Riots need one grievance more; Broken charter fades twice as fast Master of works Buildings and roads 25 % cheaper and twice as fast; burned tiles rebuilt twice as fast Muster master Recruits refill 25 % faster Customs officer +15 % trade gains Chaplain Faith mix moves twice as fast toward the ruler's faith Schoolmaster Language mix moves twice as fast toward the ruler's language; students graduate a year sooner Warden Garrison fights 25 % better; walls repair twice as fast; castle store rots half as fast Colonial governor No effect of his own: founds a colony, then becomes its ordinary official. Needs a colonial governor slot and doesn't count against the officials cap while holding one Officials are gained by hiring one of a chosen type (gold up front, wages yearly; a foreign specialist costs more), by school graduates (a madrasa gives judges and chaplains, a university judges and stewards, an academy masters of works and wardens), and by a lord's line dying out. They are lost to old age and death, dismissal, unpaid wages, being killed when rebels or an enemy take their province, and a richer neighbour hiring them away. Your country card's Officials count is the sum of your officials. Filling posts without the busywork. With Auto-fill posts on (the switch at the top of the Officials tab, on in a new campaign), the crown fills its empty royal posts at the start of each month, most people first, each with the best fit for the province: a judge where it riots or plots, a steward where the store holds under a month of food, a warden where walls face an enemy at war, a customs officer where at least 3 traders passed last month, and otherwise a tax collector. It hires at home when someone of that type already serves in one of your royal posts, else a foreign specialist, and always keeps 20 gold back and stays under your officials cap. Land you take is filled straight away and doesn't hold up End turn. All the hires of a month come as one line of news. Every AI realm fills its posts the same way. Turn it off and empty posts wait for you, and new land waits for a decision before the turn ends. Fill all fills every empty post at once by the same choices. An empty post's screen puts the best fit first as a single Hire button, above the officials who could move in and the full list of types. An official's screen offers Replace with the best fit (when he isn't it) and Dismiss , which asks once more before he leaves your service. A commissioned official whose post was filled while he was away takes another empty post when released, or waits until one opens. Lords in the province - A lord always holds at least one province; someone with no land is a courtier . A lord who loses his last province stays at court as a courtier who can be granted land again, or, if you took it by force, flees abroad and becomes a pretender to it. - A lord hires and pays his own officials from his wealth. A lord's province with none of his officials pays him half and has Ungoverned . - You can lend a lord one of your officials: it costs your wage and wins his loyalty, and the official works for him until called back. - Lords spend their own wealth on buildings by their traits: Builder the most, Greedy markets and mines, Pious houses of worship, Warlike castles. - If you pay for a building in a lord's province, it is his, and his loyalty rises one step (unless he is in revolt). When a lord's land comes back to you, its buildings come with it. More on lords in Your Realm. Charters The ruler may grant a charter to one province or town: Charter Gain Cost Market charter A market that can grow into a yearly fair A little gold Tax cap Tax rate no higher than light Tax from it Town law Townsfolk run the town; it needs no official Nothing may be seized there without breaking it No quartering No armies winter there Winter quarters there Faith tolerance Its minority faith worships openly Clergy lords' loyalty; Wrong faith ends there Free trade No tolls Toll gold Mining right A merchant house runs the mine, digging faster and finding new ore deposits Half the mine's output Charters are granted, demanded by lords and towns for loyalty or a loan, or forced by rebels. Revoking one gives Broken charter for 20 years, and every lord notices. A conqueror may keep or revoke the charters of a province he takes. Defence - Castle : none, earthwork ring fort, stone castle, bastion fort or star fort. Gained by building or upgrading (gold × build cost, and years) or conquest; lost by siege, demolition in a peace, or one step per 10 years without upkeep. An enemy must besiege it to take the province; on hills or mountains it is far harder to take; on a shore tile it can be supplied by sea. - Walls : whole or with 1 to 3 breaches. Repaired with gold and months; breached by siege guns, mining and earthquakes. Each breach shortens a siege and allows an assault. - Garrison : soldiers inside, counted from the army. A castle with no garrison falls at once. - The Garrison tab : the province card lists the troops in the province without a commander (by thousand, troop type and drill), levies still gathering with the days left, and the commanders here who can pick them up. Freshly raised levies wait here and man the castle until a commander takes them. See Warfare for sieges. Grievances and rebels There is no anger meter. A province has a list of grievances , each a named cause you can point at and fix: Grievance Starts when Ends when Heavy taxes The rate is heavy (crushing counts as two) The rate drops; a tax cap charter Hungry Local food store under 1 month Above 3 months for a full season Homeless Homeless over a tenth of the people (two above a fifth) New buildings, an almshouse, people leaving or sent as settlers Soldiers quartered Any army stays more than a season It leaves; a no-quartering charter Burned homes Any burned tile All tiles rebuilt Conscription Recruits below a quarter of the pool Refilled to half Foreign rule A homeland held by a ruler of another language Enough years held; a lord of the local language; the majority changes Wrong faith Most people don't share the ruler's faith Conversion; a faith tolerance charter Ungoverned No official (a royal province without yours, or a lord's without his) An official is assigned Harsh lord The lord is Cruel or Greedy, or hostile to the people's faith or language The lord changes Broken charter A charter revoked in the last 20 years Time Far from the throne Days to capital above the limit A seat nearby; roads; moving the capital Plague An outbreak here It burns out Bloodshed A rising of the same faith or language was massacred in the last 20 years Time Requisitioned An army, yours or anyone's, takes food from the store A season after the last taking Neighbour in revolt A neighbouring province has rebels with a grievance this one shares Those rebels are beaten or satisfied Grievances Mood 0 or 1 Calm 2 Grumbling: growth slows; scholars and craftsmen start to leave 3 Riots: tax and recruits halved; traders avoid it; the lord wavers 4 or more Rebels: a share of the recruits take up arms each month under a named leader, with a demand from their biggest grievance Under a judge, riots need one grievance more. Rebels are gained from four or more grievances, a disloyal lord raising his retinue, a pretender landing, or foreign gold. They melt away when beaten, when their demand is granted, when grievances are fixed, or when their leader is killed or bribed. Rebel armies fight as the Rebel band kind under the battle rules. A province with riots or rebels counts toward your country's In revolt . At 4 or more grievances a province is Plotting : each month it may rise, with a 5 % chance at 4 grievances, 15 % at 5 and 30 % at 6 or more (an event can spark a rising at 3). The rebels are men from the province's recruits. More on Rebellions. Health and the land - Plague : none, rumour, outbreak, burning out. It spreads with traders along roads, rivers and sea routes, and with armies and refugees; crowded towns catch it first. It burns out after a season or two. Quarantine (you close the province) stops trade; hospitals, wells and drains slow it. It kills townsfolk first, then countryfolk, and buildings go fallow. It runs weekly while an outbreak lasts. How plague works in the game today is under Plague in the game. - Fever land : none, mild, harsh or deadly, set by ground and climate, with marsh tiles adding to it. Lowered by draining marsh and later inventions (quinine, sanitation). Soldiers and settlers from elsewhere die there; locals mostly don't. - Smoke : from era V, factories and coal mines make smoke. Townsfolk get sick and tiles become worn. Closing them and later inventions reduce it, and smoke feeds the event tree's climate stats. Colonies and the people already there - A colony is founded only in a province no country owns . Land held by any country, tribal countries included, is gained only by war, treaty, marriage or a lord joining. - A colony takes only the free tiles that nobody works. Tiles the local people work stay theirs, with their buildings and lords; once the province is owned they can be taken only by conquest or treaty, and each tile taken adds grievances and starts resistance events. - Settlement : none, trading post, settlement or colony. A trading post is a market that draws traders without taking a tile. Settlement is gained by founding a colony, founding a post (envoy and gold), settlers arriving, or a treaty; lost to the local people driving it out, disease, abandonment, or another power taking it. - Settlers are sent from provinces with homeless people, live on the colony's free tiles, and stop the colony growing when those are full. They are lost to fever land, war with the local people, and leaving. See Exploration and Colonies. Adding up to the country card Each province supplies your country card's sums: gold income, people (people plus refugees), recruits (royal provinces only), food, horses, ships, castles, faith and language, in revolt, schools, students and scholars, and officials. See Your Realm. When events touch a province The event tree speaks in abstract province stats, and each becomes a concrete change: Event stat Example Lands as population −10 % People −10 %, townsfolk first in plague events prosperity +2 Two new buildings that fit the province devastation +30 30 % of tiles burned unrest +20 One named grievance from the event control −20 The official flees, or the road breaks fort level +1 Castle one step up infrastructure +1 Road one step up industry +1 One factory food security −0.3 Harvest two steps worse disease burden +40 Plague outbreak Starting values At the start each province takes its tile count from its size on the map, its ground from terrain, its tile mix from ground, its shore tiles from coast and rivers, its people from population, and how many buildings start built (and its town size) from wealth. Wealth then stops being a live stat. The rest comes from the catalogue, the research tree, region tables and event anchors; see The 1378 Start. What is stored and when it updates A province stores about 95 small numbers and works out food made, wares made, tax owed and reaching you, town size and country sums when needed. Cadence What happens Monthly Births and deaths; overflow and homeless drift; rebels take up arms; sickness for armies staying; occupation months; grievances evaluated Each season Food check and famine; Hungry , Requisitioned and Soldiers quartered timers Each autumn (twice for rice) Harvest roll Yearly Recruits refill; tax owed; years held and years served; one burned tile rebuilt; worn tile checks; mine ore deposits fall; woods regrow after 10 unworked years; refugees settle after 2 years Weekly, during an outbreak Plague In the game now: the land Every province is laid out in 4 to 16 tiles from the map: bigger provinces have more. One is the Town , a coast gives 1 to 3 Shore tiles, and the rest are Fields , Pasture , Woods , Marsh or Waste in the share of the ground under the province (farmland is mostly fields, mountains mostly waste and pasture, forest mostly woods). Food comes from the tiles. A farm in the province works all its fields: each fields tile has work for 30,000 farmers, who feed 1.1 people each at a plain farm, 1.3 at a mill farm and 1.5 at an enclosed farm. Farmers past that, or with no farm at all, work bare land and feed 0.67 each. Ranches do the same for herders on pasture and fisheries for seafolk on the shore (1.33 each). The ground matters too: farmland farms better, mountains and marsh worse. At the start every province about feeds itself: its people's own ways of working the land (terraces, ditches, herding on the move) make up what its buildings leave short of 110 % of its needs in a normal year. That stays fixed, so as the people grow, a better farm or another ranch is what feeds them. A poor harvest bites. Hunting. Woodsmen hunt in the woods: each woods tile has room for 3,750 hunters, who feed 0.67 each, more in the northern forests and tundra, less in thin woods. Woodsmen past that room scrape by on half. Crowd the woods and the game thins, year by year, down to a third; fewer hunters let it come back. A hunting lodge makes the hunters in the woods bring in half as much again, and gives furs in the north. In the north a hard winter (about one year in five or eight) cuts the catch to 0.6. Changing a tile. You can clear woods into fields (3 years), turn fields to pasture or plough pasture back (a season each), drain marsh (3 years, needs Polder drainage ) and irrigate dry waste (2 years, needs Qanat and canal irrigation ). Each costs gold up front, more on hard ground; a province changes one tile at a time, and stopping gives half the gold back. The ground itself never changes. Lords change their own land, and other countries change theirs, by a simple rule: a province that can't feed itself drains, irrigates or clears woods. Mines and salt. A province in hills or mountains may have an ore deposit under its waste: iron, copper, tin, silver, gold or rock salt, with so many years of digging left. Tap the waste tile on the Land tab to see it. A mine needs the ore deposit and timber from a lumber camp in the province or next door; it gives work for 6,000 miners and adds trade, three times as much for silver or gold. Each January it digs a year off the deposit, and when it runs out the mine closes. Kutná Hora's silver (in Středočeský) and Falun's copper (in Dalarna) are already dug at the start. On a dry or warm coast, saltworks on the shore make salt and add trade too. Worn fields. Fields farmed year after year with more farmers than they hold wear out: after 30 years of it one fields tile turns worn and gives half, then the next 30 years another. Each rotation invention your realm knows ( Three-field rotation , Fodder crops , Four-field rotation ) makes that half as long again. Farmers work the sound fields first, so once the sound fields hold them all, the worn tile rests, and after 5 years of rest it is sound again. A better farm, fewer farmers (settlers, recruits, a new town building) or clearing woods for more fields lets it rest. Grassland and savanna start mostly as pasture. Fever land. Every province has a fever land of none, mild, harsh or deadly: jungle is harsh and marsh and savanna mild, a step worse in the tropics and for every two marsh tiles. By the rules, soldiers and settlers born elsewhere die there at 5, 15 or 30 % a year and the people born there at a tenth of that; the game shows it on the Land tab now, and armies and colonies will count it when their sickness is played. Draining the marsh lowers it. How you use it. Tap one of your provinces, then its Land tab. The first line says how much of its people the land feeds in a normal year, in red under 100 %; under it, a line names the province's fever land, if it has any. Below is the grid of tiles; a worn field is striped and marked "worn", and its sheet says how long it has rested, each coloured by its use and naming the building that works it. Tap a tile to see who works it, what it feeds or gives a year, and the building that would work it better, with its Build button or why it can't be built yet. Under the sheet are the one to three changes that tile allows, each with its gold and time. On the country card, Provinces → Short of food lists the provinces whose land doesn't feed them and what would fix each; tap one to open its Land tab. Plague in the game Plague is in the game now, as it was in the century after the Black Death: it comes back to a region about once every ten years, not all the time. A large realm sees it somewhere in its land every few years. How it starts. Now and then plague breaks out by itself, most often in crowded towns (a province where many of the people are townsfolk) and in shanty camps of the homeless. Land no realm holds has no towns, and plague does not start or spread there. How it spreads. Every week (on the 7th, 14th, 21st and 28th of the month) plague can spread from a province where it rages: - to the provinces next door, along the roads, and more easily down a river both share; - by ship to the other coasts of the same sea; - with an army that stood in a sick province: for about a month after, the army can bring it wherever it goes. Crowded towns catch it more easily than the countryside. How it runs. First comes word of plague (about a month), then the outbreak (a season or two), then it is burning out (about a month), and then it is gone. A province that has just had it is spared for about twelve years: its survivors don't catch it again soon. Who dies. While plague is there, people die faster: a little at first and at the end, more during the outbreak, most of all in shanty camps. The dead are townsfolk first, so towns lose their craftsmen, market folk and clergy faster than the countryside loses its farmers. Fewer children are born while it lasts, and the outbreak is a grievance ( Plague ) that adds to the province's mood. Quarantine. You can close any of your provinces, sick or not, and open it again whenever you like. While it is closed: - its trade stops (its trade ratio falls to 0) and it pays only half its tax ; - nothing spreads out of it along roads, rivers or by ship; - plague gets in only a quarter as easily. An army still carries plague in and out. A closed province stays closed until you lift the quarantine, and its trade grows back slowly after. Other realms close their crowded towns when an outbreak starts there, and open them when it is over; they leave their countryside open. How you use it. A sick province has a pale door with a red cross over it on the map when you zoom in to regions; a plank across the door means it is closed. Tap it: its Overview has a plague card with the step in words and about how long it lasts yet, how many have died so far, whether it is closed and what that costs, and a Quarantine or Lift quarantine button. A healthy province of yours shows the card when plague is next door, so you can close it before plague comes. On your country card, the Provinces tab says how many of your provinces have plague and how many are closed, and its Sick tab lists them, worst first. The Lands tile of your realm's Overview says "Plague in N provinces". You hear once when plague reaches one of your provinces, and how it came, and once when it burns out there, with its dead. Not in the game yet: hospitals, wells and drains that slow plague, refugees that carry it, and buildings going fallow when their workers die. What you see The province card , when you tap a province at close zoom: The tile row is the province: tap a tile to see its building, its workers and what it makes. Tap any other line to open its gain and lose list. The Tax screen sets the realm default rate, overrides per province and presets. The province map modes (Food, Tax reaching you, Days to capital, Grievances, Ground, Recruits) and what shows at each zoom are on Map and Map Modes. Things you can do : set a province's tax rate, the realm default or a preset; set a toll; change a tile's use (clear woods, fields to pasture and back, drain marsh, irrigate waste); burn your own fields; pay to rebuild a burned tile faster; assign, dismiss and hire officials; lend an official to a lord and recall him; pay for a building in a lord's province; grant or revoke a charter; build a road; quarantine a province; assign a garrison; repair walls; send settlers. Rebellions: Rebellions turn a province's grievances into a rising. There is no anger meter: a province simply counts its named grievances, and as the count grows it grumbles, riots, plots and finally rises. This page covers how a rising starts, how strong and how severe it is, how you can answer it, and what the rebels get if they win. How it works From grievances to an uprising Every province counts its grievances (the list, and when each starts and ends, is on Provinces). The count sets the province's step: Grievances Step What happens 0 to 1 Calm Nothing 2 Grumbling Growth slows, scholars and craftsmen start to leave. No danger of a rising yet. 3 Riots Tax and recruits are halved, traders avoid the province, and its lord wavers. A spark now starts a rising at once. 4 or more Plotting The province may rise by itself each month. Its card shows the monthly chance and a named plotter. Each step shows on the map. The Homeless grievance counts fully, and as two grievances where the homeless are above a fifth of the people. While a province is plotting, it rolls each month to rise by itself: Grievances Chance each month 4 5 % 5 15 % 6 or more 30 % When a province rises, rebels muster and the rebellion card appears. Sparks A spark is a single happening that turns a rioting province (3 or more grievances) into a rising at once. The rebellion card shows the spark as the reason the rising began. In a grumbling province with only 2 grievances, a spark does nothing. Kind Sparks A new burden The province's tax rate raised; a levy called at harvest time; an army quartered for the winter; an army requisitioning food while the province is already Hungry A failed harvest A failed harvest roll while the province already has Hungry An insult to faith A house of worship of the majority faith demolished; a faith tolerance charter revoked A death or execution The province's lord executed, or dying without an accepted heir; a popular official dismissed A defeat Your army loses a battle in or next to the province; the capital falls An outsider A pretender lands with men; a rival's envoy arrives with gold; a preacher of a new faith arrives The ruler The ruler dies with a child heir or none An event can also act as a spark directly. When a revolution event fires, a rising starts in every province that meets its conditions: if the French revolution fires and Paris and Troyes meet its conditions but Rouen doesn't, Paris and Troyes rise at once and Rouen stays quiet. Cause, demand and who joins A rising's cause comes from the province's heaviest grievance. The cause sets what the rebels demand and who joins them most: Cause From Demand Who joins most Hunger Hungry Food, the castle granary opened to them Farmers and homeless Tax Heavy taxes or Conscription The tax rate back down and the levy ended Farmers, craftsmen, market folk Faith Wrong faith or a faith Broken charter A faith tolerance charter, or a ruler of their faith Everyone of that faith Homeland Foreign rule or Far from the throne Self-rule, then independence Everyone of the homeland's language Town Homeless , Broken charter or Soldiers quartered A town law charter, work, the soldiers gone Homeless, craftsmen, market folk Lord Harsh lord , or a disloyal lord's own choice The lord's want (land, an office, lower taxes, independence) The lord's retinue and officials, plus people of his land who share his faith and language Pretender A pretender with a right to the province, plus any grievance The pretender on the throne, or the province handed to them Lords who back the pretender, plus anyone with a grievance New ideas From the age of revolutions, any grievance plus support of 0.3 or more for liberalism, socialism, communism or nationalism A new kind of government Townsfolk and scholars first Resistance. When settlers take local people's tiles in a colony, the local people raise a resistance instead of rebels. It works by the same rules, with its own named leaders, and its demand is to get their tiles back. A resistance can win. The leader Every rising has a named leader drawn from the province, with Might, Cunning and Logistics like a commander: Leader When Brings A local (dyer, miller, village elder) Hunger, tax and town risings Cunning and little Might A preacher Faith risings The faith spreads to neighbours twice as fast A veteran Any province with returned soldiers among the homeless Might; the rebels fight as if one arms step better The lord himself A lord's revolt His retinue, wealth and officials The pretender A pretender's war The lords who back them and foreign help Strength: how hard an uprising is to beat Strength = Men × Arms × Leader × Ground , and food decides how long they last. In battle, rebels fight as the Rebel band kind under the Warfare battle rules. Men. Rebels are taken out of their classes, their job slots go empty, and they are no longer recruits for you. While a rising grows, each month it draws these shares of each class's men: Who Share each month Homeless 30 % The class the cause speaks to 10 % Everyone sharing the faith or language (faith and homeland risings) 8 % Other classes 2 % Clergy and scholars only in faith and new-ideas risings A lord's retinue all of it at once So in Troyes with 1,000 men in a class: a town rising draws 300 homeless or 100 craftsmen, a hunger rising draws 100 farmers but only 20 craftsmen, and a tax rising draws no clergy. A rising stops growing once it has drawn its share or its cause is fixed. Arms. Each step above Tools needs one source: Arms step Multiplier Sources Tools × 0.4 Any rising Old weapons × 0.6 A forge in the province, or a veteran leader Armed × 0.8 A forge and a market, a captured castle's store, or foreign gold Soldiers × 1.0 A lord's retinue, deserters, a rival's troops, or a pretender's army Ground and walls. Rebels fighting in the hills, mountains, forest, jungle or marsh of their own province get the province's Locals know the land bonus. Rebels holding a castle fight from its walls. Food. Rebels eat from the local store of the provinces they hold, then by foraging, which burns tiles. With no food, a tenth of their men are lost each month to hunger and desertion. If you burn tiles to starve a rising, Burned homes is added wherever the burning happens. Worked example. A rising in Troyes has 3,400 men carrying Old weapons. Its strength is 3,400 × 0.6 × its leader factor × its ground factor. Severity: how much harm it does Severity is separate from strength. It follows the rising's size: Tier Size What happens Riot One province, no rebel army Rising One province with a rebel army The province sends you no tax, recruits, food or trade, and its official flees Rebellion 2 to 5 provinces Rising effects in each province; neighbouring lords of the same faith or language waver; rebels can besiege castles Great revolt More than 5 provinces, in or next to the capital's province, or a whole lord's land Civil war: every lord picks a side by loyalty, allies may stay out, and rival AIs may attack A rising that starts in or next to the capital is a great revolt at once. Spreading. Each month a rising may spread to each neighbouring province. The chance is higher when the neighbour: - has the same grievance (it also gets Neighbour in revolt until those rebels are beaten or satisfied), - shares the rebels' faith or language, - is connected by roads, rivers and traders, - has many homeless, and when your army is away at war, you answered the last rising with a massacre, or a rival pays the rebels. The chance is lower when the neighbour shares no grievance, a garrisoned castle sits on the road between, a judge runs the neighbour, your army is in the region, you pardoned the last rising, or an almshouse stands in the neighbour. What makes it worse. - A disloyal lord whose faith or language matches the rebels may join with his retinue, turning the rising into a lord's revolt with Soldiers' arms. - While rebels hold a province, they loot one town building a season (the market first), kill or drive out officials, burn tiles when they forage, and make scholars flee. - A rising keeps pulling in more men every month until its cause is fixed. - A massacre adds Bloodshed for 20 years to every province of the same faith or language. Answering an uprising You have five answers: Answer Cost What happens Grant demand What was asked (the tax lowered, a charter, granary food, the lord's want) The rising ends at once, rebels go back to their classes, the grievance goes. Other provinces with the same grievance become more likely to rise and ask for the same. Talk An envoy or a judge, and some gold A partial deal of half the demand. Usually works on hunger, tax and town risings; rarely on faith or homeland risings. Bribe leader Gold, more for a lord or a pretender The leader and his bonus are gone, and the rebels may split or melt away. A faith rising finds a new preacher quickly. Wait The lost tax and output each month Rebels with no food or arms shrink. Rebels who hold a castle, have a lord or have foreign gold don't. Attack An army that can reach them A battle under the warfare rules. If you win, the rebels scatter: a third die, a third flee abroad, a third go home as homeless. Hunger and tax risings end when their need is met. Faith, homeland and pretender risings don't end by gold or grain. Worked example. With a tax rising in Troyes and Heavy taxes also in nearby Sens, granting the demand lowers Troyes's tax rate, ends the rising at once, sends the rebels home and removes Heavy taxes from Troyes. Sens becomes more likely to rise and ask for the same. After a victory you choose how to treat the beaten rebels: Treatment Effect Pardon Survivors return to their classes and the province calms faster, but the leader may rise again Punish the leaders The leader is executed; that province gets no new rising from the same cause for 10 years Massacre No rising in that province for 20 years; Bloodshed across every province of the same faith or language; lords of that faith or language waver Preventing uprisings - End grievances: once a grievance ends, it no longer counts. - A judge running a restless province raises each step's bar by one grievance. - An almshouse sheltering the homeless keeps them from counting toward the trouble. - A garrisoned castle on the main road limits the spread along it and gives the rebels a siege to fight. - Loyal lords stay out of risings, and their retinues fight for you. If the rebels win Rebels win when they have held their provinces for 12 months with no army beating them, or when they take the capital. What they win depends on the cause: Cause Result Hunger The castle's food is handed out, Hungry ends, and the province's lord turns disloyal Tax The tax rate in their provinces is fixed at light for 10 years Faith A faith tolerance charter in every province they held, or in a great revolt a ruler of their faith Homeland Their provinces break away as a new country, from the catalogue if a record fits, or a new one named for the homeland Town A town law charter, and the quartered army leaves Lord The lord gets his want, or leaves the realm with his land as his own country or under a neighbour Pretender The pretender takes the throne (in a great revolt) or the province passes to them New ideas The government changes to theirs (through the event tree's revolution events) How other systems use it - The country card's In revolt counts provinces with riots or rebels. - A lord whose loyalty reaches In revolt starts a lord's revolt, and in a great revolt lords pick sides by loyalty. - An event's unrest lands as a named grievance (for example "unrest +20" on Troyes gives Troyes one named grievance), separatism risk reads homeland risings, and revolution and reformation events act as sparks or set the cause. - A rival paying your rebels is a hostile act you can find out about through envoys. While a rival funds a rising, its arms count as Armed from foreign gold and it doesn't shrink while you wait. The computer players AI countries use the same answers as you. Rivals and opportunists pay rebels and attack countries in a great revolt. Opportunists and hegemon seekers fund rebels in a rival's provinces that already have two or more grievances, when they have a free envoy seat and gold to spare. Cautious AIs grant demands early; harsh AIs massacre. Each month A turn is one week, so these steps run once a month, in the turn in which a new month begins. 1. Recount each province's step from its grievances. 2. Apply this month's sparks. 3. Roll the rising chance for each plotting province. 4. Draw new men into each growing rising. 5. Feed the rebels (store, then forage) and apply hunger losses. 6. Roll spread to each neighbour and apply Neighbour in revolt . 7. Apply damage in held provinces (looting once a season). 8. Count months held and check whether the rebels have won. What you see - Steps on the map : each province's step (grumbling, riots, plotting, risen) shows on the map, with rising icons and a Grievances map mode. - The province card : while plotting, the monthly chance to rise and the named plotter. - The rebellion card : the rising's name, cause and demand, its leader and a skill, who joined, men, arms and multiplier, what it holds, food in months, severity with its province count and neighbours sharing the grievance, who backs it, where it may spread next month, and the five answers. Worked example: the Troyes weavers' rising. A tax rising holds Troyes town but not the castle, led by Jehan the Dyer (Cunning 3), with craftsmen, homeless and some farmers. The card shows: - Cause "Heavy taxes", demand "tax back to normal". - "Men 3,400" and "Arms: tools and old weapons (x0.6)". - "Holds Troyes town (not the castle)" and "Food: 2 months". - "Severity Rising · 1 province · 2 neighbours share the grievance". - "Backed by nobody yet", and where it may spread next month. - The buttons Grant demand, Talk, Bribe leader, Wait and Attack. In the game today The first slice plays risings on the eight grievances the game tracks, so the risings you meet are hunger, tax, homeland and town ones. They start from a plotting province's monthly roll, or at once in a rioting province when you raise its tax or your army loses a battle in or next to it. - Where : an alert over the map says a rising has begun, with Go there. The province's card opens with the rebellion card, and the five answers under it as big buttons with their gold and odds. Grant asks once more before it gives anything up; Attack sends your nearest free army; Wait folds the card. - On the map : the band stands in its province as a dark rider with its men, and the land it holds is hatched dark. It besieges the castles of its land; once it holds two or more provinces it marches a province a week on the nearest castle beside its land. A taken castle arms it. - What it costs you : a province the rebels hold sends you no tax and no recruits, and its men are taken from its recruits. - Beating them : march an army with a commander onto the band. If you win, the rebels scatter and the same card asks for your verdict: Pardon, Punish the leaders or Massacre. Massacre asks once more. An army that stands four weeks in a held province the band has left takes it back. - Overview : your realm's Provinces tab opens with an Uprisings block listing every rising and every beaten rising waiting on you, and the Lands tile on your Realm book's Overview turns red and names the uprisings; tapping it opens the Provinces page. A plotting province's mood line gives its chance to rise each month. - Answers today : granting a tax demand puts the tax back to normal and ends the musters there. A hunger demand opens the castle granary (up to 4 months of food). A homeland demand gives self-rule, so Foreign rule no longer counts there and the tax stays light for good. A town demand sends your armies out of their land. Talks cost 10 gold a province, once a month. A bribe costs 1 gold per 100 rebels. - If they win (a year held, or the capital's castle taken): tax and town risings keep their tax light for 10 years; hunger risings empty the castles into their stores and turn their lords disloyal; a homeland rising breaks away to the realm that held it at the start, which comes back if it was gone; a people that rose in their own realm's land found a new realm named for their homeland, with a founding card and a truce with the realm they left. How it connects - Provinces: grievances, homeless, classes and slots, the local store, judges, almshouses, charters and castles; rebellions writes Neighbour in revolt , Bloodshed and Burned homes . - Your-Realm: lords' loyalty, wants and retinues; the In revolt count; lords waver or pick sides. - Warfare: the Rebel band kind, battle rules, break point and sieges. - Troop-Movement: armies in or away from the region, and marching to attack rebels. - Revolutions: risings tagged by a revolution, its camps, and what happens when they win or are crushed. - Historical-Events: the rebels effect, rebels active , unrest as grievances, sparks from events. - Diplomacy: secretly funding rebels, and envoys fleeing when a host falls to rebels. - Religion: faith risings' demands, preachers as leaders, sparks from faith policy and houses. - Culture: homeland risings draw 8 % of the language and, with nationalism 0.5 or more, demand a new country; Banned language . - Government: a won New ideas rising sets a form; over-cap lords become disloyal. - Subjects: a lord leaving with his land. - Recruiting: recruits lost to rebels. - Buildings: looting one town building a season; town walls stop looting without storming. - Trade: traders avoid riots, bandits appear, and rebels act as an enemy army for trade. - The 1378 Start: a new country for a won homeland rising. - Exploration-and-Colonies: colonies, local people's tiles and resistance. - Map and Map Modes: steps on the map, rising icons and the Grievances map mode. - Time-and-Turns: where the monthly steps sit in the turn.
