Recruiting: Recruiting is how your realm turns the people of its provinces into soldiers. You call men up with one slider (the levy), train them into regiments of one troop type at a castle or drill yard, keep the best as standing regiments, and take officials out of their provinces to lead your armies. Every step has a price in gold, food, work at home and goodwill, and this page explains each one. How it works Who can be called Only fighting-age men can be called, and they are a quarter of a province's people, in every realm. The levy calls men only. Each class gives at most a share of its fighting-age men, its call share: Class Call share Homeless 24 % Herders 16 % Farmers 12 % Woodsmen 12 % Miners 8 % Seafolk 8 % Craftsmen 8 % Market folk 6 % Clerks 4 % Students 4 % Clergy and scholars 0 Add these up over a province's classes and you get its men who can be called , the ceiling. The ceiling is hard: no levy, war or invention ever takes a province past it. In Troyes that works out at about one man in eight of the fighting-age men. Students can be called from the same pool at the clerks' share (1,000 students give 10 men), while clergy and scholars cannot. Students who are called stop making research. The class a man comes from does not change the soldier he becomes. Every levied man arrives as levy infantry , the weakest troop type, with farm tools. Classes only matter for how many men you can call and what you lose at home when they leave. With the invention W15 Mass conscription every class's call share rises by half (homeless 36 %, farmers 18 % and so on), and the ceiling stays a share of the fighting-age men. The levy Tap one of your provinces, then its Garrison tab, and press Recruit 1,000 men once for each thousand you want. Under the button you see what that thousand is as a share of the province's men who can be called, and when all the thousands queued there will have gathered; when the button can't be pressed it says why (queue full, too few men, over your troop cap, not enough gold). Up to 10 thousands wait in a province's queue, one row each with the days left, and the × on the last row takes it back with its levy money and men. There is no levy for a whole region or the country: you recruit one province at a time. The costs below are the design's full levy screen; the game shows the levy money on the button. - Gold now : levy money of 20 gold per 1,000 men, paid up front for food on the road. - Food now : while they gather, levies eat 1 ration a man a month from the province's local store. - Pay : free for the first 3 months, then 0.15 gold per man a month. - Harvest : how much of the harvest you lose by taking farmers. - Pool left : how much of each province's recruit pool remains. - Ready in : when each thousand will be ready. The men gather a thousand at a time, 14 days for each thousand (provisional), so 10,000 men take months to assemble. A warning sign shows when the season is wrong, and every cost line opens its own gain and lose list so you can see where the number comes from. There are no class or province settings, and a region or country levy draws only your royal provinces; lords' men come as their retinues. The screen names the bigger classes and sums the small ones as "others". A levy takes men from every class in proportion to its share of the men who can be called, and from every province of a region by its share of the region's men. Veterans come along by their share of the pool too: if Troyes has 2,000 recruits of whom 400 are veterans, a levy of 1,000 brings 200 veterans. Each thousand gathers in 14 days (3 days once you know W18 Railway mobilization, so several can come in one week) and joins the province's garrison : troops without a commander. They man the province's castle if it has one, and wait on the province card's Garrison tab, listed with their arms and drill; only you see them. They can't march, fight in the field or train until a commander picks them up into his army, which happens at once. A commander standing in the province does it from the Garrison tab ("La Hire takes 1,000" or "takes all") or from his own screen ("Take in 1,000" or "Take in all"); a commander waiting at court can be put at their head with "Lead". A commander can also leave men behind as a province's garrison. While they are away their job slots stay empty, so a building that falls under half filled goes fallow and pays no tax and makes no wares. This worked example comes from the design and is drawn as a region levy; today the same levy is raised province by province. Champagne, late summer 1444. France is at war with Burgundy. Champagne has 4 royal provinces, about 260,000 people, 65,000 fighting-age men and 7,900 men who can be called, 65 % of them farmers. It is 3 weeks before harvest. A levy of 5,000 costs 100 gold and 2,500 rations, cuts the Champagne harvest by 6 %, and leaves each province 37 % of its pool. The levy takes 3,250 farmers, 550 herders, 500 homeless, 300 woodsmen, 200 craftsmen, 150 seafolk and 50 others. The screen reads "Ready in 2 weeks at Troyes" as 5,000 levies, with a harvest warning. Push the slider to 6,000 and each province keeps only 24 % of its pool, so all four get the Conscription grievance. The recruit pool Each province keeps three soldier counts: - Recruits here : the men who can be called right now, never above the ceiling. - Fallen from here : men from this province killed in the last 10 years. - Veterans here : men home from war who were trained or stood in a battle. Every January the pool refills by a quarter of the gap to the ceiling, or a third with a muster master as official: Troyes with a ceiling of 2,200 and 1,000 recruits gets back to 1,300 (1,400 with a muster master). It grows when disbanded men come home, and a growing population raises the ceiling. It shrinks for levies, students enrolling, famine, plague, men dying in war and the men of a rising. While a province riots, only half its recruits can be called; the ceiling stays the same, and the whole pool can be called again when the riot ends. Conscription. If a levy leaves a province's recruits below a quarter of its ceiling, the province gets the Conscription grievance. If the province has Fallen from here, the line is a third instead. With W15 Mass conscription it is only below a tenth, fallen or not. The fallen. Each soldier levied in a province who dies adds one to its Fallen from here, which fades by a tenth each January. For each 1 % of a province's people fallen, its births fall by 0.2 % for 10 years. Veterans. Disbanded regiments and levies who were trained or stood in a battle come home as Veterans here. They fade by a tenth each January from old age, and also leave by dying or going off as settlers. What a levy costs at home - Births : while fighting-age men are away, births fall by the share of them away. - The harvest : a levy in the sowing or harvest season cuts the harvest by twice the share of farmers taken, and by 1.5 times that at harvest. In the north, sowing is in March and April and the harvest season is August and September; in the south, sowing is in September and October and the harvest season is February and March. A winter levy costs no harvest. Rice lands have two crops a year: sowing in May–June and November–December, harvest in February–March and August–September. In a pastoral province, taking herders during the spring move (March to May in the north, September to November in the south) cuts herd growth by twice the share of herders taken, and the harvest is untouched. - Food : men in a training camp eat 1.5 rations a month and horses 3, from the training castle's store first and then its province. A man eats 2 rations on campaign and 1 at home. Before an army marches abroad it fills a reserve of reserve size × 2 rations per man per month, from the castle store first, then the locals. Training Training is ordered from the commander screen , for the levy infantry in that commander's army, while the army stands at a castle or drill yard of yours: set how many thousand with − and +, then tap the troop type, which shows its months and gold. Away from a training place the screen tells you to march there first, and training already under way holds while the army is away. The commander screen also shows the army's men by troop type, drill and break point, the commander's skills, its companies to split, merge or leave as garrison, its food reserve and food used a day and a month, and its pay. Levies can only be trained at a training place : a castle or a drill yard of yours. Each has a training room, the number of men it trains at once: Training place Training room Earthwork ring fort 1,000 Stone castle 3,000 Bastion fort 5,000 Star fort 8,000 Drill yard 1,500 of any troop type Barracks (drill yard step) 4,000 of any troop type A castle and a drill yard in the same province add their rooms together. You pick the troop type, how many men and the place; the men walk there and start. If you order training from a town with neither, the men march to the nearest place that can train. You can only train into troop types your realm has unlocked, and training takes the months, gold and goods in this table (per 1,000 men): Arm Months Gold Needs Levy infantry 0 0 nothing Heavy infantry 2 80 10 loads of arms Pikes 3 60 10 loads of arms Archers 4 60 10 loads of arms Hand gunners 3 120 10 loads of arms, 10 powder Pike and shot 4 150 20 arms, 10 powder Musketeers 5 180 20 arms, 20 powder Line infantry 6 220 20 arms, 20 powder Riflemen 6 300 30 arms, 30 powder Light cavalry 3 100 1,000 horses Camel riders 3 100 1,000 camels Horse archers 6 150 1,000 horses, 10 arms Knights and lancers 9 300 1,500 horses, 20 arms War elephants 6 400 125 elephants Gun crews 4 200 the guns, horses or oxen for them, 20 powder Some things speed training up or change it: - A Marshal as the province's official makes training there 25 % faster. - Veterans train in half the time, so a regiment made mostly of veterans finishes early. - Retraining a regiment to a newer troop type takes half the months and half the gold, and it keeps its drill and scars. - Until the order is done the men are still levies. If you call them out of training to fight, they go as levy infantry and the months spent are lost. - A castle or town under siege stops all training in it. - The 3 free months count from the day the levy has gathered. If training runs past them, you pay for the extra months. Pikes and light cavalry (3 months) finish inside the free months; musketeers (5 months) cost 2 months of pay and knights (9 months) 6. When training finishes, the regiment has its troop type, drill 3 (drill 4 if trained under a Marshal), pay by its troop type and a break point of 30 % plus its troop level. Untrained levies stay at drill 0 and break at 25 %. Training never changes a regiment's kind: a trained levy regiment is still a levy. No levy, trained or not, goes home on its own: it stays until you disband it or leave it as a garrison. Pay by troop type, per 1,000 men a month: foot 200 gold, gunners 250, horse 400, knights 600, and gun crews 1 gold per crew of 15 (10 gold for 150 men). Each troop type belongs to one of these groups: Pay group Troop types Foot Heavy infantry, pikes, archers Gunners Hand gunners, pike and shot, musketeers, line infantry, riflemen Horse Light cavalry, camel riders, horse archers Knights Knights and lancers, war elephants Gun crews Gun crews Champagne continued. Of the 5,000 levies, 2,500 train into pikes at the castle of Troyes and 500 into light cavalry at Reims, while 2,000 march at once as levies. The pikes cost 150 gold and 25 loads of arms and eat 11,250 rations in 3 months. The light cavalry cost 50 gold and 500 horses and eat 6,750 rations. Training eats 18,000 rations from the castle stores at Troyes and Reims, and no pay is owed. Filling a 2-month reserve then takes 23,000 rations. From the 4th month the army costs 1,000 gold a month in pay and eats 11,500 rations a month on campaign, about 6,500 more than the men would eat at home. Standing regiments and retinues With W12 Standing regiments you can sign on a trained regiment. It stays under arms in peace, keeps its drill and scars, and is paid 1.5 times, all year round. Its men are gone from their province's pool and their slots stay empty. Housed in a barracks in peace, a standing regiment gives the province no Soldiers quartered; without a barracks it is quartered on the people like any army in winter. Lords raise their retinues by the same rules, with their own wealth and at their own castles. Their traits decide what they train: a Warlike lord trains knights and heavy infantry, a Greedy one keeps levies. What recruiting gives back - Taking homeless men means less theft and begging, and the province may lose the Homeless state. - While men serve abroad, their home province has fewer mouths to feed. - Each month a fifth of the pay of soldiers training, standing or quartered in one of your provinces is spent there, as trade for its market folk, and its tax owed rises by the same amount. - Disbanded men can go as soldier settlers to a frontier or colony province with free tiles. They clear tiles twice as fast as other settlers and become farmers, and that province needs one grievance more to riot for 10 years. - When an army disbands, a tenth of its loot goes to the provinces its men came from, split by how many men each gave, raising their local store and tax owed for a year. What recruiting takes - Disbanded men go back into the emptiest slots of their province; those with no free slot become homeless. - On disbanding, the arms always go back to the store. You are not asked. - An army that disbands within 3 months of a plague or high-sickness campaign brings a plague rumour home to 1 in 4 of the provinces it disbands into. - Students called to arms stop making research. Commanders from officials Every army has a commander, and no army gets one by default. Your way to new commanders is to commission officials; your ruler and heirs may also lead, lords lead only their own retinues, and hired companies bring their own commander. A captain who rises from the ranks, an academy graduate or an exile first joins your service as an official. Any official can be commissioned to lead an army or stand in one as a captain. They leave the province they ran and start with the skills and trait offer of their type: Official type Might Cunning Logistics Trait offered Warden 2 1 1 Steady or Siege master Steward 0 1 3 Careful Muster master 1 1 2 Beloved or Old soldier Master of works 0 1 2 Siege master Tax collector 0 2 2 Greedy Customs officer 0 3 1 Careful Judge 1 2 1 Steady or Cruel Schoolmaster 0 2 1 Old soldier Marshal 2 2 2 Any At 5 years served the type's highest skill gains +1, and +1 more at 10, and no skill goes past 5. When skills tie, Logistics gains first, then Cunning, then Might, so a Marshal with 5 years served has Logistics 3. You pick the offered trait or keep the one rolled. A commander gets the realm's current style for their era and country; a Marshal may take any style your realm has seen in a battle it fought. Years served count where the official was assigned. The costs. A commission costs 50 gold once (a provisional number, raised from 10 so commanders are not handed out freely). In the field an official earns their wage ×3 as commander or ×2 as captain. They bring a staff of 100 (commander) or 50 (captain) who eat 2 rations each a month from the army's reserve, and their horses (30 for a commander, 15 for a captain) eat 3 each. Staff eat but are not soldiers: they do not count toward foraging or the column size. The empty province. When you commission an official you choose how their province is run: Choice Effect Leave it Half tax, half recruits, and the province is Ungoverned Move another official in The moved official starts at half effect, and their old province becomes the empty one Name a deputy Full tax and recruits, no type effect, for 1 gold a month; needs 20 clerks in the province Ask the lord next door A loyal neighbouring lord takes the recruits for his retinue and half the tax, grows a step more loyal, and may ask for it as a fief when the war ends When you release the official you send them to a province of your choice. Their years served restart at half, unless they return to the province they left and a deputy ran it. The steward of Reims. The steward of Reims has 8 years served and Reims has at least 20 clerks. Commissioned as commander with a deputy named, the steward has Might 0, Cunning 1, Logistics 4 and the trait Careful, the deputy costs 1 gold a month, and the army eats 20 % less. When the lords are called, the Proud Count of Foix refuses to bring his retinue and the Duke of Bourbon comes. After two wins the army comes home in spring with 700 of the 5,000 dead: the steward returns to Reims at full effect at once, Troyes' births dip for a decade, and 1,400 veterans return to Troyes who will train in half the time. The Marshal The Marshal is an official type trained for war. You get one from an academy, by hiring one at three times a normal official's price, or by raising a captain who stood in 3 won battles (one offer per won battle). While a Marshal runs a province, training there is 25 % faster and regiments leave with drill 4. A Marshal is paid twice an official's wage in war or peace, and one who spends 10 years in a province with no war loses 1 from their best skill. What official commanders mean - They never refuse a command, never go home with their men mid-war, and never defect with land. - When their army wins a battle, every lord grows one step more loyal (up to Loyal; a lord in revolt stays there), the ruler's victories rise by one, and no single lord grows from it. - An official who returns with 3 or more victories gives 1.5 times their type's effect where they serve, for as long as they hold that post. - A Proud lord serving as captain under an official wavers a step each season, and refuses to bring his retinue unless the war aim is his Want. - An official commander brings no retinue of their own. - If one is killed or captured you lose a commander and an official; a ransom brings both back. - Any commander with 8 victories who has led the same regiments for 5 years becomes "their man". An official at 6 victories asks for land: refusing makes them Ambitious, granting turns them into a lord with their old soldiers as his retinue. Other leaders: the ruler and heirs can lead, lords lead only their own retinues (as captains in a royal army), hired captains come with their mercenary companies, and exiles who ask to serve become officials of the type closest to their past. Names and ranks Every commander is named the way his own people name someone: a Castilian is "Rodrigo Manrique", a Hungarian "Hunyadi János" and a Japanese "Hosokawa Katsumoto", family name first where the language puts it first. The great commanders of the start go by their own names too: Bertrand du Guesclin, Gazi Evrenos Bey, Vettor Pisani, Xu Da. He also carries the rank of his post in that language: a Portuguese commander leading an army is "Marechal Fernão Coutinho" and the same man at the head of a fleet is "Almirante Fernão Coutinho"; an Ottoman admiral is "Kapudan Mehmed Pasha", a Japanese general "Hosokawa Katsumoto Taishō". The rank changes with the post, so an admiral sent back to court is a general again. A mercenary company's captain is named and ranked in the language of the land the company gathers in ("Hauptmann Ulrich von Hallwyl", "Condottiero Niccolò Piccinino") and keeps that name in your service. A people with no word for a post in the game's data shows the name alone. The ranked name is used on the army row of a province card, the commander screen, the Military tab's Commanders list, the army picker, fleet names on the Navy tab and in port, and the Mercenaries tab. Under it, the small line with his skills starts with his post in plain English (commander, admiral or hired captain), so you never need to know the word. Dispatches and short buttons use the plain name. The computer players The AI uses the same levy and training commands. Its catalogue personality sets how much of its pool it dares to levy and what it trains: a militarist levies deep and trains expensive troop types, a merchant republic levies little and hires companies instead, a steppe realm trains horse archers. It avoids levying in harvest months unless an enemy army is in its land, and it commissions stewards and wardens first, keeping tax collectors in their seats. It commissions an official only when at least 1,000 of its men have no commander and no free commander can go to them, so it never keeps more commanders than its armies need. Each month A turn is one week. Everything below happens once a month, at the end of the turn in which the new month begins, with the same amounts as before. Each province is updated once a month: training months tick down and finished regiments come out, births are cut by men away and fallen, pay starts for levies past their free months, a fifth of pay is spent where soldiers are, the empty province's effects apply, and Marshal idleness counts up. Once a year, in the turn in which 1 January falls, the pool refills and Fallen and Veterans fade. A levy itself is worked out in one calculation when you tap it. What you see - The levy screen , opened from a province card: one men slider in thousands; Gold now, Food now, Pay, Harvest, Pool left and Ready in; a season and harvest warning sign; a gain and lose list behind every cost line. - The commander screen : the army's stats, troops, food and pay, and the training choice (troop type, thousands of men, castle or drill yard). - The Garrison tab of the province card: troops without a commander, levies still gathering and the commanders who can pick them up. - Where to settle men : soldier settlers for a frontier or colony province. - The commission choice : commander or captain, the trait to pick, and the four ways to run the empty province. - Province stats : Recruits here, Fallen from here and Veterans here. How it connects - Provinces: classes, job slots, homeless, officials, grievances and births; recruiting writes back empty slots, Conscription and the three soldier counts. - Your-Realm: gold, food and arms stores, lords and their loyalty, officials' wages, schools and academies. - Warfare: takes the companies and commanders recruiting makes, and reports deaths, victories, loot and sieges back. - Buildings: castle steps, the drill yard and its barracks step set training room. - Research: W12, W15 and W18 unlock signing on, raise call shares and speed gathering. - Troop-Movement: gathered levies and trained regiments become movers, and levies walk to their training place. - Naval: recruiting sailors reuses the levy with its own ceiling for seafolk (sailors at sea are not at home to be levied), and admirals reuse the commission and the empty province. - Rebellions: armed veterans, a rising's men drawn from the pool, and the Conscription grievance. - Historical-Events: plague rumours brought home and generals who grow too big. - Time-and-Turns: the month tick, the seasons and the order of monthly steps. - Government: the Ungoverned state and lords' fiefs. - Diplomacy: war aims (a lord's Want) and exiles asking to serve. Numbers The numbers live in the recruiting config file. Most are provisional and waiting for a balancing pass. Value Design number Fighting-age share a quarter of people, men only Call shares see table above; W15 raises them ×1.5 Pool refill each January 1/4 of the gap; 1/3 with a muster master Riots half the recruits can be called Students' call share 4 % Conscription line 1/4 of ceiling; 1/3 with Fallen; 1/10 with W15, fallen or not Fallen and Veterans fade a tenth a year each Births cut per 1 % fallen 0.2 % for 10 years Gathering 2 weeks; 3 days with W18 Levy money 20 gold per 1,000 men Free months 3, from the day the levy has gathered Levy pay 0.15 gold per man a month Pay by troop type (per man a month) foot 0.2, gunners 0.25, horse 0.4, knights 0.6; gun crews 1 per crew of 15 Standing pay ×1.5 Rations gathering 1, camp 1.5, campaign 2, home 1; horse 3 Lost harvest ×2 share of farmers taken, ×1.5 at harvest Lost herd growth ×2 share of herders taken in the spring move Training room, troop type table see tables above Veterans / retraining half the time / half months and half gold Marshal 25 % faster, drill 4, hired at 3×, paid 2×, −1 skill after 10 idle years Drill and break point trained 3 and 30 % + troop level; levies 0 and 25 % Pay spent at home a fifth Soldier settlers clear ×2; +1 grievance to riot for 10 years Loot home a tenth, for a year Armed veterans garrison +10 % for 5 years Sickness brought home within 3 months; 1 in 4 provinces Years served bonus +1 at 5 years, +1 at 10, up to 5 Commission 50 gold (provisional); wage ×3 commander, ×2 captain Staff 100 or 50, 2 rations each; 30 or 15 horses at 3 rations Victory under an official every lord one step more loyal; ruler's victories +1 Deputy 20 clerks; 1 gold a month Returning official 3+ victories gives 1.5× effect Land request / "their man" 6 victories (officials) / 8 victories and 5 years (any commander) Still open Nothing in recruiting is waiting on a decision. The numbers above still need their balancing pass. Religion: Religion decides which faiths exist, how the faith mix of every province slowly changes, and how you rule a realm where people pray in different ways. Faiths spread through things you can point at on the map: houses of worship, preachers, schools, traders, rulers and lords. You set a policy for each faith, from Established to Persecuted, and every choice has a price in grievances, lords' loyalty, tax and people. There is no faith meter, piety, fervour or unity score, and no "convert province" button. Every change on the Faith line comes with a named reason. How it works Faiths and families The game uses the event tree's list of faiths plus three added ones: hussite, jain and asian traditional. Each faith belongs to one family: Family Faiths christian catholic, protestant, anglican, orthodox, oriental christian, hussite islamic sunni, shia, ibadi indic hindu, sikh, jain buddhist theravada, mahayana, vajrayana east asian shinto, confucian ritual, daoist jewish jewish traditional indigenous american, african traditional, pacific traditional, siberian steppe traditional, asian traditional none secular Each faith shows by its local name from the catalogue, while the rules use the faith id. Yazidi, Druze and Zoroastrian communities stay as named minorities in the catalogue rather than faiths of their own. Faiths relate to each other in three ways: - Layered. Some faiths live in the same people at once. Shinto, mahayana, confucian ritual and daoist are layered with each other, and a traditional faith becomes layered with any faith once they have shared a province for 100 years. Layered faiths don't pull against each other, and a layered community gets no Wrong faith under a ruler of a faith it layers with. So Ming, with a confucian ritual court and Beijing 30 % mahayana and 30 % daoist with no houses of their own, has no Wrong faith there. - Rooted. The five traditional faiths need no house to be served, hold twice as hard (see below), and where they are a quarter or more of the people, their sacred places count as one house of worship (pull 1). - Kin. Faiths of the same family are kin. A kin faith's house can serve a community under 20 %. The faith mix Each province holds up to three faiths, as shares of its people. Once a year, every faith's pull is added up from the sources present: Source Pull A house of worship at step 1 / 2 / 3 (at least half filled with clergy) 1 / 1.5 / 2 The same house when fallow (short of clergy) half Each preacher of the faith stationed there 2 Each school of the faith (temple school, madrasa, monastery or cathedral school, seminary) 0.5 The ruler's faith in the ruler's capital 1 A lord's faith in a province he holds 0.5 Sunni, shia and ibadi: per 100 traders passing from markets of that faith 0.5, up to 2 A faith wave covering the province the wave's pull per carrier The ruler's faith where another faith is Restricted +1 The ruler's faith where a Chaplain official serves pull from houses and preachers doubled The ruler's faith where another faith is Persecuted doubled Each faith also has a hold , its resistance to change: its share times 4, or times 8 for a rooted faith. At the end of the year each faith gets a target share : its hold plus its pull, divided by all holds and all pulls in the province. Its share then moves 3 % of the way toward that target. If no faith has any pull, nothing moves. Worked example: one year. A province is half catholic and half protestant. Catholic has 3 pull and protestant 1. Both have a hold of 0.5 × 4 = 2. Catholic's target is (2 + 3) ÷ (2 + 2 + 3 + 1) = 0.625, and its share moves 3 % of the way there, from 0.5 to 0.50375. Hold slows change but never stops it. A province where one faith has three houses and another has one, with nothing else pulling, ends up about three to one after many years. Worked example: East Bengal, 1444 to 1700. East Bengal is 70 % hindu, 25 % asian traditional and 5 % sunni, with 2 hindu temples and a sunni lord, under a sunni ruler. The forest is cleared and a mosque is granted on each of 3 new field tiles. Now sunni has 3.5 pull (three mosques and the lord), hindu 2 (two temples) and asian traditional 1 (its sacred places). The mix settles toward sunni 54 %, hindu 31 % and asian traditional 15 %. Once asian traditional falls below a quarter it loses its sacred-places pull, and by about 1700 East Bengal is mostly sunni. Small and new faiths. A faith under 1 % with no house of its own is removed. A fourth faith arriving gets in only if it is larger than the smallest of the three. Then the smallest of the four joins the province's majority faith, so nobody simply vanishes. Languages work the same way. Hidden believers. For 100 years after a Persecuted faith's houses in a province are closed, that faith stays at 2 % or more there, unless an Inquisition removes the floor. If catholic is Persecuted in Japan and its houses in Nagasaki were closed 40 years ago, it stays at 2 %; after 100 years, or with an Inquisition, it may fall lower. People on the move. Refugees, settlers, migrants and soldiers settling at home shift the mix by their headcount at once, outside the pulls. Faith buildings The buildings themselves are described on Buildings. Religion decides what they do for the mix: Building Pull Serves its community House of worship, step 1 / 2 / 3 1 / 1.5 / 2 yes Landmark house (step 4) 3 in its province, 0.5 in every province of the owner's realm within 3 rings yes Minority house of worship 0.5 yes Monastery 1, plus 0.5 as a school once it has seats yes Religious school 0.5 no Pilgrimage shrine (holy places only) 1 yes A house of worship can be built for any faith present, not only yours. A minority house needs a community of a tenth of the people, or a Faith tolerance charter. Taking over a house. You can convert a house to another faith at any time. It costs half of building it, its pull flips to the new faith, its clergy's property gold goes to your treasury (twice over for monastic land), an "insult to faith" spark is raised in the province, and lords of the old faith waver one step. Worked example. Anglican England converts a catholic monastery with monastic land in Yorkshire. England pays half its building cost, the pull goes to anglican, the property gold is paid twice over, an "insult to faith" spark rises in Yorkshire, and the catholic lord Percy wavers a step. Tithes. Each year the clergy of each faith get 1 gold for every 10,000 people of that faith into their own purse, which they spend on a house in every town of their faith first. A Restricted faith's clergy keep their houses but can't build new ones. When a faith becomes Persecuted, its purse is seized. Preachers found houses. A preacher who spends 10 years in a province with no house of his faith founds a step-1 house there. Losing pull. A house loses its pull when it is burned or sacked with its town, or closed or converted under a Persecuted policy or a change of state faith. It gives half while it lacks clergy. Clergy. Faith buildings, almshouses and hospitals are where the clergy work, and the clergy are the pool for preachers and Chaplains. Whether clergy marry follows the faith. Communities and the Faith policy screen Any faith with at least 10 % of a province's people is a community there. A community of a faith other than yours is served when its faith is Tolerated or Restricted and it has a house of its own faith in the province (or of a kin faith if it is under 20 %), or needs none because it is rooted or layered. Otherwise it is unserved , and a Persecuted community is always unserved. You keep one policy row for each faith in your realm. Exactly one is Established : your state faith. The others are set to one of: Policy What happens Tolerated Keeps its houses, its clergy may build new ones, normal tax. If the faith is 10 % or more of the realm, Pious and clergy lords of the state faith waver once. Restricted Keeps its houses, no new ones. Its share of tax is 25 % higher (faith tax). The state faith gets +1 pull wherever it lives. Its lords waver one step. Persecuted Its houses are closed or handed to the state faith (your choice for the realm). No tax from it. The grievance Persecuted , counting as two, in every province where it is 10 % or more. The state faith's pull is doubled where it lives. 2 % of its people flee each year as refugees, craftsmen and scholars first. Its lords waver two steps. Every ruler of that faith on your border gets the Defend the faith war aim against you. The flag religious persecution active is set. A policy change takes effect at the next New Year. Each step toward Persecuted raises a spark for faith risings where that faith lives; a step back is not a spark. A Faith tolerance charter makes a faith Tolerated in that province whatever the realm row says. When a faith stops being Persecuted, the Persecuted grievance ends. Wrong faith. A province gets Wrong faith when a community of another faith is a third or more of the people and unserved, or is Restricted where it is the majority (unless protected; see Islam below). Worked example: La Rochelle under catholic France. Protestant share Policy House Wrong faith ? 40 % Tolerated none yes 20 % Tolerated none no 40 % Tolerated a protestant church no 60 % Restricted a protestant church yes 40 % Restricted a protestant church no Wrong faith ends when the community's house is built and its faith is Tolerated or Restricted, when it converts, or when a Faith tolerance charter is granted. Expulsion and the Inquisition Expel is a one-off decision, offered only on a Persecuted faith. Within a year, 70 % of its people leave as refugees for the nearest realm where it is Established or Tolerated, keeping their class where a slot is free; the rest convert or hide, and the hidden-believer floor still applies. The expelling realm gets the faith's houses and the gold of its property, the Persecuted grievance ends, and every province where they lived gets Bloodshed . Harm is never rewarded: an expulsion can never leave the expelling realm better off in people or skills; the host realm gains both. Worked example: the Alhambra decree. In 1492, with jewish Persecuted in Castile and the Ottomans the nearest realm that tolerates it, Castile expels the jewish faith. Within a year 70 % leave for the Ottomans, Castile takes their houses and property gold, the Persecuted grievance ends, and every province where they lived gets Bloodshed . The Inquisition is a decision only for realms ruled by a house (feudal realm, diet monarchy, household realm, bureaucratic empire, elective monarchy, absolute monarchy or constitutional monarchy) whose Established faith is catholic. While it runs it costs gold upkeep each year, removes the hidden-believer floor, adds +1 state-faith pull in every province with a Restricted or Persecuted community, and makes 1 % of the scholars and craftsmen in those provinces leave each year. It sets the flag inquisition established , and you can close it again. Lords and faith A lord loses one step when A lord gains one step when His faith is set to Restricted (two steps for Persecuted) The ruler builds or pays for a house of his faith in his land He is Pious or clergy of the state faith and the realm tolerates a faith of 10 % or more of the realm He is Pious or clergy of the state faith and the ruler takes over another faith's houses The state faith changes away from his The state faith changes to his Preachers Preachers are named agents of your state faith. You get one for each monastery or religious school of the state faith, one for every 5 houses of the state faith, one for each holy place of your faith you hold, plus any granted by events and some inventions. Worked example. Catholic Castile has 2 monasteries, 1 religious school and 10 houses of worship, and holds Santiago de Compostela. That is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 preachers. A preacher travels like an envoy and, once there, adds 2 pull for the state faith each year. He can go to your own provinces, to a subject's provinces without asking, to a foreign realm whose ruler has given leave ( Allow preachers , a diplomacy action), or to a foreign realm without leave. Without leave, that ruler may expel or execute him each year; if so, the flag missionary persecution is set and you get the Defend the faith war aim. You lose a preacher when he is killed or expelled abroad, when you recall him, or when your state faith changes (then all of them go). A preacher of a Persecuted faith inside the realm can lead a faith rising, which then spreads twice as fast. Changing the state faith The decision Adopt a faith is offered when that faith is at least 30 % of your capital province, or 40 % or more of the realm, or when an event offers it. When you adopt: - The old Established faith becomes Tolerated at once (you can change it from the next New Year). - Every preacher of the old faith is gone, and you have none of the new faith until its houses exist. - Lords' loyalty moves as in the table above. - You choose to keep the old faith's houses (serving it as a community) or take them over (pull flips, property gold paid, twice for catholic and orthodox monastic land, and an "insult to faith" spark where each is taken). - You choose to close the other faith's schools or keep them. Worked example. Catholic Sweden with 3 catholic preachers adopts protestant, takes over the catholic houses and closes catholic schools. Catholic becomes Tolerated, Sweden has no preachers at all until protestant houses exist, the houses become protestant with their pull, the property gold is paid (twice for monastic land), sparks rise where houses were taken, catholic schools close, catholic lords lose a step and protestant lords gain one. You can't adopt by decision again within 30 years; events aren't limited. After the event peace of augsburg , rulers inside the Empire can switch between catholic and protestant without the capital test (cuius regio). Holy places Holy places are a fixed list of named provinces, each with its faiths and its holder on 20 September 1378: Holy place Faiths Held at the start by Rome catholic Papal States Jerusalem catholic, orthodox, oriental christian, jewish, sunni, shia Mamluk Sultanate Mecca and Medina sunni, shia, ibadi Hejaz (the Sharifs, not their Mamluk overlord) Karbala and Najaf shia Jalayirids Constantinople orthodox Byzantium Echmiadzin oriental christian Jalayirids Aksum oriental christian Ethiopia Varanasi hindu Delhi (Jaunpur is not yet born) Lhasa vajrayana Tibet Temple of the Tooth theravada Gampola, then Kandy from 1592 Mount Wutai mahayana Ming Qufu confucian ritual Ming Ise shinto Japan Santiago de Compostela catholic Castile Bodh Gaya theravada, mahayana, vajrayana Delhi Amritsar appears as a holy place only once the founding of the Sikh Panth has happened, not before 1577. A holy place is always held by whoever owns its province. Holding a holy place of your own faith gives +1 preacher, the pilgrimage shrine there and 200 more traders passing through each year. Holding one of a faith you don't share lets every ruler of that faith use Defend the faith against you with that province as the prize. Pilgrims still come if you tolerate their faith and keep a house of it there. The holy places where church heads sit (the Pope, the Ecumenical Patriarch, a Caliph's claim, the Dalai Lama from 1578) are marked, and the heads have rules of their own, below. Heads of the faith Five faiths have a head with a seat. Nothing here is a meter: a head works through ties, wrongs, preachers, lords, war aims and calls to arms. Head Faith Seat How the patron is chosen The Pope catholic Rome A conclave when the Pope dies, or whoever holds Rome if the Papal States lose it The Ecumenical Patriarch orthodox Constantinople Whoever holds the seat, or its overlord The Catholicos oriental christian Echmiadzin Whoever holds the seat, or its overlord The Caliph sunni Mecca and Medina A Sunni ruler who holds both, directly or as overlord, and takes Claim the caliphate The Dalai Lama (from 1578) vajrayana Lhasa Whoever chose him in Altan Khan and the Dalai Lama , until Lhasa changes hands Anglican and Protestant churches are headed by their own crowns, and every other faith has no head. - The patron of a head who shares his faith gets the tie The Pope favours us (+15) with every realm of the faith and 1 more preacher. He owes them help: when a ruler of another faith attacks a fellow believer who holds a holy place, the patron gets a call to arms, and refusing it is an oath broken. A patron who changes faith loses the patronage and is Betrayed the faith (−30, fading over 30 years) with all of them. - A patron of another faith (the Ottomans in Constantinople, say) gets nothing but this: every community of the head's faith in his realm counts as served. - Taking a seat by war from a fellow believer of the head is Seized the seat (−20) with his faith; taking it from a ruler of another faith is Freed the seat (+20). - The conclave sits for one month when the Pope dies. Each Catholic realm casts a vote per cardinal and may send gold, 20 gold a vote, up to as many gold votes as it has cardinals. Rome casts 10 votes; if Rome wins or ties, the Pope is Italian and has no patron. - Censure. Declaring war on a ruler of your own faith, to take land, for tribute, to raid or with no aim, brings the head's censure: Censured by the Pope (−25) with every realm of the faith while the war lasts and fading over 10 years after, your lords of the faith waver once, and every fellow believer holds the Punish aim against you. A peace that gives back everything you took ends it at once. Crown-headed churches are never censured. - Raise our own patriarch , once, for an Orthodox realm with a great Orthodox house in its capital while Constantinople is held by another faith, for 40 gold: its church becomes crown-headed and it gets 1 more preacher. The Schism. On the start day there are two Popes: Urban VI in Rome, and Clement VII, elected at Fondi that day, who goes to Avignon. Each Catholic realm holds an obedience to one of them, and its Pope is the one whose censure, patronage and calls count for it. On 20 September 1378, 150 realms and lords follow Rome (the Empire, England, Hungary and Poland, Scandinavia, most of Italy), 30 follow Avignon (France and its great fiefs, Scotland, Naples, Savoy, Cyprus) and 22 have not chosen, among them Castile, Aragon, Portugal and Navarre. The Council of Pisa (1409) can add a third Pope and the Council of Constance (1414 to 1418) can end the Schism; both are events. At the start Byzantium is the Ecumenical Patriarch's patron, the Jalayirids the Catholicos's, and the Mamluks hold the Caliph's claim as overlord of the Hejaz. What each faith does differently Faith Its own rule Catholic Clergy don't marry; taking over monastic land pays double; the Inquisition Protestant +0.5 pull for each press and each school in the province; clergy marry Anglican (state faith) The crown heads the church: clergy lords never waver over faith policy Hussite Kin of protestant once the Reformation starts; at the end of the Reformation period or in 1620, whichever comes first, its shares merge into protestant, or into catholic where there is no protestant house Sunni, shia, ibadi (ruler) Protected communities: a served Restricted community gets no Wrong faith even as the majority Hindu A step-3 temple draws 150 traders a year Sikh Each gurdwara shelters 1,000 homeless, like an almshouse Theravada Each house of worship gives 20 student seats, like a small temple school Vajrayana A step-3 house or monastery can be granted as a lord's land, its abbot being the lord Orthodox Taking over monastic land pays double Secular No houses; a secular state may only Tolerate or Restrict other faiths; after 1850, +0.5 pull from each school in a town with a factory, once the realm has mass schooling Faith waves and events A faith wave is a temporary source of pull started by an event. It starts from a place, grows outward each year by its reach in rings of provinces, never past its limit, and ends after a number of years or with a period. In each province it reaches, it adds its pull for each carrier there: Carrier Counts Presses per press Schools per school Towns per town of market-town size or bigger Traders per 100 passing Rule the province is owned by the wave's starting country Army an army of that country stands or passed there this year Preachers per preacher of that faith, on top of his usual pull A wave never converts anyone by itself; it only adds pull. Worked example: the Reformation. When protestant reformation fires with the option to protect the reformer and the reform centre in Saxony, a protestant wave starts from Saxony. It gives 1.5 pull per press, school and market town or bigger in each province reached, spreads half a ring a year, never leaves Europe, and ends with the Reformation period. Other events also start waves: the catholic renewal after council of trent , Safavid shiism after safavid rise , the Sikh Panth, the Futa Jallon and Sokoto jihads, and the Mongol conversion to vajrayana after Altan Khan meets the Dalai Lama. Religion adds ten new events: the princes adopting the Reformation (1525 to 1563), the expulsion of the Moriscos (1609 to 1614), Altan Khan and the Dalai Lama (1578), the jizya reimposed (1679), the Raskol and the Old Believers (1653 to 1667), the revolution and the church (1790 to 1801), the separation of church and state (1905 to 1928), the missionary societies (1792 onward), court conversion to Islam (1444 to 1750) and court conversion to Christianity (1790 to 1914). For event writers, religion provides the conditions faith policy , holds holy place and faith wave active , and the effects faith wave , faith policy (Tolerated, Restricted or Persecuted; Established is set only by religion ) and preachers (extra preachers for some years, or for good with 0). The religion and religion share conditions read the mix and the state faith directly, and spread still shifts a share at once. The start Each country gets its ruler's faith from the catalogue, and each province the mix of the record that owns it, adjusted by region overrides. Where the people's majority differs from the ruler's faith, the ruler's faith starts at 15 % (court, garrison and town), as for sunni Delhi over a hindu people, pagan Lithuania over orthodox people, or sunni Mali over african traditional people. A community not otherwise sized starts at 5 %. Region override Starting mix The Balkans under the Ottomans orthodox 85 %, sunni 15 % Granada sunni 95 %, jewish 3 %, catholic 2 % The north Java coast hindu 55 %, sunni 25 %, asian traditional 20 % Punjab hindu 55 %, sunni 45 % Persia sunni 80 %, shia 20 % Egypt sunni 88 %, oriental christian 10 %, jewish 2 % Polish towns 5 % more jewish There are no Hussites at the start: Bohemia is Catholic until Hus is burned (1415) and the Defenestration of Prague (1419), and only then does the Hussite mix (hussite 70 %, catholic 27 %, jewish 3 %) come in by event. Lithuania and Samogitia keep their own Baltic traditional faith until their baptisms (Jogaila's in 1386 and 1387, Samogitia's in 1413), which are events. What religion gives other systems - Faith risings demand that their faith be Tolerated in the provinces they hold, or a house of worship there (a smaller demand rebels accept in a Talk). - Defend the faith also opens when a neighbour persecutes your faith in a province bordering yours, when your preacher is killed or expelled, and when a holy place of your faith is held by another faith. - Schools have a faith, and persecution drives scholars abroad. - Diplomacy gets the fact "same faith" (better starting opinion) and the Allow preachers leave. - Faith and language stay two separate mixes with two separate grievances. The computer players - They build a house of the state faith wherever it is below half, if gold allows, and a minority's house when that community has Wrong faith and its lords are wavering. - They tolerate any faith above 20 % of the realm unless zealous. A zealous ruler restricts, and persecutes only after an event or a war of religion. With jewish at 25 % of the realm, a mercantile AI tolerates it, a zealot restricts it, and a zealot after a war of religion persecutes it. - They send preachers first to their own provinces where the state faith is under half, then abroad where they have leave. - They adopt a new faith only when an event offers it or it is above 60 % of the realm. When it happens Once a year, alongside traders and the trade balance: pulls, hold and the 3 % move, small shares, hidden-believer timers, tithes, persecution flight (2 %), Inquisition flight (1 %), wave growth, preachers founding houses and the Hussite merge check. At New Year, pending policy changes take effect. Each month, preachers travel and expulsions progress. What you see - Province card, Faith line : each faith's share and whether it is rising or falling. Tap it to see this year's pulls for each faith with their sources, each community's state, and how fast the mix is moving and toward which faith. For example, Rouen at catholic 61 % falling, protestant 37 % rising and jewish 2 % shows the protestant community served by its own church and Tolerated, and the jewish 2 % as below a community with no grievance. - Country card, Faith row : for example "Catholic · 78 % of people · 3 more faiths · 2 preachers · holds no holy place". Tap it to open the Faith policy screen , with one row per faith. Preachers are also listed under Abroad. - Faith % is the share of people of the state faith or a faith layered with it. Ming, with 10 % confucian ritual, 50 % mahayana, 30 % daoist and 10 % asian traditional not yet layered, has a Faith % of 90. - The Faith map mode : at world zoom, provinces coloured by majority faith, hatched where another faith's community is 30 % or more, with holy-place icons. At region zoom, houses as town sprites, preachers as walking figures and waves as a spreading tint. At local zoom, the Faith line. Communities of a tenth or more start with a house of worship where their faith has one. - Province card, Faith line : each faith's share with ↑ or ↓. Tap it for this year's pulls per faith and their sources (houses, your capital, your policy), each community's state, any grievance, and how many points a year the mix moves toward which faith. - Your realm card, Peoples tab : the state faith, Faith %, and a card per faith in your realm with its share, people and provinces. The state faith is Established; every other faith has three buttons, Tolerated , Restricted and Persecuted , which are your tolerance for that faith. A change is shown as pending and takes effect at New Year; tap the current policy to cancel it. - Tolerated: houses stand, normal tax. - Restricted: a quarter more tax from its people, no new houses, your faith pulls harder; Wrong faith where it is the majority. - Persecuted: its houses close at New Year and its people pay no tax, your faith pulls twice as hard; Persecuted , which counts as two grievances, wherever it is a tenth or more. - The Faiths map mode : provinces coloured by majority faith, hatched where a second faith holds 30 % or more. - Faiths move each New Year, a fraction of a point at a time. - Head of the faith card , on the Peoples tab under the faith cards: the head, his seat and who holds it, the patron, what the patron gets and owes, and the one action open now ( Send gold to the conclave with − and +, Claim the caliphate , Raise our own patriarch ), or why it is not open. The Faith line on every realm's General tab carries a badge: Patron of the Pope , Caliph , Heads its church or a red Censured . Before you declare war, the Diplomacy tab warns you if the head will censure it and what it costs. The Faiths map mode marks each seat; tap one, or its button in the key, to open that head's card. - For now a cardinal is a Catholic house in a province of 300,000 people or more, and a great Orthodox house is any Orthodox house in the capital. Research: Research is how your country learns. You build schools, fill their seats with young men from the same recruit pool your army draws on, and after five years they graduate as scholars whose work, counted in scholar-years, unlocks new inventions. Every country climbs one shared invention tree that reaches back before the start, through the Ancient and Medieval eras, and on to the radios and tanks of the 1930s. Not every country starts at the same place on it: some begin the game still missing the plough, the horse or iron, and have to catch up. And every seat you fill is a soldier you didn't raise. How it works Schools, students and scholars Schools are town buildings with student seats. You get one by building it (gold up front), by a lord or the clergy founding one, or by conquering a town that has one. A school closes if its upkeep isn't paid, and schools are also lost when sacked in war or when a change of religion closes the other faith's schools. The school types come from the invention tree: School Seats Unlocked by Temple and monastery school 20 L1 Temple and monastery schools Madrasa 30 L2 Madrasa networks University 60 L7 Universities Academy 100 L12 Academies of science Village schools every province gets seats L18 Mass literacy schooling Students. You set how many seats to fill. Students are enrolled from recruits, local recruits filling local seats first, then the realm's. Students are lost by graduating, being called back into the army, famine and plague. Graduation. After 5 years a student graduates as a scholar, a year sooner where a Schoolmaster official runs the province. A graduate may instead become an official of the types his school trains: School Graduates can become Madrasa Judges or chaplains University Judges or stewards Academy Masters of works or wardens With G4 Examination system , scholars can become officials directly. Official types are described on Provinces. Scholars are gained by graduation, by hiring foreign scholars (gold), and by scholars fleeing war or persecution abroad to you. They are lost to old age, war in their town, persecution (they flee abroad) and being poached by a richer neighbour. Progress Each year, every scholar gives 1 scholar-year and every student 0.2 to your current study. When progress reaches the invention's cost, your country knows it, and the next invention in your study queue starts at once (see What you see); you're asked to choose only when the queue is empty. A known invention is never lost. If your schools close, progress on the current study stops, but nothing already known is lost. A country can also gain an invention by stealing it in war. You study one invention at a time , or two once you have an academy-level school (L12 Academies of science ). Why war and research don't mix - Every school seat filled takes one man from the recruit pool the army can raise. - Schools cost gold every year, from the same treasury that pays soldiers. - If you call students to arms, the schools empty back into recruits at once, research stops, and those students never become scholars. - Fighting in a province with a school can sack it and scatter its scholars, who may flee to a peaceful neighbour. What an invention costs Each invention costs scholar-years by its era: Era Years Cost in scholar-years Ancient before 600 10 Medieval 600 to 1377 15 I the start (1378) to 1500 20, raised for the long Era I of the 1378 start (see below) II 1500 to 1600 40 III 1600 to 1700 80 IV 1700 to 1800 150 V 1800 to 1870 250 VI 1870 to 1914 400 VII 1914 to the end of the campaign (31 August 1939) 650 - Studying ahead : an invention from an era later than the current date costs double for each era ahead . - Spread : each neighbour or trade partner that already knows an invention makes it 10 % cheaper, up to 60 % off . A trade partner is a country whose traders deposit or collect in your cities, or yours in theirs (see Trade). So in 1460, an Era II invention costs 40 × 2 = 80 scholar-years; with three neighbours who know it, 30 % off brings it to 56. Ancient and Medieval inventions are never ahead of their time, so they always cost 10 or 15, and the spread discount applies to them like any other: a country next to countries that know them catches up fastest. Ox plough with four neighbours who know it costs 10 − 40 % = 6 scholar-years. What you may study You may study any invention whose parent you know plus everything listed under also needs . Where alternatives are given ("or"), either one is enough. Contact inventions open only after a contact event, for example the Atlantic crossing for maize and potatoes, and, for a country of the Americas, first contact with a country from across the ocean for F03 Riding and pack animals (see Without it). Era VIII is out of the game, and Era VII only within the campaign, which ends 31 August 1939. Some inventions change research itself: L5 Printing (inventions spread +20 %, schools cost less), C1 Paper making (schools cost less), L4 Metal movable type (students cost less), L6 Humanist learning and L11 Experimental science (scholars +research), L3 Observatories (+research for learning and sea inventions), L10 Spectacles and telescopes (scholars work into old age), L14 Encyclopedias (spread +20 %), L20 Research laboratories (research +50 %) and L21 Radio (faster spread of news and inventions). The tree There is one tree , from the root Settled life , which everyone knows. It splits into four branches (called boughs before), which every country also knows at the start: - R1 Tilling and building - R2 Fire and metal - R3 Counting and records - R4 Boats The tree reaches back before the start with two past eras , Ancient (before 600) and Medieval (600 to 1377), and then runs through Eras I to VII. Era I runs from the start to 1500: a campaign from 1378 plays all 122 years of it (the 1444 checkpoint only its last 56), so an Era I invention costs about 2.2 times as much as it would from 1444 and a realm still reaches Era II around 1500 (the number is a first guess for balancing). Inventions grow era by era, and many need an invention from another branch. The letter in an invention's id only says what it is about (F food, C crafts and industry, T trade, S sea, W war, B building, G government, L learning); it is not a separate tree. Each invention is one config row ( id , parent , also needs , era , unlocks , start regions ), so new inventions such as Andean terrace farming, Ethiopian church schools or Javanese irrigation can be hung anywhere on the tree without code. The tree holds 187 inventions : 13 past inventions and 174 from Era I on. Twenty of them keep ids the event tree uses (marked "event id" below) so events keep working; the event tree's technology and innovation stats read them from the tree. Where another system gives an invention's effect in numbers (Warfare, Trade, Exploration and Colonies), that system owns the numbers. Nuclear physics and Rocketry are never studied, and the other Era VII inventions stay in play until August 1939 with what they did by then. For example, Venice also knows Double-entry bookkeeping, Bills of exchange, Glass and lenses, Tax registers and Lateen and junk rigging; Portugal and Castile have the Carrack and caravel; the Ottomans also know roads, tax registers, the compass and rigging, bombards, gunpowder infantry, glass and variolation; the Inca also know stone castles, roads, raised fields and temple schools; Scotland and Switzerland know Pike squares; Muisca lack Dressed stone and Sail, and the Purépecha lack Writing, Written law codes and Temple and monastery schools. At the 1378 start. The start groups were drawn up for 1444, so the examples above include realms that are not born yet in 1378 (Kazan, the Crimea, Malacca, Kongo and others, which form later). New campaigns start on 20 September 1378, and the same groups apply with a few changes for that year: the Ottomans don't yet know bombards, gunpowder infantry or tax registers; Bohemia and Hungary have no wagon fort; Portugal and Castile have no carrack and caravel (Genoa and Venice do); Ming has no tax registers yet (the Yellow Registers come by event in 1381); Timur's realm stands with the settled khanates and has no observatory, while the Jalayirids keep the Maragha tradition. The realms of 1378 that the 1444 map lacks, such as the Jalayirids, the Anatolian beyliks, the White Horde or the Tepanecs, start in the group of their neighbours. Goryeo, in the Korea group, keeps metal movable type (Jikji, 1377). A start set is always complete : every invention in it has its parent (or one of its alternatives) and everything it also needs in the same set, and the game's data check refuses a set that isn't. So with the 1444 sets the Latin, Orthodox, Islamic, South Asian and East Asian countries stand in Era I with 23 to 38 inventions, maritime Southeast Asia in Era I with 21, and mainland Southeast Asia is split between Medieval and Era I. The khanates, hordes, Tibet, Ethiopia, the Swahili coast and the Sahel stand in Ancient with 7 to 15. Forest Africa stands in Ancient with 3 or 4 (iron but no horses), and Mesoamerica, the Andes and North America in Ancient with 2 to 10, without iron or horses. No African country south of the Sahara starts with B1 Stone castles : they defend with B4 earthworks until they learn dressed stone. Standing. Your standing is the latest era, from Ancient on, of which you know at least a quarter of the inventions, and a quarter of every earlier era's too. Ancient is the floor: no country stands lower. If your standing is earlier than the era of today's date, you are behind the times by the eras in between: a country standing in Ancient at the start, in Era I, is behind the times by 2 eras. Standing changes nothing by itself; it tells you, and the AI, how far behind a country is. See The 1378 Start. Research elsewhere - The event tree's literacy stat reads your scholars and schools per thousand people. - Your inventions known, each weighted by its era cost, make up the Technology win score on Your Realm. Each month A turn is one week. These steps run once a month, in the turn in which a new month begins. Cadence What happens Monthly Progress from scholars and students is added; if it reaches the cost, the invention is learned and the next queued study starts (you choose only when the queue is empty) Yearly Student cohorts age and 5-year cohorts graduate; scholars age; spread discounts are worked out again with trade partners At each era boundary The cost of studying ahead changes Progress moves every month by a twelfth of the yearly rate, and an invention is known in the month it is paid for. With two studies, each gets half. The AI An isolationist AI fills its schools and avoids war; a hegemon seeker keeps its recruits for the army instead of students. Every AI country studies the invention it can study that costs it least right now (ties go by id), fills every empty seat while at peace and none at war, and calls its students to arms only when it is at war with no recruits left. A country behind the times therefore studies its missing past inventions first, since they cost least. The AI picks one study at a time and keeps no queue. What you see Everything about research and schools is in one place: the Research tab of your country card (called Learning before; tap your realm's name or flag, then Research). Studying all happens on one screen: the queue, the tree and the invention you've picked sit together. Schools is one button in the tab's header. - The overview. At the top: your scholars, students, scholar-years a year, how many of the tree's inventions you know, and the era with your standing: "Era I · abreast of the times", or "Ancient · behind the times by 2 eras · 9 past inventions to catch up". Tap the catch-up line to open the tree at the first one. When nothing is studied, the card says so in red. - The queue strip. Along the top: your current study (two with an academy) with its progress bar and the time left, then up to 5 queued inventions in order, each a chip with its time. Tap a chip to show it in the tree; drag it, or use its ◀ and ▶ buttons, to change the order; ✕ takes it out. When a study is learned, the first queued invention whose needs you now know starts at once, with nothing lost. A queued invention whose needs aren't met when its turn comes is skipped, stays in the queue and is marked waiting. - The tree. The whole tree as one picture: the root Settled life at the left, then a column for each era ( Ancient , Medieval , I to VII ), with the era headings pinned along the top and today's era marked Now . The four branches are four bands across the picture, each with its name pinned at the left edge. Lines run from each invention to the ones that grow from it, across bands too; the "also needs" lines are drawn only for the invention you've picked, highlighted. Each invention reads as known (✓), being studied, can be studied (◆) or locked. Queued inventions carry their place number (1 to 5), and when you pick an invention whose needs you don't know yet, the path to it is highlighted, so you see in the tree what the queue would study. Drag inside the frame to move around. - Close up shows named inventions; Whole tree fits the full tree in the frame, each invention a dot in its state's colour, so you see at a glance how far each branch reaches. Switch with the Whole tree / Close up button or by pinching inside the frame; tap a place in the Whole tree to go Close up there. - Above the tree, chips jump to what matters and open its sheet: My study , Can study ◆ n (each tap goes to the next one) and, while you lack any past invention, Catch up n (each tap goes to the next past invention you can study). - The sheet. The invention you've picked (or, with nothing picked, your current study): what it does, what it grows from and what it also needs (each marked ✓ or ✗; tap one to jump to it), its cost in scholar-years, about how long it takes at your pace, how many neighbours already know it (each makes it cheaper) and whether it is ahead of its time. A past invention's sheet also says what it opens and what you lack without it. The sheet has one action that fits: - Study now when nothing is being studied; - Add to queue when you know its needs, or they are queued ahead of it; - Queue the path when you don't: it lists the missing steps in an order you can study them, then the invention, with the total scholar-years and time, before you tap. If the path would make the queue longer than 5, the sheet says so and queues none of it. A known invention has no action. Study now never drops progress; to replace a study under way, the sheet offers Switch to this study and says how many scholar-years you would lose. - Schools. Your students: the −5 and +5 buttons set how many seats to fill. Each student is a man the army can't raise: more students fill from your recruit pools at once, fewer go back to them. In need of soldiers? folds out Call students to arms , which empties every school back into recruits at once; research stops until you fill seats again, and those students never become scholars. Then each school, where it is (tap to see the province) and its students, schools being founded with the months until they open, and their upkeep a year, also shown as the Schools line of the Treasury. Found a school opens the list of your towns without a school: a temple school costs 60 gold and opens after 12 months (a madrasa, with 30 seats, if you know Madrasa networks). You need Temple and monastery schools or Madrasa networks. On a phone. Where the tab is at least 500 points wide (Wide), the sheet stands beside the tree and the branch names sit in a pinned column. On a narrower screen (Tall), the queue strip, the tree and the sheet stack: the strip scrolls sideways inside itself, the branch names shrink to a coloured strip with the branch's first letter, and the sheet slides up from the bottom when you pick something and closes with its own ✕ . Everything stays inside the safe areas, every chip, node and button is at least 44 points, nothing needs hover, and the page never scrolls sideways. Elsewhere: - The Overview of your Realm book has a Research tile, "Three-field rotation · 40 %", that opens the tab; it turns red with "Choose what to study" when nothing is studied. - Another country's card shows its standing, how many inventions it knows and what it studies, and how many inventions it knows that you don't: those are the ones it makes cheaper for you as a neighbour or trade partner. - The nation picker at the start of a campaign shows each country's standing next to its name ("Starts in Ancient", "Starts in Era I"), so you know a country starts behind before you choose it. - When you learn an invention and your queue is empty, an alert says "Learned X. With something queued, the next study simply starts. - A commander's Train list offers only the troop types your realm knows; the rest are named with a button to the Research tab (pikes need Pike squares, knights Heavy armoured cavalry). In the game now Research plays one study at a time, with a queue of up to 5 behind it. Every country starts with a school in its capital (a madrasa where it knows Madrasa networks, else a temple school), half its seats filled and a few scholars, so research moves from the first month. The tree reaches back to the Ancient and Medieval eras, every country starts from its start group, and the four penalties for lacking a past invention are in: worse harvests without the Ox plough, no horse regiments or camel caravans without Riding and pack animals, half the food carried without Wheel and carts, weaker regiments without Iron smelting. Inventions already change harvests (Three-field rotation and later farming inventions make each harvest a band better), which troop types can be trained, and the troop cap (Standing regiments, Mass conscription, Railway mobilization). Castles and roads follow with buildings. Not yet in the game: the academy's second study, stealing and sacking in war, poaching, foreign scholars and the Atlantic crossing for maize and potatoes; the other effects are shown as text.
