Subjects: Subjects are countries on the map that answer to another country, their overlord. This system decides what types of subject exist, what each side owes the other, how loyal a subject is and why, and how a subject is made, tightened, loosened, folded into your realm, released or lost. Loyalty is never a hidden number: it is one of four steps, moved each season by named reasons you can read on the subject's card. How it works The ladder of rule All land sits on one ladder of rule : royal land (run by your officials), lord's land (run by a named lord inside your realm), subject realm, and independent. The one rule that separates a lord from a subject: a subject has its own country on the map with its own treasury, army, lords and diplomacy, while a lord is a card inside your realm. At the start, any catalogue subject that is not its own map nation becomes a lord of its overlord, his card filled from the catalogue's history. Six types of subject Vassal Tributary Union March Colony Protectorate Icon shield chest two crowns watchtower anchor key Pays you 10 % of its taxes 15 % of its income, in gold or grain 5 % nothing 25 %, and its trade goods flow home first 10 % Fights for you when called, by loyalty, like a lord never always, if Loyal or Wavering only in wars on its own frontier; raids your enemies there defends itself only when called Own diplomacy yes, but no wars or alliances against you or your allies yes, fully no: your envoys speak for it yes, but no alliances no no Own subjects yes yes yes no no no You owe it defence when attacked defence against anyone but you defence; one ruler for both a yearly stipend of gold or titles defence; ships on its sea route defence Weight toward the subject limit 1 ½ 1 ½ 1 1 Drift none −1 none −1 none −1 Fold in yes no: tighten to Vassal first yes, as Merge the crowns yes yes, into royal land yes Examples at the 1378 start Brittany under France; Wallachia and Bosnia under Hungary; Naples held of the Pope Goryeo, Ryukyu, Dai Viet to the Ming; Byzantium to the Ottomans; Tver and Ryazan to Mamai's Horde; Tenochtitlan to the Tepanecs Sardinia under Aragon; the Lordship of Ireland under England the Tibetan and Western Guards commanderies on the Ming frontier Genoese Gazaria; Cypriot Korykos Bukhara under Russia; Indian princely states under the Company (event tree) A subject pays its share from its own treasury each month, so a poor subject pays little. Tribute taken in grain arrives at your nearest castle and counts toward Food. Protectorates exist only from era VI, or from era IV for an overseas trade empire. Ties are labels on the bond that change one or two rules: Tie Set when Effect Kin its ruler is of your ruling house (appanages) +1 loyalty reason; if your line dies out, its ruler has a claim to your throne Held of the Church the overlord is a religious head (the Pope's fiefs) pays a token (1 %), never fights Held in fief a sovereign kingdom holds its crown from someone else pays a token (1 %), never called to war; counts ½ toward the subject limit Second master it also pays tribute to someone else the second master gets a small tribute (5 %) and no other rights; if the two masters fight, it leans to the stronger Hostage at court you hold its heir +1 reason; −2 if he is mistreated or lost Colony stages: Stage When Change Outpost founded pays 25 %, no army of its own, your governor (an official) runs it Settled 5+ provinces, more than half settler people raises its own militia; its settlers become a peace voice that can be Wavering; from here its loyalty is counted each season (an Outpost stays Loyal) Self-governing 10+ provinces and 50 years, or an event (dominion) pays 10 %, keeps its own lords; can no longer be folded in, only released or kept When a Settled or Self-governing colony turns Disloyal, Revolutions gets the settler-independence trigger. The subjects at the start The relations data has eight subject types, which are mapped onto the six: vassal to Vassal; fief to Vassal with Held of the Church or Held in fief (Naples from the Pope, Andorra from Foix); appanage to Vassal with Kin ; tributary to Tributary; personal union to Union; frontier commandery to March; colony to Colony; and estate (Catalonia, Flanders, the Castilian magnates, Moravia and others) to a lord of its crown, never a separate country. Event subjects map the same way, with protectorate and puppet becoming Protectorate and dominion a Colony at Self-governing. On 20 September 1378 the 228 subject records minus 24 estates give 204 subjects : 126 vassals, 68 tributaries, 4 unions, 4 marches and 2 colonies. (The 1444 checkpoint has 135.) Loyalty A subject has one of the lords' four steps: Step Pays When called to war Foreign envoys Other Loyal all it owes comes at once, whole army turns them away can be folded in Wavering half half its army, late; home after 6 months unless the war is on its border listens Disloyal nothing refuses; each further call is another down reason bargains for a backer hides its army's size In revolt nothing at war with you: the independence war Reasons are named badges pointing up or down, each worth one or more arrows. At the end of every season (3 months) the arrows are added: +2 or more moves loyalty one step up, −2 or less one step down, anything else stays. Loyalty never moves twice in the same direction within 12 months. Up Arrows Down Arrows You are much stronger (your soldiers ≥ 3 × theirs) +1 You are not much stronger (theirs ≥ ½ of yours) −1 Same faith as your ruler +1 Different faith −1 (−2 if you persecute it) Same people as your ruler +1 Different people, not accepted −1 You defended it in the last 20 years +1 You left it alone (attacked, you didn't join), 20 years −1 Gift in the last 5 years +1 Heavy / crushing tribute −1 / −2 Marriage between your houses +1 You lost a war in the last 10 years −1 Kin; Hostage at court (each, so both is +2) +1 New ruler on your throne (first 5 years) −1 Your resident at its court +1 Courted (a foreign envoy stationed at its court) −1 Common enemy (the same rival) +1 Stretched thin (over your subject limit) −1; −2 for the furthest few Long held (30+ years) +1 Far away (no land border, and no sea route: both of you holding coast on a linked sea) −1 Light tribute +1 Outgrown (more provinces than you, or than its type allows: a Vassal over half of yours) −1 Given a crown (raised while Wavering), 10 years +1 Master of others −3 Loosened, 10 years +2 Hostile / Rival stance toward you −2 / −1 Type's drift −1 Force used (you folded in, deposed or restored another subject by force), 5 years −1 Another subject deposed, 5 years −1 Doctrine of lapse used on another, 10 years −1 Refused a call again, 12 months −1 Missed march stipend, 12 months −1 You left another subject alone, 5 years −1 Two quarrelling subjects forbidden, 5 years −1 Events can add or remove a reason by id, or add a one-off named reason with its own arrow for a stated time. Starting loyalty comes from the dataset's autonomy: very low, low and moderate start Loyal; high and very high start Wavering; one step lower if the subject is Hostile toward its overlord in the data. What an overlord can do Each action is a button on the subject's card; a locked button names its first missing requirement. Action Cost Effect Set tribute (none, light, normal, heavy, crushing) none pays ×0, ×0.5, ×1, ×1.5, ×2 of the type's share; light +1, heavy −1, crushing −2 Take tribute in grain none arrives as grain at your nearest castle Call to war none answered like a lord, by loyalty and type; tributaries are never called Send a gift 6 months of its income +1 for 5 years Station a resident one envoy while it stays +1; reveals a courting foreign envoy; shows its true army even when Disloyal Lend an official one official's wages +1; the official's type effect applies there Take a hostage only from a Loyal or Wavering subject, or as a peace term Hostage at court ; the heir returns when its ruler dies; harming him −2 Arrange a marriage an heir or princess the marriage reason; a path to a Union Tighten (Tributary to Vassal only) one envoy for 6 months; subject Loyal a Wavering subject refuses and drops a step; Vassal to Union is not possible Loosen (Vassal or Protectorate to Tributary) none +2 for 10 years Fold in see below it becomes one of your lords Release none independent and Friendly toward you; no other subject's reasons change Depose its ruler a pretender of yours, or its ruler Disloyal (if In revolt, win first) your candidate rules, starting Loyal; every other subject −1 for 5 years Raising a lord. A Loyal or Wavering lord holding at least 3 provinces can be raised to a Vassal, or to a March if his land borders a foreign realm (you choose): his provinces become his own country on the map and his retinue its army. A Wavering lord raised gets Given a crown +1 for 10 years; a Loyal one gets nothing extra. He leaves your lord capacity and counts against your subject limit; his land leaves your realm, you get a share instead of half his taxes, and he may make his own friends abroad. Obligations both ways - When anyone but you attacks a subject you owe defence, you are called as if you were its ally. Refusing gives you an Oath broken, the subject You left it alone , and every other subject −1 for 5 years. - Each year a March's stipend is missed, it gets −1. - A Union shares your ruler, so every war of that ruler is the Union's war, and its lords' peace voices add to yours. - Two subjects of one overlord can't fight without leave. You pick a side (the loser drops a step) or forbid it (both −1 for 5 years). Subject limit The subject limit is how many subjects your ruler can watch over. It comes from Government, starting from the catalogue's administrative capacity: very low 2, low 3, moderate 5, high 7, very high 9. It is a separate number from lord capacity. Each direct subject counts by its weight (Tributary, March and Held in fief ½, the rest 1). Over the limit, every subject gets Stretched thin −1, and for each point you are over, one more of the furthest subjects takes −1 more (11 of 7 hits the four furthest). Subjects with subjects. A subject that holds subjects counts 3 times its type's weight plus 1 for each of its own subjects, and gets Master of others −3, which goes away when it releases them. Only the direct overlord acts on a subject; a subject's own subjects pay you nothing and count nothing toward your subject limit. When a subject is folded in or falls, its subjects step up to you, keeping their loyalty. March, Colony and Protectorate can't hold subjects. Folding in Folding in makes a subject's ruler one of your lords and removes its country from the map. It needs: Loyal for the last 10 years, a subject for 20 years or more, a land path or your sea route to it, room for one more lord in lord capacity, and a type other than Tributary or Self-governing colony. At the start each subject counts as held since its dataset start date (20 years when unknown), and one Loyal at the start counts as Loyal for 10 years. You keep one envoy at its court for 1 month per province; if the subject drops to Wavering, the folding stops and the envoy comes home. When it completes, its ruler becomes one lord holding all its provinces (its own lords merged into his card), with its buildings, its army as his retinue and its treasury as his wealth. Its provinces get Foreign rule for 10 years unless it shared your faith and people. - An Outpost or Settled colony folded in becomes royal land at once, needing your officials. - Merge the crowns folds in a Union after 50 years in union with the junior crown Loyal: its provinces join the realm, its lords become yours one by one keeping their loyalty, and its laws become a charter in its provinces. - When the ruler of a Loyal Vassal or Union dies without an heir, you can inherit and fold it in at once, ignoring the 10 and 20 years. For other subjects its lords pick a new ruler, and you may back a candidate with an envoy. - With the event flag doctrine of lapse , any subject whose ruler dies without a natural heir is folded in, and every other subject takes −1 for 10 years. Losing subjects - Drifting. A Disloyal subject stops paying, refuses calls, and bargains with foreign envoys for a backer that agrees to declare Break a subject when it rises. - Rising. A Disloyal subject rises to In revolt when it has a backer at peace and willing, or its overlord is at war elsewhere with over half its peace voices for peace, or an event says so; the seasonal count alone never goes past Disloyal. Every other Disloyal subject of yours that borders it or shares its backer rises too. The independence war starts with its aim fixed as Independence and its backer joining. If you win, the peace can restore it one type tighter, or fold it in at once if it shares a border. If it wins, it goes free with a Hostile stance toward you. - Changing masters. A Disloyal subject bordering a rival of yours can ask to pass to that rival; the rival takes it when it fits within the rival's subject limit. It becomes the rival's subject of the same type, and you and the rival turn Hostile toward each other. - Taken by force. Break a subject is a war declared on you, the overlord; the subject answers by its type and loyalty like any call. If the attacker wins, it chooses whether the subject goes free or becomes its own. - The overlord's fall. If an overlord is destroyed or becomes someone's subject, its Tributaries and Marches go free, and its Vassals, Unions and Colonies go to whoever took its capital if it wants them, otherwise free. Making a subject - A peace term Become a subject (over three quarters peace voices): the winner picks Vassal or Tributary, or Protectorate from era VI (era IV for an overseas trade empire). A distant loser with no land path can only be a Tributary. - After a 20-year tribute term has run, the receiver can offer the payer Tributary by envoy, which a weaker payer accepts. - Winning a war to seat a pretender: the realm becomes your Vassal or ally, the new ruler starting Loyal. - By agreement through Diplomacy: when its count says yes to Offer overlordship or Ask for protection , the smaller country becomes a Tributary, or a Vassal if it asked for that. - A ruler inheriting another crown after a marriage makes a Union. - A frontier grant : give your titles and a gift to a frontier chief who is nobody's subject and shares your border, and he becomes a March. - Chartering a group of your colonial provinces in one distant region makes one Colony. - Events ( vassalize , create country … subject of , relation: personal union ) create the type they name; a created country is a Colony at Self-governing unless named otherwise. France, 1444 to 1453 (on the 1444 checkpoint world) France has high administrative capacity and a subject limit of 7, with 10 vassals and the appanage of the Dauphiné. - The start. Brittany starts Wavering and Armagnac Loyal. France uses 11 of its subject limit of 7, so every subject, Brittany and Foix included, has Stretched thin , and the four furthest take −1 more. - Folding in the Dauphiné. The Dauphiné is a Loyal Vassal with Kin , a subject since 1349, with 3 provinces. France sends one envoy for 3 months; the Dauphin becomes a great lord inside France, which now uses 10 of its limit of 7. - Two small vassals. Folding in the French minor lordships and Nevers over the next years brings it to 8 of 7, and lord capacity fills up instead. - Brittany is courted. England stations an envoy at Brittany's court; France stations a resident there and arranges a marriage. The season ends at 3 up and 3 down, so Brittany stays Wavering. When war with England resumes in 1449 and France calls, Brittany comes with half its army, late. - Armagnac. France sets Armagnac's tribute to heavy to pay for the war. Armagnac turns Disloyal, and an event makes it rise. France wins, the peace folds Armagnac in at once because it shares a border, and every other subject takes Force used −1 for 5 years. Playing as a subject Every playable subject at the start (94 on 20 September 1378) can be played. You see your own card from below with the same badges, and can pay and be protected, stop paying, find a backer, wait for your overlord's bad war, or marry into its house to inherit its crown (a union can run either way). A Loyal subject that politely asks by envoy for a looser type gets it if the overlord's AI is cautious or over its subject limit. A subject that wins its independence war can make its old overlord its own subject in the same peace if the voices allow. The computer players As overlord, an AI folds in Loyal subjects when lord capacity allows and its personality likes centralising, loosens a Disloyal subject when at war elsewhere, stations residents on its biggest Wavering subjects, and never goes more than 1 over its subject limit. As a subject, a Disloyal AI looks for a backer; an opportunist rises the moment its overlord is losing a war, a cautious one waits for a backer and its neighbours. As a rival, it courts its rivals' Wavering subjects and picks Break a subject against the overlord with the most Disloyal subjects. Loyalty is worked out once a season per subject from cached reasons. Each month A turn is one week; these steps run once a month, at the end of the turn in which the new month begins. Each month tribute is paid, tighten and fold-in envoys progress (stopping if the subject wavers), and risings are checked. At each season's end reasons are recomputed and loyalty moves. Each year march stipends fall due and colony stages are checked. What you see - The subjects list (a tab on the country card): how much of the subject limit is used, monthly tribute in gold and grain, and one row per subject with its type icon, loyalty, up and down arrow counts, what it pays and its worst reason, sorted worst first. - The subject card , in the lord card's frame: type, ruler, provinces, army, treasury, its own subjects, loyalty with its reasons, what it pays and how it comes when called, and the action buttons. - World zoom : a subject in its direct overlord's colour with a 2-pixel diagonal hatch in its own colour and a dotted border with the overlord, never two hatches stacked. - Region zoom : the type's icon on the subject's capital, its frame tinted by loyalty (green, yellow, orange, red). - The subjects map mode : your subjects coloured by loyalty, with a line to each courted subject from the courting country's capital. - Long-press a subject on the map (or select it and press the card button on a controller) to open its card. Subjects in the game today - Where : your realm's Diplomacy tab lists your Subjects : how much of your reach they use (from your administrative capacity: 2 to 9, 5 where it is unknown), the tribute they send each month, and a row per subject with its type, loyalty, arrows up and down, what it pays and its worst reason. Tap a subject to open its card. - The subject's card (its own Diplomacy tab): its loyalty and every reason behind it as a badge, what it pays and how it comes to your wars, and your actions: set the tribute ( None , Light , Normal , Heavy , Crushing ), Send a gift (six months of its income, +1 for 5 years), Loosen to tributary (Vassal or Protectorate, +2 for 10 years) and Release (it goes free as your friend). - What they pay : the type's share times the tribute level, all of it while Loyal, half while Wavering and nothing while Disloyal. A Vassal pays 10 in 100 of its taxes; a Tributary 15 in 100 of its income. It shows as Tribute in your Treasury tab. - Loyalty is counted at the end of every season: two more arrows up than down raise it a step, two more down lower it, never twice the same way within a year. You hear when it moves. A Disloyal subject refuses your calls to arms. - Making subjects : send an envoy to Offer overlordship to a smaller realm (it becomes your tributary) or Ask for protection of a larger one (you become its vassal), or demand tribute. The other realms offer overlordship too. - Your envoys at their court : Station a resident (+1 loyalty, takes one of your envoys while he stays), Tighten to vassal (a Loyal tributary, one envoy for 6 months) and Fold into your realm (Loyal for 10 years, a subject for 20, sharing a border, and room under your lords cap; one envoy for a month per province). When folding in completes, their land is yours, held by their ruler as one of your lords, and the country leaves the map. Other realms fold in their subjects too, one at a time. - Rising : a Disloyal subject may rise and declare its independence war. The other realms' subjects rise when their overlord is losing a war elsewhere or a stronger enemy of it waits next door, and their Disloyal neighbours rise with them. Lose land in the peace and the subject is taken back one type tighter (its fellow subjects remember the force used); otherwise it is free. If you are a subject and Disloyal, Rise for independence is on your Diplomacy tab. - Their heir : Take a hostage from a Loyal or Wavering subject: his heir lives at your court (+1 loyalty) until you Send the heir home or 20 years pass. - Backers : a Disloyal subject with a stronger enemy of its overlord next door rises with that realm at its side; the backer declares war on the overlord at once. - The Subjects map mode : from the map mode menu, your realm in its colour, your subjects green, amber or red by loyalty, your overlord purple. Tap one for its Diplomacy tab. - On the realms map, zoomed out : every subject is washed in its direct overlord's colour with thin diagonal stripes (2 map pixels wide) of its own colour, and its border with that overlord is dotted instead of a solid line, so Brittany reads as part of France at a glance; a subject of a subject shows only its own overlord's colour, never a second set of stripes. Occupied land keeps its occupation hatch, and zoomed in each realm is drawn in its own colour again. - Personal unions : a marriage is a path to a crown. When a ruler dies without a son, because his heir died first or none was born, each house married into his has a 1 in 10 chance of a claim on his throne, held for 20 years. One such death in 4 leaves no heir at all, and the crown passes to the ruler of the house married most often into his, as a Union , if neither realm is at war and the inheriting realm answers to no one. Your own line is spared that: you can inherit, but are never inherited. Your Diplomacy tab's Your house lists the houses married into yours and your claims; another realm's tab says when your houses are married or you claim its throne. - Playing as a subject : on your own Diplomacy tab, or your overlord's card, Your overlord shows your card as they see it, with the same badges, then Your choices . Stop paying keeps your tribute but makes you Disloyal a step each season ( Withholds tribute −2); Pay tribute again ends it. Ask to loosen (Loyal only) makes you a tributary when your overlord is cautious (unrest or outside threats high) or over its reach, and says when they would refuse. Find a backer names the rivals of your overlord, at peace, next door and as strong, who would join your rising; the first of them does. Their wars show how many of their voices want peace, the moment to rise. Marry into their house opens their card: if their line dies out and your house is married most into theirs, you inherit their crown and they become your union. - Turning the tables : in your war for independence, once you hold more provinces than your old master and over three quarters of its voices want peace, Make them your subject ends the war with them as your vassal (or tributary without a land border). - The subject card : framed like a lord's card, with its kind, its ruler as the start data names him (Duke John IV, age 39 · House Montfort), provinces, army, treasury and its own subjects. - Long-press : hold a finger on a realm on the map (for the Settings long-press time) to open its card at the Diplomacy tab. - Merge the crowns : a Union cannot be folded in. Once it has been in union 50 years and is Loyal, Merge the crowns on its card joins its provinces to your realm at once, its lords serving you with the loyalty they have. When the ruler of a Loyal Vassal or Union dies with no heir, its overlord takes it at once. - Courting : on another realm's subject, Court their loyalty stations one of your envoys at its court: it counts Courted (−1) against its overlord, and a Disloyal subject may rise. Each season there is 1 in 4 they find out (−25 with the overlord, fading over 10 years) and he comes home. Your own subjects' cards show Courted when someone courts them, and name who once you have a resident there; the Subjects lens draws a dotted line from the courting realm. Rival and hostile neighbours court your Wavering and Disloyal subjects too. - Events : historical events can make a subject ( becomes a protectorate of … ), loosen or tighten it, add or lift a loyalty reason for some months, and break the tie ( released … goes free as a friend ). What the event will do is written on its card before you choose, and the change lands on the subject's card and the Subjects lens like any other. Events can also ask how loyal a subject is, or how many subjects you hold. - Not yet : the succession war of an inherited realm's lords, and harming a hostage come later; distance gives no reason yet. Faith and language do: the same state faith or court language pulls a subject closer, a different faith pushes it away, more so where you persecute it. How it connects - Diplomacy: the Subject relation record, independence wars, release, envoys, marriages, protection asks, courting and inherited crowns. - Your-Realm: lords and their loyalty steps, the lord card, ruler and heirs, soldiers, treasury, Oaths broken and Food from grain tribute. - Government: the subject limit, lord capacity, and which types a government may hold. - Warfare: calls to war, Break a subject and Independence , peace terms, a Union's peace voices. - Provinces: royal land from folded colonies, charters from merged crowns, lent officials. - Rebellions: the Foreign rule grievance and lords rising with land. - Religion and Culture: same faith, persecution, Held of the Church , same people and accepted cultures. - National-Strengths: changes to the subject limit, drift or types. - Revolutions: settler independence, type changes and releases by revolution. - Naval: the sea route for Far away , colony defence by sea. - Trade: colony goods flowing home; what an overseas trade empire is. - Exploration-and-Colonies: colonial provinces chartered into a Colony. - Historical-Events: vassalize , release , relation , subject count , create country … subject of , doctrine of lapse and new keys. - The 1378 Start: the 1378 subject records, autonomy, start dates, playable subjects. - Map and Map Modes, Screens-and-Navigation, Time-and-Turns: hatches, icons, the list and card, and the month, season and era. The-1378-Start: Every campaign begins on 20 September 1378 , the day the Western Schism begins. The world is built from research: every realm that existed that autumn, from great kingdoms to stateless societies, put onto the map with its ruler, its government, its strengths and weaknesses, its friends and enemies, and the goals it was really pursuing. Realms that were not yet born wait asleep and can form later. This page explains what the world looks like on the first day, which realms come later, how history guides the computer realms without forcing them, how a country's starting gold, soldiers and officials are worked out, how each province gets its starting people, wealth and castles, which realms you can play, and which campaign rules you pick before you begin. Once the first turn starts, other systems take over. How it works The start day: 20 September 1378 On 20 September 1378 the cardinals meeting at Fondi elect Clement VII against Urban VI, the Pope they had chosen in Rome that spring. From that day Latin Christendom has two Popes, and every Catholic realm must decide which one it obeys. That is why the campaign starts here: the first years hand almost every realm a choice. Some things have already happened by the start day: - On the Vozha (11 August 1378) Moscow has beaten Mamai's Horde for the first time. - The Ciompi have risen in Florence, and a regime of the minor guilds rules the city. - Tokhtamysh has taken the White Horde with Timur's help. - Ayutthaya has made Sukhothai its vassal. What history did next, and what your rivals will be reaching for: When What happened in history Who it hands a choice to Autumn 1378 Every Catholic realm picks a Pope. The Emperor Charles IV dies (29 November) and his son Wenceslaus follows him. France seizes Brittany. Catholic realms, the Empire, France, Brittany 1379 The War of Chioggia, Venice against Genoa. John V retakes Constantinople from his son with Ottoman help. Venice, Genoa, Padua, Hungary, Byzantium, the Ottomans 1380 Kulikovo. Charles V and Du Guesclin die. Tokhtamysh unites the Golden Horde. Muscovy, the Horde, France 1381 and 1382 The Peasants' Revolt in England. Timur takes Herat. Louis the Great dies, and Hungary and Poland part. Tokhtamysh burns Moscow. Ming takes Yunnan. England, Herat, Hungary, Poland, Muscovy, Ming None of this is forced. Each of these is something a realm wants, and whether it happens depends on what you and the other realms do (see History is a reference). The campaign runs from 20 September 1378 to 31 August 1939, one week per turn: about 29,250 turns. The tutorial, Murad's Frontier , starts on the same day, playing the Ottomans under Murad I (see Tutorial and Help). The world on 20 September 1378 About 315 realms hold land on the map at the start, many more than in 1444, because the world of 1378 is more divided. These are the big stories you start in the middle of. The Church: two Popes. Urban VI sits in Rome and Clement VII goes to Avignon. Each Catholic realm holds an obedience to one of them, and its Pope is the one whose censure, patronage and calls count for it. On the start day 150 realms and lords follow Rome : the Empire, England, Hungary and Poland, Scandinavia and most of Italy. 30 follow Avignon : France and its great fiefs, Scotland, Naples, Savoy, Provence, Lorraine, Cyprus and the Knights of Rhodes. 22 have not chosen yet , among them Castile, Aragon, Portugal and Navarre. In history Castile went to Avignon in 1381 and Aragon in 1387. The Council of Pisa (1409) can add a third Pope, and the Council of Constance (1414 to 1418) can end the Schism. There are no Hussites yet: Hus is not burned until 1415. The Empire. Charles IV of the house of Luxembourg is Emperor and King of Bohemia, aged 62. His son Wenceslaus, aged 17, is already King of the Romans and follows him without an election. The seven electors are Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bohemia, the Palatinate, Saxe-Wittenberg and Brandenburg, which the Luxembourgs also hold, so the house has two votes. Meissen and Thuringia belong to the Wettins, who are not electors yet, and Nuremberg is still only a burgraviate of the Hohenzollerns. Austria is shared by the brothers Albert III and Leopold III. See Institutions. The Hundred Years' War, its Caroline phase. Charles V of France and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin are winning back the land England took. England's king, Richard II, is 11. England and France are at war; Castile fights beside France at sea and against Navarre, whose Norman lands Charles V has just seized. England keeps Calais and Gascony, Scotland keeps an uneasy truce with England, and Brittany under John IV is France's most restless vassal. Italy. Venice and Genoa are at war over Tenedos and the straits: the War of Chioggia. Padua, Hungary and the Patriarch of Aquileia join Genoa, while Bernabò Visconti of Milan backs Venice. The Visconti lands are split between Bernabò at Milan and his nephew Gian Galeazzo at Pavia. Joanna I rules Naples and backs Avignon. Hungary and Poland under Louis. Louis the Great is king of both, aged 52, with no son. His daughter Mary, aged 7, is heir. Poland is governed for him by his mother Elizabeth, and its lords want a king of their own. Hungary holds Wallachia, Bosnia, Vidin and Ragusa as subjects and is at war with Venice. The north and east. Lithuania is still pagan, ruled by Jogaila beside his uncle Kęstutis, and at war with the Teutonic and Livonian Orders, whose crusades raid it every year. Moscow under Dmitry Ivanovich, aged 27, has stopped paying tribute to Mamai and is at war with him. Tver, Ryazan and Nizhny Novgorod still pay the Horde. Albert of Mecklenburg is King of Sweden, and a child, Olaf II, is King of Denmark. The Hordes, Tokhtamysh and Timur. The Ulus of Jochi is broken in three. Mamai , a beylerbey who is not of Genghis Khan's line, holds the west through puppet khans and wants to punish Moscow. Arab Shah holds part of the Volga. Tokhtamysh , khan of the White Horde since this year, wants Sarai and the whole Ulus. Behind him stands Timur , Amir of the Chagatai ulus since 1370, aged 42, who shelters and arms him. Iran is split among five successor states (the Jalayirids at Tabriz and Baghdad, the Muzaffarids, the Kartids of Herat, the Sarbadars and the Sufids of Khwarazm) and Timur means to take them. Murad's Ottomans and the beyliks. The Ottoman Beylik of Murad I, aged 52, is a rising frontier state on both sides of the straits. Byzantium is its tributary, and Ivan Shishman of Tarnovo, Marko of Prilep and Constantine Dragaš are its vassals. In Anatolia the beyliks still stand: Karaman (the Ottomans' great rival), Germiyan, Aydın, Menteşe, Saruhan, Hamid, Teke, Candar and the Eretnids. In the Balkans Lazar's Serbia, the Lands of Vuk Branković, the Balšić Zeta, two Bulgarian tsardoms (Tarnovo and Vidin) and Dobruja stand between the Ottomans and Hungary. Kosovo is still ahead. The Byzantine civil war. Andronikos IV holds Constantinople and his father John V and brother Manuel are his prisoners. He owes his throne to Murad. In history John V retakes the city in July 1379, again with Ottoman help. The Despotate of the Morea holds the south of Greece, beside Latin Achaea and Catalan Athens. The Mamluks rule Egypt and Syria under a boy sultan, al-Mansur Ali II, hold Jerusalem, and protect the holy cities of the Hejaz. South Asia. Firuz Shah Tughlaq, aged 69, rules a Delhi sultanate far larger than the one of 1444: it still holds Gujarat, Malwa and Multan, and Sindh pays it tribute. Bengal is free and at peace with Delhi. In the Deccan the Bahmanis and Vijayanagar under Harihara II are rivals. East Asia. The Ming under the Hongwu Emperor, aged 50, are ten years old. They are still at war with the Northern Yuan on the steppe and with Naghachu in Manchuria, and a Yuan prince still holds Yunnan. Goryeo , not yet Joseon, rules Korea under King U, aged 13. Japan has two courts at war: the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimitsu, aged 20, and the weakening Southern Court. Southeast Asia. Champa under Chế Bồng Nga has sacked Thăng Long and is at war with Dai Viet. Majapahit under Hayam Wuruk holds tribute from much of the archipelago and the Malay peninsula, Singapura among them. Ayutthaya has just made Sukhothai its vassal. Africa. Mali under Mansa Musa II still rules the western Sahel. Ethiopia under Newaya Maryam is at war with Ifat. The Bulala are driving the Sayfawa out of Kanem. The Americas. In the valley of Mexico the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco under Tezozómoc are the great power, and the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, under their first tlatoani Acamapichtli, are their tributaries. In the Andes Cusco is one small lordship among its rivals, and Chimor at Chan Chan is the strong power of the coast. Mayapan still rules in Yucatán. Realms that come later A realm that was not yet born in 1378 is a sleeping realm . It is listed from the start but hidden and landless until it wakes. 67 realms sleep on the start day, among them: - Europe: Spain, the Dutch Republic, Wales, Transylvania, Poland-Lithuania and Russia, and Albanian lordships such as the Kastrioti and the League of Lezhë. - The steppe: Kazan, the Crimea, the Nogais, the Uzbek Khanate and the Oirats. - South Asia: Jaunpur, Gujarat, Malwa, Multan, Kabul, the Mughal Empire and the Sikh Empire. - Southeast and East Asia: Malacca, and Japan's great warrior houses (the Hosokawa, Ōuchi, Takeda, Date, Shimazu and others). - Africa: Kongo, Mutapa, Adal, Ajuran, Kaffa, Buganda, Rwanda and the Aïr Sultanate. - North America: the Cherokee, the Creek and Coosa. A sleeping realm wakes when its conditions hold: by a decision, which you or a computer realm can take once it holds the land and shares the faith and tongue, or by an event. A computer realm usually forms one when its goals lead there, near the historical date, but it stays formable for the whole campaign. Its record from the 1444 catalogue is its blueprint: its name, colour, capital and home land. If you never take the steps, Spain may never be. History is a reference History in Pocket Hegemony is a reference, not a script. No event is forced by its date. History still tends to run its normal course, because every realm pursues the goals it really had, for the reasons it had them . Each goal names what the realm wants, why, when it is likeliest and when the goal ends. Some goals from the start data: Realm Goal Because Ottomans Take Sofia, Serres and Niš Ghaza and timar land for the frontier lords Ottomans Keep Byzantium a tributary and play its civil war The straits and the Gallipoli crossing Muscovy Break Mamai and stop paying tribute Mamai is a usurper, not of Genghis Khan's line White Horde Take Sarai and unite the Ulus of Jochi Tokhtamysh's claim to the whole ulus Timur Conquer Khorasan: Herat, Sabzevar, Tus Rich, divided neighbours, and land for his amirs Timur Punish Tokhtamysh Only once Tokhtamysh turns on him Hungary Secure the crowns for Louis's daughters No male heir Lithuania Stop the crusade and defend Samogitia The Orders raid every year - A goal ends when its reason does. If Tokhtamysh is dead, Timur stops chasing him. If the Ottomans already hold Niš, that goal is done. - The computer weighs goals like any other wish. A goal makes a war aim, an alliance, a marriage or a decision more attractive while its reason holds and its time is near. It never makes a realm do what it can't afford: a weak Timur doesn't march on Anatolia. - Realms sometimes go their own way. At the start of each campaign the seed shakes every realm's goals. A goal can be eager in one campaign and half-hearted in the next; some goals are dropped or swapped for a plausible alternative (the Ottomans may turn on Anatolia first, Venice may look to the mainland); a new ruler may bring a goal of his own. The big picture usually holds, but no two campaigns run the same. - The events choice sets how closely history is followed. Historical leans harder on history, Plausible (the default) is in between, and Free loosens it. - You are never steered. Your own realm has no goals forced on it. Other realms' goals show on their realm card, so you can see what Florence or Timur is after. Research and the eras The research tree keeps its eras, and Era I is stretched back to the start: it runs from 1378 to 1500 . The Medieval era ends in 1377, and inventions from before then stay "known before the start". Era I is now 122 years long, so its inventions cost more and a typical realm still reaches Era II around 1500. A few start inventions differ from 1444, because they had not spread yet. The Ottomans don't know bombards, gunpowder infantry or tax registers. Bohemia and Hungary have no wagon fort (that comes with the Hussites). Portugal and Castile don't have the carrack and caravel, while Genoa and Venice do. Ming keeps its handgunners but has no tax registers until the Yellow Registers of 1381. Timur's realm has no observatory, while the Jalayirids keep the Maragha tradition. Goryeo knows metal movable type. See Research. The 1444 checkpoint The world of 11 November 1444 , the day after the battle of Varna, is still in the game as the main history checkpoint . Its map and catalogue are the reference that a test run from 1378 is compared with: who holds the key places, which realms exist and who the great powers are. Eight other dates are checked beside it, from Timur's death in 1405 to Sarajevo in 1914. The check runs only when the designer asks; the game itself never corrects a realm that wanders off history. A tester can still open the 1444 world by adding ?start=1444 to the address. A campaign you began in 1444 keeps playing in its own world: opening its save reopens the game in 1444 and loads it, and going back to the start screen returns to 1378 for new campaigns. The country catalogue The starting world comes from the country catalogue : 963 researched records of the political entities of the 1440s, and a 1378 pass over them region by region. The 1378 pass dates each record, makes the realms born later sleeping realms, and adds records for the realms of 1378 that were gone by 1444, such as the Hordes, the Iranian successor states, the Anatolian beyliks, the Bulgarian tsardoms, Padua, Verona, Goryeo, the Tepanecs and Mayapan. The catalogue is history, not game balance: it holds no numeric game statistics at all. Population appears only as a published range with a source, and army sizes or budgets only when they are directly sourced. Who gets in. The catalogue follows a few inclusion rules: - Date test : an entity is included only if it existed on the start day with the identity recorded. Entities founded later become sleeping realms or wait for events. - Agency test : subordinate entities are included when their internal politics mattered. Pure administrative subdivisions are excluded not distinct or merged into other . - Groups : where hundreds of micro-polities existed, the significant ones get their own record and the rest go into a named group record (such as silesia or tusi group ), which never implies a single state. - No forced states : societies without a state are recorded as such (stateless, segmentary lineage and so on), as a decentralised polity or a non-state actor, never forced into a nation-state. - Disputes are kept : where existence or classification is disputed, the record is kept as included disputed with the dispute described, never resolved silently. Ids. Every record has a stable snake case id that is never reused (for example ottoman , mamluk , chimor ). A renamed id goes into an alias list. Relationship edges live in separate relationship files, never inside records: a hierarchical edge is stored with the subordinate party and a symmetric one with party a . Nothing from commercial games. The catalogue carries no tags, statistics, values, mechanic names or text from commercial games. Every record carries every section, whatever its importance: region, names, classification, existence, identity, leadership, government, geography with capital, society, economy, military, diplomacy, gameplay data, event links, sources, confidence and open questions. Each record belongs to exactly one of 29 regions, by its core or seat. Detail tiers set only how much prose a record has: A for major powers, B for significant secondary states, C for minor ones. Representations: what each record becomes in the game Representation What it is Records (1444 catalogue) Playable country Has its own AI, can be played, not under an overlord 274 Playable subject Has its own AI but sits under an overlord 218 Decentralised polity A society without a state, recorded as such 214 Background only Flavour or territory holder without AI 115 Non-state actor For example a movement or order 68 Internal estate Simulated as a faction or region inside another country 58 Collective institution The Empire, the Hanse, confederacies, councils 16 The collective institutions are bodies such as the Holy Roman Empire, the Hanseatic League, the Swiss Confederation, the Livonian Confederation, Mount Athos, the Japanese imperial court and the Kamakura kubō. They are not realms of their own, unless a map nation stands for one: Switzerland plays as the Swiss Confederation, which in 1378 is eight cantons. The rest are background that events can draw on. Some institutions of the 1444 list are not there yet in 1378 and come by event: the Kalmar Union, the Council of Basel, the League of Lezhë and the Triple Alliance of Mexico. Starting assessments Instead of numbers, each record has a qualitative assessment on a set of dimensions, each one very low, low, moderate, high, very high or unknown, with a justification and a confidence. There is deliberately no overall power score . Kind of dimension Dimensions Judged… Size-dependent economic strength, manpower potential, military capability, naval capability, diplomatic influence, trade access on one global scale Quality political stability, administrative capacity, fiscal resilience, institutional development, territorial cohesion, long-term potential relative to the entity's own size and type Risk (higher is worse) unrest risk, external threat exposure as risks Each record also has an AI personality : historically informed tendencies (priorities, ways of expanding, diplomatic style, economic focus, doctrine, risk tolerance, constraints, opportunities, failure conditions, how it adapts). These are tendencies the AI reads, not scripts. The realm's goals (see History is a reference) grow from them. Start forms of government Every country starts with its historical form of government, assigned by rules tried in order: 1. Hand-set overrides (75 of them, each with a reason), which win over everything else. Examples: the Ottomans as a household realm, the Mamluks as soldier emirs, Venice as a merchant republic, England as a diet monarchy, Hungary as an elective monarchy. 2. Text rules (12), tried in order on the lower-cased government text in the catalogue, honouring each rule's allowed and skipped entity types. 3. Entity type (52 entries). A record of type kingdom takes its form from its region: Region Kingdom starts as Latin Europe; Anatolia and the Caucasus feudal realm Levant, Egypt and Arabia; Iran and Transoxiana; North Africa household realm South Asia; China and Inner Asia feudal realm The steppe and Siberia horde Japan and Korea warlord domain Southeast Asia tribute empire (tiers A and B), paramount chiefdom (tier C) The rest of Africa, the Americas and Oceania paramount chiefdom 4. Default : chiefdom . No country ever starts as an absolute monarchy, constitutional monarchy, constitutional republic, military junta, party state or company rule. Those forms are reached later by reform, revolution or events (see Government). The summary of start forms is generated by a tool, never edited by hand. Starting counts for each country Each country's starting counts are set from its assessments: Assessment Sets Economic strength and fiscal resilience Gold and Debt Manpower potential Recruits Military capability Soldiers, Commanders, Horses Naval capability Ships Administrative capacity Officials, and how many provinces start as royal land Political stability and unrest risk Lords' starting loyalty, and provinces in revolt Territorial cohesion Number of lords, the land they hold, and Language Institutional development Schools and Scholars (starting inventions come from the realm's start group: see Research) Trade access Merchants and access to grain prices Diplomatic influence Extra officials at court ready to go abroad How the numbers come out (all provisional, in starting in realm.json ): Starting number Set by Very low → very high Gold Economic strength 1, 2, 3, 5 or 8 months of the realm's tax and trade (at least 10 gold) Debt Fiscal resilience 1.5, 1, 0.5, 0.25 or 0 times its starting gold, never more than lenders allow Levies already gathered Manpower potential 50, 65, 80, 90 or 100 % of each province's levy ceiling Officials at their posts Administrative capacity 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1 or 1.2 per royal province; the posts farthest from the capital stand empty Envoys at court Diplomatic influence 0, 1, 1, 2 or 3, each an extra envoy seat Each number is spread at random by how sure the catalogue is of that assessment: up to 25 % either way for low confidence, 10 % for medium and 5 % for high, so an uncertain realm starts a little differently each campaign. The campaign's seed fixes the spread, so the same seed gives the same start. An unknown level counts as moderate. The country card's Heritage tab shows each assessment with the starting number it sets under its bar. Other starting facts: - Rulers : every realm starts with its real ruler of 20 September 1378, with his age, his years on the throne and his heir: Murad I, Charles V, the boy Richard II, Louis the Great, Timur, Hongwu. See Your Realm. - Relations : allies, rivals, subjects and enemies come straight from the 1378 relations data: 503 relations and 128 facts on 20 September 1378, with each Catholic realm's obedience. Wars under way include England against France, Venice against Genoa and its allies, Mamai against Moscow, Lithuania against the Orders, Champa against Dai Viet, Ming against the Northern Yuan, and Japan's two courts. See Diplomacy and Subjects. - Lords : for major countries, lords come from the great houses the catalogue's history names. A country with only one province has no lords. See Your Realm. - Traders : starting traders follow trade access (very high 6, high 4, moderate 2, low 1, very low or unknown 0); trade ships for coastal countries with ports, caravans or barges inland. Starting trade ratios are set by running the starting traders for 24 months before the first turn , so busy roads start busy. Genoa's Black Sea trade through Caffa and Tana and Venice's routes are at their peak. See Trade. - Faiths : each record's ruler's faith, its people's majority faith and other communities come from the catalogue. Lithuania and Samogitia keep their own Baltic faith until their baptisms. See Religion. - Exploration : no realm can explore at the start. Genoa and Venice know the carrack, but the Age of Exploration has not begun; Portugal and Castile must learn the ocean ships first. See Exploration and Colonies. Town size follows population, and town slots fill by a regional template, for example a European market town gets a market, a church and a loom house, and a Sahel trade town a market, a mosque and a caravanserai. See Buildings. Ports come from the start's port list: a great port gets harbour 2; a port harbour 2 or 1; a small harbour 1; a canoe landing no harbour but extra seafolk and small craft. See Naval. The province faith mix follows the record that owns it, adjusted by a region table. Population, wealth (1 to 10), terrain, coast and neighbours stay as starting inputs . Wealth stops being a live stat once the buildings are placed. Charted map : every country starts having charted every province within 6 steps of its lands, plus every sea zone touching them. The 1378 map today The 1378 map is built from five regional parts (western Europe, the east, Asia, Africa and the Americas, and Arabia), joined into one start: - About 315 map nations , each with a capital, a colour and commanders with might, cunning and logistics (for example France's Bertrand du Guesclin, England's Sir Robert Knolles). - Owner rules hand provinces to nations, checked in order, first match wins, by modern country, region name or a longitude and latitude box. Borders are an approximation of 1378, not an atlas. The borders that differ most from 1444 are in Anatolia (the beyliks), Iran (five successor states), the steppe (the Hordes), North India (Delhi still holds Gujarat, Malwa and Multan), France (English Gascony and Calais, Brittany, the Navarrese lands), the Low Countries, Italy, Mexico (the Tepanecs) and the Andes (a small Cusco and a strong Chimor). - A realm added from the catalogue whose capital lies in another realm's province is left as reference data (for example Timbuktu in Mali's land). - Each nation's colour is one of 32 palette colours not taken by a neighbouring nation. Population of a province, in thousands of people: - Land area times the density of the first matching settlement region (default 0.8 people per km²), - ×0.35 in mountains, desert and tundra; ×1.3 in farmland and marsh; ×2.5 for a capital, - spread by 0.7 to 1.3 per province, - unowned land capped at twice the default density. Wealth of a province: - The first matching settlement region's wealth (default 1; always 1 for unowned land), - +1 if owned and coastal, +2 for a capital, - spread by 0.75 to 1.25 and kept between 1 and 10. Settlement regions range from dense, rich ones (the Low Countries at 30 people per km² and wealth 6) to sparse ones (Africa at 3 and 2). Castles (a stand-in until real castles are researched): Province Castle Capitals, and provinces of 400 thousand people or more Stone Frontier provinces on high ground with 30 thousand or more, or anywhere with 200 thousand or more Stone Other frontier provinces Earth About 15 % of other owned provinces An old ring fort Unowned provinces None A realm the catalogue does not assess starts with the engine's 50 gold, every province's levies at their ceiling, and 20 % horse in starting armies (all placeholders). A realm's men under arms all start in armies under a commander, spread over its land: one army per commander, the first in the capital. It gets one commander for every 8,000 men, at least one and at most eight (more only if an army would pass 30,000). From catalogue to map A mapping plan says which catalogue record owns which provinces, with capitals, colours, rulers and commanders. The nations on the map are the realms. Where a map nation's id differs from the catalogue (for example the Mexica are Tenochtitlan and Chimú is Chimor), a rename table links the two. A catalogue record that owns no province on the map is background only, and land nobody owns stays free to settle. A colony can be founded only in a province no country owns. Land of a tribe that is a country (a chiefdom or clan council in the start list) can only be taken by war or treaty. Good realms to start with - The Ottomans (free): Murad I's frontier state, with Byzantium as a tributary in civil war, Balkan lords as vassals, the beyliks of Anatolia to win by marriage, purchase or war, and Lazar's Serbia and Kosovo ahead. This is the tutorial's realm. - France (free): Charles V and Du Guesclin, winning back the land England took, with Brittany and Navarre to settle and an English boy king across the sea. - Muscovy : fresh from the Vozha, with Mamai coming for revenge and Tver and Ryazan to master. - Venice or Genoa : the War of Chioggia, decided at sea in the first two years. - Hungary : two crowns, a ring of Balkan subjects and no son to inherit them. - Lithuania : a pagan realm between the crusading Orders and Moscow, with a crown and a baptism on offer. - Timur or the White Horde : Timur's rise to empire, or Tokhtamysh's road to Sarai, and the break between them. - Ming : a young dynasty still fighting the Yuan on three frontiers. - The Mexica : a small tributary city of the Tepanecs that can become an empire. Playable realms and the free tier - The free tier offers the Ottomans and France . The tutorial is played as the Ottomans. - Without the full game, the realm picker shows other realms with a padlock and a button to the Unlock screen. Coming back from a purchase keeps the realm you chose. - Every realm on the map is playable. A sleeping realm can't be picked at the start; you form it in play. Campaign rules At new game you set the campaign rules : difficulty, AI temper, fog, historical, plausible or free events, ironman, and the end date (default 31 August 1939). Presets fill the whole step at once. The rules are saved with the campaign, can't be changed afterwards, and are shown read-only under Pause, Campaign rules. A new game starts from a seed , your nation and the options, and gets a random campaign id. The same seed and the same rules always give the same starting world, including how each realm's goals are shaken. Each save header records your nation and whether it needs the full game. Loading a save of a locked realm asks you to unlock it; the save is never deleted. What you see - Realm picker : the "Choose your realm" sheet over the map, titled Autumn 1378 . It opens on the suggested realms : the great powers of each part of the world and a start for each part of Africa (Mali, Benin, Tio, Ethiopia and Kilwa; Kongo is not founded yet). Or tap any realm on the map. A realm's card names its ruler on the start day and says the campaign starts on 20 September 1378. Locked realms show a padlock and a button to Unlock. - Region : the select at the top of the sheet lists every region that has realms, with how many: Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Central and North Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, North America, Mesoamerica and Central America, and South America. Choosing a region frames its realms on the map, and the sheet lists every realm of the region from A to Z, one row each with its pennant, name, size and its standing at the start. A realm of one province is never only a speck to hit: tap its row. Regions follow the event tree's macro-regions; the Sahel, West, Central, East and Southern Africa (Ethiopia and the Somali coast too) are Sub-Saharan Africa, the Maghreb, Egypt and the Sahara are North Africa. - The realm's card : tapping a row, or one of a realm's provinces on the map, shows the realm at a glance: its ruler, its form of government, provinces, people and what it is strong in, and one line Ways to grow , for example "Ways to grow: 3 smaller neighbours · 4 free provinces · 1 port". It counts the realms next to it by land that have fewer provinces (tributaries it could make), the free land that borders it, and its trade at the start: gold fields, trade and caravan towns, and ports. Rule starts the game as that realm; ✕ goes back to the list. - On a phone held sideways the sheet sits at the left with the map beside it; held upright, or in a narrow window, the sheet sits along the bottom under the map. Every row and button is at least 44 points high and nothing needs hover. - Campaign rules step : difficulty, AI temper, fog, events, ironman and end date, with presets. - Quick start : skips to Begin with the last options used and the realm last tapped (or the first suggested one). - Pause, Campaign rules : the rules of the running campaign, read-only. The screens themselves are on Screens and Navigation. Time-and-Turns: Pocket Hegemony is played one week at a time, from 20 September 1378 to 31 August 1939. You give your orders, press End turn, and the game plays out the 7 days of that week for every army, fleet and trader in the world at once. This page explains the clock: how a turn runs, how battles slow it, what happens daily, weekly, monthly, seasonally and yearly, and how the campaign is won and ends. How it works One week per turn Every turn is one week: 7 days on the real calendar. The very last turn ends on 31 August 1939 and may be shorter. Months have their real number of days, 28 to 31, with leap years in February (every fourth year, except years ending in 00 that can't be divided by 400; the game uses these rules for every year, before 1582 too). Things counted per day, like marching, sailing, traders and battles, use the real number of days. Things counted per month, like tax, wages, upkeep and growth, still come once a month, in full: they are paid at the end of the turn in which the 1st of a new month falls, whatever the month's length. Seasonal and yearly things work the same way. No rule counts turns: anything that lasts or waits is measured in days, weeks, months or years on the calendar. Only orders, End turn and the turn report are once per turn. When a turn is processed, the date moves on by 7 days and the turn counter goes up by one; a campaign is about 29,250 turns. Every campaign starts on 20 September 1378 , the day the cardinals at Fondi elect Clement VII against Urban VI and the Western Schism begins, the day the realms and their relations are drawn from. The tutorial, "Murad's Frontier", starts on the same day. The turn counter starts at 0, and loading screens call the start "Autumn 1378". The world of 11 November 1444, the day after the battle of Varna, stays as the main history checkpoint; testers can open it with ?start=1444 in the address (see The 1378 start). Before the first turn, the game sets up the world and lets the traders warm up their routes. All of that uses the campaign's one random seed and does not move the date. How a campaign is won and ends There are two ways to win. - World domination. If your realm owns, or holds as subjects, half of the world's settled land provinces, you win. This is checked in the turn in which 1 January falls, and the win counts at once. You may keep playing to the end date afterwards. - Best at the end. The campaign ends on 31 August 1939 . On that day the realm leading the Economy score, the realm leading the Power score and the realm leading the Technology score each win in that score. No margin is needed, and realms that tie share the win. The scores are worked out each January for the realm book, but the winner is only judged at the end. A campaign that reaches the end without a win shows the final scores and your rank. The end date is chosen when you start a campaign and saved with it. When it is reached, the campaign ends with the final wrap-up events, a closing sequence and the final result. There is no playing on past it. Nothing after 1939 is in the game: no Era VIII, no Second World War events, and no Decolonization, Cold War or Globalization ages. Orders and End turn Every command that changes the world is an order , for example "move this army to that province". The player and the AI send exactly the same kinds of order through exactly the same pipeline. There are no player-only shortcuts. - Orders you give during your turn are queued, not applied . If you tell Bertrand du Guesclin's army in Paris to march to Dijon, it still stands in Paris until you press End turn. - When you press End turn, your orders are applied first, then each AI realm's, realm by realm in a fixed order. - If an order can't be applied, it is rejected with a plain-language reason, listed in the turn report, and the rest of the turn still runs. - An army can take only one move order per turn. A second one is rejected with "army already moved this turn". - While the turn is being processed, orders are frozen. You can still pan and zoom the map. Unanswered events block End turn. If any event is still waiting for your answer, End turn opens the first unanswered event instead. Nothing ever answers an event for you. Warnings never block. If the End turn confirmation setting is on, the game asks first and tells you how many warnings are open, for example "3 warnings wait for you". You can look, or end the turn anyway. Auto turns In a single-player campaign you can let the weeks play one after another. Tap Auto , just above End turn, and the next week starts by itself as soon as one has played and been saved, at your Turn playback speed. Auto turns change only when End turn is pressed, never what happens in a week. Pausing finishes the week. While Auto turns run, a tap on End turn or on Auto (or Space) doesn't stop the clock mid-week: the week plays to its end, then the game stops and you can give orders. Until then both buttons say "Stops at the end of this week"; tap Auto again to keep going. On a keyboard, Shift+Space switches Auto turns. Auto turns stop by themselves at the end of a week in which something needs you, and the alert over the map says what: an event, one of your battles or sieges, a war of your realm, a call to arms, a peace offer or an envoy waiting, beaten rebels waiting for your verdict, scholars with nothing to study, or one of your armies reaching the end of its march. An event, a revolution or one of your battles still makes the week wait at once, as it always does. Auto turns are off every time you load a campaign. The order of a turn Every turn runs the same steps in the same order: 1. Orders : yours first, then each AI realm's. 2. The 7 days of the turn (the day loop, below), then the weekly steps. 3. Monthly steps , only in the turn in which a new month begins: sieges first, then armies and fleets settle their month (sickness, pay, ship states, colonies), then provinces (people, food and tax), buildings, recruiting, the realm (treasury and lords), research, trade upkeep, subjects, government, diplomacy, culture, religion, rebellions and revolutions. 4. Seasonal steps , in the turn in which a season begins. 5. Yearly steps , in the turn in which 1 January falls. 6. Events , then the national strengths tick. 7. Achievements , always last. 8. Autosave . 9. The date moves on 7 days. Because provinces run before buildings, a building finished this month takes in homeless people from next month on. What a turn looks like Inside one turn you see, in this order: 1. The week playing out on the map, at about one second per ten days, slowing down while one of your battles runs. 2. Each of your battles, followed while it runs. 3. The events that fired, one at a time in date order. 4. The turn report. Events and the report are skipped when there is nothing in them. Watching time pass When you end a turn, the date doesn't jump a week. It ticks day by day while the week plays on the map, armies walking their routes, battles fighting and sieges going on as the days pass. While one of your battles runs, the clock slows to 4-hour steps and shows the hour. The day loop: the days inside a turn The turn is played out day by day, all 7 of them, for every mover at once: armies, fleets, traders and trade ships, and exploration ships. They all share one clock, so a trader and an army can meet on the same day, and a fleet that closes a strait on day 12 matters to an army trying to cross on day 13. Each day runs these steps, always in this order: 1. Move : armies first, then fleets, then traders, then exploration ships, each kind in a fixed order. So an army crossing a strait on the very day an enemy fleet arrives there gets across. 2. Stop checks : movers that arrived somewhere check what stops them. 3. Contact : hostile armies in the same place meet, and a battle may begin. 4. Battles : every running battle fights its rounds. Armies in a battle don't move while it lasts. 5. Standing orders : for example armies set to attack look at visible enemies next door. At the end of every turn armies eat (from home or from their reserve), hunger bites, plunder and raids burn a tile, forced marches lose men, and plague spreads while an outbreak runs. Sieges are worked out once a month, at the start of the monthly steps. Days already walked toward the next place are called progress and carry over into the next turn. At the end of every day, every mover stands in exactly one place, never between two. Battles inside the turn A battle begins on the day two hostile armies meet, and it is fought over time, round by round, until one side is beaten or retreats. While a battle your army or fleet is in is running, time keeps passing but slows down : each day is played in six steps of 4 hours. Each step fights one round of every running battle and moves every other army, fleet and trader a sixth of a day, so your armies (and anyone else's) can march in and join the battle while it lasts. When no battle of yours is left, the days go back to whole days. At any step you can change a battle's standing orders or order a retreat. There is no skip: you watch each of your battles to the end. If several of your battles run at once, you can switch between them to follow each one and decide when to retreat. Battles between other realms never slow the game. They fight their six rounds a day all at once, so they last just as long as yours, and other armies can still join them at the start of a day. Any battle, yours or not, can be replayed afterwards from its notice. If the app is killed while a battle runs, the turn is played again from the save taken before it, with the same orders, and the battle comes out the same. Determinism: same world, same orders, same result - All randomness comes from one seeded random generator, never from the device. The same seed gives the same sequence on every phone, PC and server. - The turn always runs its steps in the same order, and ties on the same day are broken by a fixed rule. - The same world plus the same orders always gives the same result, which tests and a later server can check. - The random generator's state is saved with the world, so a loaded campaign continues the same sequence. - Nothing outside the simulation changes it: not the music, not the interface, not any setting. Anything that changes rules, balance or the AI is a campaign rule chosen at new game. Turn boundaries and saves A save always holds the world between two turns . If your phone puts the app in the background while a turn runs, the turn pauses and carries on when you come back. If the app is killed, the turn is played again from the last save with the same orders and gives the same result. If a balance change is loaded with a campaign, the new rules apply from the next turn on. See Saving. Seasons and the hemispheres Season North South Spring March to May September to November Summer June to August December to February Autumn September to November March to May Winter December to February June to August Snow peaks with no pass and no road are closed December to March June to September Which hemisphere a province is in comes from its latitude. Wet seasons follow the climate: monsoon Asia June to September, the Sahel and savanna July to September, the Amazon December to May. If you set the autosave to "every 12 months", it falls in each January turn. The rotating autosave goes by the calendar, at most once a month, so it doesn't write every week. Ages and eras Ages are history's big situations, owned by Historical Events. Each starts and ends by its own conditions inside a window of years, and each has forced dates so a stalled game still moves on. Ages may overlap. The ages in the game are Schism and Conquerors, Gunpowder Empires, Exploration, Reformations, Atlantic Empires, Crisis and Absolutism, Revolutions, Industrialization, Imperialism and World Wars. An age whose window runs past 1939, like World Wars, simply runs to the end date; an age that would start on an event after 1939 never starts. Trade: Trade in Pocket Hegemony is carried by units you own and steer: caravans, barges, wagon trains and rail freight on land, and trade ships at sea. You give each trader a route between cities; every province it walks through gets busier, it collects value into its purse in every province it enters, and it empties that purse into your treasury when it reaches a city of your own. You can watch the gold travel home. How it works The idea in one card 1. Found a trader in one of your cities with a market. 2. Set its route by tapping where it starts and where it goes. The way between them is found for you, through the most populated land. 3. Every province the trader passes gets busier : its trade ratio rises, more with more traders, yours and everyone else's. 4. In every province it enters , it collects a share of that province's trade value, times its trade ratio, into its purse. 5. When it reaches a city of your own country , it deposits the purse into your treasury. Traders and trade ships Each trader is one unit on the map with a kind, a home city, a crew, a route, a purse, a hold, a position and progress toward the next province. Without a route it goes to its home city. Gaining traders: - Found a land trader in one of your cities with a market, or in a trading post once you know T8. You pay its founding gold up front, and its crew leaves the home province's job slots like a levy. - Ships : buy a ship in a port with enough sailors (see Naval) and set it to Trade, or turn a cog, junk, dhow, carrack or galleon to trade. Caravels cannot trade. - Capture in war (an army taking a caravan may keep it), a lord's gift, or an event. Losing traders: dismissing one removes it and its crew overflow into the emptiest slots of its home. If a trader's or trade ship's upkeep is unpaid for 6 months, it is lost and its crew leave. A trade ship pressed into war stops trading and keeps its purse until it next reaches one of your ports. Upkeep is charged every month, even with an empty purse and no route. There is no cap on how many traders you run. Lords run their own traders from their own cities with their own wealth. They deposit into the lord's wealth, and you can see them but not steer them.
