A province with no market (a village like Langres) still has a trade value, gets busier and pays traders who walk through it; it just can't be a route stop. Trade ratio: how busy a province is When the month's day loop ends, every province's ratio (0 to 100 %) updates: - Every trader of every country counts in traders passing, once in every province it stood in during the month, whether it stopped or walked through. - A trade ship sailing through a sea zone counts as half a trader in every port province on that zone's coast (a sea lane). Steady ratios: 1 trader a month gives about 23 %; 2 about 37 %; 5 about 60 %; 10 about 75 %; 20 about 86 %. A road nobody uses loses half its ratio in about seven months. Ratio gain modifiers: Condition Gain A customs officer in the province +15 % Road one step better than every neighbour's +10 % 10 years of peace +10 % Riots −50 % Homeless over 5 % −5 % for every 5 % homeless Enemy army or siege in the province no gain that month Plague quarantine ratio 0, and no trader enters Blockaded port no ship enters, no sea-lane gain The modifiers add together (riots count as −50 %), and the total never drops below no gain. Collecting When a trader enters a province, it collects that day: - It doesn't collect in the province it sets out from, or while it waits somewhere, until it enters another. - A full purse collects nothing more until it deposits. - Market fee : collecting in another country's province pays that country 10 % of the collection, except with a trade pact. A French caravan collecting 0.55 gold abroad pays a 0.055 fee. - Crowding : each province serves a number of visits a month at full value (2 with no market, 4 weekly market, 8 fair, 16 trading house). After that, each further visit's collection is multiplied by served ÷ visits so far. Geneva, with a fair, serves 8; the twelfth trader that month collects 8/12 of the full amount. Routes - A stop must be a city : a settlement of city or great-city size, or one with a market or trading post. Troyes with its weekly market can be a stop; Langres, a village with no market, can't; Elmina, a hamlet with a trading post, can. - A route is a start and an end , two different cities. You never draw the way or add stops between them. It runs there and back (the default) or once (wait at the end for orders). - The way comes from the shared route planner: fewest days by the trader's step days and where it may enter, drawn toward the most populated land (a province's days count for less the more people live there, up to three times the average), avoiding forbidden provinces, and preferring lower tolls when two paths are close (a toll counts as 2 days). Busy land is where the trade is, so a caravan goes through the towns, not around them. - Every province walked through gets the ratio gain and a collection. A route from Lübeck to Bruges busies the whole coast road in between. Route preview , before you confirm: Expect is the planned collections over one trip there and back at this month's ratios, minus fees and tolls, divided by the trip's months. Provinces you cannot see count as nothing. Red marks show embargoes, quarantines, enemy armies and passes shut by snow. When a route breaks (war, a closed border, quarantine, a snowed pass, a blockade), the route is checked again. A closed way is replaced by a dashed detour if one exists, otherwise the end is skipped. A closed end (war with its owner, an embargo, a quarantine) is skipped, shows red, and the turn report says so once. If both ends are closed, the trader goes to the nearest of your cities, deposits and waits for orders. Deposits and trade income - When a trader enters any city of your own country , stop or not, it deposits its whole purse into the treasury that day: "Caravan of Troyes brought 6.1 gold to Troyes." - Depositing in a lord's city pays the whole purse to the treasury, with no fee to the lord. - No deposits in a city of a subject (unless the subjects design says otherwise for a kind of subject), or in one of your cities an enemy occupies. - With T3 Bills of exchange , your traders may deposit in a foreign city with a counting house or bank that you are at peace with, paying 10 % to its owner. Trade income = your traders' deposits + market fees paid to you + tolls at your toll points. It replaces the old trade balance and merchants' earnings on Your Realm. Who may go where - Land traders may enter your own, your lords' and your subjects' provinces, and those of countries at peace with you unless closed or embargoed. Trade ships the same, ports only. - No trader enters a country at war with its owner, its occupied land, or a quarantined province. - Land traders can cross unclaimed land but collect nothing there unless it has a trading post. They never enter sea zones. - Trade ships enter only sea zones their country knows. - Borders at peace need no passage. - Tolls : passing a toll point (bridge, ford, pass, river mouth, strait), a trader pays the owner's rate (none, low or high) from its purse. Rates are set on Provinces. - Trade pact : no market fees and no tolls between the two countries, both ways. - Embargo : the embargoed country's traders can neither enter nor stop in the other's provinces or ports. - War sends traders inside enemy land at once to the nearest own or neutral city, where they may be caught. - The peace term Open the roads (10 years) lets the winner's traders pass the loser's tolls free. - A tributary's traders pay no tolls in its overlord's cities; a subject's traders deposit into the subject's own treasury. Risks - Enemy army : a trader that meets an army at war with its owner loses its purse to the army's owner and is captured (the army's owner may keep it), unless it can step back the way it came that day. By default a trader that sees an enemy army ahead waits a day and goes round. - Raids : an army on Raid takes the purse; the trader escapes half the time. - Bandits : in a province with riots, rebels or homeless over 20 %, each land trader has a 1-in-20 chance a month of its purse being stolen; halved with T1, none where there is a caravanserai or a garrisoned castle. - Rebels holding a province count as an enemy army. - Plague : a trader passing through an outbreak carries it onward. - At sea : a hunting fleet captures trade ships in its zone with their purses, and routes avoid zones where an enemy hunts when they can. Your warships escorting a zone protect your trade ships until the escort is beaten. A ship lost in a storm loses its purse; with T11 Marine insurance half is refunded. If naval adds pirates, they act as a hunting fleet with no country. What trade does elsewhere - Tax : tax owed in a province rises 1 % for every 4 points of its trade ratio. - Crafts appearing : craft buildings appear by themselves only where the trade ratio is 30 % or more. - Inputs : a building's input ware is supplied if it is made in the province, within reach (one ring, more with roads and rivers), or anywhere on a trader's route that passes through; otherwise the building works at half. - Research : when your traders deposit or collect in another country's cities, that country counts as your trade partner for invention spread (see Research). - Food is never carried by traders; hungry cities are fed by castles (see Your Realm). Events - trade power of a country changes its traders' collections by the same share for the duration. - trade access of a province changes its ratio gain by that share (−0.2 means −20 %). - world trade index changes every province's trade value by that share. - trade index reads a country's trade income over the last 12 months as an index against 100 gold a year. - trade presence(who, hub, value) reads a country's share of all collections in a hub's provinces over the last 12 months. - trade route(from hub, to hub, open) makes a sea passage's zones known to a country for routes, or marks the link closed. - trade good reads wares made. Hubs (Alexandria, Amsterdam, the Malacca Strait and 20 more) are named sets of provinces and sea zones used only by event triggers, never as route targets. The start and the warm-up Each country starts with traders by its catalogue trade access: very high 6, high 4, moderate 2, low 1, very low or unknown 0. Coastal countries with ports get trade ships, inland ones caravans or barges, in the proportion the catalogue's trade routes suggest. Starting routes are seeded from a hand-made list (Venice, Genoa, Lübeck, Florence, Mali and Timbuktu, Kilwa, Calicut and Gujarat, Malacca, Ryukyu). Before the first turn, the starting traders run for 24 months so busy roads start busy. See The 1378 Start. The AI - Scores possible routes from a trader's home to its own cities and enterable foreign cities within reach (about 12 provinces for caravans, 40 sea zones for ships) by expected gold a month after fees, tolls and crowding, minus upkeep, weighted down by danger. - Founds a trader when the best unused route beats upkeep by a margin set by its personality (merchant republics found more); dismisses one whose route has lost money for a year. - Reroutes once a year, and at once when a route breaks. - At war, pulls traders off roads near the front and uses trade ships as transports if short of carriers. Each turn, each month, and keeping it fast 1. During the day loop (the 7 days of each weekly turn): traders move; on entering a province they count as passing, collect (with crowding), pay fees and tolls, meet risks, and deposit in your cities. 2. After the day loop, in the turn a new month begins : every touched province's and sea zone's ratio updates. 3. Trader upkeep is charged and unpaid months counted. 4. Every turn, the turn report gets one deposits line for the week and lines for problems. Yearly: trade value is worked out again with the year's wares (and also on events or burned tiles); the AI reroutes and dismisses. On a phone, each province and sea zone stores only its ratio and traders passing; each trader about 12 small numbers. Paths are cached per city pair and cleared only when something on them changes, and ratios on quiet roads decay lazily (×0.9 for each untouched month). What you see - The trader card (above): kind, crew, route and its days there and back, position, purse bar, last collections, fees and tolls, danger and upkeep. - Found a trader : Trade, Found a trader, choose a kind, from a city with a market. Ships are bought on the port screen and switched to Trade. - Setting a route : tap where it starts, then where it goes (another tap moves where it goes), and tap the end again to finish; the preview updates with each tap; then Confirm. You can copy another trader's route. - The Trade screen : every trader and trade ship with kind, route, purse, last deposit, expected gold a month and problems, sortable by gold a month. - Turn report : deposits summed into one line ("Traders brought 23 gold this week"); only problems (robbed, route broken, ship taken) get their own line. - On the map : at world zoom the Trade map mode coloured by trade ratio and the busiest roads and sea lanes; at region zoom thicker roads with more traders, trader icons (caravan, barge, ship) with a purse bar, and a coin on market cities; at local zoom caravans, barges and ships moving. Map modes: Trade ratio , Trade value and Traders (your traders and routes). See Map and Map Modes. In the game now Trade runs in the game as a first slice: traders you own walk there and back between two cities, and what they bring home is your Trade line in the treasury. The old flat trade sum from a province's wealth is gone. - Goods. Each January every province counts what it makes: the wares of its works (timber and furs, stone, ore, salt, wool and hides), the food it does not eat (as grain), and crafts made by its craftsmen (finished goods, until the loom houses and forges make their own). Priced by tier, with a market's weight added, that is its trade value in gold a month. A harbour adds its weight for ships. - Trade stops. A city, or any town with a market, is a stop for caravans and barges; a port with a harbour is a stop for ships. - Traders. Pack caravans, camel caravans (from desert or drylands, or with Caravanserai networks), river barges (on rivers only) and the cog. Each walks its way there and back a month at a time: every province it stands in gets busier, it collects as it enters (10 % to the owner of a foreign province, nothing on unclaimed land) and it empties its purse in every city of yours it reaches. Its upkeep is paid each month; six months unpaid and it is given up. - Trade ratio. Each month a province's ratio rises with the traders passing (a customs officer helps, riots hurt, an enemy or a siege stops it) and loses a tenth. Every 4 points of ratio raise the tax the province owes by 1 %. - Your Trade line is last month's deposits plus market fees paid to you, less your traders' upkeep. - At the start every realm gets its traders by its trade access (Venice six, France four), on hand-made routes where their cities are on the map and otherwise on the best route from each of its best cities, and two years of their walking set the starting ratios. - The AI looks at each trader once a year and finds it a better route when its own pays little or is broken, and founds one more a year where a route pays well, up to twice its starting traders. Where you find it: - The Trade tab of your realm card, next to Treasury: last month's deposits, fees and upkeep; your traders, best first, each with its route ("Paris → Lyon and back"), its days there and back, a purse bar, about what it brings a month, what it deposited last month and what is wrong, with Route , Show and Dismiss ; then two folds you open with a tap: Found a trader (its line says how many cities can; it starts open while you have no trader), with one button per kind with its gold and upkeep in each city, greyed with the reason when it can't; and Busiest cities (its line names the busiest). - Setting a route : tap Route on a trader. The map switches to the Trade map mode and a bar along the bottom asks you to tap where it starts, then where it goes; a third city moves where it goes. You never draw the way: it is found through the most populated land and drawn on the map, with the preview (days there and back, provinces collected in, about how much a month, the best provinces). Then Confirm (or tap the end again), Undo or Cancel . - The Trade map mode : provinces coloured by trade ratio, what you don't see in parchment; zoomed in, your traders' ways there and back as dotted lines with each trader and its purse, and a coin on every trade stop. - The province card has a Trade line: value a month, ratio, traders passing and its top goods. - The Overview of your Realm book has an Economy tile with your gold and gold a month; the Trade page sits beside Treasury and Food in the Economy section. Not yet: tolls, trade pacts and embargoes, bandits and capture on the road, lords' traders, ships other than the cog, copying a route and the "once" mode. Tribes-and-Hunting-Grounds: The peoples of North America cannot colonise, so a tribe starts with two or three provinces and empty land all round it. Hunting grounds give it room to grow: a tribe walks a few unowned provinces next to its land, lives off them, and after years makes them its own. Every number here is provisional and lives in tribes.json . Which realms are tribes A realm is a tribal realm while its form is a clan council, a chiefdom or a confederation and its capital lies in North America. At the 1378 start that includes the Iroquois and the Huron; the Cherokee and the Creek are not born yet and form later (see The 1378 start). The Pueblo are a city commune: their towns grew by farming, so they walk no grounds unless a reform makes them a tribal form. A realm that reforms out of a tribal form loses its grounds at once. The range Form Hunting grounds : Clan council 2 Chiefdom 3 Confederation 4 At the start each tribe fills its range with the unowned land nearest its own, the most peopled first, walking out one province at a time; the tribes take their turn in map order, so a province the Cherokee took first is not the Creek's. Claiming and leaving Open the province card of an unowned land province touching your land or one of your grounds and tap Claim as hunting ground · 3 months . After three months it is yours to walk. One claim runs at a time, and only while your range has a free place. When the button is greyed, the reason is written under it: no free place, a claim is under way, it is another tribe's ground, or a colony is being founded there. Leave this ground (it asks first) frees the place; you may not claim that province again for five years. A ground is lost when it gets an owner (a colony, a treaty, a war) or, at the next month, when it no longer touches your land or another of your grounds. What a ground gives - Furs and hides : 0.5 gold a month for each ground, on its own line of the Treasury ledger. - Food : your armies and your allies' refill their wagons there as in your own land; an enemy's army strips it as enemy land. - Neighbours : two tribes whose grounds touch are neighbours, which counts for the confederation reform's "allied with 2 neighbours of the same people". A ground stays unowned in every other way: it pays no tax, needs no official, raises no levy and does not count toward world domination. Taking them in A ground you have held for ten years can be taken in while you are at peace and no colony is being founded there: it becomes your province, with its people, their tongue and faith, and its place in the range is free again. If its people speak your tongue, a clan council or chiefdom needs no official there; otherwise it needs one, counted against your officials cap. Settlers on our land A colony founded on a tribe's ground meets fiercer locals (one step: Peaceful becomes Wary, Wary Hostile, Hostile Fierce), and the tribe holds the wrong Settlers on our land (−30, fading over 20 years) and the war aim Punish against the founder for 10 years. A tribal player gets an alert over the map with Go there. A colonial power can instead ask for the land : from the province card, the tribe's Diplomacy tab or the fleet card's Colony section, offering 10 gold or more. The tribe answers a month later by its reasons count: Reason Number : Base −5 Gold offered +1 a gold (at most +40) Standing / 4 Settlers on our land held against the asker −25 Hostile toward the asker −30 Only one ground would be left −10 It is our last ground −100 A yes pays the tribe, gives up the ground (the tribe may not claim it again for 10 years), and the asker's next colony there is founded in peace with the consent of the local people (achievement Treaty on the Shore ). A tribal player answers asks for its land on the Hunting grounds tab. The Hunting grounds tab A tribal realm's card has a Hunting grounds tab in the Lands group, beside Colonies: settlers on your grounds at the top in red with Go there, asks for your land, "Hunting grounds n of m" with a bar, the claim under way and its end date, then one row per ground with its people, years held and furs, a ground ready to take in first. When settlers or asks wait, the Lands tile on your Realm book's Overview turns red and opens it. On the map, grounds are a light diagonal hatch in the tribe's colour at every zoom, in the political and Charts lenses. In the Charts lens an empty coast that is someone's hunting ground is amber, not green, so you see before sailing that settling there angers a tribe. The computer's tribes Each month a tribe of the computer with a free place claims the most peopled province it may; each January it takes in every ground it may, oldest first, while within its officials cap. A colonial power of the computer that holds twice the price asks for the land before settling on a ground, and founds there only after the answer.
Troop-Movement: Troop movement is where your armies stand on every day of the turn. You draw a route with your finger, see how many days it takes and how much food will be left on arrival, and the week then plays out day by day for every army at once: armies cross rivers and passes, get stopped by castles and borders, meet the enemy, withdraw, retreat and chase. The same rules move fleets, trade ships and traders, so the whole map runs on one clock. How it works The day loop A turn is one week : each turn plays out 7 days , and the calendar runs through months of their real length, 28 to 31 days (February has 29 in leap years). On each day, for every army at once, the game runs four steps in order: 1. Move : every marching army walks a day further along its route, tile by tile, and enters the next province on the day it reaches that province's first tile. 2. Stop checks : an army that arrives somewhere is checked against the list below. 3. Contact : hostile armies that come within engagement range of each other, 10 tiles plus one for every 2 points of the better commander's Cunning, at most 15, start the battle rules from Warfare where the defender stands, with a chance to withdraw first. 4. Standing orders : armies set to attack may turn to intercept. Every mover steps in a fixed order each day: armies first, then fleets, then traders, then exploration ships, each in the order they were raised. After the moves come arrivals, then battles. Battles are fought over time, in rounds of 4 hours, six a day, and while a battle runs its armies don't move. Other armies that march into the province join the side they belong to. While one of your battles runs, the whole map slows down: each day is played as six 4-hour steps, every other army, fleet and trader moving a sixth of a day per step. At every step you can change your army's standing orders, order a retreat or switch between your running battles; the result can't be skipped. When the battle ends, days go back to normal. Battles between other realms never slow the game: they fight their six rounds a day at once, and others can join them at the start of a day. At the end of every turn the weekly steps run: armies eat (and go hungry when the food is gone), plunder, raids and plague. An army standing in your own land refills its food there at each weekly step, from the castle store first and then from the locals, without having to stop. Sieges, sickness and pay run once a month, at the end of the turn in which a new month begins. A mover always stands on exactly one map tile, and so in the province that owns that tile. You can follow every army across the map tile by tile as the days pass: its commander's banner stands where the army is. If two hostile armies walk the same border in opposite directions, they fight in the province of the army with more days still to walk. Days already walked toward the next province carry over into the next turn. How long a step takes Routes run over the map's tiles, not from province to province. Each tile has a weight , the days it takes to cross its kind of land (grassland is quick, mountains, jungle and marsh are slow), and the route planner picks the path of least total weight. Snow makes a tile slower still: in winter, land from latitude 50° toward the pole and every mountain lies under snow and costs more to cross. The tile weights are provisional, tuned so marching keeps its pace: an army on foot can't walk from Mexico to Canada in 2 months (it takes about 4 to 6). The factors below still apply on top of the tiles: days = tile weights walked × road × season × march order × guns × column ÷ horse bonus ÷ Cunning bonus + river days - Crossing used to be counted per province by its ground (farmland, grassland and savanna 1; drylands and hills 1.5; desert, forest and tundra 2; mountains, jungle and marsh 3); these are now the starting weights of the tiles of those grounds. - 6 days per crossing unit , so a step across farmland takes 6 days. - Road : the worse road of the two provinces counts: track 1, road 0.75, paved road 0.5, turnpike 0.4, railway 0.1. - Season : in winter (December to February in the north, June to August in the south) step days double in tundra, mountains and forest. In the wet season of the climate they are ×1.25 in paddies, marsh and jungle (monsoon Asia June to September, Sahel and savanna July to September, Amazon December to May). - March order : Normal 1, Forced 0.67, Careful 1.33, Raid 0.67 (horse-only armies). - Guns : an army with any guns other than light field guns takes ×1.25 once for the whole army into hills, mountains, forest, jungle and marsh. Bombards can't enter a mountain province without a road. - Column : an army bigger than the forage limit of the province it enters adds 1 crossing. - Horse bonus : step days are divided by 1 + 0.5 × (horses ÷ men), so a horse-only army goes 1.5 times as fast as foot. - Cunning bonus : divided by 1 + 0.05 per point of the commander's Cunning. Fractions are kept, and rounded to whole days only for display. Rivers, passes and hard ground - Rivers : entering a river province with no bridge adds 1 day per 10,000 men or part of it, 2 for a great river (the biggest rivers on the map, such as the Rhine, Danube, Volga or Nile). A bridge removes river days for any army size, but a bridge province held by an enemy army is no use to you. Named fords count as bridges in summer and autumn: June to November in the north, December to May in the south. A flood (an event) doubles river days in a province for 3 months. Frozen rivers : from December to March a river at latitude 55° or more freezes and is crossed like a bridge, with no river days and no penalty for attacking across it. - Passes : mountain provinces marked as passes (Great St Bernard, Khyber, Brenner, Roncesvalles and others) count as having a road (×0.75) even before roads are built. - Snow : from December to March (June to September in the south) snow-peak provinces with no pass and no road are closed, and routes go round them. - Sea : armies enter sea and ocean zones only aboard ships. - Glacier is impassable. - Dunes : a province that is mostly dunes takes 3 crossings instead of desert's 2, allows no foraging, and guns can enter it only with camels. Glacier and paddies likewise count when they are most of the province. - Straits : some land neighbours across a narrow strait (Bosporus, Øresund, Messina, Kerch, Gibraltar and others) can be crossed without your own ships where there is a ferry (a harbour on either side owned by you, an ally or someone granting passage), at 2 days per 10,000 men or part. An enemy fleet in the strait closes it. What stops an army When an army arrives in a province, the checks run in this order: enemy army here, enemy garrisoned castle here, border closed, snow pass closed, halt when the enemy is seen, food runs out. When a check stops a march, the rest of the route stays drawn in grey so one order resumes it. - Enemy armies stop you only in the province they stand in. - Castles always block. An army that enters a province with an enemy garrisoned castle stops there, and no army marches on past until the castle is taken (stormed, surrendered or bribed). While there it can only stay (besiege or wait), go back the way it came or into a neighbour it came from or its side holds, or march on once the castle has fallen. A castle with no garrison doesn't block. An ally's garrisoned castles block that ally's enemies the same way. The planner treats every such province as the end of a route and shows "stops at Langres on day 14 until the castle falls". An arrival in the middle of a day counts as that day, so 13.5 days is day 14. - Borders. An army may enter its own land, its subjects', the land of an enemy at war with it, rebel-held provinces, an ally's land or a realm granting passage, and land nobody owns, and no other realm's land. No order can march an army into any other realm, not even as an act of war: declare war or get passage first. If passage is withdrawn while it marches, the army stops at the border that day. If a destination can't be reached without passage, the planner routes round or says "needs passage from Savoy". - Snow. If a pass closes while an army is in it, the army stops and winters there, hungry. - Halt when the enemy is seen stops the army in the province before the one where an enemy is seen. - Food. An army whose food runs out on its route is not stopped; its route turns red from that step and you get one notice. What an army eats from depends on the land: its own land feeds it from the locals and refills it; a subject's land uses the reserve unless the subject's terms feed it; enemy, rebel-held and unowned land use the reserve and then plunder; an ally's or passage land use the reserve. Meeting the enemy Withdrawing. Before a battle each side checks its standing order "retreat if outnumbered" against what it sees, a rumour counting at its shown size. Only an outnumbered side wants to go; the stronger side never withdraws. A side that wants to go steps back to the province it came from, or if it was standing still to the friendly neighbour with the fewest enemies. It gets away only if its commander's Cunning is higher than the enemy's and it isn't trapped; otherwise it fights. Broken armies. A side that breaks in battle drops half its wagons, and its guns if the winner held the field with horse. It marches on forced march by the fastest route to the nearest refuge (an own-side province with a castle, or any own-side province with no enemy) up to 3 steps away, never through an enemy castle. While broken it takes no orders, doesn't besiege and doesn't stop for its own side's castles. An enemy that meets it fights at once; the broken army can't withdraw and breaks again at the first lost sector. With no refuge within 3 provinces, it surrenders: its men become prisoners and its commander is captured, unless he has Cunning 4 or more and gets away alone to the capital. At the refuge it becomes an ordinary army again and fled men who come back rejoin it. Interception. Once a day an army with standing order "attack" looks at seen enemies in neighbouring provinces (an army known only as a rumour is never a target) and turns to march on one if it isn't on a player route (or Attack on the way is set), its men are at least the enemy's (or what its AI personality's retreat ratio allows), and its step there is shorter than the enemy's remaining step. An army on "wait" never intercepts. Chasing. An army following an enemy re-plans its route each day to where the enemy was last seen. If the enemy vanishes from sight, the follower walks to where it was last seen and stops there with a notice. Friends and neutrals in the same province don't fight or block, and share the province's forage limit by men. Food on the road The route preview shows the food reserve on arrival at each province, counting meals abroad, refills at home and the forage limit: green while it covers the march, yellow under half, red where empty. On a route that leaves your land, the point of no return is flagged: the last province from which the army can still get home before its reserve runs out. Refill and go adds a stop at your castle with the most food above its siege reserve, or the richest of your provinces on the route, and waits a day per 10 % of the reserve refilled. Marching through your own provinces refills the reserve at each weekly step, not only where it stops at month end. A route that stops at a castle abroad shows its colour for the end of the turn there. Splitting and joining Splitting an army takes 2 days before W14 Army divisions and no time after, and each half gets its share of food, wagons and companies. The commander stays with the half you pick; the other needs a captain or new commander, or is led by its senior company captain with Cunning 0. Joining two armies in one province takes 1 day: food and wagons add up, the commander with more victories leads, and the other becomes a captain if there is room. Moving many armies - March together : several armies get one destination, each with its own route. With "arrive together" on (the default), the faster ones start later so all arrive the same day, and that day is shown. - Rally point : armies march there and join on arrival in the order they come. - New regiments go to : set a province (or one per front) and trained regiments march there on their own when ready and join the army standing there. Newly raised levies don't: they wait in their province as its garrison until a commander picks them up (see Recruiting). - Fronts (W14): draw a line of provinces and give it armies, which split it into even stretches, march to the middle of their own stretch, intercept only within it and retreat to a castle on the front. Orders You can change an army's orders as often as you like before ending the turn; the last order stands. Every army can March to (fastest route to a province it may enter; marching to the province it stands in is a Halt), March by (through waypoints), Halt (stop, keeping the rest of the route greyed), Return home (to the nearest own province with a castle) and Follow / Join (follow a friendly army and join when you meet, or chase an enemy). Horse-only armies can Raid , walking each step at raid pace and then spending 7 days in each province they enter before riding on. Any army in a province with an enemy castle can Besiege , and can't march on until the castle falls. Armies in a port with ships, or at sea, can Board ships / Land . To stop a march, tap Halt beside Move on the army's card, tap Halt it where it stands in the commander list, and it stops on the spot. A fleet under sail has Stop here beside Sail on its card. These show only while there is a route to cancel. Each army remembers two route settings: Pace (Normal, Forced, Careful) and On the way (keep marching, halt when the enemy is seen, attack what we see). There are no standing orders beyond warfare's. Every order is data, the same for player and AI; an AI army's standing orders come from its realm's personality. One way of moving Armies, fleets, trade ships and traders are all movers . Each has a place, a route, progress, and three rules of its own: how many days a step takes, where it may enter, and where it stops. Land provinces and sea zones form one graph, and each mover's may-enter rule picks its part. All movers step in the same day loop and use the same route planner. A port province with a harbour on a shore tile neighbours its sea zone. - Boarding : an army in a port with enough of its own or an ally's ships boards at a day per 5,000 men and becomes cargo , moving with the fleet. Aboard, it eats from its reserve as if abroad. - Landing : a fleet lands its army on a neighbouring coast at a day per 5,000 men, twice as long with no port, and the army is a mover again with the stop checks applying. - If you route an army onto water, the planner asks Naval for a combined route (march, board, sail, land, march) when you have ships, or stops at the coast with "needs ships". - Traders use the same roads, rivers and passes. A trader's stop rule reacts to enemy armies, and raiding armies can attack traders they pass; Trade sets the amounts. Dunois marches to Dijon, March 1450 France is at war with Burgundy. Jean de Dunois (Cunning 4) leads 14,200 men with 3,200 horse and 8 bombards from Paris. Paris and Troyes are French farmland, Langres is Burgundian hills, Dijon is Burgundian farmland, and Troyes sits on the Seine with no bridge. Step Days Paris to Troyes 6.5 Troyes to Langres 7.0 Langres to Dijon 5.6 Langres has a stone castle with 400 men and every other road to Dijon runs through Burgundian castles. Dragging the banner to Dijon gives a route ending at Langres: "stops at Langres on day 14 until the castle falls", with the leg to Dijon in grey. The food line is green to Troyes and yellow at Langres. In the month, Dunois arrives at Langres on day 14 and besieges it. The Bastard of Burgundy (Cunning 2) leads 8,000 men, seen by France only as a rumour of "about 6,000 near Beaune". His standing order is retreat if outnumbered 3 to 2. When he stands in Langres at the end of day 22 he wants to withdraw (14,200 against 8,000 is more than 3 to 2), but must fight because his Cunning is lower than Dunois'. The garrison joins him from the walls, and while the battle runs the month slows to 4-hour steps, where the player can change standing orders or order a retreat. If Dunois wins and the castle falls, tapping the grey leg resumes the march to Dijon. What you see - Selecting an army : tap it (banners take big taps) or tap its commander in the Army list, and its card slides up halfway; provinces it could reach this turn are lightly shaded, those next turn lighter still. Selecting never moves or zooms the map. Select several armies at once with more taps or a drag-box and give them one march order together. - Drawing a route : drag from the army's banner and the route is drawn live with days and food on arrival, set when you lift, cancelled by dragging back onto the army. A drag that doesn't start on the banner pans the map. Tapping a province draws the same route and waits for confirmation. Drag the middle of a route to add a waypoint; drag a waypoint off to remove it. A two-finger tap deselects. - The order pill : at least 44 points high, at the route's end, with March and its days, pace, on the way and cancel. Changing a setting redraws the route and its days at once. - The route preview : a light dashed line over a dark outline, so it shows on every map colour; turn marks (every 7 days) where the army will stand at the end of this and each later turn; day counts at each province and the total; food colour and the point-of-no-return flag; icons for river, snow pass, stopping castle, border needing passage and enemy seen (with shown size); other selected armies' routes thinner in the same colour. - Stacked armies : one banner with total men and number of armies; tapping opens a picker (name, men, food, commander) with Select all here and, at region zoom, Select all in sight. - Zoom : at world zoom, arrows thick by men and coloured by owner, long routes in weeks; at region zoom, the full preview; at local zoom, marching columns as sprites sized to the army. - Watching the turn : when the turn ends its week plays at about one second per 10 days with a skip button, the date ticking one day at a time while armies walk their routes. The army walks exactly the route the preview showed. While one of your battles runs, the playback slows to 4-hour steps where you can change standing orders, retreat or switch battles. Battles between other realms only flash for half a second, and stopping castles ring red. Any battle can be replayed from its notice. - Notices , only for: an army stopped short (enemy, castle, border or snow), a battle fought (with its reason), a route that turned red, and an enemy first seen marching into your land. Nothing for an army that walked where it was told. - Accessibility : every gesture has a tap-only version (tap army, tap province, tap March; Go by… for waypoints); food colours also carry a pattern (solid, dashed, dotted); day counts stay at least 10 points tall at region zoom and hide rather than shrink. How it connects - Warfare: contact leads to battles; warfare supplies withdraw and break results, standing orders, sieges, food reserve, forage limit, plunder, raids, scouting and Cunning. - World-Map: the province and sea-zone graph, ground, rivers and their rank, hemisphere and climate. - Provinces: days to cross per ground, roads, bridges, castles and the inputs to the forage limit. - Buildings: bridges, roads and harbours as built. - Naval: shares the mover rules, day loop and planner; fleets' step days, boarding and landing, enemy fleets closing straits. - Trade: traders move on the same day loop and roads. - Diplomacy: passage, war state and allies decide where you may enter. - Subjects: a subject's terms may feed your army. - Recruiting: gathered levies and trained regiments march to "New regiments go to", and levies walk to training places. - Research: W14 Army divisions for same-day splits and fronts. - Historical-Events: floods. - Time-and-Turns: the weekly turn, real month lengths, turn order and seasons. - Map and Map Modes and Screens-and-Navigation: the route preview, replay and notices. - Rebellions: rebel-held provinces may be entered and plundered. Numbers Values live in packages/rules/data/domain/troop-movement.json . Values marked provisional may change in balancing. What Value Status Days in a turn 7 (a week) fixed Days in a month the real length, 28 to 31 fixed Days per crossing 6 fixed Days to cross by ground farmland 1, hills 1.5, forest 2, mountains 3, dunes 3 … provisional Horse speed bonus 0.5 provisional Column too big for the forage limit +1 crossing fixed River days 1 per 10,000 men, 2 for a great river or a ferry provisional Road 1 / 0.75 / 0.5 / 0.4 / 0.1 provisional Season ×2 winter; ×1.25 wet season provisional March order Normal 1, Forced 0.67, Careful 1.33, Raid 0.67 provisional Guns ×1.25 fixed Cunning 0.05 a point provisional Flood 3 months provisional Frozen rivers latitude 55° or more, December to March provisional Battle steps six 4-hour steps a day while your battle runs fixed Raid stay 7 days per province provisional Refuge search 3 steps provisional Split / join 2 days / 1 day provisional Refill and go 1 day per 10 % of the reserve provisional Replay speed 1 second per 10 days, battles flash 0.5 s provisional Boarding / landing a day per 5,000 men; ×2 landing with no port provisional Captured commander escapes Cunning 4 provisional The march code also uses warfare's food values: 2 rations a soldier, 3 a horse, 2 months carried and 5 % less food per Logistics point. Still open Nothing in troop movement is waiting on a decision; the provisional numbers above are tuned in balancing. For developers - Spec: domain/troop-movement/spec.md in the game repository. - Features: domain/troop-movement/features/ , including day-loop.feature , step-days.feature , what-stops-an-army.feature , movers.feature and the worked example dunois-1450.feature . - Code: packages/engine/src/domain/troop-movement/ ( model.ts , planner.ts , day-loop.ts , food.ts , army-rules.ts , army-ops.ts , many.ts , orders.ts , preview.ts ), with balance numbers in packages/rules/data/domain/troop-movement.json . The older march code in packages/engine/src/march.ts and turn.ts is replaced by these rules.
Tutorial-and-Help: Pocket Hegemony teaches itself in four layers: a short tutorial campaign, "Murad's Frontier", played as the Ottomans under Murad I from 20 September 1378, the day every campaign starts, to late 1383; guided first turns for your first real campaign; a Needs attention list that tells you what needs you; and tooltips, "Why?" and the Almanac, which explain every number in the game. You can skip any of it, and nothing in the game is locked behind it. How it works The principles - Teach by doing. Every lesson is something you do on the real map with the real screens. No slideshow, and no tutorial-only screens the real game does not have, apart from the tutorial's own pacing tools and its note. - One idea per step. Each step names one thing to look at or one thing to do, in one or two short lines. - Short sessions. Chapters last about 5 minutes. Close the app mid-chapter and you come back to the same step. - Never trap. Every step and every chapter can be skipped, and you can leave the tutorial at any time. - Same lesson on every device. Each step is written once, with button tokens that become the right prompt for touch, mouse and keyboard, or controller. - Teach the start first. The tutorial teaches the game as it starts, in 1378. Systems that only matter later are taught through New entries on the Needs attention list and the Almanac, not through tutorial chapters for later eras. - Our own words. No tutorial text, character name or screen name comes from other strategy games. If you skip the tutorial and the guided turns, you still get the Needs attention list, tooltips, "Why?" and the Almanac. Murad's Frontier The tutorial is played as the Ottomans, from 20 September 1378 to late 1383, in ten chapters. Like every campaign it starts on 20 September 1378. Murad I rules from Edirne, with Bursa across the water as the second seat of his house and his son Bayezid as heir; Gallipoli is his again, so the crossing between Anatolia and Thrace is safe, but Venice and Genoa rule the sea. In Constantinople Andronikos IV sits on the throne he took in 1376 with Genoese and Ottoman help, and pays Murad tribute, while his father John V and brother Manuel II sit in his prison. The tutorial keeps history's own dates and never moves an event to suit the lesson plan; where historians disagree on a date, it uses the dating the 1378 start uses and says so in the event's history. The Ottomans are in the free tier, so the whole tutorial works without a purchase on every store and in the Steam demo. Each chapter starts from its own fixed chapter save, so you can play or replay any chapter on its own. Chapter Date Turns What it teaches Done when 0 The map September 1378 0 Pan and zoom through world, region and local view; select a province; open its card; switch map modes (Food, then Faith); find Edirne, Bursa, Gallipoli and the straits, and Constantinople You have opened Edirne's province card and seen the Food and Faith map modes 1 A week at a time September to November 1378 3 Country card; gold and food at a glance; End turn; the turn report; the first event (Tribute from Constantinople: take the tribute, or ask after the imprisoned John V) The tribute event is answered and the turn report read 2 The bey and his lords December 1378 to February 1379 3 Ruler and heirs (Murad, Bayezid and Yakub, and what Savcı's revolt in 1373 showed); why frontier lords waver when there is no war or new land; the lords Evrenos, Mihal and Timurtaş; what a lord wants (Evrenos: a march on Serres); royal provinces and lords' lands; hiring an official; tax rates An official is placed, and the wavering lord has been given his want, a gift, or left alone (each is fine; the turn report shows the result) 3 Schools and inventions March to May 1379 2 plus Advance Madrasas, students and scholars (the madrasa in Bursa); schools have a faith; a served, protected community on a Faith line; choosing what to study; every student is a recruit the army cannot raise; ends when news comes that John V and Manuel have escaped An invention is chosen and you have seen the recruit pool shrink 4 Two emperors June 1379 3 John V and Manuel reach Murad: back John V, or keep Andronikos IV; the Italian partner each brings (Venice or Genoa) and their war over Tenedos; the war aim Seat a pretender; a partner's reasons; the Faith policy choice for the Orthodox; crossing at Gallipoli; the levy in Thrace; levies against trained regiments; the first Janissaries and how they were raised; calling the lords' riders; making Lala Şahin Pasha Marshal; standing orders An emperor is chosen, and an army of levies, lords' riders and Janissaries stands with a commander 5 The walls of Pera July 1379 to May 1381 4 to 6 plus Advance Marching and days to cross; the food reserve; Constantinople opens to John V (1 July 1379); seeing the enemy (Andronikos's sally from Genoese Pera, first as a rumour); a small clash before Pera; what the faith choice and the Venetian galleys changed; terms; peace voices; making peace (the settlement of May 1381) Peace is signed (losing the battle is allowed; the chapter adapts) 6 Bread and castles June to September 1381 1 plus Advance Food lives in provinces; castles collect and spread it; reach rings; the Food policy screen and presets; a bride for Bayezid (the Germiyan marriage, whose dowry castles of Kütahya, Simav, Eğrigöz and Tavşanlı would join your reach, or press Germiyan by war); the September harvest; ends with the Hamid towns for sale (buy them, knowing Karaman wants them, or leave them) A preset is chosen, the harvest turn played, and one hungry province's "Why?" opened 7 The soldiers' pay 1382 3 to 4 A rising of unpaid soldiers in Edirne, owed since the Pera years; the rebellion card; the five answers (grant, talk, bribe, wait, attack); then the news that Manuel II has made Thessaloniki his own base The rising ends by any means 8 The road to Serres August to September 1383 4 to 6 Declaring a war yourself (Evrenos's march on Serres); marching from Komotini; besieging Serres month by month; storming the breach; terms (Serres fell on 19 September 1383) Serres falls or terms are agreed 9 Your realm now late 1383 none A one-screen recap with Almanac links, and what lies ahead: Thessaloniki, Karaman, Sofia and Tarnovo, the road to Kosovo; keep playing these Ottomans or start a new campaign You pick one In all, about 30 to 40 turns and 45 to 50 minutes, in sessions of about 5 minutes. A turn is one week, so each chapter uses Advance to… to skip the quiet weeks between its lessons. The chapters follow the calendar: the choice of emperor has to come before John V's return on 1 July 1379, and no harvest falls before then, so the food lesson waits for the harvest of September 1381. History and your choices. When your choices differ from history, the chapter carries on from what actually happened, as a real campaign would. When the next chapter starts, its chapter save puts the world back on its historical course, and its opening card says so in one line. Nothing you did off script carries into a later chapter. Every scripted event keeps the event tree's history block with its sources. The Germiyan marriage and the Hamid sale are dated 1381, as the Ottoman chronicles have them and as the 1378 start leaves them still ahead; their history blocks give the other dating (1378, and 1374 to 1375). The recruiting, battle and siege lessons use their own Ottoman set of worked numbers (for now: 1,000 Janissaries, 4,000 levies, 2,000 lords' riders, an army of 6,000 at Pera, and a Serres that holds 2 months). How you use it You find the tutorial on the first-launch question ("Play the tutorial"), under Tutorial in the main menu (under More once you have finished it) with its chapter list, and through Practice this on any How to play page of the Almanac. Every lesson happens on the map and on the real cards over it; the parchment note says in one line what to look at or tap, and a spotlight sits on it. The historical choices (which emperor to back, the Germiyan marriage, the Hamid towns) are ordinary event cards with their options. One chapter is one subject, one step is one thing, and one note shows at a time. The chapter list's ticks show how far you are through the ten chapters, and the note's counter how far through the chapter. On a phone in landscape the note runs along the bottom inside the safe areas and moves under the top bar when what it points at is low, so it never covers it, and it never takes more than a third of the screen. Skip step, Free look, event options and every button a step points at are at least 44 points; the spotlight takes no taps, a "look" step ends on a tap anywhere, and nothing needs hover. Turn the phone upright and the game asks you to turn it sideways again; the tutorial waits on its step. Pacing tools - Advance to… runs several weekly turns in a row to a named date and shows one combined turn report. - Input focus. During a "do" step only the controls on the step's allowed list respond; everything else is dimmed, not hidden. Free look , a small button, lifts the focus for that step. - Quiet world. While the tutorial runs, every computer war against the Ottomans except the war for John V's throne is held back, and so is every computer war in the Balkans and western Anatolia (Karaman and Germiyan included). - Battle at watch speed. The chapter 5 clash before Pera always opens the battle screen, slowed to one bell every 3 seconds. The tutorial scenario The tutorial is one scenario file holding its start state, world rules, scripted events, chapter saves and steps. It starts from the normal 20 September 1378 setup, which already has Murad I and Bayezid, Andronikos IV on the Byzantine throne, Shishman at Tarnovo, Germiyan holding Kütahya, and Serres, Thessaloniki and Sofia still beyond the Ottoman border. It overrides only where the tutorial needs them: Çandarlı Kara Halil as grand vizier; the Evrenos, Mihal and Timurtaş families as lords, Evrenos wavering; one royal province in Anatolia with no official; a fixed seed; the Christian sipahis' lord card (Wavering); and the Orthodox row of the Faith policy set to Restricted. The computer is steered: in chapter 5 Andronikos IV holds Pera with the Genoese and leads their sally, and in chapter 8 Manuel II accepts terms once Serres has fallen. The scripted events are Tribute from Constantinople (autumn 1378), John V and Manuel reach Murad (June 1379), John V back in Constantinople (1 July 1379), the settlement of 1381 (May 1381), A bride for Bayezid (1381), The Hamid towns for sale (1381) and Manuel goes to Thessaloniki (1382). Each is marked tutorial only and never fires in a real campaign. The rising of chapter 7 is not a scripted event: its chapter save leaves the soldiers unpaid, and the rebellion rules do the rest. Chapter saves are rebuilt by a tool whenever rules change, by playing the previous chapter's recommended path in the engine; they are never edited by hand. The same chapter save and the same orders always give the same result. A CI test plays each chapter's recommended path from its save and checks it reaches "Done when". Going off script If you… Then… Asked after John V in chapter 1 Andronikos's envoy leaves cold until chapter 1 ends; chapter 2 starts from its own save with the tribute taken as in history Lose the clash before Pera The step changes to "Your army broke. Fall back behind the walls of Edirne and call the levy." Andronikos IV's side offers terms after failing to take one castle in two months, so the chapter still ends in peace Ignored the wavering lord His loyalty drops one step, and the turn report shows it; later chapters start from their own saves Sit idle on a "do" step After 8 seconds the pointer pulses on the target again; after 20 the note adds "Stuck? Skip this step." After the Food map mode you switch to the Faith map mode: Rumelia shows as Orthodox under a Sunni realm, hatched where a community is 30 % or more, with the line "Most of your people in Rumelia are Orthodox Christians. You rule them as a Sunni bey." - The news. On chapter 3's last turn the news comes that John V and Manuel have escaped to Murad, and the country card shows "Two emperors: Andronikos IV (Genoa) and John V (Venice)". Venice and Genoa are already at war over Tenedos, and each backs one emperor. - Which emperor (chapter 4). The event "John V and Manuel reach Murad" (June 1379) hands you the choice: Choice What follows Back John V (as history) Venice and its galleys are your partner; Andronikos IV and Genoa are the enemy; John V at your court gives you the war aim Seat a pretender Keep Andronikos IV Genoa's galleys from Pera are your partner; John V and Venice are the enemy; the emperor on the throne is already yours, so there is no war aim to win The war screen shows the aim, its cause and one linked line on why this aim and not Take land. A shared rival, not faith, binds this war. - The faith choice (chapter 4). While the Genoese galleys of Pera hold the Bosporus, that crossing shows as closed with Genoa's banner on it, so you send your Anatolian troops over the Dardanelles at Gallipoli: 2 days, plus a day per 10,000 men. - After the clash before Pera , the turn report shows the battle's result together with the faith choice (how many Christian sipahis rode at Pera, or why they stayed home) and what the Venetian partner brought. The madrasa in Bursa is Sunni. The tutorial calls the civil war what it was, a father and a son fighting for one throne with Ottoman and Italian help, names neither emperor the rightful one, rewards no harm, and counts the dead of the clash on both sides the same way. The Janissaries In chapter 4, after the Janissaries join the army, a step opens their regiment card and the "Why?" on its men. The recruits line reads "War captives: the bey's fifth of every haul (the pençik), trained as the new troops (yeniçeri)." These are the first Janissaries, raised under Murad in the 1360s to 1380s; the later levy of Christian boys is not part of a 1378 story. Tapping the line moves the camera to the border lands the raids took captives from. Then one illustrated vignette card, in the style of an event and marked narrative only, shows three panels: the captives brought back from a raid, the young man's years of training, and the soldier he becomes. It has only Continue and Read more; no option gives you anything. The step ends on a raided border province's card whose People line shows the captives taken and whose grievances show Sons taken , with its Orthodox lords one step lower in loyalty, and the vizier's line "The corps is strong. This is what it costs the villages that fill it." The Almanac's entry is sourced from the catalogue's Ottoman record and standard histories, with no invented numbers. Steps and how they look Each step has an id, a kind, its text (a string key), an anchor, an allowed list, a done condition, whether the guide's face shows, and a length limit of 140 characters. Kind Ends when look You confirm, or tap anywhere; never auto-advanced do Its condition is met; there is no Next button choose You make any choice; the next step reacts to which watch What it plays (a turn, a battle) ends; it can be paused Text tokens: {btn:…} becomes the prompt for your current input; {ui:…} the screen's name in bold with its icon; {stat:…} the stat's icon and name linked to the Almanac; {place:…} and {lord:…} a linked name that moves the camera there. The step note is a parchment strip at the bottom edge, never over the target, moving to the top when the target is low, and at most a third of the screen tall. A spotlight with a gold edge sits on the anchor, and the rest of the screen dims to 50 % (not black). The guide's face is the grand vizier Çandarlı Kara Halil, Murad's vizier, labelled "The Grand Vizier", and he appears only in the tutorial. A new step plays a soft hint sound and a finished step a confirm sound; neither lowers the music. A counter shows the steps of the chapter ("2 / 6"). First-campaign hints Until the Murad's Frontier chapters are playable, the first-campaign hints are the tutorial you meet. In your first campaign a small parchment note says what to tap next, and a brass ring pulses around the exact button, card or spot on the map it means, one tap at a time. There are thirteen, one after another, and together they walk you through the main systems: Hint What you tap 1 Choose a realm The Ottomans under Murad I (the tutorial's realm), or any realm you like 2 Open a province's card Your capital on the map, then its name at the bottom left 3 Open your realm's book Your banner in the top bar 4 Change the map mode Map mode, then Wealth 5 Move an army Commanders, a commander, then a province next to the army 6 End the turn End turn 7 Read the news The scroll in the top bar 8 Choose a study Your banner, Research, Can study, then Study now 9 Recruit Your capital's card, the Garrison tab, then Recruit 10 Build The Build tab, then Build 11 Meet your lords Your banner, Lands, then your lords' page 12 See your gold The gold in the top bar 13 Send an envoy A neighbour's land on the map, its card, its realm, the Diplomacy tab, then a mission Doing the thing ticks its hint off, in any order, and the next one appears; an order the game refuses ticks nothing, and a hint you have already done (a study already chosen) is skipped. When what to tap is not on screen, Show me opens the card that holds it or turns the map to it. The × dismisses one hint, and Stop hints turns them all off. The note sits between the overview button and End turn. When that would cover the ring or an open card, it moves beside the card, or under the top bar, so it never covers what it points at; a button half hidden at the bottom of a card is scrolled into view first. The ring takes no taps, so the button under it works as ever. The counter ("3 / 13") shows how far you are. Hints wait while an event card, the game menu or the loading screen is up, or a week plays. Which hints are done stays with you, not with the save: a second campaign picks up where the first left off, and once all thirteen are done they never come back. In Settings (the cog in the side tools, or the game menu), Gameplay holds the Tutorial hints switch with "n of 13 done" and "Reset tutorial and hints", which brings them all back. Tutorial on the start screen does the same and starts you at the realm list. Needs attention There is no advisor in a real campaign; the vizier belongs to the tutorial. Instead, the Needs attention screen holds one-line entries, each with a Show button that moves the camera or opens the screen. It has two groups: Warnings first, then Waiting for you , which holds opportunities and then New entries. Opportunity lines state a fact; they never tell you what to do. An entry leaves when its cause ends or you dismiss it, and a dismissed entry does not return before its check's cooldown ends (a province's famine warning at most once a year). Long-press, right-click or the info button on an entry offers "Mute this" (just that line) and "Don't list this kind again"; you can undo any mute in Settings. Warfare: Warfare is everything that happens once your soldiers are under arms: how they are organised into companies and armies, what they cost, how they are fed, who leads them and in what style, how a battle is fought bell by bell, how castles fall, what holding enemy land means, and how a war drifts toward peace. It runs from era I (from the start on 20 September 1378) to the end of the campaign on 31 August 1939, changing as inventions arrive. How it works Companies, troop types and kinds Every army is made of companies of usually 500 to 1,000 men. Each company has exactly one troop type (how it fights, such as pikes or knights) and one kind (where its men come from). A company keeps its own men, drill, scars, loads of arms, pay owed and months out. - Drill is months spent training together, from 0 to 24. A company in camp, garrison or winter quarters and not marching gains 1 drill a month; standing regiments drill all year. A hungry month takes 1 drill away. When new men join, drill and scars are diluted: drill becomes drill × old men ÷ all men. Disbanding resets drill and scars. - Scars are battles stood through without breaking, from 0 to 5. A company gains 1 scar for standing through a battle and 1 more if its side won. Five years without a battle takes one away. - Loads of arms come from the store at raising and from won fields, and are lost with killed and fled men, on a lost field, or sold at disbanding. A company short of the loads its troop type needs fights as the next troop type down (heavy infantry as levy infantry). - Men join by raising, refilling from recruits, wounded coming back and enlisted prisoners, and leave by being killed, wounded, fleeing, deserting, falling sick, going hungry or being disbanded. Troop level is read from drill and scars: 1 Raw, 2 Drilled, 3 Seasoned, 4 Veteran, 5 Elite. In eras I and II, Drilled comes at 3 months of drill, Seasoned at 6 months and 1 scar, Veteran at 3 scars, and Elite at 5 scars and 12 months of drill. Levels drop when new men dilute a company, after 5 years without a battle, when hungry, and all at once on disbanding. Standing regiments (W12) never drop below level 2.
