Kinds set pay and base break point: Kind Base break point Pay Levy 25 % free for 3 months, then normal pay Retinue 35 % paid by the lord Hired company 35 % three times normal pay Standing regiment 30 % 1.5 times normal pay, all year (needs W12) Garrison 40 % on the walls normal pay Rebel band 20 % loot Levies have no service term: once raised they stay until you disband them or leave them as a garrison. Levies away at harvest cost their province that share of its harvest. A wavering lord may take his retinue home mid-war. A hired company owed 1 month of pay won't fight; owed 2 months, it loots the province it stands in or takes the enemy's offer if higher. Standing regiments keep drill and scars through peace. Garrisons count against their castle's room. Rebel bands fight by the same battle rules whatever the rebellion rules decide about how they form. A company's break point is changed by its troop level, the Might of the leader in its sector, +5 % defending its own homeland, −10 % if hungry, −5 % per month of pay owed, and commander traits. The realm's soldier stats - Soldiers : all men in all companies, garrisons included. - Arms store : fed by forges, buying, captured fields and companies handing arms back; emptied by issuing, battle losses, rust of 2 % a year and selling. - Powder store : fed by powder mills and buying; emptied by firing, damp of 5 % a year and a castle magazine being captured. - Prisoners : from battles won, surrenders and pursuit; each eats 1 ration a month. - Victories and defeats over the last 20 years, which feed lords' loyalty, neighbours' fear and the event tree's prestige. The troop cap The troop cap is the most soldiers your realm may keep: 2 % of the people in royal provinces with an official (3 % with a muster master), plus 1 % of the people in royal provinces without one, plus the garrison room of your castles. Levies, hired companies and standing regiments count toward it, and garrisons only above their castle's room. Provinces occupied by the enemy or in revolt count nothing. W12 adds 0.5 % of people, W15 doubles the shares, W18 adds 1 %. Lords' retinues don't count: each lord has his own cap by the same rule on his lands (2 % with one of his officials, 1 % without), and allies count only against their own. Over the cap you can't raise or hire, every soldier over it costs double pay, and levies desert 5 % a month until you are back under. There is no cap on the size of one army; food is its limit. France, 1444 (on the 1444 checkpoint world). With 4,000,000 people in royal provinces with an official, 1,500,000 without and 31 castles, France's cap is 95,000 plus the garrison room of the 31 castles. The Duke of Burgundy's 6 provinces of about 430,000 people, all with his officials, give him a retinue cap of about 9,000, outside France's cap. Raising and keeping an army Levies come from Recruiting as levy-kind companies of levy infantry, gathered a thousand at a time in their province, where they wait as its garrison until a commander picks them up. No army exists without a commander : soldiers without one are a province's garrison. An army that loses its commander with no captain to step up halts; in your own land it becomes that province's garrison, abroad it waits for a commander to join it. Calling the lords. Each lord answers by his loyalty. A loyal lord brings his whole retinue in 3 weeks and may lead it as a captain. A wavering lord brings half, after 6 weeks, and goes home after 6 months unless the war aim is his Want. A disloyal lord refuses, and calling him again makes him angrier. A lord in revolt's retinue is a rebel army. When the war aim is his Want, a lord comes even when wavering and stays to the end, and a lord whose lands are occupied leaves to defend them. Lords' men in play. A lord's lands' recruits are his retinue, not your levy: your levies and troop cap count only royal provinces, and each lord's retinue can grow to his own cap. At war, open your country card's Army tab: the Lords' men section sums what your lords have ready, gathering, in the field and refusing, with Call the lords to call them all; you can also call one from his own screen (Lords tab), where Retinue shows his men and Call him . A called retinue gathers at the lord's seat (his most peopled province) and takes the field as its own army, led by the lord himself. You march it like any army, but it is his: it can't be split, trained, joined to another army or handed to another commander, and he leads no other army. It costs you no pay and doesn't count toward your cap. It goes home to his lands when peace comes, when he turns disloyal, when a wavering lord has served 6 months (unless the war is for his Want), or when you tap Send him home . Every battle his men help win raises his loyalty a step. AI realms call their lords whenever they are at war. Not yet in play: a lord leaving to defend his occupied lands. Mercenary companies. Named companies with a captain are offered in the regions where they historically gathered (Swiss and German foot, Italian condottieri, Scottish and Irish gallowglass, Turkic and Afghan horse, Javanese and Japanese sword bands and others). Each shows men, troop type, drill, scars and price. A contract brings the company for the agreed months for gold up front plus monthly pay, using no recruits. The company isn't there at once: it marches from where it gathers to your capital, and the hire screen shows how many days that takes. It always comes led by its own captain as its commander, and he leaves with it. It leaves when the contract ends, when pay is owed as above, or when an enemy outbids you. Keeping. Each month the treasury pays every company except retinues and levies in their first 3 months. An army eats 2 rations per soldier on campaign, 3 per horse and 1 per prisoner, from the province at home and from its reserve abroad. Disbanded men go back to their home province's recruit pool and their arms to the store; a disbanded standing regiment loses all its drill and scars; soldiers home from a long war with no free slot become homeless, a source of rebels. Commanders and captains Every commander has Might , Cunning and Logistics from 0 to 5, a style, one trait, victories, defeats, wounds, age and origin. Jean de Dunois of France has Might 3, Cunning 4 and Logistics 2, the style Three battles and the trait Careful, with 6 victories, 1 defeat, 1 wound and age 47. How skills move: Skill Grows Fades Might +1 per 2 more victories; +1 at once for a win while outnumbered −1 for a serious wound; −1 every 5 years past 60 Cunning +1 for a win where he gave more orders than the enemy, or a clean withdrawal from a lost battle −1 every 5 years past 65; −1 when ambushed and beaten Logistics +1 for a full year in the field without a hungry month; years as a steward or warden before command with age past 65; −1 when an army starves under him Academy graduates, and officials you commission as commanders, start with +1 Cunning or Logistics and no victories. A commander takes a serious wound with a 1 in 10 chance per lost battle and 1 in 20 per won one (twice as likely if Reckless), and wounds never heal. Traits: Trait Effect Steady +5 % break point for his army Reckless +10 % strength, −5 % break point, losses ×1.3 for both sides, wounds twice as likely; never retreats Careful never ambushed while marching Careful; spots hidden companies as with +1 Cunning; retreats at 3 to 2 Beloved halves desertion, keeps levies 3 months longer Cruel sacks pay 50 % more, Burned homes come faster where he occupies, enemy garrisons won't accept his terms Siege master breaches 25 % faster Horse lord +10 % Shock; Turn with Shock hits ×2 instead of ×1.5 Old soldier his companies drill 2 a month instead of 1 Greedy keeps a tenth of all loot; takes bribes from garrisons Ambitious may grow too big (see below) At 10 victories a commander may gain a second trait. If you have not set an army's standing orders, the commander's trait sets them. Where commanders come from : the ruler or an heir, a lord, a hired captain, a captain risen from the ranks after a victory (one offer per won battle), an academy graduate, a foreign exile, or one of your officials commissioned as a commander (who counts as an academy graduate), each with its catch (a succession crisis if the ruler dies or is captured, Proud lords refusing a lower-born commander, a hired captain leaving when unpaid, the exile's old ruler insulted). Women can be commanders where the country's history supports it, more often in later eras. Recruiting adds commissioned officials. Commanders are lost to death in battle (1 in 20 for the loser's commander, more if Reckless), capture, old age, dismissal (a dismissed lord wavers), defection, or a grant of land after which he leads only his retinue. An army has one commander and up to two captains , each standing in one sector. A captain who wins 3 battles under a commander learns his style. Generals who grow too big. A commander with 8 or more victories who has led the same standing regiments or hired companies for 5 years makes them "his men", who follow him before the crown. If he is Ambitious, pay is owed, or the ruler is a child or newly crowned, events may offer him the throne or a march on the capital. Seeing the enemy and marching You see enemy armies in your own provinces, next to your armies and castles, and as far as your scouts ride: every 500 light cavalry, horse archers or camel riders see one province further. Armies further away show as rumours of size and place that can be wrong by up to a third. Scouting and rumours are only worked out near the player. A forced march doubles sickness, makes levies desert 2 % a week, and gives −10 % strength for the first day of a battle the army arrives into. A Careful march can't be ambushed and its scouts see two provinces ahead. An army with guns heavier than light field guns marches ×1.25 slower into rough ground (once for the whole army), and an army too big for a province's forage limit takes one extra crossing (6 days) to enter it. The march itself belongs to Troop-Movement. Supply Food is counted in rations (food for one person for a month). A commander cuts what his army eats by 5 % per point of Logistics. In the game today (feedback 83): men eat 1 ration a month at home and 2 on campaign (at war or abroad), and a horse eats 3. Every day an army eats from its wagons, which hold two months of campaign food, and refills them from the store of the province where it stands: in friendly land the locals keep two months for themselves, in enemy land the foragers take what they find on that ground. The food leaves the province's store. Castle stores, plunder of the standing crop and the Requisitioned and Hungry marks below are still to come. See Your-Realm for what the province and army cards show. - At home an army takes only what it needs (each week's meals plus what its reserve is missing), from its own castle store first, down to the castle's siege reserve, then from the local store. - Anywhere else (enemy, neutral or allied land, or at sea) it eats from its food reserve , which shrinks every week. - Plunder : abroad with an empty reserve, an army takes from the local store at the ground's foraging rating (rich 100 %, fair 60 %, poor 30 %, almost none 10 %), then from the standing crop, one tile a week turning burned and giving one season of that tile's food at once. Plunder never refills the reserve. - The reserve sits in wagons of 1,000 rations, each pulled by 2 horses that eat. Wagons are built (gold, timber) or captured, and lost in defeats, raids and when horses die; W10 adds 50 % to their load. You set the reserve size at 1, 2 or 3 months as a standing order. - The reserve grows by refilling at home, capturing an enemy's wagons when it breaks, and taking a fallen castle's store. It shrinks by eating abroad, losing half the wagons when the army breaks or is raided, and rot of 5 % a month (half as fast with Logistics 3 or more). - Taking food from a province's local store makes it Requisitioned for a season, and Hungry if it drops under a month of food. Taking a lord's grain lowers him a step of loyalty, and taking from a province with a no-quartering charter also counts Broken charter. - The forage limit of a province is its local store × foraging rating ÷ 2 rations, shown when you drag an army over it. - Hunger : each week with no food, 5 % of men desert (levies first, then hired, then retinues, standing regiments last), 2 % die, 1 horse in 10 is eaten, and the army fights at −20 % strength and −10 % break point. - Sickness each month by ground: low 0.5 %, medium 1 %, high 3 %, heat or cold 2 % (cold only in winter), plus the fever land rate for men not born on that ground, cut by 10 % per Logistics point. - Winter quarters : an army stopped for winter in a province with a town eats 1 ration a man from its store and drills, and the province gets Soldiers quartered after a season. A no-quartering charter refuses. Armies left in the field in winter eat 2.5 rations a man. - Burn the fields in your own province burns all its food tiles, moves the local store to the nearest castle or destroys it, and leaves Burned homes and Hungry. - With W10 you can build magazines in occupied provinces, where an army refills as if at home. Battle A battle starts when two hostile armies end a day in the same province, unless one withdraws first. An army may slip away before battle if its commander's Cunning is higher than the enemy's and it isn't trapped. Before any fighting the armies spend a contact day scouting and deploying, as armies of the age did; nobody is lost, others can march in and either side can still pull out. Then a battle day has 3 bells , fought by daylight from 8 to 20 o'clock (4 hours each in eras I to V), the nights resting, and a battle lasts at most 5 days of fighting. A typical battle runs 3 to 4 days from contact to rout. Battles are decided by the commanders' styles and skills, the troop types and levels, the realm's inventions and the place, with no dice and no player orders during the fight . The battlefield is the middle 7 tiles of the province's tile row (all of them if fewer), each a sector with a room: Sector Room Effects Fields, pasture, burned 3,000 open: horse can charge; pasture +10 % for horse Woods 1,000 no charges; shooting into it halved; companies can hide Marsh 500 no charges; everyone −25 % Waste (rock, sand) 1,500 open in drylands and desert; rough on hills and mountains Shore (river bank) 1,000 attacking across it −20 % without a bridge, none when the river is frozen Town 1,500 defender +50 %, shooting into it halved, no charges; fighting burns town buildings Castle its garrison the garrison joins from the walls The province's ground applies on top (foot, horse and gun modifiers, the defender bonus, +10 % for locals in rough country). Men beyond a sector's room stand behind it as depth and step forward at the end of each bell. Each army has a camp behind it with its wagons, food reserve, wounded and unplaced guns. A narrow field favours the small army. Roles: - Line holds and fights hand to hand. - Brace reverses a charge into it (chargers take double and deal half) but takes ×1.5 from shooting. - Shock doubles hits the first bell it meets an enemy and again after a bell out of contact, only in open sectors. - Shot shoots before the lines meet and every bell after while it has ammunition. - Light can step back a sector without counting as fleeing and shoot again, and scouts. - Heavy halves arrows and spears against it (not hand guns or later shot). - Guns shoot into their own and neighbouring sectors and have no melee. - Air (era VII) hits any sector or camp. War elephants whose sector loses a bell badly panic and trample their own side for −10 % of their men. Troop levels in eras I and II: Raw −10 % hits and can't fall back without breaking; Drilled can fall back a sector on orders; Seasoned +10 % hits, +5 % break point, can shift to a neighbouring sector within one bell; Veteran +20 % hits, +10 % break point, Line counts as half Brace; Elite +30 % hits, +15 % break point and one free order of its own each bell. Approaches. Every commander has a style of his own (not picked per battle), and every style rests on one of eight approaches that sets how he deploys and which orders he gives first: Approach How it deploys Shines Struggles Breakthrough all Shock massed in the best one or two open sectors against Line and Shot in open fields against Brace; narrow, wooded fields Steadfast Line evenly in every sector, Shot behind, a quarter in reserve defending; against Breakthrough and Assault slow to win Envelopment strong end sectors, thin Drilled centre; needs 5+ sectors against Breakthrough and Assault against Skirmish and Bombardment Skirmish Light and Shot over open sectors, Shock waiting behind against Line and Brace in open country against Shock; woods, marsh, towns Ambush up to half hidden in woods, marsh and town sectors broken, wooded or swampy fields open plains Entrenchment spends the first bell digging in; never advances dug-in sectors: defender +50 %, charges reversed attacking (fights as Steadfast) Bombardment guns massed in the centre, Line guarding them against Brace, Entrenchment, any army that stands still before W8; against Skirmish and Assault Assault everyone in front, no reserve, no shooting phase against Shot and Bombardment against Brace and Steadfast; losses ×1.25 for both sides Leaders in battle. The commander and each captain stand in one sector, where men get +5 % hits and +2 % break point per point of Might (era III and IV values); if that sector is lost the leader may be wounded, captured or killed. A commander gives 1 order per bell, +1 at Cunning 2 and +1 at Cunning 4, and the one with less Cunning gives his orders first, so the cleverer one answers. A commander whose Cunning is at least the Ambush commander's sees hidden companies. Shot and guns shoot for 3 bells + 1 per Logistics point (+1 with W10) before falling back to the camp for a bell. Each bell up to Logistics sectors swap a tired company for a fresh one for free; a company that has fought 3 bells in a row loses 10 % of its hits for each further bell until rotated. The orders: Commit reserve; Shift (Seasoned or better arrives the same bell); Turn (from a won sector into a neighbour: hits ×1.5, enemy −10 % break point); Drive (from a won sector into the enemy camp: take wagons and food, free prisoners, spike guns, enemy army −10 % break point); Fall back (no hits that bell; Raw companies break instead); Rally (half the men who fled from one sector this bell return); Spring (Ambush only: reveal hidden companies, hits ×1.5, enemy there −10 % break point); Rotate. The bell runs in order: orders (less Cunning first, then the other, then Elite free orders), shooting, charges, melee, breaking, then depth and rotation. The first bell is shooting only, unless an Assault commander advances. Hits. Each company takes out 2.5 % (by era) × men in the front × strength per man × roles × level × leader's Might in its sector × sector and ground × inventions × tired × hungry (−20 %) × forced march (−10 % on the first day). Each hit takes one man out of the line: a share flees and the rest are split evenly between killed and wounded. The flee share is 50 % − 30 % × the content share, where the content share is the share of your people living in calm provinces (0 or 1 grievances). Levies and standing regiments use their home provinces; retinues use the lord's lands (half for a wavering lord, zero for a disloyal one); hired companies always flee at 30 % plus 10 % per month of pay owed; garrisons use their home provinces and are fully content defending their own castle; rebel bands flee at 50 %. Fled men count toward the break point. Breaking. A company whose losses pass its break point leaves the line. A sector with no company of one side is lost by that side and won by the other, who may Turn or Drive next bell. An army breaks when it has lost more than half the sectors it started in, or its total losses pass its men-weighted break point, or its camp is taken by Drive and it has lost at least a third of its sectors. If both break in the same bell, only the one further past breaks. Night. After a day's 3 bells without a break, night falls. Either side may withdraw by its standing orders; the withdrawal is clean if its commander's Cunning is at least the enemy's, otherwise it counts as breaking with half the pursuit. Overnight, fled men who will come back return and ammunition refills. Troyes, 1450. Troyes' sectors are Fields, Fields, Fields, Pasture, Pasture, Woods, Town. Dunois defends for France in Three battles (Might 3, Cunning 4, Logistics 2) with 4,000 levy infantry, 2,000 archers and 1,000 knights. The Bastard of Burgundy attacks in Charge en haie (Might 3, Cunning 2, Logistics 1) with 5,000 hired heavy infantry and 2,000 knights. With 70 % of the French living in calm provinces, the French flee share is 29 %. In bell 2 the Burgundian knights charge the pastures and both pasture sectors break. In bell 3 Burgundy gives 2 orders first and France 3 after. After the day's last bell neither army has broken; at night the Burgundian withdrawal counts as breaking with half the pursuit because his Cunning is lower, and France holds the field. Battles play out over time: the contact day, then a bell every daylight 4 hours. On the map and in the battle viewer you see the phase ("In contact, deploying", "Day 2, fighting", "Night after day 2, the camps rest") and each side's men and a bar of men and morale left, updated every step; morale shows how far a side still is from breaking. The contact day and the nights pass quickly, so you wait only through the bells. After a rout the winner's horse catch 1 in 4 of the fleeing men. After the battle - Two thirds of the field-holder's wounded return after 5 weeks if the army is fed; the rest die. The broken side's wounded become the winner's prisoners. - Half the field-holder's fled return within 2 weeks and half go home to recruits; of the broken side's fled, half return if the army reaches a friendly castle and half go home. - The winner's Shock and Light companies that didn't break pursue: 1 in 4 of their men catches one fleeing man, killed or taken. - The field-holder takes the arms of the loser's killed and wounded, and half the loser's wagons and food reserve (all if the camp was taken). - Each captain and the commander of the broken side has a 1 in 10 chance of capture, more if pursued. - Victories and defeats are added to the commanders and countries, scars are awarded, and all killed count as Fallen. - Prisoners can be ransomed (gold by rank), exchanged, released (a gift that wins goodwill), enlisted as a hired company at level 1, or held (they eat). Realms with capture warfare (Mesoamerica and some forest-zone realms at the start) take half the enemy's killed as prisoners instead. Standing orders apply to every battle: retreat if outnumbered 2 to 1, 3 to 2, or never (checked before battle and each night), and attack or wait. Battles start on the day two hostile armies meet and are fought over time: after the contact day each bell is one round of 4 hours on the map, three a day by daylight. While one of your battles runs, the map slows to those 4-hour steps; at every step you can change standing orders, order a retreat (it takes effect at once, cleanly if your commander's Cunning is at least the enemy's) or switch between your battles, and the result can't be skipped. Armies that march in join their side's reserve. Afterwards the battle report shows, and any battle can be replayed later from its notice. Battles between other realms never slow the game: they play their steps of the day at once and go to the log. Commander styles Each country has its own list of styles: catalogue styles whose From names it or its people and whose inventions it knows. A new commander takes one by origin: a noble or lord takes the country's horse style if it has one, a risen or hired captain its foot style, an academy graduate the style the academy teaches. Hired captains bring their own people's style wherever they serve. A country with no named style in an era uses the nearest one from its region by culture group (for example Sahel takes Furusiyya, the Andes Three battles until contact). Adopting a style needs its inventions, plus one of: hiring 3 commanders or captains who use it and waiting 5 years, setting an academy to teach it with a teacher who knows it, losing 3 battles to it within 10 years, fighting beside an ally using it in 3 battles, or taking the capital of a country that uses it. An adopted style works as at home, except its special rule is at half strength in a commander's first battle with it. A style is stale when the enemy has the inventions or styles that historically beat it: the commander loses its special rule and one order per bell, and the report says why. A commander knows one style, a second at 10 victories, and learns a newer style from his country's list 3 years after it arrives if he served in that time, or at once by graduating from an academy that teaches it, or after losing a battle to it. A castle with no garrison falls at once. A castle besieged by at least 3 men per garrison man is closed : nothing reaches it. Otherwise it can be fed by road from its own side, and by sea if it stands on a shore tile and the sea isn't blockaded. Each month of a siege: - The garrison eats 1 ration a man from the castle store, and so do the castle tile's townsfolk unless the commander drives them out (adding refugees and Burned homes next door). Besiegers eat from their own supply. - Guns add shot (each bombard 2, each field gun 1, ×1.5 with B7); without guns the besiegers mine. Each castle's shot or mining months per breach opens a breach, and each breach takes a third off the walls bonus. A Siege master breaches 25 % faster and Logistics digs 10 % faster per point. - A garrison with a warden or 200 spare men repairs one breach a month, and may sally once a month with a third of its men in a one-bell battle against the siege camp. - An empty castle store costs the garrison 10 % a month to hunger and desertion and −10 % break point. - After 3 months the besiegers' sickness doubles. Storming needs a breach, or an earthwork ring fort (scaled at double losses). It is up to 6 bells on one sector with room 500 per breach; the garrison gets the walls bonus less a third per breach, and stormers' losses are ×1.5. A siege ends by honours of war (the garrison marches out armed to the nearest friendly castle and the castle is taken whole; keeping terms builds trust, breaking them is an oath broken), surrender (the garrison become prisoners), storm (the garrison killed or taken; you choose Spare, Plunder or Raze), relief (an army from the castle's side beats the besiegers and the garrison joins as a reserve at +10 %) or lifting (the besiegers leave). Plunder gives gold equal to a year of the province's tax owed, burns 1 in 3 town buildings, kills or drives off 10 % of townsfolk and adds Burned homes; Raze destroys the castle. An AI garrison accepts honours when it has a breach or under a month of food and no relief army within 10 days, and never from a Cruel commander. A besieger can bribe the garrison's captain only when its pay is owed 2 months or more, the castle belongs to a disloyal or wavering lord, or the captain's language differs from his ruler's. A Greedy commander inside takes the bribe; a Greedy commander outside pockets a tenth. Taking a castle gives you its store and the province's food spread. The castle of Troyes. A stone castle with a garrison of 300 and 6 months of store is besieged by Burgundy with 6,000 men and 4 bombards. It is closed, and the besiegers add 8 shot a month. After 3 months it has 1 breach and a walls bonus of about +67 %. Burgundy offers honours, no French relief army is within 10 days, so the garrison accepts and marches to Reims, and Burgundy takes the castle whole with its store and control of food spread in Champagne. A siege shows its progress on the map: how long the castle has held, its breaches, and the garrison and food left inside. Occupation and raids Taking a province's castle, or holding a province with no castle for a season, occupies it: you get its tax, recruits, food and trade, and its lord wavers toward the side holding his land. A horse-only army set to Raid can't besiege or occupy; each week it burns one tile and takes loot (gold from market and town, herds and horses from pasture) up to 1 load per 50 riders, then moves on, and castles there may sally. War and peace Every war's aim is shown to everyone; it decides which lords come and how peace voices speak. A war with no fitting aim counts Lands taken for every province taken, makes your non-Warlike lords waver, and doesn't oblige allies to join. Breaking a truce counts an oath broken and makes every lord waver a step. Peace voices are recomputed from the war's current state, never stored as a score: - Each lord has one voice per province he holds. He says peace when any of his provinces is occupied, his retinue has lost half its men, he is wavering or disloyal, or his lands are hungry; war when he is Warlike, the aim is his Want, or he is loyal and his side has more victories in this war. - Each royal province says peace with 2 or more of Conscription, Soldiers quartered, Burned homes, Hungry or Heavy taxes, or when occupied; otherwise it has no voice. - The capital is a third of all voices, saying peace when occupied or besieged. - A Warlike ruler ignores a quarter of the peace voices; a child ruler's regent counts as a lord. With over half saying peace, the ruler must accept a peace asking only for provinces the enemy occupies and gold up to the treasury. A player who refuses loses a step of loyalty from every lord each season and levies desert twice as fast. With over three quarters, the ruler must also accept tribute, a pretender, or becoming a subject. The AI makes and accepts peace by the same counts. Peace terms and what they need: Cede a province only one the asker occupies (or a swap); Pay gold up to the treasury or as debt; Tribute (yearly gold or grain for up to 20 years) only with over three quarters peace voices or as overlord; Seat a pretender only with their capital occupied; Become a subject only with over three quarters peace voices; Demolish a castle in a province they keep; Open the roads means no tolls for 10 years; Give back occupied provinces, ransom or exchange prisoners, a marriage and white peace are open to either side; Renounce a claim by a pretender. What each war aim gives: Take land gives those provinces; Seat a pretender replaces their ruler and makes the realm your ally or subject; Tribute gives yearly gold or grain; Free a people releases a new country; Break a subject makes it independent; Defend the faith gives a faith tolerance charter there, or the province; Punish gives gold and a humbled ruler; Raid ends after 12 months with raids only. Wars also end when one side has no soldiers and no castles left (the winner takes all it occupies), when a Raid war reaches 12 months, or when a ruler dies with no heir and his lords fall into a succession war (a white peace unless the enemy backs a claimant). A signed peace starts the truce set by Diplomacy: 5 years, +5 if provinces moved or a subject was made. The price of war Every war costs gold, men, people and your lords' patience, and one peace takes only part of a realm, so war is a choice with a price and not the best answer to everything. - The declare sheet. Declare war on a realm's Diplomacy tab no longer acts at once: it opens a sheet with the Price of war above Confirm . It lists who will be called against you (each realm with its soldiers and how it comes in: an ally, a protection pledge, a league against you or a subject), your allies who will come to your side, both sides' soldiers, the neighbours who will hold Threatened us for a war with no aim, how many of your lords (or boyars, beys, daimyo: your realm's own word) will waver, a truce you would break and when it would have ended, the monthly pay of your armies at war, and the most one peace can take ("at most 5 of their 14 provinces"). Lines that hurt are red with a "!" mark, and every line opens its reason when you tap it. A faith head's censure warning sits above Confirm , and a button opens your Your name abroad card. On a phone held sideways the price sits on the left and the terms on the right; in the Tall layout it is one scrolling column. Confirm stays pinned at the foot; with a truce it reads Break the truce and declare war . - Levies at war are paid from their first month (in peace they serve three months free), and occupied provinces pay their occupier only half their tax and no trade, so occupation doesn't pay for the war. - The dead are missed at home : men killed in a levy are lost from their province's peasants and counted among its fallen. - One peace takes at most a third of the loser's provinces, rounded up, and the capital only with the last one. Swallowing a realm takes several wars. - Long wars tire lords : after 2 years, lords who aren't Warlike, and whose Want the aim doesn't name, all say peace. - The war card. Each running war has a card on your Diplomacy tab (and on the enemy's): the aim, both war leaders' peace voices as bars with a mark at half and the numbers written beside them, months at war and the long-war mark, provinces occupied each way, and how many provinces one peace could take from each side now. The At war plaque in the top bar carries a small bar of your side's peace voices with its number: amber past a third, red past half, when you must take a fair peace. Tapping the plaque opens the war card. - The computer counts the same price : it declares only when its side, with the allies who will answer, is clearly stronger than everyone who will be called against it, when it holds gold for some months of war pay, when its own people don't want peace, and (unless Warlike) when its notoriety is under 50. The computer players The AI's risk tolerance sets its standing orders: a careful realm waits and retreats when outnumbered at all, a middling one attacks and retreats at 3 to 2, and a bold one attacks and retreats only at 2 to 1. Only a bold realm sends horse-only armies raiding instead of besieging. Its commanders start with its country's styles from the style catalogue. Its personality also sets which kinds it raises (Castile noble retinues and frontier light cavalry, a city republic hired companies) and how many peace voices it needs before talking peace (a low-risk AI offers at a third, a hegemon seeker only when forced). It sees only the forage limits, food reserves and peace voices the player sees, and doesn't cheat on food. Each turn and each month During the turn, inside the day loop: contacts, the withdraw check and battles; raids burn a tile a week; forced marches and hunger cost men weekly; weekly meals and refills at the end of every turn (a turn is one week; each meal is 7/30 of the month's rations). Monthly rules keep their size and run at the end of the turn in which a new month begins, in order: pay and pay owed; supply (rot, quarters, Requisitioned and Hungry); sickness and wounded returning; sieges; occupation by holding a season; drill, months out, levies and lords going home; the troop cap; peace voices. Yearly: arms rust, powder damp, scars fade, ageing, and victories older than 20 years drop off. What you see - The army card : name, owner, place, destination, commander and skills, captains, men by foot, horse and guns, companies by kind and level, food days and reserve size, pay and months owed, break point and flee share, orders, sick and wounded. Every line opens its gain and lose list. - Your running battles : shown step by step every 4 hours, with standing orders, retreat and a switch between battles. - The battle report : who fought, where, the result, the losses and a one-line reason. Any battle can be replayed later from its notice. - The battle playback : the tile row, companies as blocks with level chevrons, the camps, and a one-line action per bell ("Dunois commits his knights to the pastures"). - The forage limit , shown when you drag an army over a province. - Rumours of unseen armies. - Notifications for battle won or lost (with the reason), a breach, terms offered, peace voices passing half, pay owed and an army hungry. - The war aim , shown to everyone. How it connects - Troop-Movement: supplies daily positions and contacts; warfare supplies march effects, scouting, standing orders, the battle-start rule, forage limit and the broken army. - Recruiting: delivers levies, trained regiments and commissioned commanders; gets back disbanded men, deserters and Fallen. - Naval: uses warfare's bell rules for sea battles on 3 sectors, and its commanders' skills for admirals; naval decides ship damage (a ship hit and still afloat loses one hull step, hits equal to its strength sink or take it) and storms. - Diplomacy: declares wars with aims and sides, carries peace and sets the truce; receives peace voices, occupation and oaths broken. - Provinces: supplies ground, tile rows, stores, sickness and grievances; receives Requisitioned, Hungry, Soldiers quartered, Burned homes, burned tiles and sacks. - World-Map: tile rows, ground, shore tiles and bridges. - Your-Realm: treasury, lords and loyalty, ruler, the siege reserve and academies; receives Fallen, victories, stores, prisoners and the troop cap. - Research: the W, B and S inventions known. - Buildings: castle types, powder mills, forges, drill yards and magazines. - Rebellions: rebel bands fight as the Rebel band kind. - Government: Warlike rulers, regencies and succession wars. - Subjects: subject armies and the Break a subject and Become a subject terms. - Culture: homeland language, culture group for style fallback, a captain's language for bribes. - Religion: persecution for the Defend the faith aim. - Historical-Events: prestige from victories, war weariness from Fallen and peace voices, throne offers to generals. - The 1378 Start: starting styles, capture warfare realms, starting castles and inventions. - Map and Map Modes and Screens-and-Navigation: army cards, battle playback, reports and notifications. - Trade: occupiers take trade; the Open the roads term. - Time-and-Turns: the weekly turn, the day loop and the order battles resolve in. World-Map: The world map is the ground every other system stands on: about 4,400 land provinces and about 4,700 sea zones covering the whole world, each with its terrain, rivers, coasts and neighbours. It is built once from real-world data and never changes during a campaign, so every army, fleet and trader plans its way across the same fixed geography. This page explains how the map is made, what each place knows about itself, and how the map keeps old saves working when it changes between versions. How it works The grid The world is a pixel image 5,760 by 2,144 pixels , at 16 pixels per degree, which is about 7 km per pixel at the equator. It runs from 78° north to 56° south. Every pixel belongs to exactly one place (a land province or a sea zone), or to no place at all: large lakes are punched out, and the polar band is left empty. The map is build data. Nothing in it changes during a campaign, and none of it is stored in a save. Land provinces Provinces start from modern first-level admin regions (states, counties, oblasts and so on), which are then merged or split until they are roughly even in size. The target size is set per part of the world, so Europe, India and China are cut more finely than Siberia or the Sahara. The default target is 1,100 pixels; Western and Central Europe aims for 380 and the far north for 3,200. - A province is named after the modern admin region that covers most of it, plus a compass point when it was split (for example "West Pskov"). Provinces keep these modern names; there are no historical names. - Large lakes are punched out of the land, and connected pieces of one admin region (exclaves, islands) become their own pieces. Islands smaller than 10 pixels are dropped. - The current build has 9,158 places : about 4,400 land provinces ( p0 to p4410 ) followed by about 4,700 sea zones ( sea0 onward). Each land province carries: Fact What it means Id p plus a number Name Modern region name, plus a compass point if split Centre x and y on the grid Size Its size in pixels Ground One of the 11 grounds (see below) Coastal Whether it touches a sea zone River Whether three or more river pixels run through it Neighbours Every land province and sea zone it touches A province's size on the map sets how many tiles it has on its Provinces card: 4 for the smallest, 16 for the largest. Only provinces on a coast, lake or navigable river get shore tiles , 1 to 3 of them, set from their coast and rivers. Sea zones and straits Water is split into sea zones that are equal in kilometres at every latitude, so the number of zones a fleet crosses really measures how long it takes: Kind Terrain value Size Coastal zone sea about 150 km across Open-ocean zone ocean about 300 km across Sea zones take real sea names from Natural Earth's marine areas. Some narrow waters are closed on a 7 km grid even though ships sailed through them. A config list of straits joins those seas: the Bosporus, the Dardanelles, the Kerch Strait, the Øresund, the Great Belt, the Strait of Gibraltar, the Strait of Messina, the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab-el-Mandeb, the Strait of Malacca, the Garabogaz strait and the Strait of Maracaibo. A separate config list of strait crossings names land neighbours across a narrow strait that armies may cross by ferry, such as across the Bosporus, the Øresund, Messina, Kerch and Gibraltar. The rules for crossing belong to Troop Movement. Armies have no way into a sea zone at all except aboard ships. Terrain: 22 tile types, 11 grounds The map draws 22 tile types so the world looks varied, but the simulation plays every province as one of 11 grounds . The ground is what matters for troops, buildings and people; the tile type is mostly how it looks. Category Tile type Plays as ground Temperate grassland grassland farmland farmland broadleaf forest mediterranean grassland paddies farmland Boreal and polar forest (pine, taiga) forest tundra tundra glacier tundra Dry lands steppe grassland drylands drylands desert (stony) desert dunes (sand sea) desert colddesert desert Tropical savanna savanna jungle jungle Wetlands marsh marsh swamp marsh Hills and mountains hills hills mountains (grey rock) mountains snowpeaks mountains badlands (red rock) mountains highlands (green) mountains The 11 grounds are farmland, grassland, savanna, drylands, desert, hills, mountains, forest, jungle, marsh and tundra. How each pixel gets its type. The generator decides every pixel in four passes: 1. Climate , from the Köppen-Geiger climate map: rainforest, savanna, steppe, desert, Mediterranean, temperate, taiga, tundra or ice. 2. Mountain ranges , from Natural Earth, each with a rim of hills 1 to 3 pixels wide. The mountain type follows the climate: badlands in desert climates, highlands in tropical climates, snowpeaks in alpine and polar climates, in the high core of large ranges and north of 50°, and grey-rock mountains everywhere else. 3. Wetlands , from Natural Earth: swamp in the tropics (the Sudd, the Pantanal), marsh elsewhere (the Pripet, the Fens). 4. Woods and fields break each zone up. How wooded the land is follows the climate's natural forest (after the WWF ecoregions), blurred across climate borders by a degree or two and wobbled with noise, so taiga, mixed forest and broadleaf fade into each other. Where 1444 was crowded, some wood is cleared for fields: rice paddies in monsoon Asia and farmland elsewhere (the Paris basin), in proportion to how crowded the region was. How a province gets its ground. Each province takes one ground by the province ground rule: Province is… Ground More than half mountain mountains A quarter or more hills or mountain hills Temperate land more than 60 % wooded forest Otherwise the most common ground under it So a province that is 55 % mountain is mountains; one that is 20 % mountain and 10 % hills is hills; one that is 10 % of each and mostly grassland is grassland. Grassland in the most crowded parts of 1444 counts as farmland ground, and the config can force lowland valleys such as the Po valley. Each tile type also suggests starting tile uses for the province card: farmland suggests fields, steppe suggests pasture, badlands suggests waste with mines, and so on. A few terrain effects adopted by Troop Movement hold as map facts: snow peaks close passes in winter, dunes need camels for guns and give no foraging, glacier is impassable, and paddies are slower in the wet season. No other terrain effects exist: broadleaf, mediterranean, pine forest, steppe, cold desert, swamp, badlands and highlands play only through their ground, and mediterranean and steppe land plays as grassland. Each land province also stores its most common tile type, so these effects know where they apply. Ocean depth is stored for every water pixel in five bands from Natural Earth's sea-floor data: under 200 m, 1 km, 3 km, 5 km, and deeper. Rivers Rivers come from Natural Earth's river centre lines (scale ranks 0 to 8), traced as paths of map pixels. Each pixel knows the river's size and which neighbouring pixels it flows to, so every river draws as one clean line. - Rivers of scale rank 0 to 4 are great rivers (size 2); the rest are size 1. - A province with three or more river pixels is a river province . - A config list of fords names river crossings that count as bridges in summer and autumn, such as the Ebro at Tortosa and the Danube at Vidin. A province has a navigable river when a great river runs through at least three of its pixels. Only coasts, lake shores and navigable rivers give a province shore tiles; a small river does not. In winter, from December to March, rivers north of latitude 55 freeze : crossing them costs no extra time, as if they were not there. Passes and roads A config list of passes marks mountain provinces with a historic road through them: the Great St Bernard, the Khyber, the Brenner, the Pyrenees at Roncesvalles and others. Movement rules for passes belong to Troop Movement. Each province has one road step for the whole province: track, road, paved road, turnpike or railway. The map only holds it as a fact; building roads belongs to Provinces and Buildings, and movement and Trade read it. One graph for land and sea All land provinces and sea zones form one graph of places and their neighbours. A province neighbours the sea zones it touches, and any province with a sea-zone neighbour is marked coastal. Neighbour lists are always two-way: if A lists B, B lists A. Every mover, player or AI, plans on the same graph. Regions The map uses the Historical Events geography: 13 macro-regions (Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Central and North Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania, North America, Mesoamerica and Central America, the Caribbean, South America) with their sub-regions and 257 areas. The event tree also names anchor provinces such as Constantinople, Potosí and Malacca, and each resolves to one province on the map. The map generator has its own density and settlement regions, and modern admin regions supply names. Map versions If the map generator splits or merges provinces, it writes a rename table ( old id → new ids, with shares ) that ships with the map. Every built map has a mapHash , and saves record it. When a save made on an older map is loaded, its provinces are mapped through the rename table. See Saving. Sources and credits The map credits its data: Natural Earth (public domain), the Köppen-Geiger climate maps of Beck et al. 2018 (CC BY 4.0, attribution required), and the WWF terrestrial ecoregions of Olson et al. 2001. What you see The world map has no screen of its own; Map and Map Modes draws it. What it hands over for drawing: - The province id image , which says which place each pixel belongs to. - The terrain image : terrain per pixel in the red channel, ocean depth in the green channel (0 on land, otherwise depth band plus one), and river size and links where a river runs. - Province and sea zone names, rivers and depth bands. How it connects - Provinces: reads ground, size (tile count), coastal and river (shore tiles) and the road step. - Troop Movement: plans on the graph; reads ground, river and great-river flags, passes, fords and strait crossings. - Naval: reads sea zones and their kind, coasts and straits. - Trade: routes over the graph, roads, rivers and sea zones. - Warfare: reads ground for battles, roads and rivers. - Exploration and Colonies: graph steps for the charted start; coastal provinces. - The 1378 Start: places to own; size, terrain and coast for starting population and wealth; asks for rebuilds when provinces must be split. - Historical Events: shares region ids, areas and anchor provinces. - Map and Map Modes: draws the id image, terrain, depth and rivers. - Saving: mapHash and the rename table; map data is never saved. - Buildings: ground (build cost), shore tiles, anchors for fixed mines and markets. When a rebuild splits provinces, Naval reruns its port placement. Numbers These are the map generator's settings. None are game balance placeholders except where noted. Value Config key Design value Provisional? Pixels per degree pxPerDeg 16 No Latitude band latTop , latBottom 78, −56 No Largest lakes punched out lakeMaxScalerank 3 No Smallest island kept minIslandSize 10 pixels No Merge and split thresholds minFactor , maxFactor 0.4, 1.7 of the target No Target province size defaultTarget , density[] 1,100 px; Western and Central Europe 380 … far north 3,200 No Forced lowlands lowlands[] Po valley No Sea zone seeds and sizes seas.coastSpacing , oceanSpacing , coastBand , minSeaSize 22, 44, 20, 150 pixels No Sea straits straits[] 12 named No Province ground thresholds MOUNTAIN SHARE , HILL SHARE (in mapgen.ts ) 0.5, 0.25 No Tiles per province tile count range (province config) 4 to 16 Yes Great rivers great river ranks scale ranks 0 to 4 No River province river province threshold 3 river pixels No Strait crossings, passes, fords troop-movement march config named examples only Yes (lists still to fill) Frozen seas Seasons show on the map. From December to March the far northern seas freeze: the Gulf of Bothnia, the White Sea, the Arctic seas, Hudson Bay, Foxe Basin and the North Western Passages. Fleets cannot enter a frozen sea, and a port on a frozen sea cannot be used until the ice goes. Other map facts - Crossing a strait on foot. Armies cross five straits as if they were land borders: the Bosporus (Istanbul holds both shores), the Øresund, Messina, Kerch and Gibraltar. These are not the same as the sea straits fleets use. - Lakes. A lake shore gives shore tiles, but a harbour needs a real sea next to it. Fleets can sail the large lakes, such as Ladoga and the Great Lakes, but not smaller ones. - Map size. The map keeps its 4,411 land provinces. Some ports share a province, and Melos and Malé are not on the map. - Hills and mountains. A province that is at least half mountain is mountains, and one that is at least a quarter hill or mountain is hills. Still open Nothing about the map is left open. The frozen months and the latitude for frozen rivers are first values that balancing may change. Your-Realm: Your realm is your country as a whole: the treasury, the food network that runs through your castles, your people and land, your named lords, your army and navy at a glance, your ruler and family, your standing abroad, and how a campaign is won. Most of what the realm shows is the sum of its Provinces, gathered on one country card where every number is something you can count, with a list of how you gain it and how you lose it. How it works The country card The country card has four tabs: General first, then Diplomacy , Trade and Army . Your own realm's card is the Realm book, in six sections that open on the Overview (see Screens and Navigation); another realm's card keeps these tabs. General is the one-screen summary of your country; Allies, Enemies and Oaths broken sit on the Diplomacy tab, where war and peace are declared, trade lines on Trade, and soldiers, commanders and ships on Army. France's General tab at the start might look like this: It shows the ruler (title, name, age, years on throne, heirs), Gold, Food (how many castles feed how many provinces, and how many are hungry), People, Soldiers (plus recruits), Horses, Ships (war and trade), Castles, Officials (for how many royal provinces), Lords (named, by loyalty), Schools (students, scholars, current study and progress), Faith, Language, In revolt, Allies, Enemies, Oaths broken, Fallen in the last 10 years, and your rank in each win score. People, recruits, food, horses, ships, castles, faith, language, in revolt, schools and officials are always sums over your provinces , never stored separately. Every number here is a placeholder until balanced. Treasury Gold is the coins in your treasury. You gain gold by You lose gold by Taxes from royal provinces Soldiers' pay (every month) A share of lords' taxes Officials' wages Trade School upkeep Tribute from subjects Building Selling grain Debt interest Loot and ransoms Gifts and bribes Selling titles Buying grain Debt records how much you owe and to whom: a bank, a merchant city, a lord or another ruler. You take it on with a loan, or when lords lend in exchange for favours. It goes away when you repay it, when the lender dies or is conquered, or when you default . Debt costs yearly interest. Defaulting wipes the debt but counts as an oath broken . A lord you owe money to gets more demanding. Tax is set per province, with a realm default (see Provinces). A revolt can force it down. Heavy taxes fill the treasury but make lords waver and provinces revolt. Tax and the treasury in play Every province pays at its own tax rate or, until you give it one, at your realm's default, which starts at normal. Against normal, none pays nothing, light half, heavy one and a half times and crushing double. A province whose official has been made a commander pays half, and so does one that riots or plots. Heavy tax gives the province the Heavy taxes grievance, and crushing counts as two. A lord's province gives you only your share, and raising its rate to heavy or crushing makes its lord waver. A busy province owes more: every 4 points of its trade ratio add 1 %. Trade itself comes from your traders (see Trade), whatever the rate. The treasury keeps a ledger for the month: Tax and Trade coming in, Army pay, Officials and Interest going out. Their sum is your change a month, paid in on the 1st. Each official at his post earns 0.1 gold a month; a commissioned official draws no wage while he commands. Wages and interest are paid a twelfth each month. Lenders let you owe up to one year's tax and trade . A loan costs at once: the gold you borrow plus 10 % interest goes onto your debt the moment you take it, and the debt keeps costing 10 % a year while you owe it. Borrowing also makes the crown look weak: every lord falls a step in loyalty , at most once a year. You can repay any part at any time. AI realms tax at normal in peace and heavy at war, borrow only when their gold falls below zero, and repay once they hold a year's army pay and wages. Where to find it: the gold plaque at the top of the screen shows your gold and change a month; tap it for the Treasury tab of your country card: your purse with how long the gold lasts, the month's gold in and out as bars, the realm tax default, and your debt as a meter against what lenders allow, with Borrow buttons that say what you will owe before you tap. To tax one province differently, open it: its Overview tab has a Tax line and a row of rate buttons, from Realm default to Crushing . Food: provinces grow it, castles move it Food lives in provinces: each grows, stores and eats its own. Castles are the hubs that collect it and spread it. In each province: - Harvest : bumper, good, normal, poor or failed. Better with farmland, people working it, inventions and peace; worse with weather, armies marching through, burned tiles, plague killing farmers and cold periods. It is the province's main food each autumn. - Local store , in months of food: filled by what is left after collection and by castle deliveries; emptied by people eating, armies refilling their reserve, yearly rot and raids. When it hits zero, the province starves. - Herds (pastoral provinces), in thousands of head: grown on good pasture, by raiding and tribute; lost to drought, hard winters, raids, disease and slaughter in famine. Pastoral peoples eat from herds, which move with their owners and can't be besieged. - Fish (coastal provinces): a steady catch, improved by salting inventions, lost to blockade and war at sea. - Grain price at each market, per sack: up with bad harvests across the region, war and blockades; down with good harvests and trade routes. You can buy and sell grain for gold. In each castle: - Castle store : filled by collection, deliveries from other castles and buying; emptied by feeding the garrison, spreading to the land around, handing out to armies refilling at home, rot and capture. - Granary size : raised by building granaries (gold) and inventions such as Ever-normal granaries ; lowered by siege damage and neglect. Bigger granaries hold more and rot less. - Reach , in rings of provinces: raised by roads, rivers, canals, wagons (horses) and research; cut by enemy armies on the roads, winter and burned land. A province outside every castle's reach lives on its own harvest. The Food policy screen One Food policy sets realm-wide defaults on the realm's Food tab, and a castle can have its own collection and siege reserve. Set those on the castle's own province, under Castle food on its Overview; tapping a castle on the Food tab takes you there, and Realm puts it back on the realm's setting. The Food page shows how many provinces are hungry or running low and the presets; the five settings sit in a Customise fold whose line reads your current choices, and the castles in a Castles fold that opens by itself while one is besieged or its roads are cut. Setting Options Collection : share of each province's surplus sent to the nearest castle 0 %, 25 %, 50 %, 75 % Castle shares : how collected food is divided between castles by people, frontier first, capital first, equal, or custom (a slider per castle, summing to 100 %) Sharing out : how a castle hands out food by ring (own province / next ring / ring beyond) default 50/30/20; Tight 80/20/0; Wide 30/35/35 Siege reserve : months a castle keeps and never spreads 0, 3, 6, 12 Army refill : how armies refill their own reserve at home locals only (default, from the local store), castles hand out first, no refill in lords' lands Famine relief : below this, a province's castle feeds it first, ignoring how food is shared out off, 1 month, 3 months Surplus above granary size keep (it rots), sell on the market, send to the capital castle, send to subjects or allies Lords' castles follow the policy by loyalty: loyal lords follow it, wavering lords half of it, disloyal lords keep their food. Presets fill the whole screen at once: Preset Collection Castle shares Sharing out Siege reserve Army refill Feed the people 25 % by people Wide 3 months castles hand out first Fortress realm 50 % frontier first Tight 12 months locals only War footing 75 % frontier first 50/30/20 6 months castles hand out first Merchant 50 % capital first 50/30/20 3 months no refill in lords' lands; surplus sold The year of food 1. Autumn : every province rolls its harvest. Weather is rolled by region, so neighbours suffer together and grain prices rise for all of them. 2. Collection : the collection share of each province's surplus goes to its nearest castle in reach. 3. Castle shares : castles exchange food until each holds its share. Food moving between castles loses some of its load for every province it travels. 4. Sharing out : each castle keeps its siege reserve and hands out the rest to the rings around it by its sharing-out pattern. 5. Through the year people eat. Soldiers on campaign eat double, and a horse eats like three men. Stores rot a little each season, less with granaries. Under pressure: - A besieged castle stops spreading and lives on its own store. - An enemy army sitting between a castle and its outer ring stops food spreading past it, so cutting the roads starves the outer ring without a battle. - Rice lands get two harvests on irrigated land, but war can wreck their canals. Maize, potatoes and cassava arrive through the research tree after Atlantic contact. - When a province runs out of food, people die, survivors flee to neighbours or abroad, revolts become likely, and the lord of that land turns disloyal. The event tree's famine events read the same stores. - You can burn your own fields ahead of an invader (scorched earth) to starve him. Harvests and army supply in the game today - Each province rolls its own harvest : 1 in 10 poor, 7 in 10 normal, 15 in 100 good and 1 in 20 bumper. Its region's weather, an enemy in the province and your harvest inventions then move it a step each, so a failed harvest comes from a poor roll in a bad year, or bad weather with an enemy at the gates. - Weather depends on the climate. A region rolls once, and each province reads it by its climate: temperate land has bad weather 1 year in 6, dry land (desert, drylands, savanna) a drought 1 in 4, and the monsoon lands of Asia floods 1 in 5. Neighbours still suffer together. - When the harvest comes in : once a year in September in the north and March in the south. Rice lands from India to South China and the Indies harvest in both March and September once their realm knows Wet-rice terracing , each harvest bringing half the year's food, so one bad season costs only half. The tundra grows no crops; it lives on herds, hunting and fishing, which bring food every month. - Armies eat from the land. A man eats a month of food a month at home, double on campaign (while your realm is at war or the army is abroad), and a horse like three men. An army refills its wagons from the store of the province where it stands. In your own or friendly land the locals keep two months for themselves; in enemy land the foragers take what they find on that ground. What an army takes leaves the store, so a long stay or a march through poor land brings hunger to the province, and then to the army. - Where you see it : the province card's Overview shows the last harvest and why ("poor · drought in the region"), when it comes in, and how many months of the store the armies standing there eat a month. The Provinces tab counts your last harvests and marks poor and failed ones on each row. A failed harvest sends a news item. The army's supply line says how long its wagons last, whether it eats double on campaign, and what the land there gives it. The Food map mode shows how many men on campaign each province could feed. A royal province gives full taxes and recruits, but without an official it pays half taxes and gives half recruits . One official runs one province with G1, two with G9 and three with G16, plus one more each for B2, G11 and T14. A low Faith share means religious revolts and wavering clergy lords; a low Language share means separatist revolts and slower officials. Provinces in revolt lose taxes and recruits and spread trouble to neighbours. Under half counts as low: risings of that kind come half again as often, the lords seated among another faith waver each January (in a theocracy, all of them), and with a low Tongue officials' years count at half pace. The General tab marks a low Faith or Tongue with a warning line under it. A rising spreads to a restless neighbour at about a tenth a month. Lords Each lord is a named character with a card: Field Meaning Lands Provinces he governs, always at least one, run by his own officials Retinue His own soldiers from his lands; he brings them when called, if loyal Wealth His own gold; he can lend to you or fund a revolt Traits Two words that shape what he wants and how he reacts Want One concrete goal: a province, an office, a marriage, lower taxes, a war against someone Loyalty Loyal, Wavering, Disloyal, In revolt Heir Who inherits his land The lord card is the same in every society; only the label changes: nobles, merchant houses in city republics, bishops and abbots in theocracies, clan chiefs on the steppe, elders and lineage heads in chiefdoms and stateless societies. Where you find them. Open a province and the first thing on it is who governs it: its lord, with his loyalty and buttons to open him or seize the land, or Royal land with a Grant as fief button that lists your lords, neighbours first. Its official sits under him; a lord's official serves the lord, so you can't make him a commander. The country card's Lords tab is the overview: how much of the realm is royal land, and a row per lord with his portrait, house, lands and loyalty. Tap a lord to open his screen: his lands as a list, a gift while he is not loyal, royal provinces you can grant him (nearest first), and Show his lands on the map , which fades the rest of the map and frames his provinces. On the map a lord's land always carries a fine pattern of crosses and a dashed border, and the Lords map mode colours each of your lords' lands in his own colour. Lords versus officials. A lord costs no gold, but keeps half the taxes of his provinces and keeps their recruits as his retinue. He obeys according to his loyalty, and can be removed only by force, a trial, an assassin or his line dying out. At war you call his retinue from the Army tab or his screen, and he leads it himself (see Warfare); each row of the Lords tab shows his men's state beside his loyalty. Sending an assassin. A lord who grows too troublesome can be killed. On his screen, Assassinate… opens a card that shows the cost (25 gold, spent either way), the chance it works (60 %, 15 points less for each Great lord reason, never below 20 %) and what follows. If it works he dies: his heir takes his lands as a wavering lord (with no heir, a kinsman may, or the lands return to the crown), the rest of his house turns disloyal, and every other lord of yours falls a step of loyalty. If the assassin is caught, the lord turns disloyal and every other lord still falls a step. Murder at court is never a secret, so use it when one lord costs you more than the trust of all the others. The computer players never send assassins. All the numbers are in lords.assassination in the realm data. How you gain lords: - Grant a fief of one or more royal provinces to a commander, relative, favourite or loyal official: a new loyal lord, whose provinces no longer need an official. - Keep a defeated local ruler after a conquest: he becomes a lord who starts disloyal, with no officials needed and the people calm. - Sell a title : a rich merchant buys a province as a fief, giving gold now and a weak but loyal lord. - Marriage can bring a foreign or local house in as a lord with its land. - When a lord dies with several sons, his lands pass by the realm's inheritance law, possibly split between them. - A disloyal lord across the border can defect to you with his land. - At the start, major countries have their historical great houses from the catalogue, and smaller countries a few generated lords sized to their realm. How you lose lords: - His line dies out: his land returns as royal provinces needing officials. - You seize his land by decree: other lords waver, and he may rebel. - You try and execute a disloyal lord: all lords of his house become disloyal. - His revolt is defeated: his land returns to you, or to a loyal claimant you pick. - A disloyal lord defects to a neighbour with his provinces, or rebels. - Two lords' houses join by marriage and merge into one bigger lord. Loyalty: Rises with Falls with Granting his want Heavy or crushing taxes Gifts of gold, offices at court Seizing land from him or another lord Marriages into the ruling house Lost wars and battles Victories he took part in A child ruler, a disputed heir or a new ruler A long secure reign with a clear heir Requisitioning his grain Feeding his lands in famine A foreign rival's bribes and promises Sharing your faith and language Paying for a building in a lord's province raises his loyalty one step. A famine in his land turns him disloyal; riots or a heavy demand on his province make him waver. At New Year, each lord over the government's cap drops one loyalty step (see Government). What your lords and officials are called Every realm names its lords and officials in its own words. A Russian prince has boyars and voivodes, the Ottomans beys and subashis, Japan daimyo and daikan, Ethiopia rases and shums, the Inca kurakas and tocricocs, and the peoples of the Americas and much of Africa chiefs and headmen. The word comes from the family of your court's language, and a realm ruled by kin calls them chiefs and headmen where its language has no word of its own. Everyone else keeps lords and officials. The words show on the country card's tabs, the Stability pillars, the Lords map mode, a lord's and an official's screen and a province's "Governed by" card. Another realm's card uses its own words. Only the words change: chiefs and daimyo follow exactly the same rules as lords, and post types such as Warden or Tax collector stay the same everywhere. Stability Stability tells you at a glance how well your realm holds together. It is not a hidden number: it reads four pillars, and your realm is only as steady as the weakest of them. A judge holds riots off one grievance longer. Lords' own provinces are run by their own officials and do not count. The stability plaque in the top bar shows the step (amber when Uneasy, red when Troubled, blinking when Crumbling). Tap it to open your Realm book's Overview, where each pillar has a row; tap a row to open the Lords, Diplomacy, Officials or Provinces tab and mend it. The details live in Recruiting, Warfare and Naval. Ruler and family - Age rises each year, and old rulers die. A child ruler needs a regent: a lord, or a queen mother. - Years on throne rise each year and reset on death, deposition or abdication. New rulers start with more wavering lords. - Heirs are gained by births, marriages and adopting or naming an heir; lost by death, marrying daughters abroad, and heirs going over to a rebel lord. If the ruler dies with no heir, the realm falls into a succession war among the lords. - Traits : two (for example Pious, Warlike, Builder, Greedy), given at birth and sometimes gained or rarely changed by events. They give small bonuses and lean event options. - Marriages are living ties to other ruling houses and your own lords, arranged with an heir or a princess, ended by death, divorce events and war between the houses. They give goodwill, loyalty and a path to inheriting another realm. In the game now. Your ruler is on the Overview of your Realm book, under the section tiles: name, age, years on the throne, the regent while a child rules, the two traits with what each does, and the heir (or who would follow under your law). Most realms start with their real ruler of 20 September 1378. Each January rulers and heirs grow a year older and may die, by the table below that every person shares. The heir takes the throne and every lord wavers a little; with no heir a kinsman takes it and the lords dispute it. An heirless ruler of 18 to 50 may have a child. A dispatch with the crown tells you of a death, a birth or a child coming of age, in your realm and on your borders. Traits: Pious makes faith risings a quarter rarer, Warlike refills recruits 10 % faster, Builder makes works 10 % cheaper and Greedy brings 5 % more tax to you; each also leans the choices an AI ruler makes in events. Everyone ages and dies. Not only the ruler: every person the game names grows a year older each January and may die, by one table for all of them (about 3 in 100 a year for a small child, 1 under 40, 2 in their forties, 4 in their fifties, 8 in their sixties, 16 older). A battle can kill the losing commander (1 in 20, more if he is Reckless), and other causes, an assassin or an event, end a life the same way. Who Where you see his age When he dies Your heir General tab, beside the ruler Your ruler has no heir until a child is born; die then, and the lords dispute the throne. Abroad, a ruler who dies without a son may give married houses a claim A lord His row on the Lords tab; his age and heir on his screen His heir takes his lands, loyalty and want; with no heir, a kinsman of his house half the time. Otherwise his line dies out and his lands come back to you as royal land, with their posts empty An official His card on the province and the Officials tab His post stands empty: fill it from the province card. AI realms and lords fill theirs at once A commander or admiral With his skills on the Military tab and the army card He leaves your service and his army or fleet has no commander until you name another. Past 60 his Might falls, past 65 his Cunning. A lord leading his own retinue is the lord himself: if he falls, his heir leads the men on, and with no heir they go home A colonial governor The Exploration tab His colony is lost if he was founding one Each death in your realm reaches your dispatches in one line saying what follows. Women in roles. Women can hold every role: ruler, lord, commander, official, scholar. The chance is set per country (or culture) per role from the catalogue's history and succession customs. Where the crown passes only through men (France), no woman inherits the throne, though a duke's daughter can inherit his duchy; where a daughter could inherit (Castile, Navarre), a queen regnant is possible. Wherever a ruler is a child, a queen mother can be regent. The chance rises as history's ages arrive: a little in the Age of Revolutions, more in the Age of Industrialization, more again in the Age of World Wars, and events and reforms can raise one country's chance earlier. Women who held roles at the start (Joanna I of Naples, say) or appear in events are placed as they were; the chances apply only to characters the game generates. Inheritance law is fixed by each country's culture and history from the catalogue. You can't choose it, though events and reforms can change it. It decides who takes the throne (eldest son, eldest child, a brother or the eldest of the house, the strongest claimant among the lords, or an election by lords or a council) and whether a lord's land passes to one heir or is split among his sons. Starting values At the start, the catalogue's assessments set your counts: economic strength and fiscal resilience give gold and debt; manpower potential recruits; military capability soldiers, commanders and horses; naval capability ships; administrative capacity officials and royal provinces; political stability and unrest risk lords' loyalty and provinces in revolt; territorial cohesion the number of lords, their land and language; institutional development schools, scholars and inventions; trade access starting trade; diplomatic influence extra officials ready as envoys. A low-confidence record starts with a wider random range. Allies, rivals, subjects and enemies come from the 1378 relations file. See The 1378 Start. Events and the AI The event tree's abstract country stats each map to concrete realm stats: legitimacy to loyal lords, heirs and years on throne; stability to loyal lords and provinces in revolt; war weariness to Fallen; prestige to battles won and lands taken; administrative capacity to officials; technology and innovation to inventions; literacy to scholars and schools per thousand people; food security to stores, harvest and herds; debt and treasury to debt and gold; navy strength and naval reach to warships; army strength and manpower to soldiers and recruits. The AI reads the same counts as you and doesn't cheat on food. An opportunist (the Ottomans eyeing Hungary) attacks when a neighbour's lords waver or its soldiers drop; an isolationist (Korea) fills its schools and avoids war; a hegemon seeker (France) keeps its recruits for the army. How a campaign is won You win by world domination or by leading one of three scores , each built only from realm stats: Score Built from Economy Yearly income (taxes, lords' share, trade, tribute) plus the bank (gold minus debt) Power Provinces held (subjects' provinces count half) plus army power (soldiers weighted by kind, warships, commanders) Technology Inventions known, each weighted by its era cost; nothing removes a known invention - World domination : you and your subjects hold half of the world's settled land provinces (land with people) in the turn in which 1 January falls. Allies by marriage do not count. - Score victory : lead a score when the campaign's end date (default 31 August 1939) arrives. Leading earlier wins nothing, however wide the margin. Army power counts foot as 1, horse as 2, guns as 3, a warship as 100 men and a commander as 1,000, all over 1,000; the weights are provisional. Scores are worked out at the start and every January. A domination win happens at once and you may keep playing. At the end date the leader of each score wins, and ties share the win. Where you see it. Every realm's General tab has a Score line: its Economy, Power and Technology with its rank in each. On your own card the line opens the Score tab: how each of your scores is made (income and bank; provinces and army power; inventions), your rank of how many realms still stand, and the five leading realms beside you. When the campaign ends the clock stops and the end card opens by itself (see Screens and navigation). Each month A turn is one week. These steps run once a month, in the turn in which a new month begins. Cadence What happens Monthly Pay soldiers; add income; desertion if unpaid or unfed; apply loyalty causes; check the ruler's death and succession; check score victory Each season Eating and rot of castle and local stores; famine relief releases Each autumn Harvest roll by region, collection, castle shares, sharing out Yearly Debt interest; officials' wages; recruits refill; ruler and lords age; years on throne; old entries drop out of Fallen, Oaths broken and Lands taken New Year Lords over the cap lose a loyalty step What you see - The country card , as above, including your rank in each score. - The lord card for each named lord. - The Food policy screen , with realm defaults, per-castle overrides and the four presets. - The treasury : gold, debt and lenders. - The top bar : your realm, the date, gold and its change a month, stability, the war plaque while at war, and the News button. Things you can do: set food policy, override a castle, apply a food preset; take a loan, repay or default; hire and dismiss officials; grant a fief, keep a local ruler, sell a title; seize a lord's land, put a disloyal lord on trial; give a lord gold, an office or a marriage, or grant his want; call a loyal lord's retinue; name an heir; burn your own fields.
